SUKP local search algorithms are available at: https://github.com/fernandocosta/SUKP-LocalSearch. These resources include the state-of-the-art algorithm for SUKP, adaptive, variable, and efficient local search algorithms, and instance generators alongside the metrics used to assess the performance of local search algorithms. Churn prediction is a prevalent method for identifying at-risk customers across various settings, including every second transaction in online gambling and the first month of service for mobile operators. Early and precise customer loss detection enables businesses to implement timely retention strategies, while frequent, predictable losses reduce the need for such interventions. This study examines churn forecasting models for online gambling transactions, presenting a case where predicting loss within the first second significantly improves feature engineering. Furthermore, we compare diverse classifiers and ensembles, identify hyperparameters that enhance model performance, and evaluate the impact of sampling methods on balanced accuracy and precision at the 50% cutoff. This framework for assessing churn prediction models can be adapted to other use cases, such as those used in online services. Our findings indicate that XGBoost with a random forest estimator achieves the highest balanced accuracy at 81.8%, followed by LightGBM at 81.2%. Additionally, we observed that resampling techniques improve balanced accuracy but result in a decline in precision at the 50% threshold. The complete code is accessible at https://github.com/edwardosborn/churn_forecast.git. Describing risk in advanced safety systems is crucial for ensuring human-machine collaboration. However, existing techniques for generating contextual risk descriptors are immature, particularly within cycling. This paper introduces a lightweight, video-driven approach to create momentary risk descriptors for cyclists. By leveraging deep neural networks, the method analyzes video streams to generate continuous and discrete descriptors representing momentary and temporal risk, utilizing acceleration and velocity data alongside semantic context. Experiments using ground-truth ground-level videos demonstrate that the method achieves high accuracy in risk detection and description, performing effectively even in night and rainy conditions. Furthermore, human evaluations of the descriptors reveal that they are intuitive and deliver consistent and accurate results. Consequently, this method offers the potential to generate intelligent risk descriptors for cyclists, enhancing human-machine collaboration in next-generation smart cycling systems. Additionally, the study explores the unique challenges and opportunities presented by cycling risk description, advocating that momentary risk descriptors should incorporate both physical and psychological dimensions. The inherent uncertainties in robotic motion planning, stemming from imperfect state measurements and environmental unpredictability, can compromise system safety. This work introduces a comprehensive framework for motion planning in robotics by integrating control barrier functions (CBF) with model predictive planning (MPP), specifically addressing motion constraints related to collisions, obstacles, and the dynamic obduracy of the robot itself. Planners that fail to account for CBF constraints on collision avoidance may result in unsafe trajectories. CBF constraints enforce robustness in collision-avoidance filters, preventing the final state estimates from violating CBF safety guarantees. Furthermore, CBF constraints ensure that robot dynamics remain obdurable, meaning no state is reachable from the current configuration within a specified time horizon. CBF constraints define the robot's reachable set, which serves as a low-level collision avoidance filter and constitutes the primary constraint for higher-level motion planning. Finally, this work proposes secure motion planning strategies utilizing CBF-MPC, demonstrating their efficacy through numerical simulations and experiments on a robotic platform. The simulation results indicate that CBF-MPP outperforms low-level CBF filters and basic motion planning algorithms in terms of safety, robustness, and efficiency. Key benefits of this approach include efficient computation, effective collision avoidance, and strong efficiency and safety performance, even under significant state estimation uncertainties. CBF-MPP can address various safety-critical constraints, such as maintaining a minimum distance from obstacles and enforcing speed limits. By solving a single optimization problem, CBF-MPP simultaneously satisfies collision avoidance, obstacle clearance, and speed constraints, offering a promising solution for real-world motion planning applications. The resulting CBF-MPP motion planner is versatile and applicable to diverse robotic systems, including ground vehicles, unmanned aerial vehicles, and autonomous systems. This work paves the way for future research in safe and robust motion planning for dynamic robotics. The CBF-MPP framework can be extended to other robotics applications, such as path planning and trajectory generation. Additionally, the CBF-MPP motion planner can be adapted for use in real-time applications by leveraging hardware accelerators, such as FPGAs and GPUs. CBF-MPP offers a versatile and flexible solution for motion planning in dynamic robotics. This paper introduces the concept of enveloping numbers for rings and investigates various properties of these numbers. We establish multiple characterizations of enveloping numbers and demonstrate how to calculate them for specific types of rings. Additionally, we examine the environmental function of rings, which maps a ring to its enveloping number, and various interconnections between rings and these numbers. The study concludes with several examples and a list of open problems. Overall, this work addresses numerous related issues concerning enveloping numbers, their properties, characterizations, and computations, providing numerous examples and inquiries for future research. Specifically, the paper introduces the concept of enveloping numbers, which are closely related to other invariants such as Jacobson radicals, center, commutators, and dimensions. Enveloping numbers also address issues related to Jacobson's Common Commutant Problem, examining the relationship between a ring and its centralizer. The definition of enveloping numbers is also explored in the context of algebras, where an algebra is considered pure if its enveloping number equals that of the algebra. Deep neural networks face significant threats from adversarial examples, which are subtle perturbations applied to benign images that cause misclassification. This study introduces a novel framework for developing natural resilience against such adversarial inputs. The approach relies on the concept of feature diversity, which measures the variation in activation patterns across an network's layers. The proposed training method consists of two components: feature diversity regularization (FeDeR) and feature diversity regularization enhancement (FeDeR-e), both applied to the first convolutional block. FeDeR encourages activation diversity through a composite loss function that penalizes uniform distributions and rewards diverse ones. To strengthen this resilience, FeDeR-e functions as an auxiliary, class-specific loss that rewards activation patterns demonstrating robustness against perturbations. Extensive evaluations on MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet datasets reveal that the FeDeR+FeDeR-e framework surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, offering superior accuracy, generalization, and resilience, even when evaluated on natural images never encountered during training. Furthermore, the mechanism successfully identifies interpretable features that aid in withstanding attacks. The comprehensive code and datasets required to replicate this research are publicly accessible at https://github.com/rahul-agarwal1994/Natural-Resilience. Nonlocal conservation laws, arising from both continuum physics and discrete agent-based models, are characterized at their core by partial differential equations featuring integrals or in general nonlocal terms dependent on the unknown function. Although extensive research has been conducted on specific instances of these equations, this study addresses the general scenario where integral or local dependence terms involve a function $m$ of the conserved variable $u$, written as $m(t,x;u)$. We demonstrate that the singular limit of variable-speed Boolean equations is well-posed within the Besov space $B^s_{\infty,0}$ for $s>1$. Furthermore, we establish the entropy admissibility criterion for shock waves in nonlocal equations possessing concave flux and derive the corresponding Rankine-Hugoniot condition. Finally, a stability result is obtained for sequences of Riemann problems, which facilitates the derivation of error estimates regarding the difference between the Boolean equation and its hydrodynamic limit. These findings are supported by several numerical examples. Notably, our findings regarding the singular limit and the $L^2$ convergence rate for piecewise constant solutions are new and represent significant advancements over previous work. The primary innovations of this study include: (i) the generalization of prior work by formulating and solving the hyperbolic equation $u_t + (mu)_x = 0$ instead of the classical conservation law $u_t + uu_x = 0$ for variable-speed Boolean equations; (ii) the first established result with an explicit convergence rate for the hydrodynamic limit of variable-speed Boolean equations; and (iii) the extension of entropy admissibility criteria and Rankine-Hugoniot conditions to nonlocal conservation laws, accompanied by the first explicit shock speed estimate for a variable-speed Boolean equation. These results hold significant implications for understanding the general structure of nonlocal conservation laws. Specifically, our work provides the first explicit estimates for shock speeds in nonlocal conservation laws with nonlocal interaction, a topic where existing literature offers only implicit conditions. These contributions are achieved through the application of novel techniques and a unique perspective on the problem. We present a topological generalization of the affine properties seen in closed hyperbolic surfaces, termed "Morse-Smale dilation surfaces." These structures arise by gluing together horizontal strips using complex conjugates under dilations; they feature a horizontal singular lamination that acts as the boundary to an ideal triangle within a surface of constant curvature. Our work offers a topological characterization of the Morse-Smale condition for the return map on sections with horizontal cores and connects the homotopy classes of horizontal saddle links to the dynamics of these return maps. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the space of Morse-Smale dilation surfaces encompasses a subset isometric to a subset of the space of horizontal saddle links on a constant curvature surface, bridging the findings of W. Goldman ("The symplectic geometry of Teichmüller space via cluster algebras," *Compositio Mathematica* 146 (2010), 1323–1362) and F. Leininger ("Teichmüller spaces, flat surfaces, and saddle connections," *Surveys in Differential Geometry* 16 (2011), 151–205). This connection establishes direct links between the geometries of Teichmüller space and the Teichmüller迷乱 space. Additionally, we prove that Morse-Smale dilation surfaces constitute a closed subset within the space of all dilation surfaces by verifying the continuity of the holonomy map and the projection onto the Teichmüller space of Morse-Smale dilation surfaces. This result strengthens the validity of the dynamical characterization of the geodesic flow on the Teichmüller space of dilation surfaces, originally proposed by Ch. Bonahon and W. Goldman (*J. Geom. Phys.* 110 (2017), 1–19). The paper concludes with several open problems. This study introduces a total correlation (TC) based measure, denoted as TotalNet, to capture multi-directional and bidirectional influences between brain regions within functional networks. By extending the concept of mutual information to higher-order dimensions, TC serves as an effective metric for quantifying dependencies between random variables beyond simple pairwise interactions. Utilizing resting-state fMRI data, we established a connection between high and low mobility modes in human motion and low and high total modularity (low-TC and high-TC) in functional connectomes. We calculated the total modularity (TCNet) of functional connectomes across 61 subjects, revealing that participants with high mobility dominance in their high mobility modes associated with low-TCNet, whereas those with low mobility dominance exhibited high-TCNet. Furthermore, we found that TCNet is a more robust indicator of mobility dominance than either the functional connectivity strength or the graph-theoretic metric of global entropy. These findings suggest that TotalNet effectively characterizes long-distance, multi-directional connectivity between brain regions, highlighting its value for understanding the complex dynamics of the human mind's functional architecture. Total-Connectome analysis offers a promising framework for investigating the intricate dependency structures of brain regions and for designing novel network-based biomarkers to detect and track neurological and psychiatric conditions. We present an explicit unitary transformation linking two $n$-dimensional Clifford algebra-valued Hilbert spaces derived via Segal-Bargmann extensions of the exponential maps for logarithmic vector fields and their time-reversed counterparts. This approach yields a novel proof of a generalized form of the Delsarte-Genin-Verdu pointwise inequality, thereby confirming the extended SB-VR conjecture in $n$ dimensions. Furthermore, it establishes an alternative proof for the Taylor isomorphism between the symmetric tensor algebra and the Clifford algebra extension of the polynomial algebra, while also deriving several new integral inequalities with application potential. Notably, we explicitly construct orthogonal kernels and orthogonal bases within the generalized Clifford algebra-valued Segal-Bargmann space. Additionally, we explore an extension of the classical Segal-Bargmann formula for Hermite polynomials into the domain of Clifford algebra extensions, specifically identifying the extended kernel as a generalized form of Paul matrices. Finally, we substantiate the reverse validity of the Segel-Bargmann transformation. These outcomes represent the first applications of global transformation techniques to the SBLV framework, offering a fresh perspective on the theory. The novel findings not only advance research into novel mathematical tools for analyzing vector fields in both classical and quantum physics but also hold significant promise for developing mathematical models in machine learning, genetic engineering, and neurology. Finally, we outline potential directions for future investigation based on these results. A comprehensive list of 107 references is included. A detailed table of contents is also provided for your convenience. Keywords: Global transformation method; Vector fields; Segal-Bargmann space; Tensor algebra; Polynomial algebra; Machine learning; Genetic engineering; Neurology.

Over the past few decades, particle physics has unveiled a host of enigmatic phenomena, with numerous clues pointing toward new sources of interaction beyond the Standard Model. In the late 1990s, observations by Super-Kamiokande and SNO revealed that neutrinos undergo flavor oscillation, demonstrating that at least one neutrino possesses non-zero mass. This discovery indicated that beyond third-order corrections in the inverse mass scale, lower-order terms must also exist. To address these implications, researchers must pursue more precise measurements of the nonperturbative parameters governing the relevant processes. The upcoming DUNE experiment, situated 1,300 meters underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota, aims to deliver high-precision data on the neutrino mixing matrix. Shapley values originate from cooperative game theory and have recently been suggested as a technique to interpret the input features of neural networks. This study examines the implementation of Shapley values applied to the CTPP's description of TCP data, comparing this approach to classical top taggers that utilize the same network inputs. Results indicate that the method achieves an enhanced top tagger, demonstrating a four percent improvement in efficiency over the traditional alternative. Furthermore, Shapley values offer the distinct advantage of quantifying the reliability of network predictions, a critical metric for experimentalists. We also explore alternative methods for feature importance assessment using the CTPP, demonstrating that combining the proposed top tagger with an algorithm for feature selection yields a further performance gain of two percent. Additionally, network training was conducted with varying top and b-jet fractions, revealing that incorporating b-jets results in a tagger with an efficiency 10 percent superior to a tagger trained without them. Finally, we illustrate how to quantify the uncertainty of the proposed feature selection technique by analyzing the variance in importance across multiple trained top taggers. Incorporating feature selection enables the construction of importance distributions for each variable, thereby quantifying uncertainty in a manner complementary to that provided by Shapley values. This offers a comprehensive approach to understanding input features that can be extended to other inputs within the CTPP. Ultimately, the paper underscores that the effectiveness of the presented methods is contingent upon the specific training conditions of the neural network. Consequently, the final output of any analysis should explicitly reflect the training conditions used for that specific network. The CTPP serves as a versatile tool for evaluating new techniques and training networks for a wide array of physics scenarios. The ultimate goal is to refine existing techniques by learning from the insights gained through the CTPP's analysis. The paper concludes by discussing how to quantify the uncertainty inherent in trained tagger decisions. The growing availability of online online video platforms has made online video consumption a ubiquitous activity, with online video consumption having become a common pastime. A primary obstacle to achieving a superior user experience (UX) in online video is the limited buffer duration, which is often long and cumbersome. Recent research indicates that detailed aspect pre-fetching can significantly enhance UX by reducing the buffer time. However, existing approaches either fail to predict the entire video or overlook the fine-grained requirements of aspect pre-fetching. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel deep learning framework called MoDeRNN (Motion and Description Recurrent Neural Network) for predicting spatiotemporal data at a fine-grained level. By leveraging spatiotemporal data, MoDeRNN accurately forecasts online video content aspects, such as the beginning and endings of clauses and sentences. Furthermore, MoDeRNN employs recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to capture fine-grained semantic context, enabling the prediction of aspects like the topic, summary, and emotion within online video consumption. Experimental results demonstrate that MoDeRNN significantly improves UX. Specifically, it achieves a $3.2\times$ increase in Average Session Time (AST) and a $2.5\times$ increase in Average Session Video Count (ASVC) compared to the TensorFlow Hub (TH) baseline. Additionally, MoDeRNN reduces average buffer time by 40% relative to TH. These metrics indicate that the proposed model effectively predicts various aspect contents at a granular level, thereby enhancing the overall online video consumption experience. This study explores the integration of Rust and closure-based programming languages to construct more resilient and efficient software systems. By leveraging the definitive memory management mechanisms of both paradigms, we leverage the advantages of each language to their fullest potential. Our findings demonstrate that this hybrid approach offers greater safety and expressiveness compared to using either language in isolation. Furthermore, building on Rust's strong type system, we introduce Josephine, an open-source library that utilizes JavaScript to securely manage the lifetimes of Rust data. Josephine enhances the security of built-in JavaScript closures by providing additional safeguards for data accessed within closed-over variables. Through this work, we illustrate the benefits of combining closure-based and object-oriented languages and highlight the security implications associated with closed-over variables. While standard models featuring right-handed neutrinos predict neutral states capable of triggering neutrinoless double-beta decay, similar mechanisms can arise from charged lepton flavor violation. This work demonstrates that such "charged pathways" can significantly influence neutrinoless double-beta decay rates in models with Majorana neutrinos, potentially dominating over traditional "neutral pathways" that rely on heavy neutral gauge eigenstates. These findings highlight the necessity of exploring both neutral and charged sources of the phenomenon within experimental settings, such as the FCC-eh, to effectively constrain relevant model parameters. Furthermore, we illustrate that the interference between neutral and charged pathways can lead to either suppression or enhancement of the decay rate, a critical factor for accurate experimental interpretation. Finally, relevant processes are also expected to generate lepton-number-violating signatures in collider experiments. However, due to the intricate interplay between neutral and charged contributions, the resulting rates may be substantially suppressed relative to simple na\"ive expectations based on heavy neutral or charged states. Consequently, careful consideration of these effects is essential when interpreting the (non)observation of such signals. Finally, we outline the strategies of the LEPS collaboration for investigating these phenomena at the future European hadron collider, the ILC, and the HHCC. This study introduces a novel belief propagation (BP) list decoder designed for polar codes of arbitrary length. By employing polar subcodes, the proposed method effectively manages multiple hypotheses, enabling the construction of a list decoder capable of achieving the polar coding capacity threshold. The approach is implemented within a hybrid coding framework that combines polar codes with low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, for which an enhanced BP list decoder was previously developed. Simulation results indicate that the subcode-based BP list decoding technique for polar-LDPC codes delivers performance comparable to that of polar codes under the same list decoding architecture. Furthermore, the paper provides an analysis of the subcode-based message passing algorithm's computational complexity and memory requirements. Finally, the study explores the potential of this design for high-speed transmission systems by evaluating its power efficiency through gate count estimation. Numerical simulations confirm that the proposed decoder is highly suitable for high-speed transmission systems. The code construction algorithm is detailed in our prior work, which is cited throughout this paper. This paper focuses exclusively on the development of the subcode-based belief propagation list decoder for polar codes. The results presented herein support the claim in our previous research that belief propagation list decoding is a viable decoding strategy for polar codes. Additionally, this paper demonstrates the feasibility of using belief propagation list decoding for high-speed transmission systems. To the authors' knowledge, this represents the first work to address the speed issue associated with polar code decoding. The paper is structured as follows: Section II presents the system model and introduces the subcode-based belief propagation list decoder for polar codes. Section III outlines the overall system design. Section IV provides a detailed description of the subcode-based belief propagation list decoder for polar codes. When two objects with identical shapes are depicted, the resulting image's full width at half maximum (FWHM) broadens by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$ compared to a single object, even though its peak intensity remains unchanged. This paper examines how the profile of a combined image changes when the number of objects with similar shapes varies. We derive analytical expressions for the profiles of two identical squares and equilateral triangles, as well as for a collection of discrete points, which all yield exact results. Additionally, we provide an approximate expression (AP) incorporating a single free parameter for the profile of all considered objects. We also approximate the profile of a profile sum using a fit-for-purpose (FF) approach, which relies on the profile of a discrete point set and also features one free parameter. When the number of objects increases, the profile of the combined image becomes sharper, and we approximate this sharpening effect by analyzing the profiles of the combined image and the discrete point set. We address the appropriate scaling of the free parameter for increasing image particle counts. Finally, we evaluate the accuracy of these approximation methods. For the AP model, we determine the optimal free parameter value to minimize errors in approximating the combined image profile. For the FF model, we demonstrate that it remains a reasonable approximation even at the limits of the parameters used in the AP model. In both scenarios, the primary source of error is the flattening of the combined image profile. The AP method proves more accurate for images with fewer particles, whereas the FF method achieves the same level of accuracy with more particles. The total number of particles in the combined image required to match the accuracy of the other method differs between the objects considered. Furthermore, the particle count required for either approximation method to achieve equal error is not consistent among the analyzed objects. The tensile fracture strength of crystalline solids is governed by the initiation and propagation of cracks along various crystallographic planes. This study identifies the ultimate tensile strength by pinpointing an unstable configuration within a periodic crystal structure, thereby bypassing the nucleation and growth of cracks. Through extensive testing across numerous materials, we observe that tensile strength is generally governed by the weakest plane within the crystal lattice. Our theoretical findings align with existing experimental and computational data. Furthermore, we develop a model to explain why certain fracture planes demonstrate greater resistance to crack propagation than others, ultimately deriving an analytical expression for ultimate tensile strength as a function of this plane's fracture toughness. The validity of this model is supported by both computational and experimental evidence. We contend that this represents the first instance where the tensile strength of crystalline solids has been characterized without relying on external input from experimental or computational data. This framework provides a comprehensive understanding of the fracture behavior of crystalline solids, elucidating both fracture initiation and propagation phenomena. Additionally, we demonstrate that our approach yields accurate predictions regarding the plane along which cracks will travel, even under mixed-mode loading conditions. This represents the initial report on predicting fracture planes, thereby resolving a long-standing challenge in fracture mechanics. Consequently, this work paves the way for advancing materials design by enabling the prediction of tensile strength for various materials and identifying optimal composite configurations to further enhance material performance. This design methodology constitutes a significant advancement in materials science. Moreover, the ability to predict optimal composite designs facilitates the identification of promising candidates for further exploration, substantially accelerating the materials discovery process. This connection provides a rationale for the orientation of fracture planes in amorphous materials and offers a means to predict their paths. This represents the first report on predicting fracture planes in amorphous materials. We believe this constitutes a significant advancement in fracture mechanics. We introduce and investigate random surfaces generated by a one-to-many coupling of chordal Gaussian free fields (CFF) and Schottky groups generated by points drawn from random log-gases. These surfaces are defined through holomorphic quadratic differentials expressed as a product of factors, where each factor corresponds to a CFF driven by a Schottky generator and coupled with the others. Leveraging this random surface, we examine a variant of the Dyson-Specht process, which describes the dynamics of random log-gases. This process is driven by a random time change associated with the area increase of a growing domain within the unit disk. We demonstrate that the distribution of the driven multiple Schottky group remains invariant under this area increase, thereby extending the concept of stationary domains for multiple Schottky groups as defined by Dyson-Specht. Furthermore, we explore the connection between our findings and Dyson's conjecture regarding the joint distribution of eigenvalues in GUE matrices. Additionally, we analyze specific instances of random surfaces derived from Cardy's formula and observe that our framework unifies previously unconnected results, such as those concerning the dynamics of eigenvalues in GUE matrices and double-scale stochastic processes on the unit disk. Finally, we outline various open problems stemming from these research questions, including the necessity of defining and analyzing a random time change for area increase, the development of a cardy-type formula for double-scale stochastic processes on the unit disk, and the generalization of GUE matrices beyond pairs of matrices linked by multiple commutators. These generalizations are essential for formulating analogous questions regarding the dynamics of eigenvalue distributions in random Hermitian matrices linked by multiple commutators. Consequently, these issues extend the scope of free probability, originally centered on free products of random Hermitian matrices, to the case of free products of random log-gases. Notably, the random log-gases driving the multiple SLEs in our construction include the Dyson-Specht process, which unifies Dyson's conjecture and double-scale stochastic processes on the unit disk, as well as the Brézinski-Randall-Shepp process, which is driven by Gaussian free fields. Furthermore, the random log-gases we consider encompass the Brézinski-Randall-Shepp process, which is driven by Gaussian free fields. This observation underscores the unity of our results with those arising from Gaussian free fields and their interactions with random log-gases, thereby extending the domain of free probability beyond its traditional focus on free products

Traditional verification of quantum computations is typically carried out via quantum tomography, which demands a resource expenditure that scales exponentially with the number of qubits. In this study, we present a traditional verification protocol that scales linearly with the size of the quantum circuit. We illustrate this approach using a Tomographic Interim Verification (TIV) scheme applied to the simulation of a Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonian. By selecting a sparse set of qubits at each circuit stage and performing state tomography on these selected qubits, we can effectively monitor the traditional verification of the entire circuit. We demonstrate a successful TIV protocol for both a recent published simulation and a newly developed state-vector-based simulation of the same Hamiltonian. Additionally, we introduce a modified version of TIV that scales linearly with the number of quantum states rather than the size of the quantum circuit. Furthermore, we show that this revised TIV protocol can detect deviations from the claimed outcomes caused by single-qubit Pauli errors injected into the quantum circuit. Overall, our findings indicate that traditional verification through quantum tomography is feasible in linear time, provided that the state description of the quantum circuit is also available in linear time. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first proposal for a traditional verification method that scales linearly with the quantum circuit size. Notably, the two state-vector-based solutions we employed are not specific to the claimed claims, suggesting that our TIV protocols may be adaptable to verify various other claims. Consequently, our proposed TIV protocols hold significant potential for the traditional verification of diverse claims in quantum computing. Finally, we outline several promising avenues for extending our TIV approach to traditional verification. Notably, our TIV method offers a promising path toward the efficient traditional verification of various quantum computing outcomes. Furthermore, our findings may help clarify the relationship between traditional verification and the emerging qubit-based E9000 verification framework. Specifically, our TIV protocols demonstrate that traditional verification can achieve linear scaling with circuit size under certain conditions, thereby challenging the hypothesis that the fundamental limitations of qubit-based E9000 verification (which scale exponentially with circuit size) also apply to traditional verification. This insight may pave the way for further research into the traditional verification of quantum computations. Ultimately, our work may inspire renewed interest in the traditional verification of quantum computing, potentially leading to the development of more effective traditional verification protocols. Ultimately, our TIV protocols may contribute to the traditional verification of various quantum computing claims, potentially advancing the field of traditional verification of quantum computing. Blockchain technology offers unique advantages, including transparency, traceability, and security. Within the Internet of Things (IoT) domain, it can validate data integrity, ensure transaction security, and manage device interactions. By creating decentralized networks, blockchain eliminates the need for a central trust authority, while smart contracts automate agreements between entities. This study presents a framework for a decentralized supply chain utilizing blockchain, IoT devices, and smart contracts, with a specific use-case focusing on food traceability. The proposed solution is assessed against key blockchain attributes such as transparency, security, and scalability, as well as IoT critical factors including cost, energy consumption, and latency. Results indicate that for short supply chains, the approach is both cost-effective and energy-efficient, though it may face scalability challenges. Conversely, in long supply chains, the method proves to be more expensive and energy-intensive but demonstrates better scalability. Ultimately, the paper argues that blockchain-enabled decentralized supply chains are the future, as they enhance trust, transparency, and security for all stakeholders. Additionally, smart contracts can automate decision-making and trigger alerts when anomalies are detected by the blockchain network. The paper details the implementation of smart contracts to detect these anomalies and automatically notify the blockchain in real time. A proof-of-concept was developed, tested, and deployed on the public Ethereum network, featuring a mobile application that allows mobile users to query the blockchain for product traceability. Given the potential of blockchain, IoT, and smart contracts, this research supports the development of innovative solutions for supply chain management and food safety. Furthermore, it aids in designing decentralized applications (DApps) that interact with the blockchain network, such as the proposed mobile application for traceability. The paper also addresses the benefits of public testnets, which enable cost-effective testing without the risks associated with mainnet deployment. Finally, the paper outlines the advantages of open-source blockchain solutions, which facilitate transparency and trust in the system. This research is part of the project \emph{Smart City of the Future}, led by the Department of Computer and Electronic Engineering at the University of Bologna. We introduce a method for modeling the shapes of living cells using a hybrid approach that combines the flexibility of neural networks with the advantages of geometric representations. By employing a multi-layer perceptron to define a cell's boundary, we successfully shape the region between the plasma and actin layers. When used as a boundary condition for the region's internal dynamics, this representation facilitates the learning of the internal vector field responsible for shaping the cell. Furthermore, the technique is demonstrated to reproduce diverse cell forms, such as those seen in *Dictyostelium discoideum*, and to generate realistic, diverse cell shapes by utilizing recent sophisticated representation learning methods. Consequently, we establish that the internal region dynamics of cells can be represented as a vector field guided by features extracted from two distinct cellular structures. Finally, a representative form is created for each combination of these structures, enabling the disentanglement of cellular structural features and their corresponding dynamics. This marks the first step toward a representation theory of cell forms and provides new insights into cell shape formation. Specifically, the results indicate that two structures are essential for understanding cell forms, and they highlight the influence of cellular structure on cell dynamics. Additionally, the proposed method offers a means to quantify the similarity between different cell forms. Through a series of experiments, the study investigates questions regarding the similarity between cell forms and their internal vector fields, as well as the influence of cellular structures on these dynamics. Ultimately, the findings suggest that cell forms are highly reproducible and that dynamics are largely independent of cellular structures. Blindness and low vision significantly hinder an individual's ability to read, comprehend, and derive meaning from printed material. While Braille offers tactile access to text for the blind, it remains less popular among people with low vision due to its tactile nature, and audio formats like CD-Audio or audio CDs face challenges regarding accessibility to textual elements such as headings, footnotes, and references. These formats also lack the inherent navigability and non-linear readability that digital text provides. We introduce the concept of Document Navigability, a requirement for the blind and low vision, and examine how the requirement applies across a spectrum of materials ranging from traditional paper to various digital media. Finally, we propose the utilization of PDF forms to enhance interactive document navigability for these users, a concept validated by a pilot study. This study compares navigability across a range of documents and formats, including CD-Audio, Braille, audio files, paper, and web-based documents. Additionally, we explore the barriers to accessibility regarding the number of users engaging with print materials and the scarcity of resources for the blind and low vision. The paper concludes by summarizing the necessity of increased awareness and access to print materials for individuals with vision impairments. Keywords: Accessibility, Assistive Technology, Blindness, Low Vision, Print Materials, Document Navigability.

Exoplanetary transits are recognized as a primary method for identifying and analyzing the atmospheres of promising low-mass worlds. However, when utilizing low-resolution spectra (R ~ 100) to detect and characterize these atmospheres, observations are often compromised by stellar activity, which can mimic or obscure atmospheric signals. This study employs synthetic data to quantify the influence of stellar activity on low-resolution transit spectra and explores the potential of high-resolution data for mitigating these effects. We demonstrate that low-resolution spectra can be acquired with minimal noise, enabling the detection of water features in small planets; yet, without adequate sampling of the Ca II H&K lines, activity-induced noise remains comparable to the target atmospheric signal. Furthermore, we show that monitoring these lines allows for the removal of most activity-related signals. Finally, we find that observing these lines at a 100 times higher resolution effectively eliminates the impact of stellar activity. These findings suggest that simultaneous low- and high-resolution spectroscopy offers a strategy for mitigating stellar activity in low-resolution spectra, paving the way for discovering and characterizing the atmospheres of smaller planets. Such an approach could enable the detection of water features in a 5 Earth radius planet around an M0V star with an activity level of log R'K = -5.0 in just 10 hours. Additionally, the high-resolution lines should be observed with R ~ 10,000 to ensure complete removal of active region contributions. Ultimately, our results indicate that the current impact of stellar activity on low-resolution transit spectra is significantly lower than previously estimated. Consequently, the search for and characterization of atmospheres around smaller planets is more feasible than currently assumed. Specifically, this work supports the feasibility of detecting water features in a 5 Earth radius planet orbiting an M0V star with an 11-day period, utilizing the ESPRESSO spectrograph at the Very Large Telescope. The analysis also provides estimates for the required number of transits to achieve the necessary precision. These conclusions are particularly relevant for the upcoming generation of medium- and high-resolution spectrographs, such as ESPRESSO, NIRVANA, and MIKE, which are being commissioned for the next decade. The findings also support the feasibility of characterizing the atmospheres of larger planets around M stars using the next-generation Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). The paper concludes with a summary of the required telescope performance and observation time to achieve the necessary precision. The analysis code is publicly available at https://github.com/afg19

We present a novel proof extending Thurston's classification of convex surfaces on compact surfaces to the case where structural maps are required to be continuous rather than smooth. This work presents an intrinsic classification of such surfaces based on their properties, while also offering a proof rooted in geometric analysis that complements Thurston's topological and combinatorial methodology. Our framework demonstrates that uniform curvature metrics on compact surfaces with prescribed pole singularities are precisely those surfaces where all structural maps maintain a consistent regularity level. We examine the moduli space of these curvature metrics, revealing that its dimension matches that of the space of structural maps with a specific maximum order of vanishing at zeros. Furthermore, we establish that the dimension of the moduli space for curvature metrics with prescribed holomorphic differentials is no greater than the number of prescribed differentials, with equality holding when the prescribed data forms a complete system. Finally, we outline an algorithm for finding curvature metrics, grounded in the continuity of solutions to curvature equations with respect to their inputs. This approach enables the derivation of various moduli properties through either numerical computation or the application of implicit function theorem techniques. Additionally, we derive uniform curvature metrics, derived from Sasaki-Einstein metrics, for a range of exceptional cases linked to Deligne-Fuchsian triangles and their covers. These findings facilitate the uniformization of holomorphic line bundles and vector bundles defined over curvature manifolds, derived from rescaling the corresponding holomorphic line or vector bundles on the moduli space. Specifically, we demonstrate that the projectivized tangent bundle of a curvature manifold is a curvature surface, and we prove that a line bundle's total space can be uniformized if its curvature bundle is. However, this method fails to uniformize general vector bundles, as the continuous dependence of curvature solutions on their data breaks down in this context. To address this, we construct a uniform curvature bundle with prescribed singularities for vector bundles, where the fiber dimensions of the bundle and the prescribed curvature surface are closely related. This provides an alternative to the classical Chern bundle formulation. Ultimately, this work serves as an introduction to our forthcoming publication. Our complete results will appear in our monograph, *Uniformization of Riemann Surfaces via Curvature*, published by Springer in the *Progress in Mathematics* series. This monograph will detail our full findings, which are currently the subject of our ongoing research. Our approach combines geometric analysis, topology, and combinatorics, with our primary technical instrument being the continuous dependence of uniform curvature surfaces on their data. Achieving efficient locomotion on water interfaces, whether biologically or by robotics systems heavier than their own fluid drag force, is a well-researched topic in fluid mechanics. However, the swimming mechanics of microorganisms and small animals that weigh less than the ambient fluid's buoyancy remain largely unexplored. This study investigates the swimming mechanics of a centipede, *Armadillidium vulgare*, by measuring its body shape and kinematics during mid locomotion and by developing a numerical model based on the Navier-Stokes equations to simulate its swimming. The results indicate that the centipede's mid-locomotion body configuration is optimized for efficient movement, while its swimming mechanics are primarily governed by the fluid's surface tension and buoyancy. The proposed numerical model accurately reproduces the biomechanics of both body undulation and lateral swimming. This study demonstrates that effective swimming mechanics can be achieved for both biological and robotic systems, even when they are lighter than the ambient fluid's buoyancy. Furthermore, the findings suggest that current scaling laws for body undulation and body displacement on the water surface may not be applicable to these lighter systems. The study concludes by discussing the potential implications of these findings for both biological and robotic systems. Finally, the authors emphasize the significance of this research for advancing biological and robotics research in fluid mechanics, as it enables the investigation of the biomechanics of biological and robotic systems operating in both buoyant and non-buoyant regimes. This could facilitate the development of biological and robotic systems capable of locomotion and manipulation in both buoyant and non-buoyant environments. Additionally, it may contribute to the creation of new biological and robotic systems, thereby fostering new research and innovation in fluid mechanics. Finally, the authors emphasize that this research has broad applications, including but not limited to biological and robotic systems, as well as floating and floating-like structures. For instance, it could be applied to the study of swimming mechanics in microorganisms and small animals, as well as the manipulation and handling of small objects by biological and robotic systems. Furthermore, the findings could be utilized to study the behavior and manipulation of floating and floating-like structures, such as oil spills and floating debris. In summary, the authors believe that this research has significant potential for application in a wide range of biological and robotic systems, as well as in the development of new biological and robotic systems for fluid mechanics research. Predicting the consequences of asteroid impacts is crucial for both scientific understanding and practical applications. While current impact models focus on the initial displacement and volume of water, hydrodynamic simulations typically initiate with a step-function release. This study aims to develop a physically accurate representation of the impact process to simulate dispersive tsunami propagation. To achieve this, we propose a straightforward new approach that couples mesh adaptation with source adaptation. We demonstrate that this method can effectively transition from a global shock to local fluid dynamics, thereby improving the fidelity of impact modeling. Furthermore, adaptive mesh refinement is shown to facilitate the smooth propagation of the tsunami from the deep ocean onto the continental shelf and across coastal areas. This work is the first step toward a comprehensive scientific and practical prediction model for impact tsunamis. All simulations were conducted using the open-source AMReX framework. Our source adaptation technique is available as an open-source add-on for AMReX and can be integrated into various fluid dynamics modeling frameworks. This paper is the first installment in a series that will explore the advantages and limitations of the coupled adaptive mesh and source functions methods for modeling the tsunami generation phase. Subsequent papers will address the propagation phase, offering the first examples of dispersive simulations regarding decay rates and the formation of bores and solitons. Finally, these methodologies will also be applied to simulate tsunamis generated by underwater landslides. For the purposes of this study, the coupled approach allows for the transition from the impact phase to the subsequent dispersive propagation of the tsunami. This transition is demonstrated by comparing the evolution of the free surface with both experimental data and non-dispersive simulations. Additionally, we examine the development of the near-field flow, including bores and secondary flows, as well as the transition to nonlinear and potentially turbulent dynamics. Finally, we demonstrate that this transition can be achieved with a fixed mesh by employing a sufficiently fine base mesh. However, such a mesh requires an extremely high cell count, making it impractical for simulations involving realistic parameters. This limitation is particularly significant when modeling real-world scenarios. For instance, simulating the 2004 Sumatra tsunami with a fixed mesh would require over 100 billion cells. In contrast, an initial mesh with 100 billion cells can be adapted to achieve the same level of mesh density throughout the simulation. This allows for a transition to a mesh density that provides sufficient resolution to capture relevant physics, such as turbulence and wave breaking. This approach is also applicable to simulating tsunamis resulting from underwater landslides.

We present early JWST NIRCam imaging of a sample of 10 optically faint ($f_{\rm opt} < 10^{-3}$), infrared luminous ($L_{\rm IR} \gtrsim 10^{11} L_{\odot}$) galaxies at redshifts $z \sim 1-3$. These objects were previously identified as radio-loud starbursts in the 8 GHz JVLA Low Frequency Array. We analyze their morphological properties, color-redshift determinations, and UV photometry, while also discussing the implications for their associated radio emission. The galaxies display a wide range of infrared morphologies, from compact and point-like to extended and clumpy. Extended sources are predominantly detected in the SWC1060 filter, whereas compact features are more prominent in SWC2000 and SWC2000W. Our photometry indicates that these galaxies are dominated by old stellar populations, with most lacking significant UV emission. We confirm that the majority of these galaxies are not obscured by significant amounts of dust. The radio emission is consistent with being driven by star formation, although a subset may harbor additional radio-loud nuclei. This sample represents a rare and valuable collection of galaxies that are bright in the optical spectrum but invisible in the optical band. We conclude that these galaxies are typically compact and compact disk-like in the infrared, with a median half-light radius of approximately 1.5 kpc. They are primarily obscured by dust in the medium-to-high infrared range ($3-5\,\mu$m), and their rest-frame UV light is primarily detected in the near-infrared filter. These findings suggest that these galaxies are dominated by old stars, with star formation rates ranging from $\sim 1-100 M_{\odot}\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$. Finally, we propose that these galaxies are likely massive, compact, and compact disk-like starburst systems that existed during the early stages of the Universe. We anticipate that future JWST observations will allow for a deeper exploration of the properties of these galaxies. This sample is ideal for investigating the relationship between radio emission and star formation in the early Universe, and for understanding the role of star formation in the evolution of galaxies. The discovery of these galaxies is a testament to the power of JWST to uncover the hidden secrets of the early Universe. We examine seven-dimensional gravity including geometrical terms. By employing the most general covariant expansions based on the metric and the Weyl tensor, we identify that the metric terms vanish unless the fourth order or higher, while the Weyl terms may appear at the first order. We construct the most general Weyl-tensor expansion that yields a second-order equation, yielding a yoked combination of the Einstein-Hilbert action and the Plebanski-Hoyle action. We analyze this yoked combination and discuss its power-law solutions. Furthermore, we investigate the most general third-order expansion and also explore its background solutions. Finally, we address the generalization to $D$-dimensions. These findings are supported by DMAPACK code. (A version of this research was previously published in *arXiv:2101.03370*.) Diameter-one disks with varying weights are arranged in alternating sequences within a horizontal channel, arranged side-by-side with no vertical spacing, such that each stack rests on the one beneath it. The challenge is to determine the channel's width that minimizes the number of stacks while ensuring each stack's total weight meets a specified lower bound. This problem was previously addressed for general alternating sequences, yielding a computable formula for the critical widths. In this study, we examine a scenario where the channel contains disks of diameter 1 and 2, and we derive a formula for the critical widths corresponding to sequences composed of blocks of varying sizes. This study investigates the transition from non-affine to affine deformation mechanisms in colloidal glasses through bulk scattering experiments. By analyzing a collection of incompressible monodisperse glass-forming colloidal systems, we demonstrate that non-affine growth exhibits either exponential or power-law behavior depending on whether the glass is near-critical. In near-critical glasses, we identify a universal crossover length scale at the point where exponential growth shifts to power-law growth. Furthermore, we establish that structural heterogeneity exhibits power-law growth up to a maximum structural correlation length, which aligns with the crossover length scale observed in non-affine growth. Finally, we show that this maximum structural correlation length serves as a significant length scale governing the dynamic susceptibility. These findings support the hypothesis regarding an underlying length scale in glass-forming liquids near the critical point. Additionally, our results contribute to the broader understanding of how scattering data can be utilized to investigate intrinsic length scales and their connection to glassy dynamics. We conclude by discussing how these insights can inform the design of future scattering experiments aimed at addressing outstanding questions regarding the glass transition. To facilitate this, we also provide an open-source Python package for analyzing scattering data. This package is designed to be user-friendly, comprehensive, and adaptable, enabling researchers to explore intrinsic length scales across a wide range of materials and experimental configurations. Its source code is available on GitHub. This study examines the effects of external electric fields on non-covalent interactions within the S66 basis set, a collection of 66 small molecules representing diverse weak molecular pairs, including both closed- and open-shell systems. The S66 dataset offers benchmark results for these pairs under zero-field conditions. The current investigation systematically analyzes the impact of applied fields on the potential energy curves of 12 representative molecules from this set. While the chosen field strengths remain significantly lower than those generated by atomic nuclei, they are strong enough to produce a substantial "electric field effect," a phenomenon of critical importance in chemical and biological processes occurring within strong intra- and intermolecular fields. Furthermore, we explore the field-induced modifications to the nature of non-covalent chemical bonds. Finally, we evaluate the efficacy of the CCSD(T) method and various density functional theory (DFT) functionals in accurately computing the energy of non-covalent interactions between electrically polar molecules subjected to strong external fields. This assessment utilizes the standard S66 benchmark data alongside our newly calculated benchmark results derived from coupled cluster methods incorporating external field effects. We demonstrate that the DFT-D3 method, enhanced with a counterpoise correction, offers a favorable balance between computational cost and accuracy for calculating weak non-covalent interactions in the presence of external electric fields. Furthermore, we show that the standard CCSD(T) method fails to adequately account for the energy of non-covalent interactions under external field influence. To address this shortcoming, we introduce a straightforward and efficient correction scheme that adjusts the CCSD(T) energy based on fields calculated at the B3LYP level. This two-level approach achieves a mean absolute error of approximately 0.2 kcal/mol when compared to the highly accurate CCSD(T') method, which was developed with external field effects incorporated from the outset. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings. In conclusion, the CCSD(T') method, combined with the fields-included DFT3 correction, is proven to be both accurate and computationally efficient for studying weak non-covalent interactions between polar molecules in strong external electric fields. This study introduces a novel heuristic that integrates clustering and linearization techniques, tailored for multi-mode multi-item scheduling under both conditions. The research emphasizes minimizing makespan and cost, with additional consideration for due dates, utilizing a flexible job-shop scenario. Notably, the proposed approach is robust, as it relies on standard scheduling data rather than requiring additional information gathering. Empirical results demonstrate the heuristic's effectiveness, achieving an average optimality gap of 1.0% for P-models and 0.5% for CC-models. Furthermore, the study finds that the uncertainty impact is more pronounced in multi-item contexts, whereas due dates play a greater role in multi-mode environments. Overall, the results indicate that handling non-deterministic uncertainty can yield scheduling improvements comparable to those achieved by deterministic models. Finally, sensitivity analysis confirms that the uncertainty's influence is greater in multi-item settings and more significant when due dates are tight. The outcomes of this research are expected to benefit practitioners by facilitating the development of efficient industrial schedulers and encouraging further investigation into various uncertainty types. Additionally, it will assist decision-makers in better understanding the implications of non-deterministic uncertainties, thereby supporting more informed choices. Keywords: uncertainty; non-convex; non-conventional; non-deterministic; industrial scheduling; heuristic.

Although the work targets the resilience of CPS, the proposed framework and metrics are applicable to any time-critical system. To our knowledge, this represents the first formal framework defining resilience in a typical system class based on time-based specifications. Furthermore, this framework offers a formal foundation that enables future research to deepen the understanding of resilience and facilitate the development of automated design and verification methods. Finally, the paper includes supplementary materials with additional proofs and an STL synthesis algorithm.

This research presents a tracking algorithm grounded in conditional probability to safeguard user privacy within location data. We introduce a novel privacy framework defined by a conditional prior, which integrates elements from both Laplacian and Gaussian priors. When pursuing location points with minimal privacy concerns, the system approximates a Gaussian prior to maintain high tracking accuracy. Conversely, when significant privacy protection is required, it approximates a Laplacian prior to shield sensitive user habits. We evaluated a privacy metric under both Gaussian and Laplacian assumptions and developed a tracking algorithm using a hidden Markov model. This approach effectively balances the competing objectives of privacy and tracking accuracy. Numerical simulations confirm that the proposed method outperforms existing privacy-preserving location tracking algorithms in terms of privacy metrics. Furthermore, we compare our conditional prior-based approach against other location privacy definitions to demonstrate its distinct advantages. This framework offers users dual benefits: robust protection against both coarse and fine-grained attacks, and the flexibility to adjust the conditional prior to prioritize either privacy or tracking accuracy according to their current needs. This adaptability ensures that location data remains secure while optimizing performance. The paper concludes with suggestions for future research directions. To address this, we introduce a statistical approach that quantifies the strength of data-driven connectivity. This method calculates a correlation metric between functional connectivity matrices derived from independent rs-fMRI scans, utilizing a bootstrap procedure to generate a distribution of connections. Its applicability to multivariate methods was validated through simulations, which also demonstrated that increasing the number of subjects enhances prediction accuracy while boosting data connectivity strength. Subsequently, the approach was employed to assess connectivity in multiple-site rs-fMRI datasets, comparing both functional and default mode networks. The findings indicate that default mode network connections exhibit higher strength than functional connectivity connections. Ultimately, the study's conclusions suggest that data connectivity strength can act as an additional quality control measure for rs-fMRI studies. Furthermore, because rs-fMRI is a noninvasive technique, future improvements in prediction accuracy will likely stem from larger sample sizes, which can be achieved by aggregating data across multiple sites. This paper examines the classical distributed naming problem within beeping networks, specifically focusing on single-input single-output (SISO) systems where a newly arrived node acquires names from existing nodes without any node initiating the process. We demonstrate that standard beeping networks operate at least an $\Omega(\log n)$ factor slower than optimal when solving this task. Consequently, we propose energy-conserving naming networks, a more flexible framework that allows nodes to execute additional actions beyond standard beepings. Code-mixed (CM) languages, formed by blending two or more languages, are ubiquitous in daily linguistic interactions. While the growing availability of multilingual data has accelerated research in CM languages, most existing approaches treat mixing as noise, segmenting texts into monolingual units for processing. This strategy often results in lost structural information and suboptimal performance. This paper introduces PESTO, a straightforward yet effective framework that treats code-mixing as a primary characteristic rather than an impediment. PESTO utilizes a novel position-wise encoding algorithm to dynamically detect language switches and generate adaptive positional encodings, alongside a proposed SwiAt (Switching Point Attention) module that integrates self-attention across monolingual segments. Experimental results demonstrate the model's efficacy, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy in speech recognition on the Indian English-Hindi dataset. Additionally, the approach proves effective on Web 1.0 CM languages, attaining 86.5% accuracy in part-of-speech tagging and 85.7% in word-level semantic role labeling. Finally, our results indicate that PESTO significantly outperforms relative position encoding, which achieved 79.1% accuracy in word-level semantic role labeling. This success underscores the advantages of adaptive encoding and confirms that PESTO effectively models the structural properties of CM languages. This study employs first-principles calculations and the deformation potential approach to analyze the pressure-dependent isotope effect on the critical temperature of the $A$34S hydride within a metallic hydrogen lattice. Additionally, the isotope effect exponent $a$ is observed to increase with pressure. These findings suggest that $\lambda$ and $T_c$ are strongly influenced by the van Hove singularity in the electron-phonon coupling spectrum, which occurs at high pressures. Furthermore, the theoretical predictions regarding the pressure dependence of the $2\Delta_0/ T_c$ ratio and the $2\pi T_c / \Delta_0$ ratio in high-$T_c$ superconductors align well with existing experimental data for the $A$34S hydride. This paper introduces a new algorithm designed to determine spatial restriction generation (SRG) for agents navigating dynamic environments. The algorithm first identifies a collision-free SRG policy for the primary agent, subsequently assessing its impact on dynamic obstacles. To ensure the SRG remains feasible under dynamic conditions, the algorithm adjusts the SRG solution derived from the static environment and extracts a corresponding collision-free trajectory. We demonstrate that this approach guarantees both the feasibility and robustness of the solution. Experimental results highlight the algorithm's performance in generating effective SRG policies and assessing their effects within dynamic settings. Additionally, the proposed method surpasses existing approaches in spatial restriction generation by successfully producing SRG policies in scenarios that previous methods fail to resolve. A simulation study further illustrates the method's performance and effectiveness. The implementation is provided in the Python-based Motion Planning Library (MPL), which facilitates low-complexity SRG policy generation. Furthermore, a 2-degree-of-freedom robot was employed to validate the approach through a motion planning case study. The results confirm that the method is effective in dynamic environments and capable of generating feasible trajectories in real time. This capability is highly relevant for applications involving multiple moving agents, such as unmanned aerial vehicles and autonomous robots. Ultimately, this method enables multiple moving agents to generate efficient SRG policies and assess their effects while maintaining safety. This work is presented as a step toward developing a universal motion planning algorithm for dynamic environments. Keywords: Spatial Restriction Generation, Motion Planning, Dynamic Environments, Decision Making, Multi-Agent Systems.

Recent years have seen significant strides in visual relocalization, driven by geometric optimization over global deep learning approaches. However, purely learning-based methods struggle to achieve generalizability across new scenes due to the immense data requirements for both scene and query images. Conversely, geometric methods depend on visual descriptors that fail to fully leverage high-level features, resulting in a performance ceiling. To address this, we introduce SumOfNormalizedDistances (SOMD), a new learning-based descriptor that integrates geometric information. Our approach begins by constructing a 3D surface normal distribution image from keyframes of both the query and target scenes, then generates SOMD representations through convolutional neural networks. During testing, 3D surfels are extracted via Geometric Scanning (GS) to compute the correlation between these SOMD representations, thereby localizing the scene. The GS algorithm also facilitates visual relocalization when geodesic distances are high, allowing the method to handle challenging scenarios. Additionally, the SOMD representation's reliance on geometric data enables relocalization over unseen scenes, provided the scene structure is first mapped. Extensive experiments confirm that our method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques in terms of accuracy, precision, and robustness. The source code and demonstrations can be accessed at https://github.com/Chenchenchen/SOMD. Furthermore, our paper has been accepted to T-RO. Chenchen, T-RO 2022. This condition represents an improvement upon previous bounds. Furthermore, we identify a specific class of tropical curves for which the rational function semifield is guaranteed to be finitely produced over $\boldsymbol{T}$ without imposing any degree restrictions. This class encompasses all smooth projective curves, as well as projective curves defined by polynomials of the form $\sum_{i=1}^d \lambda_i x^{a_i} + \prod_{j=1}^m y^{b_j}$. Our findings rely on an inductive strategy involving the contraction of divisors, which we anticipate will be a valuable instrument for investigating the Noetherian property within rational function semifields of tropical curves. Additionally, we present examples and counterexamples illustrating the necessity and tightness of our bounds. Specifically, we prove that the rational function semifield of a projective curve $C$ is finitely produced over $\boldsymbol{T}$ if the rational function semifield of the limiting curve $C^{\infty}$ is. This method yields several corollaries, including the finite production of rational function semifields for tropical superelliptic curves and those associated with Dyck paths. Our work significantly advances the recent findings of Maclagan and Rinc\'on, establishing a new criterion for the finite production of rational function semifields over $\boldsymbol{T}$. We present a theorem outlining sufficient conditions for the uniform convergence of value iteration and temporal difference learning to the optimal state-action value function. This finding serves as a sufficient-condition variant that maintains compatibility with the value function initialization framework established by Puterman (1994). Additionally, we discuss how this theorem enables the derivation of various convergence results found in existing literature through its primary mechanism: an uniform error bound across all states and actions, subject to specific initial function constraints. Our findings establish a clear equivalence: the uniform convergence of algorithms like value iteration and TD learning to their respective function targets occurs if and only if algorithm convergence to the optimal $Q$-function is achieved when starting from a sufficiently low error threshold. Finally, we highlight that, contrary to current assumptions in reinforcement learning research, algorithms do not universally converge to the optimal $Q$-function; we provide counter-examples involving (temporal difference) policy iteration, semi-gradient methods, and temporal difference learning to support this claim. Specifically, we demonstrate scenarios where these algorithms converge to the optimal policy but fail to reach the optimal value function. Furthermore, we propose a class of algorithms that converge to the optimal value function yet do not attain the optimal $Q$-function. Notably, one such algorithm is the standard temporal difference learning method, which, despite extensive empirical evidence of convergence to the optimal value function, has not yet been proven to do so. Our theorem formally establishes this lack of convergence. Temporarily allowing ties in the value function, we show that these algorithms converge to the optimal value function but only identify one of multiple possible optimal $Q$-functions. Consequently, they qualify as policy improvement algorithms rather than value iteration algorithms. This insight may offer a pathway to resolving the aforementioned gap in theoretical understanding. Finally, our theorem provides a unified foundation for proving the convergence of algorithms to the optimal value function and policy, as well as for rigorously selecting a specific set of actions to represent the optimal policy. This approach offers a more natural and straightforward alternative to the conventional method of selecting actions based on the greedy criterion. Temporarily allowing for ties in the value function, we prove that value iteration, policy iteration, and temporal difference learning all converge to the optimal policy. The structural transition from tetragonal to orthorhombic symmetry in LiFeAs, which occurs at approximately 175 K, exhibits characteristics of an nematic transition. To determine if this state results from spontaneous symmetry breaking, we analyzed the phonon dispersion relations along the a and b directions using density functional perturbation theory (DFPT). Our investigation revealed soft modes at the S point in the orthorhombic phase, though the differences between the a and b directions were minimal. Furthermore, we computed the coupling between nematic strain and these soft modes, finding no significant variation. These findings suggest that the low-temperature orthorhombic phase of LiFeAs does not arise from nematic instability, indicating that nematicity plays a limited role in this specific iron-based superconductor. Our results provide a quantitative framework for examining nematicity in LiFeAs and establish a robust DFPT methodology for evaluating nematic tendencies in other iron-based superconductors. Additionally, we compared our theoretical predictions with existing experimental phonon data for LiFeAs, finding strong agreement. This contrast between theory and experiment further underscores the complexity of the nematic phenomenon in LiFeAs. Our study offers valuable insights into the nature of nematicity in iron-based superconductors and sets a precedent for investigating nematic tendencies in other superconducting materials. Ultimately, our work advances our understanding of nematicity and its interplay with other physical mechanisms in iron-based superconductors. By demonstrating the utility of DFPT in predicting nematic strain couplings, we have created a foundation for future research into the fundamental nature of nematicity in these materials. This will contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the complex phenomena governing high-temperature superconductivity. The global alignment limit, where one Higgs boson mimics the SM Higgs boson discovered at the LHC while the remaining Higgs bosons remain non-resonant, is examined at the end of the LHC run and within the future Run 2 of the ILC, assuming $v_1 \ll v_2$ in a Higgs doublet extension. We establish conditions under which Higgs boson couplings satisfy the unitary triangle constraints set by LHC searches for $Z$-mediated $t \to c \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays. Furthermore, we derive conditions ensuring that Higgs boson couplings adhere to the LHC's $Z$-mediated $h \to cc$ and $h \to bb$ decay width limits while simultaneously satisfying the ILC's $h \to Zb\bar{b}$ and $h \to ZZ$ cross-section constraints. We further investigate how $m_A$ and $\tan\beta$ depend on the Higgs boson masses $m_h$, $mA^{(2)}$, and $m_h^{(3)}$ when $m_H = 2m_A$ and $m_h^{(3)} = mA^{(3)} = 2m_H$, a scenario consistent with the LHC $A \to h_2 h_3$ and $h \to h_2 h_3$ cross-section limits. Our findings indicate that the LHC can exclude approximately 90% of the parameter space accessible to the ILC, thereby achieving the Run 2 ILC sensitivity without requiring global alignment. The excluded regions are characterized by $m_A \gtrsim 700$ GeV for $\tan\beta \gtrsim 10$ and $m_A \gtrsim 400$ TeV for $\tan\beta \gtrsim 100$. Additionally, we note that the ILC's $h \to Zb\bar{b}$ cross-section constraint is significantly weaker than its $h \to Zc\bar{c}$ counterpart due to the LHC's exclusion of the $m_A = 2\beta v_2$ region.
