We report the discovery of a 1.21+0.26-0.22 M_Jup planet orbiting the young, low-mass star CIDA 1 (age: 11+3-2 Myr; mass: 0.18+0.03-0.02 M_Sun) and gravitationally perturb the gas disk surrounding it. This finding represents the first identification of a massive planet around such a low-mass young star. The planet's orbital period is approximately 180 days, and it is currently located at a distance of 0.60+0.05-0.04 au from the host. Our findings align with predictions from core accretion models, which suggest that a planet of this mass could form around a young star of CIDA 1's magnitude via this mechanism. Our results also contradict the limitations of the disk instability model, which requires a more massive host star. By combining astrometric data from Gaia DR2 and radial velocity measurements from the HARPS archive, we derived the most precise parameters for the system. Additionally, we present new ALMA 1.3 mm continuum imaging of the disk. The disk is viewed nearly edge-on (i = 87.7+0.1-0.1 degrees) and is dominated by gas, exhibiting a mass of 0.02+0.01-0.01 M_Sun and a radius of 11.0+0.3-0.3 au. We propose that the presence of the planet explains the observed gap in the disk's surface density. Our results support the hypothesis that a massive planet can be formed around a young, low-mass star, either by accelerating the core accretion process or by stabilizing the disk against gravitational collapse. These conclusions are consistent with recent observations of a massive planet around a low-mass, older field star, TRAPPIST-16b. This study underscores the value of combining ALMA continuum imaging with astrometric and radial velocity data from Gaia DR2 and HARPS for characterizing exoplanetary systems. The system of CIDA 1 A and B offers a unique opportunity to study the link between the formation of low-mass stars and their planets. Furthermore, the simultaneous detection of a massive planet and a gas-rich disk around a young, low-mass star provides valuable insights into the early stages of planetary system formation. Identifying outliers is a critical challenge in numerous data analysis tasks, yet existing methods often suffer from either low accuracy or high computational costs. This paper introduces a novel, highly accurate, and efficient approach to outlier detection within high-dimensional spaces, leveraging the graph structures of nearest neighbors. Our method, which is also applicable to other metric distance problems, utilizes proximity graphs to rapidly pinpoint the closest subspaces for anomaly identification. Specifically, we propose a new, efficient, and exact algorithm that operates in $O(n)$ time for $k$-annulus-based detection and in $O(n d \log k)$ time for detection relying on the nearest neighbors count of anomalous points. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach is up to $10^6$ times faster than state-of-the-art methods. The interaction between an excited atom and a cavity wall results in two primary phenomena: motion-induced stimulation, where atomic de-excitation can drive the cavity into oscillation, and the emission of measurable motion-induced radiation. At low frequencies, this radiation behaves as induced Compton scattering, whereas at high frequencies, it approximates equivalent charge radiation, exhibiting either or both characteristics depending on the specific atom-cavity system. Furthermore, by analyzing the motion-induced spectrum, one can deduce properties of the cavity's motion, enabling the detection of minute motions, such as those of light mechanical modes. This framework establishes a complete triad linking quantum radiation matter, mechanical motion, and simulated quantum motion within a cavity. Additionally, this setup facilitates the study of quantum entanglement between atomic and mechanical modes, a crucial element in developing solid-state quantum networks. Finally, this model holds significant promise for developing motion-based quantum sensors with applications in fields ranging from geophysics to quantum technology. For a comprehensive technical overview of the underlying physics, readers are directed to the accompanying review article, arXiv:1801.06223v1 [physics.atom-ph]. It presents the definition and characterization of various localized community fairness notions, along with their interrelationships. Furthermore, it examines the hardness of testing these conditions and both directly and indirectly addresses their learnability. Finally, the work validates these theoretical findings empirically. The study addresses the numerical calculation of stationary solutions to the Michaelis-Menten kinetic equation, which models the interaction between enzymes and substrates. Specifically, it examines the reversible, product-dependent case of this equation, which is notably more complex than the standard model for biopolymer reaction kinetics. By applying the successive-approximations method, the authors generate numerical solutions using a finite-difference scheme. The resulting data is utilized to construct tables of quasi-quantitative estimates for the stationary distribution function of reaction participants. These derived tables are further analyzed to formulate the approximate-derivative function, which characterizes the reaction's steady state. The final section summarizes the properties of this approximation and compares it against solutions obtained via the shooting method. The study concludes by suggesting that the proposed approach is also applicable to other reversible enzyme reaction kinetic equations. Additionally, the authors suggest that their methodology is relevant for solving the stationary kinetic equation of the phosphofructokinase reaction, a critical regulatory enzyme in glycolysis. We demonstrate that the steady-state distribution of a quantum harmonic oscillator, which has been damped and driven, can be computed using path integral methods combined with Monte Carlo algorithms. Our findings indicate that these steady-states typically display non-Gaussian characteristics. Additionally, we have employed the overcomplete coherent state basis to construct the path integral and implemented a Greenberg-Hauser type Monte Carlo algorithm to evaluate the resulting time-independent functional. Our results effectively reproduce the known Green's function for a harmonic oscillator. Furthermore, the calculated steady-states align with physical intuition and match previously reported results obtained through direct wave function evaluation. Finally, we show that the steady-state width exceeds the ground state width and remains independent of the damping rate. Our approach offers a straightforward and effective means to study quantum systems, such as Bose-Einstein condensates, within the mean-field approximation. The presented method demonstrates that, under specific conditions, path integral calculations can compete with more direct methodologies. Finally, this technique is readily adaptable to investigate quantum phase transitions in various mean-field systems. Our findings are particularly relevant for investigating the quantum phase transition between normal and superfluid phases in a superfluid $^{1}$He system, where the superfluid can be modeled as a quantum harmonic oscillator. In this context, the driving force represents the interaction with the normal fluid phase, and the damping constant reflects the ratio of particles in each phase. The quantum oscillator thus serves as an effective model for the quantum critical point, successfully reproducing critical behaviors observed in other systems. This study investigates data augmentation techniques for code-switched (CS) Arabic-English text, addressing the challenge of insufficient labeled datasets for training and evaluating CSed machine reading comprehension (MRC) models. Our approach involves augmenting training data by substituting lexical items with a vocabulary of synonyms or near-synonyms. We examine several multi-language models for this purpose, including the original X林 et al.'s Enriched BERT (EB), the recently introduced Crosslingual-EB (CLEB), and CSed-BERT (CLEB-WS). Our analysis indicates that using weighted word embeddings to identify and select synonymous words yields superior results compared to employing a simple synonym index. Furthermore, we find that the Crosslingual-WS method, which performs cross-language synonym matching, is particularly effective for CSed data augmentation. Finally, we evaluate the impact of this augmented training data on key tasks within the Microsoft Collective Intelligence (MICRI) CSed MRC dataset, confirming that training on augmented data consistently enhances model performance. Additionally, our manual analysis reveals that lexical substitutions contribute to improving model accuracy. We demonstrate that a collection of surface homeomorphisms acting without fixed points is not Roelcke precompact in the homeomorphism group equipped with the Roelcke uniformity. Furthermore, we establish that, aside from a few trivial instances, no family of surface homeomorphisms is precompact under the Roelcke uniformity. These findings stand in stark contrast to the behaviors observed on other compactly generated locally convex spaces and locally compact groups. To facilitate this comparison, we review key distinctions between the Roelcke and uniform uniformities on these varied spaces. The core of our proof relies on a general criterion (Theorem~\ref{thm:criteria}) used to identify non-Roelcke precompact families. Additionally, I. J. Farah's work \cite{I.J.Farah:2019} provides a criteria for precompactness in the uniform uniformity over $\beta G \times \beta G$ (and more broadly) for a broad class of non-abelian groups, which complements Theorem~\ref{thm:criteria} and suggests that Theorem~\ref{thm:criteria} may be extendable to the broader context of $\beta G$-continuity. Finally, we present examples illustrating the disparity between precompactness in the uniform uniformity and the Roelcke uniformity on specific groups and spaces. Through this discussion, we identify (as a conjecture) a class of spaces where the two notions of precompactness coincide. This section also addresses an open question raised by T.~Sivakumar~\cite[Sect.~3]{T.Sivakumar:2017} and includes a preliminary version of Theorem~\ref{thm:criteria} originally presented by I.~J.~Farah~\cite[Sect.~2]{I.J.Farah:2019}. The paper concludes with two hypotheses, one of which is verified, that could potentially extend Theorem~\ref{thm:criteria} to broader contexts. These extensions may offer a unified approach to understanding the relationship between precompactness in the uniform and Roelcke uniformities for groups and spaces. The strategies employed here may also be applicable to addressing the problem of precompactness in the uniform uniformity for spaces and groups that are not locally compact. This concludes the relationship between precompactness in the uniform and Roelcke uniformities. The authors acknowledge the insightful discussions

We investigate integrable dynamics arising from spin $1/2$ membranes within generalized $\lambda$-deformations linked to affine $E_{6,6}$ algebras in string theory. By performing complete canonical quantization in gauged WZW models featuring non-standard metrics and b-fields, we demonstrate membrane duality and identify hidden $sp(4)_k$ symmetries at higher loop orders. We introduce a new category of continuous finite elements, termed tets (short for tetrahedra), constructed as a composite of a simplex and a triangle. This framework extends the successful hex elements developed by Beyer et al. We demonstrate that the geometry of the tet class is simple and robust, enabling the derivation of an optimal cochain complex. Furthermore, we prove the solvability of the Stokes and elasticity equations on grids comprising exclusively tet elements. The paper also explores the theory behind the tet class, detailing specific elements within this family, their mathematical properties, and practical implementation methods. Finally, experimental results are provided, including the simulation of an anisotropic fluid flowing over a curved surface represented by anisotropic hex meshes (where faces are classified as either thin or wide). Hex meshes are increasingly popular in scientific visualization and simulation, offering a balance between the efficiency of unstructured grids and the preservation of topological duality. These meshes consist of elements arranged in a cochain complex, a property that has recently become central to research in finite element exterior calculus (FEMEC). FEMEC relies on a specific class of finite elements known as cochain elements, which maintain optimal properties across all dimensions. This article presents a series of contributions to this field, beginning with a fundamental class of geometric elements: tetrahedra. While seemingly simple, the construction of tets reveals significant complexity, leading to a rich theory encompassing various distinct elements. Relation extraction focuses on identifying entity relationships within unstructured text by mapping them to specific relation types. This task is often difficult due to the similarity between different relation labels. We introduce a method that refines relation classification by incorporating knowledge graph link prediction. Text mentions are transformed into incomplete knowledge graph triples, where missing links are predicted using a graph neural network. The distribution representations learned during this link prediction process, alongside data from the original relation extraction task, train a final classifier to determine the correct relation labels. Our enhanced system achieves state-of-the-art performance on the CoRR and WebMD relation extraction datasets and also performs well on the CoNLL-04 named entity recognition dataset. Current learning-by-interaction algorithms for continuous-state systems, such as those using discretized or Gaussian process value/policy functions, rely heavily on the assumption of locally smooth reward functions. To extend these methods to more general settings, we introduce coarse-grained continuity, a topological concept that generalizes local continuity. Our data-driven metric induces a topology where policies demonstrate coarse-grained continuity, converging to the optimal policy as the sample size increases. Additionally, we provide a local topological condition ensuring algorithmic progress toward optimality and present examples of metrics satisfying the coarse-grained continuity property. Drawing inspiration from categorical foundations, we construct this metric using a free construction on graphs. Finally, we outline an RL algorithm grounded in these coarse-grained continuous spaces and demonstrate its convergence to the optimal policy in several illustrative examples. Notably, unlike discrete or locally smooth scenarios, our examples include cases where the optimal state is isolated, meaning no neighborhood exists that contains all prior steps on a trajectory to the optimal state. These examples effectively highlight the challenges and opportunities of coarse-grained continuity in continuously stateful decision problems. The animacy category, which unites diverse objects into items capable of movement and interaction, is fundamental to understanding the visual world. While numerous studies have examined the neural bases of categorization, research specifically addressing the structure of the animacy domain remains scarce. This study investigates the organizational principles of animacy-related neurons in the human ventral temporal cortex (VTC) using high-resolution fMRI and automated machine learning techniques. Our findings indicate that the VTC employs distinct strategies to map neuronal selectivity across different levels of visual processing. In the early visual region V1, categorization relies on the independent weighting of distinct visual features, whereas in the later region VTC, it depends on a single, highly predictive feature. Conversely, neurons in V1 exhibit highly non-linear boundaries for animacy categorization, characterized by a broad distribution of entropies that fail to align with behavioral performance. In contrast, neurons in VTC display high linearity with class-adjacent boundaries that closely match the optimal Bayesian classifier, effectively separating animate from inanimate objects. The ability of VTC neurons to encode animacy using a single visual feature suggests a shift from a bottom-up, feature-based mechanism to a top-down, knowledge-driven process. This transition marks a critical step toward a cortical region capable of dynamically integrating multimodal sensory inputs and prior knowledge to facilitate complex cognitive functions. Furthermore, the high linearity of VTC neurons implies that the essence of animacy is captured by a single visual feature, offering valuable insights for developing efficient machine learning models. Finally, the gradient of representational schemes in VTC underscores the necessity of a multi-region approach in visual neuroscience. By combining these distinct mechanisms, the VTC constructs a robust and efficient representational framework that bridges the gap between low-level sensory processing and high-level cognitive functions. These findings offer valuable insights for developing next-generation machine learning models and advancing machine intelligence. This study introduces a novel, robust framework designed to preserve the geometric integrity of finite element meshes during topological events like contact, large deformation, and flow simulation. The proposed framework offers enhanced robustness, flexibility, and precision compared to conventional methods. It employs a conical, non-convex feasible region to represent the union of mesh cells, which is managed through a convex optimization-based inner approximation. For triangulated cells, this feasible region is defined by a collection of convex polytopes whose union topologically and geometrically mirrors the cell structure. The internal boundary of this conical set consists of hyperplanes derived from the facets of the constituent polytopes. By approximating the non-convex problem with a convex one, the framework ensures that simulating a mesh's boundary becomes equivalent to solving a convex optimization problem. Theoretically, the resulting simulated mesh remains well-structured, with elements that remain convex and non-overlapping while maintaining adjacency relationships. This approach is versatile enough to apply to both Lagrangian and Eulerian simulations. Theoretically, the framework guarantees the preservation of the mesh boundary and topology under arbitrary mappings, provided the mapping is injective on each individual element. Numerical experiments validate the framework's effectiveness in preserving mesh structure during large deformations, the transport of magnetic fields by fluid flows, and combinations of both. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework successfully maintains mesh quality and significantly surpasses the performance of standard J2 von Mises equivalent stress distortion metrics. Furthermore, in all tested scenarios, simulating the mesh boundary required minimal computational overhead, typically accounting for less than 1% of the total computational time of the primary simulation. Future research will focus on extending the framework to handle cases where element mappings are no longer injective, thereby enabling the preservation of mesh boundaries in more general mappings. To achieve this, we are currently developing a hypergraph-based mesh representation to better capture complex topological changes. The paper also outlines the necessary modifications to the current framework to facilitate this extension. Ultimately, we aim to create a robust framework capable of simultaneously preserving both the boundary and interior of finite element meshes. This advancement is essential for high-fidelity simulations of coupled multi-physics systems, as it will allow for the accurate simulation of contact phenomena and other topological events that are currently lost due to coarse mesh resolution. Furthermore, this development is anticipated to enhance computational accuracy in coupled fluid-magneto-hydrodynamics simulations by preserving fine mesh details near interfaces and current-carrying regions. Type-ax (Type-X) X-ray transients typically display a corona of variable size and structure, which is inferred from high-energy spectral features and the characteristics of type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs). This study investigates how the corona evolves during the 2020 outburst of MAXI J1535-571 by analyzing its high-energy spectrum and the evolution of type-C QPOs using data from the Insight-HXMT observatory. The spectrum was decomposed into a thermal disk component, a reflection component, and a thermal Comptonization component. Throughout the outburst, the corona's physical parameters fluctuated significantly, with the coronal temperature ranging from 10 to 100 keV and the coronal radius varying between 10 and 100 gravitational radii. Notably, the correlation between coronal temperature and size observed in other outbursts of MAXI J1535-571 was not detected in this event. Additionally, type-C QPOs were identified in the 2020 outburst, revealing a strong anti-correlation between frequency and luminosity, as well as a positive correlation between frequency and the size of the accretion disk's inner edge. These correlations align with previous findings from this outburst and a prior type-C QPO study of the system. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these results. Overall, this work provides insight into the nature of the corona in MAXI J1535-571. The study is available at https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stac1000. This study investigates how agents endowed with social cognitive abilities interact within dynamic cooperative scenarios. We observe that agents equipped with social intelligence can achieve their shared goals by reliably responding to their partners' actions and effectively predicting behavioral outcomes. To operate in dynamic cooperative settings, agents must develop mechanisms to anticipate partners' future moves and integrate these predictions with their own intent generation. We argue that agents require reliable feedback regarding their partners' actions and the outcomes resulting from their joint efforts. To address this, we introduce a new design for intrinsic social incentives called Transfer Empowerment, which enables multi-agent Reinforcement Learning and promotes cooperation by empowering agents to recognize the impact of their partners' actions and adjust their own behavior accordingly. We demonstrate a transfer learning approach that reduces computational costs and ensures reliable reaction to partners' actions. Through simulations of the Escape Room benchmark, we evaluate the efficacy of Transfer Empowerment in promoting cooperation between agents possessing social cognitive skills and social emotions, comparing it against other cooperative reward mechanisms. Our findings indicate that Transfer Empowerment serves as a viable mechanism for incentivizing cooperation in dynamic environments where agents must respond reliably to one another. Furthermore, we show that the proposed method facilitates the transfer of learned behavior from individual to joint settings, thereby reducing computational expenses. This research forms a foundation for developing multi-agent systems capable of collaborating in dynamic cooperative environments. To date, no general framework exists for identifying materials from images of any object. While one-shot learning has advanced significantly for standard datasets, current approaches fail to identify materials from unseen categories due to the limited number of examples. We introduce a novel framework capable of identifying materials from images of objects in completely new categories using only a few examples per material. This is accomplished without fine-tuning the network for specific categories and without requiring within-category or cross-category material instances. Our proposed framework leverages physics-based rendering and contrastive learning to identify materials across any object category. By simulating the appearance of all possible material combinations across every category of object, we can identify materials in new categories by simply retrieving the most similar image from this comprehensive dataset. We validate our approach on a newly established benchmark for material one-shot classification, demonstrating the framework's ability to identify material categories instantly and its superior generalization compared to state-of-the-art methods across all benchmarks. We examine various constructions related to Lie 2-algebras, including their equivalence to weak Lie n-algebras of dimension 2 and to lax crossed modules of Lie algebras. We introduce a new end-to-end model for keypoint-based image matching, characterized by its reliance on local image attributes without dependence on global attributes or predefined Keypoint descriptors. Specifically, our approach utilizes a two-stage transformer framework: first, a dense descriptor learning stage focuses on local attributes, and second, an attention-based stage refines match predictions. This transformer architecture enables our model to achieve state-of-the-art performance, particularly in high-resolution scenarios. Furthermore, we demonstrate that high-level supervision can be effectively incorporated into the training process. Additionally, we remove the need for a position encoder, allowing the model to operate without detecting corresponding keypoints in both images. To our knowledge, this represents the first fully end-to-end method for local image matching that relies solely on local attributes and is independent of keypoints, significantly reducing the overall pipeline complexity. Experimental results show that LoFTR consistently and reliably outperforms existing methods across various resolutions, particularly at higher ones. The surge in smart meter deployments has paved the way for personalized energy consumption scheduling. To incentivize reductions in instantaneous demand, this study introduces a novel instant load billing mechanism designed for demand-side management. This mechanism enables consumers to directly influence their costs through the timing of their usage. A aggregative game is developed to model how consumers minimize their individual expenses by balancing the cost function, available consumption capacity, and utility. The existence and uniqueness of an equilibrium solution for this aggregative game are proven. Furthermore, a distributed aggregative best response algorithm is proposed, which allows each consumer to determine a near-optimal strategy by exchanging only the difference between the current and previous estimates of the aggregative function. Simulation outcomes using both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the viability of the proposed method. Additionally, the results indicate that the mechanism successfully promotes the adoption of energy storage systems among smart consumers, thereby enhancing economic efficiency. Ultimately, consumers achieve significant cost savings, while society benefits from diminished peak-to-avg-ratio, reduced consumption, and mitigated power losses. These metrics are evaluated under varying levels of consumer participation, revealing that when 50% of consumers join the mechanism, costs drop by approximately 40% compared to traditional time-of-use pricing. Ultimately, the choice to adopt this mechanism rests with the consumer, offering them a pathway to substantial economic savings. Through this voluntary participation, consumers can also contribute to achieving a sustainable future. This work offers the first mechanism for demand-side management that simultaneously pursues both economic and environmental objectives. Consequently, consumers can select the approach that best aligns with their specific needs. Furthermore, consumers who are environmentally conscious can voluntarily join the mechanism to help build a greener society. This approach also addresses the ethical concern that algorithms should not be manipulative; instead, they should be transparent and allow users to understand the outcomes they help create. By giving consumers control over their economic benefits, the mechanism ensures that users are not merely passive recipients of costs or savings. Ultimately, consumers can actively shape their own economic advantages. This study investigates the Hawking radiation of charged black strings within Rastall theory using the state-dependent model approach. By applying the first law of thermodynamics and analyzing field equations, we determine that charged black strings in this framework emit less energy than those in the standard Hilbert deformation case. This finding supports the conclusion that charged black strings do not undergo evaporation under these conditions. Additionally, we examine various gravitational wave effects, including those from torsion, on the temperature and energy of the system. Our results indicate that the torsion effect is negligible within the charged black string context of Rastall theory. Finally, we derive the inverse square law, a hallmark of our four-dimensional analysis, which aligns with observational data regarding the redshift of distant quasars. Through this method, we also calculate the mass of the supermassive quasar 3C 273. Finally, we present the spacetime metric for a charged black string in Rastall theory, providing an alternative perspective on the solution. This study derives upper bounds for the error term in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem, incorporating spectral data of the driven dynamical system. Furthermore, we present an error bound applicable to specific scenarios even without access to this spectral information. Finally, we apply these findings to establish quantitative ergodicity rates for Euler's Lagrangian planetary $N$-body problem under appropriate initial conditions. The accuracy and tightness of these quantitative rates are subsequently evaluated through numerical experiments. The methodology employed integrates recent advancements in quantum computing, computing power, and error estimation for von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem, while the application relies on novel approaches to hyperexponential ergodic rates. Additionally, this work marks the first effort to quantify the convergence rate of von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for the planetary $N$-body problem. The associated computer program is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianSchulz1992/EulerLissajousQuantitativeErgodicRates. The source code for the numerical experiments is also available at https://github.com/SebastianSchulz1992/EulerLissajousQuantitativeErgodicRates/tree/master/src. The repository includes various orbits of the Euler Lissajous problem, demonstrating different convergence rates of von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem. The executable for the numerical experiments can be downloaded from https://github.com/SebastianSchulz1992/EulerLissajousQuantitativeErgodicRates/tree/master/src/executables. This download option provides access to multiple orbits with varying von Neumann ergodic rates. Users may also generate their own orbits and corresponding data files by modifying the computer program. To do so, one can either adapt the code or, if proficient in programming, compile the provided code using the included Makefile. **Context.** Identifying extremely metal-poor stars is crucial for astrophysics, as these objects serve as remnants of the first generation of stars formed from primordial gas. While the \textit{Gaia} mission's high-resolution spectra in the blue ($430\text{--}$) and blue ($430--}$) regions of the spectrum provide an opportunity to study these stars, the lack of detailed studies on the resulting spectra hinders the development of effective selection methods.

**Aims.** This study aims to characterize the spectral features present in the \textit{gasia} blue spectrum and evaluate their utility for selecting metal-poor stars.

**Methods.** We analyzed high-resolution spectra of metal-poor stars to compare them with lower-resolution \textit{Gaia} BP/RP spectra. Additionally, we examined a sample of 2,000 stars with metallicities ranging from $-1.5$ to $+0.5$ dex to determine how metallically sensitive specific spectral features are.

**Results.** We identified six metal-poor stars with effective temperatures between $3,500$ and $5,000$ K that exhibit clear spectral features in the BP/RP spectra. These features include the 4300 \AA\ Balmer lines, the 4555 \AA\ G-band, the 5180 \AA\ Mg~II lines, and the 6553 \AA\ G-band. We also found that the 6029 \AA\ and 6282 \AA\ regions are sensitive to metallicity.

**Conclusions.** We propose a selection technique relying on features at 4300 \AA, 4555 \AA, 5180 \AA, 6029 \AA, 6282 \AA, and 6553 \AA, which can identify stars with metallicities below $-1.5$ dex. This method is highly effective for stars with masses exceeding $0.8~M_{\odot}$. We anticipate that the features identified here will prove valuable for future analyses of \textit{Gaia} BP/RP spectra. The paper concludes with the application of this technique to the \textit{Gaia} Early Data Release 3.

This study presents a global analysis of annual severity statistics for fire seasons, defined as the product of fire count and average fire size. Utilizing CMAPRS data for fires with minimum sizes exceeding 100 km² across the USA, Canada, Russia, Australia, and Africa (1985-2019), we examine severity distributions, median values, and fluctuations. To identify the common attributes of morphological complexity, researchers can examine how corpus-based complexity metrics relate to one another. However, this correlation analysis alone is insufficient for defining the specific linguistic features these metrics capture. A more rigorous validation involves demonstrating that syntactic complexity, which serves as an external reference, aligns with morphological complexity. This study achieves syntactic alignment in two ways: first, by ranking languages according to their mean word order typology scores, and second, by linking grammatical complexity to mean sentence length. The research combines data from MorphoMap, a database of diverse morphological typology maps, with the Corpus of Modern World Languages, which contains rich syntactic annotations. Findings indicate that the inter-correlations of corpus-based measures align with grammatical complexity, as defined by mean sentence length. Additionally, word order typology ranks mirror complex morphology rankings derived from three distinct measures—morpheme-per-word ratio, disambiguation density, and canonical form ratio—thereby confirming prior conclusions about the relationship between syntax and morphology. Crucially, these results also validate the existence of an underlying construct of morphological complexity, as demonstrated by the consistent correlation of corpus-based measures with word order typology ranks. Ultimately, this study confirms that existing corpus-based measures of morphological complexity evaluate the complexity of morphological grammar. Future efforts should employ multiple measures to ensure robustness and consistency across different analysis types. Finally, the paper introduces a new measure that integrates the principles of the others. Through correlation analysis, this work advances the understanding of morphological complexity and its connection to word order, offering new insights into grammatical complexity and its relation to language size. The study also contributes to the definition of complexity in grammatical systems, which remains an underexplored area. Finally, the authors provide code to generate measures similar to those in this paper, facilitating easy replication and adaptation for researchers. The data used in this study is available at https://github.com/alexei-golovkin/complexity_measures_corpus_data. Although various methods exist for learning Markov models from data, they typically necessitate a strong prior regarding the target model's state space. This limitation hinders the application of existing learning techniques to datasets where the state space is unknown or difficult to define. To address this, we introduce an algorithm that infers the state space of a Markov model from observations of specific hidden states within that model. Our approach is grounded in the theory of state space learning via hidden observations, state reconstruction, and topological graph theory. We evaluate the algorithm using partially observed sequences of Markov chains generated by known state transducers. The results demonstrate that our method can identify state spaces comparable in size to those derived from fully observable sequences, even when only a subset of states is visible. Furthermore, the algorithm effectively handles scenarios where the initial state distribution is unknown. Finally, we apply this technique to perform model selection on Markov chains. Since state space size serves as a critical complexity metric, our method enables the identification of the most parsimonious model state space. By integrating model simplification with existing learning algorithms, we facilitate the use of those tools across a broader spectrum of datasets. Additionally, this framework offers a unique perspective on feature selection for candidate state spaces within model learning processes. Extensive experiments confirm that the approach successfully detects and removes redundant states, even in complex systems. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmed-ibrahim/model-simplification. The paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.07719. Ahmed Ibrahim, Michael Beigl, and Martin Wagner.

The mammalian visual system exhibits remarkable adaptability, adjusting to diverse lighting conditions and environmental factors. This capacity for adaptation is crucial for autonomous vehicles (AVs), which must navigate real-world settings. A primary method for AVs to handle such conditions is through image normalization techniques, which are essential for the successful deployment of deep learning models. This paper introduces M-ar-K Fast Autonomous Component Analysis (M-ar-K-Fast-ACA), a novel image normalization approach. As a multi-component technique, M-ar-K-Fast-ACA integrates multiple image features to enhance adaptability across various imaging environments. The term "M-ar" signifies "Marvellous," while "K" is a phonetic representation of the letter K, signifying that the method is low-key and unobtrusive. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this method improves the performance of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in object detection and image classification tasks. Furthermore, the adaptability of M-ar-K-Fast-ACA was validated using the Multi-domain Automotive Dataset (MAD), where deep learning models were trained without any fine-tuning. Social media platforms offer abundant data that can enhance traffic management systems. However, existing research typically concentrates on detecting traffic incidents after they occur, rather than predicting them in real-time. This study aims to detect impending incidents by leveraging high-frequency, spatio-temporal patterns within sparsely distributed geotagged social media updates. To achieve this, a geotagged sparsity-aware spatio-temporal neural network was developed to model real-time traffic demand in a probabilistic framework, specifically predicting vehicle arrival rates at given locations. Vehicle arrivals were derived from both traffic survey data and social media posts, with their distribution over time and space analyzed against incident reports from the same posts. Finally, spatio-temporal correlation metrics were computed between locations and time intervals to identify the likelihood of upcoming events. The results indicate that this approach effectively captures relevant patterns in social media activity, successfully predicting emerging incidents in upcoming time slots and their subsequent spatial distribution. Furthermore, vehicle arrival rates and their distribution were found to be highly correlated with the emergence of traffic incidents. These findings demonstrate the potential of integrating spatio-temporal patterns from geotagged posts with traffic demand models for incident prediction. The entire framework was implemented using TensorFlow on Google Colab's cloud computing platform. Additionally, the model accepts social media posts enriched with location metadata and can operate on cloud computing platforms. Future research will expand the dataset to cover longer durations and broader geographic areas. Furthermore, the model's hyperparameters were manually tuned in this study, so future work will employ hyperparameter optimization techniques to further improve its performance. Finally, the model's transferability to other regions and datasets will be investigated. These conclusions collectively highlight the model's potential for detecting emerging incidents in various locations and applying the method to other regions and datasets. This study establishes initial and boundary value problems for specific elliptic partial differential equations that involve surface measures as data terms, representing distributions supported on specific submanifolds. Representing distributions through surface measures is crucial for analyzing elliptic operators formulated as weighted integrals over weighted Riemannian manifolds, which arise in statistical mechanics. Statistically, such manifolds correspond to random walks, where the elliptic operators function as transfer matrices. The scalar fields solved by these equations describe the mean values of ensembles, such as magnetization. Furthermore, the partial derivatives of the solved fields correspond to the time and space transfer rates of the ensembles, analogous to current and velocity. In this context, surfaces denote specific configurations of the submanifolds. The second application area involves solving similar elliptic equations with surface measures in higher-order variational calculus. Here, the equations represent Euler-Lagrange equations for action functionals, where the densities are integrals combining Lagrangians for lower-order fields (e.g., the Klein-Gordon field) and higher-order Lagrangians dependent on field derivatives, such as gauge fields. Additionally, the solved scalar fields represent connections and curvature forms. In this scenario, surfaces define specific actions of principal fiber bundles. The initial section presents the mathematical foundations of this work. The second section applies these results to models in quantum field theory. The third section addresses statistical mechanics models. An appendix provides the mathematical underpinnings of physics within principal fiber bundles. These applications are explored from the perspective of a mathematical physicist. The Y-Co-B system is extensively researched for its superconducting properties, with prior studies indicating that cobalt abundance is crucial for achieving high critical temperatures. Utilizing first-principles calculations, this study examines the Y-Co-B system to investigate the link between cobalt concentration and superconductivity. Through an exhaustive search, 20 stable phases were identified, including nine newly predicted compounds. Analysis of these phases reveals a strong correlation between increased cobalt content and enhanced superconducting performance. Furthermore, several of the predicted compounds exhibit higher critical temperatures than any previously reported experimental or theoretical values. These findings offer valuable insights and new candidates to guide future experimental investigations. Additionally, the work introduces a straightforward sequential algorithm designed for automated structure prediction. This approach effectively filters out low-accuracy structures, thereby reducing computational costs, and is readily adaptable for integration into high-throughput screening initiatives. Finally, the code will be made publicly accessible to facilitate its application in large-scale screening projects. Our newly predicted cobalt-abundant compounds are expected to attract significant interest from both the theoretical and experimental research communities. We anticipate that these predictions will inspire new experimental efforts to verify them and drive theoretical investigations into their unique physical properties. Specifically, the discovery of Y6Co10B4 and Y5Co9B4 will encourage experimental studies aiming to explore their magnetic behaviors. Furthermore, Y5Co9B4, with its notably high theoretical critical temperature, is expected to motivate efforts to optimize its grain structure for improved grain connectivity, potentially leading to a significant increase in its experimental critical temperature. These predicted Y-Co-B compounds are expected to assist experimentalists in synthesizing phases with superior superconducting performance. Additionally, Y6Co10B4, characterized by its high theoretical critical current density, will encourage experimental efforts to optimize its grain structure for better grain connectivity, aiming to realize its superior superconducting potential. Overall, this work provides a solid foundation for the theoretical study of the Y-Co-B system, offering valuable guidance for subsequent research endeavors. Furthermore, the proposed method is readily applicable to other multicomponent systems, making it a versatile tool for accelerating the discovery of functional materials. Risk-aware bidding, which involves capping individual bids to preserve total budget under budgeted scenarios, is a critical capability for display advertising. While the field is largely dominated by auction-based models, budgeted auctions remain prevalent in real-world settings. Existing research on budget-aware bidding is primarily designed for first-price auctions and frequently neglects the complexities introduced by bid caps, such as the uncertainty of second-price auctions where the bidder wins. This limitation is particularly problematic in display advertising, where third-party sellers can influence bidding outcomes by adjusting their own offers. This study explores the core challenge of risk-aware bidding within second-price auctions. We introduce ARAB, an adaptive bid adjustment algorithm specifically designed for second-price auctions with budget constraints. Unlike current state-of-the-art methods, ARAB uniquely addresses bid cap uncertainty and accounts for the impact of competitor bid adjustments. Extensive simulations demonstrate that ARAB outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches, achieving up to a 14% increase in expected value. Furthermore, ARAB is easy to implement and incurs minimal computational overhead. Empirical tests using real-world data confirm that ARAB is also highly effective in practical display advertising applications. To our knowledge, this is the first application of adaptive risk-aware bidding to second-price auctions in display advertising. Additionally, our code is publicly available. In the security analysis of quantum key distribution (QKD), standard limit analysis typically assumes that random numbers used for error estimation and privacy amplification are drawn uniformly from a true random number generator. This requirement is often viewed as overly restrictive because it is impractical to verify the uniformity of randomness in real-world privacy amplification processes. Consequently, we propose a security analysis framework for QKD that accommodates non-uniform random numbers for privacy amplification, applicable to protocols utilizing specific decoding methods like the finite-key analysis based on min-entropy sampling under limited active quantum memory. Our findings demonstrate that the secure key generation rate remains largely unaffected by the entropy of the random seed used in privacy amplification, provided the seed entropy is sufficiently large. Furthermore, we illustrate the applicability of this analysis to a practical continuous-variable QKD system employing non-uniform random seeds for privacy amplification, showing that the system achieves secure key rates. These results are anticipated to provide a more flexible theoretical foundation for the practical security analysis of existing QKD technologies. Numerical simulations were conducted for the finite-key analysis utilizing min-entropy sampling. Finally, we present examples of timelike surfaces that possess both timelike and spacelike Bertrand curves, as well as surfaces featuring both timelike and spacelike Bertrand foliations. We aim to inspire a new generation of mathematicians to engage with non-Euclidean geometry and embrace "thinking outside the box." Waveguide Q marks the study of quantum emitters within one-dimensional waveguide systems, a field where light-matter interactions are typically treated as weak perturbations. However, in regimes of strong coupling, these interactions generate complex many-body phenomena that demand sophisticated theoretical frameworks for analysis. This work introduces a diagrammatic scattering method capable of rigorously calculating scattering amplitudes for multi-photon states, extending beyond standard single-photon and resonant two-particle limits. We demonstrate this approach on a paradigmatic model: a single atom within a waveguide. Our findings include the exact scattering amplitude for two-photon states, the first of its kind, alongside an approximate calculation for three photons. Furthermore, we derive corresponding scattering matrices and demonstrate their compliance with fundamental conservation laws regarding energy and momentum. Additionally, we investigate the influence of various driving configurations on the scattering outcomes. Finally, our derived formulas are applicable to broader scenarios involving multiple localized emitters in waveguide QED. These results provide a foundation for designing advanced driving schemes and controlling strong light-matter interactions in waveguide quantum systems. The accompanying code can be accessed at https://github.com/ashishkumar1989/waveguideQED. Given its ability to handle arbitrary numbers of photons, these findings may facilitate the design and control of non-linear quantum optical systems and quantum information processing within waveguide QED architectures. Moreover, the proposed formalism offers a pathway to model and control multi-photon sources and detectors using waveguide QED systems. Our approach may also prove valuable in other fields utilizing diagrammatic techniques, such as quantum field theory and many-body physics. Finally, the presented formalism offers a viable alternative to traditional quantum electrodynamics methods grounded in Maxwell's equations and boundary value problems. The paper concludes with an outlook on extending these findings to scenarios involving distributed emitters. We investigate the spin-dependent (SD) scattering of dark matter (DM) within solar material targets, with a specific focus on solar protons, to establish rigorous limits on DM-nucleon interaction cross sections using existing experimental data. By incorporating the Dirac equation, we demonstrate that for DM with a mass below approximately 10 MeV, its interaction with the quark spin within the proton is significantly weaker than its total intrinsic spin. This finding suggests that SD scattering cross sections for nucleons should not be assumed to remain constant across different DM mass states, a critical consideration for interpreting results from direct detection experiments involving low-DM-mass benchmarks, particularly for sub-MeV candidates. Furthermore, we show that the current upper limits on SD nuclear scattering cross sections are notably higher than those for spin-independent scattering, implying that SD channels could offer superior sensitivity for a given target mass. Consequently, we recommend that future experiments should prioritize searching for the DM spin-dependent axial vector coupling to the proton, as the standard convention of reporting only averaged limits across varying DM states may overlook optimal detection sensitivities. Finally, we present the most stringent constraints to date on the DM-quark and DM-nucleon scattering cross sections. These limits are applicable to dark matter scenarios ranging from the standard cold DM paradigm to lighter alternatives, including warm or superlight DM models. Notably, our derived bounds on the DM-proton axial vector spin-dependent scattering cross section reach approximately $10^{-41}$ cm$^2$ for 10 MeV DM, representing an improvement of several orders of magnitude over previous results. This level of sensitivity is highly relevant for the upcoming search efforts of the DAMIC-M experiment. This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to demonstrate why the odd Bernoulli numbers vanish. It begins by analyzing the binomial expansion of $(1+x)^n+(1-x)^n$ and substituting $x=-1/p$ for a prime $p$ greater than $n$. This approach yields not only an proof of Faulhaber's result but also a method for expressing $1/p^n$ as a linear combination of values of the Bernoulli polynomial $B_k(x)$. Finally, it proves that the coefficients corresponding to $B_k(-1/p)$ possess absolute values exceeding those of the coefficient for $B_k(1/p)$. The validity of this final assertion extends beyond its original scope to all positive real numbers, thereby offering an alternative demonstration of the property that odd Bernoulli numbers are zero. This property is attributed to R. J. Conventional differential detection for continuous phase modulation (CPM) is digital, non-coherent, and exhibits delay sensitivity; however, it is straightforward to implement and cost-effective. This paper investigates methods to enhance the delay tolerance of traditional differential detection. We demonstrate that adding a dead zone of appropriate size to the phase difference function effectively improves delay robustness without significantly degrading detection performance. Analytical and mathematical derivations are provided to determine the optimal delay bound for the phase difference function. These theoretical findings are validated through simulations using a commonly employed offset QPSK (OQPSK) scheme. Our results indicate that a full symbol period delay is sufficient to achieve robust delay performance, eliminating the need for extensive searches within the received signal space. Furthermore, the proposed analytical approach to determining the maximum allowable delay for the phase difference function is also applicable to other CPM schemes. Ultimately, our results confirm that CPM with differential detection can achieve robust delay performance when the phase difference function incorporates an optimal dead zone. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms other traditional techniques, such as the envelope transition function (ETF) differential detection. Consequently, the proposed delay enhancement improves the delay robustness of conventional differential detection, making it suitable for high-speed wireless communication systems. This offers a viable solution for future wireless applications, including millimeter-wave (mmWave) and massive MIMO technologies. Additionally, the proposed delay enhancement can be applied to other CPM schemes, such as OQPSK, to achieve robust delay performance. The core innovation lies in the dead zone selection method for the phase difference function. Reward shaping significantly accelerates the training of task-specific rewards in reinforcement learning. This paper introduces a new reward-shaping technique designed to reduce the time required to train reward functions and embed domain knowledge from human experts into task-specific rewards. By leveraging experts' knowledge of reward-shaping principles, we decompose task-specific rewards into smaller, manageable components called "visual subtasks." To identify these visual subtasks, we employ computer vision techniques and present a novel method for learning reward functions based on subtask ranking. Our findings demonstrate that subtasks facilitate easier learning and generalize effectively across similar tasks. Furthermore, we show that learning reward functions using visual subtasks results in faster acquisition of reward models compared to learning from scratch. Finally, we apply this proposed method to object pick-and-place tasks, illustrating the effectiveness of the learned reward functions. This study investigates the energy scales of the noncommutative parameter within the context of nucleon physics. Functioning as an extension of Quantum Chromodynamics, our model incorporates nucleon energy scales to assess the feasibility of experimental tests conducted at facilities like the Large Hadron Collider. Using data from deep inelastic scattering, we determine that the energy scales associated with nucleons are approximately 1 GeV. Furthermore, we present the calculated energy-dependent structure functions for the nucleon. These findings provide a crucial basis for developing new noncommutative models and for planning future experiments aimed at detecting the noncommutative nature of space-time. Our analysis demonstrates that nonperturbative energy scales, such as those of nucleons, are highly relevant for physics beyond the Standard Model. We emphasize the necessity of performing deep inelastic scattering experiments on free neutrons to refine the understanding of nucleon structure in noncommutative space-time. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive review of methods for generating free neutrons to support this research goal. Our ultimate objective is to establish a consistent framework for noncommutative extensions of the Standard Model grounded in rigorous quantitative analysis. The spectrum, composed of bulk eigenvalues interspersed with outlier eigenvalues generated by the perturbations, is analyzed using a generalized sigma-model within the framework of the local semi-circular law. Utilizing a diagonal approximation, we demonstrate that the spectral correlations are governed by the solution to a diagonal effective diagonal ensemble. Furthermore, we examine the transition between the semi-circular and circular regimes, revealing that a non-vanishing contribution from perturbations beyond the diagonal subspace drives the system into the circular regime. Finally, our findings are compared against a full effective diagonal ensemble solution and a recent extension of the strong coupling approximation. These comparisons indicate that the dominant spectral interactions can be represented by a diagonal matrix, though this conclusion is explicitly valid only for small $\alpha$. Additionally, the strong coupling approximation is shown to be applicable exclusively for very small $\alpha$. These limitations are attributed to the inability of these methods to capture important corrections involving the mixing of perturbative states. In this case, a semi-circular phase emerges when a specific parameter is sufficiently large, with spectral properties described by a semi-circular distribution exhibiting Poissonian level spacing near outliers. Conversely, task-specific models are highly effective for particular challenges but struggle to generalize across different tasks. This paper addresses the discrepancy between the broad capabilities of pre-trained models and the task-independent nature of most current dialogue initiatives. We introduce a novel, meaning-based pre-training objective aimed at enhancing the understanding of natural language semantics in dialogue contexts, particularly implicit meaning, by leveraging surrounding utterances and dialogue actions as signals. Algorithmic interpretability is essential for establishing trust, accountability, and compliance, yet it remains challenging to measure. We argue that a robust assessment of interpretability must rely on human-friendly models, such as those learnable by humans. Building on this principle, we introduce a sequence of concepts and the cognitive complexity (CC) score, which quantifies an algorithm's CC by analyzing the structure of a simulated human learning process. The CC score indicates the effort required for a human to understand an algorithm, with lower values representing algorithms of greater clarity. We demonstrate that our concept effectively distinguishes the trust and compliance characteristics of prominent machine learning methods. For instance, linear models and decision trees exhibit low CC and align with human intuition, making them highly interpretable; conversely, support vector machines, random forests, and neural networks show high CC and lack human-intuitive structures, rendering them uninterpretable. In contrast, hybrid linear models demonstrate low CC while offering interpretable outputs, and shapley values provide explanatory insights without incurring additional CC. These properties make linear models and shapley values suitable for assisting human decision-making. This framework is applied in data mining tasks, and we conclude by discussing its broader implications. An anomaly detection algorithm must be adaptable, capable of functioning across diverse domains, and efficient in both memory usage and computational demands. Isolation Forest (IF) is a widely adopted unsupervised method designed for anomaly detection. This paper introduces TiWS-iForest, a novel anomaly detection algorithm comprising three key components: (i) a three-way learning strategy that trains a model to predict normality labels alongside anomaly labels; (ii) guidance mechanisms allowing the model to leverage external knowledge during training; and (iii) a quantization technique utilizing a neural network to compress IF into tinier models capable of operating on edge devices. TiWS-iForest is straightforward to implement, demonstrating a significant performance boost over IF on eight real-world anomaly detection datasets, while reducing FPR0.001 and FPR0.01 by an average of 1.7% and 2.0%, respectively. Furthermore, TiWS-iForest successfully restores IF's performance across all GLiMMER GLUE benchmarks, outperforming various deep learning-based anomaly detection models. Bayesian inference for extreme value models is frequently hindered by non-conjugate priors and high-dimensional parameter spaces. This study proposes the Poisson max-stable process model, characterized by a low-dimensional parameter vector and an inherent Poisson structure that facilitates discrete integration. We demonstrate that this model effectively models spatial extremes and can be readily extended through covariate incorporation. By developing efficient algorithms for posterior computation via Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), we enable the construction of full joint posterior predictive distributions for spatially unobserved extremes. The model's efficacy is validated through a case study of tornadoes in the United States. Additionally, we have made the model's implementation accessible via the open-source R package {\tt extPOIMS}. This study analyzes the average differential cross section for elastic neutrino--nucleon scattering across the entire differential momentum transfer range. It is demonstrated that in the limit of asymptotically small four-momentum transfer, the average cross section converges to a constant value of $0.67\pm0.04~{\rm GeV}^2$. Furthermore, utilizing experimental data on structure functions, it is established that in the four‑momentum transfer region ranging from $-0.5$ to $-1.5~{\rm GeV}^2$, the average total differential cross section for elastic neutrino--nucleon scattering remains fixed at $0.67~{\rm GeV}^2$ within a $1\sigma$ error margin. Additionally, utilizing theoretical predictions for next-to-leading order (NLO) corrections regarding the deuteron, it is shown that the average total differential cross section for elastic neutrino--deuteron scattering also stabilizes to a constant of $0.67~{\rm GeV}^2$ in the four-momentum transfer region from $-0.5$ to $-1.0~{\rm GeV}^2$, with an accuracy of $1\sigma$. These findings support the hypothesis of QCD color transparency, indicating that the size regions of the deuteron and neutron are nearly identical within the specified NLO correction uncertainties. Finally, the paper proposes a universal parametrization for the average differential cross section of elastic neutrino--nucleon scattering and investigates its characteristics, including its dependence on four-momentum transfer, isotope, and energy. This study outlines a method for creating compact, CTIO-1000 compatible image sequences from raw data acquired by the Hi-GAL survey at the ESO's Las Campanas Observatory. By utilizing Hi-GAL-specific data reduction pipelines that generate HAWAII4R sequences, we achieved data volume reductions of 30% to 50% compared to the raw data size, resulting in more compact files without manual intervention. Furthermore, we examine how data compression can be leveraged to enhance data quality and productivity within large-scale data pipelines. Hi-GAL is a multi-year, multi-yearly survey that has accumulated over 100 terabytes of reduced data across various wavelengths. We demonstrate that implementing a data compression pipeline significantly boosts efficiency by increasing storage capacity, reducing data transfer times, and saving network bandwidth. Although our focus is on automated compression, we also argue that multi-year surveys should employ automated tools for data QC and reprocessing to facilitate the continuous improvement of large data sets. We illustrate this approach using a case study of CTIO-1000 data, which shows that compression can yield up to a 50% reduction in data volume. We have conducted medium-resolution spectroscopy on the globular cluster NGC 2808 to determine the metallicity spread within its first-generation stellar population. By utilizing a sample of 10 stars with well-identified parameters, we derived high-precision iron-to-hydrogen and oxygen-to-hydrogen ratios. The analysis yielded an average iron abundance of [Fe/H] = -0.91 ± 0.01, with an estimated total uncertainty of 0.03, combining statistical and systematic errors. Oxygen abundance results show significant scatter, indicating a metallicity spread of 0.15 dex at a 95% confidence level. These findings align with previous studies regarding the spread between [Fe/H] and log(O/C), which suggests multiple population synthesis as the underlying formation mechanism. Furthermore, we identified 10 new red giant branch overpopulations (RGBOPs) and confirmed the presence of two previously reported ones. The observed variations in iron and log(O/C) among these 13 RGBOPs are consistent with theoretical models that account for CNO processing and secondary pollution. Additionally, we detected variations in Ca/Na and Mg/Al ratios among the 13 RGBOPs, providing further evidence of nucleosynthesis occurring outside the standard single-star evolution model. These results support the conclusion that NGC 2808 is a multiple-population globular cluster. We also present preliminary evidence of a correlation between the strength of RGBOPs and their absolute magnitude. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the formation theories of globular clusters. This study demonstrates that spectroscopic analysis of RGBOPs can achieve high-precision abundance measurements, enabling the detection of metallicity spread and the investigation of the formation mechanisms responsible for it. The medium-resolution spectra utilized in this study are available at http://www.astro.ucla.edu/~wright/pec20130111.fits. The pre-equilibrium dynamics of single-file particles experiencing external potentials are analyzed using system size scaling of size-dependent net forces, which represent deviations from the ideal 1D gas. These scaling relations hold universally across different potential forms, particle number counts, and model specifications, including both continuous and discrete systems. Furthermore, they connect ideal net forces to the system size of continuous chains, as well as to the mean first passage time and the duration of the longest run of exchangeless particles, revealing power-law scaling behaviors with respect to the corresponding input variables. Finally, we demonstrate that the entropy gradient of the longest run of exchangeless particles accurately describes the deviation of the first exit duration statistics from a pure exponential distribution in the regime of large exit times. This finding offers a new physical interpretation of net forces regarding a particle exiting a potential. Additionally, we examine the validity of these findings for both continuous and discrete systems, as well as single-file chains with and without interactions. Finally, we outline a novel approach for deriving one-dimensional potential of mean forces in single-file diffusion within external potentials. This method relies on the gradient of the free energy of the longest run of exchangeless particles, which is derived from the cumulative distribution function of the first exit duration. The resulting potential successfully reproduces the mean first passage time observed in direct simulations. Finally, we demonstrate that this potential also accurately describes the statistics of the longest run of exchangeless particles. These findings suggest that the network of particle runs within a confined region is the primary driver of first passage time statistics, thereby providing a new understanding of the relationship between confinement and first passage dynamics in single-file systems. This insight is particularly relevant for the emerging field of nanoscale transport, where the interaction between particles and external potentials is anticipated to yield new functional materials. Specifically, the first passage time statistics of nanoscale transport networks are expected to be governed by the duration of particle runs within the network, which are defined by the absence of interparticle transitions (exchanges) between adjacent compartments. Consequently, the findings regarding the longest run of exchangeless particles are particularly applicable to the analysis of first passage time statistics in nanoscale transport networks. In this context, a first passage time corresponds to the time required for the longest run of empty compartments within the network. Measurement in quantum mechanics presents significant challenges, including the uncertainty principle, the disturbance caused by the act of measurement, and the problem of the past, which questions whether a measurement device can truly determine an object's state. This last issue is particularly critical for applications relying on measurement inferences, such as quantum inertia and objective collapse models. To address how one can infer an object's state through measurement in quantum mechanics, we apply the quantum Bayes' rule, which formally integrates the quantum state, measurement, and measurement outcome. The results demonstrate that this application confirms consistency in measurement inferences, as the quantum state derived from measurements in different bases yields the same predictions for future observables as the initial state. Additionally, we examine the impact of efficiency on this consistency. Finally, our findings indicate that if a position measurement accurately reveals an object's location, the quantum state updated based on this measurement functions as a localization. These conclusions offer a robust framework for analyzing quantum measurement in scenarios involving quantum inertia and objective collapse models. Furthermore, they provide a basis for developing theories to address decoy states, which arise when applying quantum inertia to photons that have undergone measurement. Finally, this approach may prove essential for developing technologies that depend on quantum measurement inferences. This study reports initial findings regarding finite-volume effects on traceable observables within the thermodynamic limit, using the Wilson loop as a representative observable. Our analysis reveals that the Wilson loop exhibits infinite multiplicity as a function of temperature, resulting in a finite-size effect that scales with $1/T$ in the thermodynamic limit. This finding contrasts sharply with hadron gas simulations, where the relevant observable varies smoothly with temperature. Consequently, the Wilson loop appears unsuitable for extracting the QCD equation of state via finite-size scaling near the crossover region. We attribute the infinite multiplicity of the Wilson loop to the non-trivial structure of its real and imaginary components, which become nearly orthogonal as the QCD scale is approached, producing a cosine-like dependence with a large amplitude. This behavior is linked to the Wilson loop's role as an order parameter for deconfinement, which drives the shift from the pure $Z_3$ symmetry to the complex domain as the bag constant is introduced, thereby generating finite-volume effects. Finally, we examine the Wilson loop's behavior alongside other thermally averaged Wilson loops and trace elements, offering potential solutions to the challenges posed by multiplicity. These insights may prove valuable for producing high-quality finite-size effects using thermally averaged Wilson loops in future investigations. Notably, our results indicate that, unlike the Wilson loop, both the Polyakov loop and trace Wilson loop observables show promising signs of convergence in the thermodynamic limit. The code utilized for these calculations is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/kevinmuller/QLattice}. Our findings have been published in Phys. Rev. D 104, 054501 (2021). Our arXiv submission, Phys. Rev. D 106, 024508 (2022), supersedes the earlier version at arXiv:2110.00001. The updated manuscript incorporates significant enhancements, including the investigation of additional Wilson loop types, the computation of Wilson loop multiplicity, and the publication of results for the Polyakov loop and trace Wilson loop. Furthermore, we have expanded the code to incorporate novel features. While the previous version of the Wilson loop results was derived from preliminary data, the current publication utilizes refined data with improved signal quality. The Lyman-alpha line serves as a fundamental tool for studying the interstellar and intergalactic media. While its optical depth sensitivity makes it ideal for investigating neutral hydrogen, it is also a potent source of background contamination in optical and optical/near-infrared data due to Lyman-series line emission from the interstellar medium. To mitigate this confusion, astronomers have traditionally relied on the Balmer continuum or utilized the blazar HE 0000-218 as a proxy for interstellar Lyman emission, although both methods possess significant constraints. This study introduces a novel approach to Lyman-alpha photometry by employing a filter designed to capture Lyman-alpha emission while suppressing the blazars-based Lyman continuum background. The proposed Lyman-alpha filter has a central wavelength ($\lambda_{0}$) of 1216 Å, a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 100 Å, and is backed by a transmission curve demonstrating $>90\%$ transparency. We demonstrate that this design effectively isolates Lyman-alpha emission, achieving a rejection ratio exceeding 1000 compared to HE 0000-218 and avoiding the confounding effects of interstellar Lyman emission. Additionally, we illustrate that the blazar-based Lyman continuum background remains unaffected by the presence of strong Lyman-alpha emission lines. These outcomes indicate that the proposed filter is well-suited for high-precision Lyman-alpha surveys and could significantly advance the investigation of the Lyman-alpha forest. Furthermore, the transmission curve was generated using a plasma filter, a material well-established in vacuum ultraviolet applications. Given the availability of high-performance plasma filters, the cost of producing such a filter is not prohibitive. Finally, we outline the future applications of this newly developed Lyman-alpha filter. The research was conducted at the Institute of Geophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China. This research focuses on graph symmetric systems (GSSs), defined as a combination of graph-based communication networks and linear time-invariant dynamical systems. The objective is to design a distributed control algorithm capable of steering these systems from any initial state to a target state that minimizes a global quadratic cost function, all while utilizing solely local information exchange among agents. To achieve this, we employ graph filters, which are straightforward iterative algorithms widely used in networked environments. We demonstrate that these filters can simultaneously serve as both a communication mechanism and computational processing step within the algorithm. Furthermore, we establish that the proposed method guarantees convergence to an optimal solution by leveraging the spectral characteristics of the graph Laplacian. Finally, a simulation example is provided to validate the effectiveness of the approach. The method's primary advantage lies in its ability to enhance both privacy and robustness, as each agent relies exclusively on local data exchange with its neighbors. Additionally, the algorithm is distributed and requires no prior knowledge of the network topology or system parameters, making it suitable for large-scale networks. Notably, this represents the first implementation of a graph filter in a distributed control context. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first application of graph filters in distributed control problems. The paper's main contributions are as follows:
\begin{itemize}
    \item We introduce a distributed graph filter designed to resolve the distributed optimal management problem for GSSs, addressing key challenges related to communication and computation.
    \item We demonstrate that graph filters can function as distributed controllers, a novel application beyond their traditional roles in signal processing and control.
    \item We prove that the proposed algorithm ensures convergence to an optimal solution by analyzing the spectral properties of the graph Laplacian.
    \item Extensive numerical simulations are included to verify the algorithm's efficacy.
\end{itemize}
