Boson sampling is recognized as the inaugural model for quantum advantage, offering a straightforward circuit architecture composed of the idealized unitary transformation applied to identical single-particle inputs, yet posing a formidable challenge for simulation. The primary barrier to classical replication of this model stems from the exponential growth of the output state vector size and the ensuing entanglement. Traditionally, the entanglement within boson sampling has been characterized by reduced density matrices; however, given the complexity of analyzing these smaller subsystems and their correlation with the full state vector, it is essential to investigate entanglement across all qubits in the complete state vector. In this study, we demonstrate that the entanglement of every qubit in the complete boson sampling state vector can be quantified using the von Neumann entropy. Furthermore, we establish an analytical relationship between qubit entanglement and the variance of local observables. These findings offer a novel perspective on the entanglement structure of boson sampling state vectors, potentially enabling the development of more efficient classical algorithms. Additionally, our results may hold significance for the broader analysis of boson sampling variants involving non-Gaussian states. Finally, the code utilized in this research is publicly available on GitHub. Mastering high-dimensional time-series data is essential for scientific research, yet it remains challenging due to information density and dimensionality. While recent deep learning advancements have addressed short sequences, they often fail with high-dimensional data due to overfitting. Conversely, models designed for high-dimensional sequences are typically too complex for deep learning. This study introduces a guided learning approach utilizing autoencoders to simultaneously compress short, high-dimensional temporal sequences. Applications in calcium imaging and cardiac electrophysiology demonstrate that our method achieves learning outcomes comparable to state-of-the-art techniques while requiring an order of magnitude fewer training samples. Reinforcement learning focuses on agents operating within partially observable settings. In such scenarios, an agent that maintains a belief concisely capturing all relevant history is guaranteed to achieve optimal control. This study demonstrates that recurrent neural networks trained via standard deep reinforcement learning techniques can reach near-optimal performance in challenging cases, effectively learning state representations that are essentially beliefs. Furthermore, we propose a novel architecture, the Recurrent State Autoencoder (R-SAE), which explicitly reconstructs these belief-like representations and validates our hypothesis. The confirmed relation between recurrent neural networks and beliefs opens this line of research to numerous opportunities, particularly for enhancing interpretability, and the R-SAE serves as a valuable architectural tool for exploring this potential. Additionally, our code and papers are accessible at https://github.com/maartenwagemansw/Recurrent-RL-Belief-Agents. Finally, this work aims to promote greater emphasis on interpretability as a core value in deep reinforcement learning research. We believe that enhanced interpretability will lead to more significant discoveries and deeper understanding within the field. The focus of human-machine collaborative systems relies on the context derived from actions, which is crucial for deriving meaningful insights from action data. However, for weakly-supervised methods, simply predicting the overall classification accuracy of a video is insufficient to determine the relevance of individual frames to that class. To address this, we introduce a two-stage learning framework for weakly-supervised action detection. In the first stage, we develop a motion-graph convolutional network to model frame relationships and learn discriminative features. In the第二阶段, we employ a motion-sampling strategy to identify frame-level annotations. Our experimental results demonstrate that this framework achieves competitive performance in action recognition and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in action detection. Furthermore, the promising context learned within this framework holds great potential for facilitating human-machine collaboration. This work represents the first step toward that goal, with applications including context provision for robotic manipulation and human computing. To support these objectives, we have made our code and data available at \url{https://github.com/leeyu1212/Action-Detection}. The datasets utilized are MPIIWEIGHTLIFTING and JHMDB. The MPIIWEIGHTLIFTING dataset was provided by the group at the University of Maryland, UMD, and JHMDB is a joint effort by the groups at CUHK, HKUST, and NUS. Given the promising context generated by this framework, it is well-suited to help realize human-machine collaboration. The 2021 Image Similarity Challenge (ISC2021) aimed to identify image pairs exhibiting strong semantic equivalence through both visual appearance and underlying meaning. This challenge reflects a critical need in contemporary computer vision to interpret not only visual data but also the intrinsic semantics of images. The objective was to determine if 2020's breakthrough methods, centered on dense image embeddings, could still dominate without significant algorithmic revisions. The competition featured two tasks: Image-KNN and Image-Image-Retrieval, engaging 109 teams across both. This technical report summarizes the top-performing approaches for each task and provides an analysis of key findings. It begins with an overview of the dataset and its inherent difficulties, followed by a description of the submission frameworks and a synthesis of results for the 2021 winners and finalists. Finally, we highlight the most promising strategies and datasets from the competition, offering insights to guide future research and potential future editions. Specifically, we advocate for the expanded adoption of modern image pre-training techniques and emphasize the value of well-curated, diverse datasets that capture a broad spectrum of real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we outline several underexplored directions within the challenge, including the distinct nature of KNN versus retrieval tasks, the necessity of cost-effective similarity computation, and the importance of evaluating robustness against adversarial attacks. These factors collectively offer valuable guidance for the continued advancement of image similarity research. Finally, we provide practical implementation code for all winning solutions at \url{https://github.com/isc2021/ISC2021}. This report was produced by the challenge organizers in collaboration with A*STAR-AgriFood Authority (SINGAPORE). The challenge was sponsored by OrCam, which specializes in wearable computer vision solutions for healthcare, security, and consumer goods. OrCam's involvement underscores the growing significance of image similarity in industry, particularly in developing wearable devices for assistive technologies. OrCam is a leading global company in this domain, with a strong market presence and a track record of driving innovation through their participation in the 2021 Image Similarity Challenge. Their commitment to the competition demonstrates their dedication to advancing the field and staying at the forefront of cutting-edge research. OrCam supports global scientific progress by fostering cutting-edge research, driving innovation, and providing funding and resources to the global scientific community. By supporting competitions like the 2021 Image Similarity Challenge, OrCam contributes to accelerating scientific progress and creating a brighter future for all.

This study examines metastability and transience within a wide range of degradation processes, encompassing algebraic decay, geometric decay, and delay effects. By employing perturbative methods and solving corresponding boundary value problems for the parabolic generator, we characterize asymptotic behavior. The analysis addresses various boundary conditions, specifically initial and boundary data within closed domains. Furthermore, we investigate the scenario where the closed boundary undergoes periodic switching, resulting in slowly evolving boundary conditions and an effective generator determined by the quasi-stationary solutions of the parabolic problem. The latter part of the work also covers an averaged boundary value problem, which serves as the effective equation for the slowly evolving domain. Additionally, we address the homogenization of these degradation processes when the periodic boundary condition becomes rapidly evolving, leading to rapidly oscillating boundary conditions and the emergence of nonlocal operators in the limit. Finally, the theoretical framework is applied to several limit examples, including algebraic and geometric degradation, delayed degradation, and boundary problems featuring rapidly oscillating conditions. The methods are also applicable to Allee degradation and other contexts involving boundary conditions subject to integral constraints. Notably, the algebraic and geometric degradation cases present unique challenges, as standard parabolic problem solvability techniques fail to yield effective boundary value problems. To address this, we develop an original approach utilizing a novel integral equation derived from the original parabolic equation. This integral equation incorporates boundary data and includes a delay term, thereby effectively resolving the core issues associated with these degradation processes. Integral equations of this nature also arise when analyzing boundary conditions subject to integral constraints. We subsequently analyze these quasi-stationary solutions to provide a comprehensive understanding of the asymptotic dynamics for degradation processes under such boundary conditions. Finally, the work concludes with an appendix detailing a solution to a specific boundary value problem involving a nonlocal operator. This study investigates the symmetric nuclear matter generated by a mixture of neutrons and protons under conditions of strong and antisymmetric magnetic fields. The multicomponent LOCV (Large Occam Counting Variable) technique is employed to address the chiral $NN$ potential and the three-body force. Our findings indicate that the magnetic field significantly influences the system when it is of order $10^{18}$ G, a intensity expected in core-collapse supernovae. Specifically, the magnetic field significantly softens the equation of state, while its effect on the symmetry energy remains negligible. Additionally, we observe that the antisymmetric magnetic field slightly favors neutronization, in contrast to the behavior seen in superfluid matter subjected to strong magnetic fields. Furthermore, we determined that the magnetic field has a minimal impact on the in-medium modification of the mass. These results are discussed in the context of their relevance to core-collapse supernovae. Finally, we note that the antisymmetric magnetic field can significantly affect the energy spectrum of nucleons, though this effect is relatively small. Last but not least, we examined the possibility of forming a quarkyonic star under such conditions within the framework of the quarkyonic scenario. Privacy and security have become central to the machine learning community, especially in light of the recently introduced federated learning (FL) framework. FL allows multiple parties to contribute to a shared model without exchanging raw data, a feature that has made it a focal point for the industry. However, FL alone does not fully ensure privacy, as model updates can inadvertently reveal sensitive information about training data. This challenge is exacerbated in modern FL deployments, which often suffer from high communication costs due to transmitting large update files over the internet. To address these issues, we introduce a novel privacy-preserving FL framework called Differentiable Privacy-based Federated Learning (DP-REC). This system employs differentially private learning to guarantee privacy while significantly reducing communication overhead through data compression. Our results demonstrate that DP-REC outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of both communication efficiency and privacy protection. Notably, under compromised conditions where the server attempts to reconstruct the model, DP-REC offers substantial protection against such attacks. Both theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations confirm that our proposed framework effectively addresses the fundamental privacy and communication challenges inherent in federated learning. We introduce the initial results from the Far Ultraviolet Survey of the Taurus-Perseus-Aquila complex, conducted using the International Ultraviolet Explorer (IUE). This survey targeted approximately 150 young stellar objects (YSOs) and their surrounding disks, utilizing a broad-band filter covering 1200-1700 A. The study reveals significant far-ultraviolet (FUV) emission from all YSOs older than 1 Myr, which aligns with expectations from their FUV spectra. However, YSOs younger than 1 Myr exhibit much weaker FUV emission, a finding that cannot be attributed to their spectral types. Additionally, we identified FUV emission from approximately 20 pre-main sequence (PMS) stars that lack visible components. These PMS stars are likely deeply embedded within dense disks or envelopes, a characteristic that may also account for the low FUV emission observed in younger stars within the sample. Furthermore, we detected FUV emission from approximately 100 molecular clouds that are not associated with any YSOs. The intensity of this FUV radiation is comparable to that seen around YSOs with spectral types later than M0, suggesting a substantial contribution from PMS stars to the overall FUV field in this region. This finding underscores the critical role of FUV radiation in driving photoevaporation processes within PMS disks. We also present new far-UV photometry for 120 previously known Taurus YSOs, extending the color-color diagram to include FUV data. The resulting diagram displays the standard M-K diagram along with a new locus for M0-M5 stars, which lies below the classical Henize diagram. We propose that this new locus represents a sequence of stars with large amounts of dust in their disks. Finally, we compare the spectral classification of YSOs in our sample with their FUV colors and discuss the implications of these relationships. We conclude that the FUV color is a reliable indicator for YSOs with spectral types later than M0. However, for earlier-type YSOs, the FUV color does not uniquely determine their spectral type. Additionally, we present a new far-UV wide-band photometric catalog for the Taurus-Perseus-Aquila complex, encompassing 270 YSOs and molecular clouds. The catalog includes FUV magnitudes and fluxes for 269 YSOs, while 1 YSO and 1 molecular cloud were excluded due to saturation.

Modern document retrieval and extraction systems depend on accurate table recognition to serve as a prerequisite for table content mining. Nevertheless, retrieving the most relevant tables from the vast collections found in today's popular PDF documents remains a difficult task, especially given the diverse formats of tabular data. This paper addresses document-based table retrieval by first tackling representation learning for them. We construct a heterogeneous graph from table metadata and model diverse table contents using natural images, then leverage the properties of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to learn representations for these documents. Subsequently, we present a neural network approach for table retrieval grounded in these learned representations, with experimental results confirming the method's effectiveness and utility. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/chenchen1992/GNNTable}. Furthermore, our method is available online at PDFTables, which offers representative heterogeneous data for table retrieval. We investigate cognitive hierarchies within multi-stage games characterized by incomplete information. Our framework incorporates both strategic thinking and belief updating, enabling the definition of cognitive hierarchy equilibria (CHE) at various levels of depth. At the foundational level, we establish the relationship between Nash equilibrium and CHE, introducing the concept of best response stability. Building upon this, we advance a sequential and recursive definition of CHE across multiple levels. Furthermore, we demonstrate that CHE is the unique refinement of Nash equilibrium that ensures a positive probability of reaching the first-order best response and the first-order neuropsychological prediction. Finally, within a recursive framework, we examine the existence and convergence of cognitive hierarchies of infinite depth. Additionally, by integrating Bayesian rationality, we show that CHE evolves into the Bayesian cognitive hierarchy equilibrium (BCHE). Our analysis confirms that the sequence of BCHE of depth $k$ converges to the unique Bayesian Nash equilibrium of a game where nature selects the depth according to a geometric distribution with a mean of $\frac{1}{1-\alpha}$ for some $\alpha \in (0,1)$. This finding generalizes a recent result by Costin, Ghosal, and Roy (2021). Finally, through agent-based simulations, we illustrate the existence of a Bayesian selection phenomenon among multiple equilibria in these games. Specifically, Bayesian cognitive hierarchies of infinite depth converge to a Bayesian Nash equilibrium with a higher payoff than the one most frequently predicted by non-strategic agents. This outcome contrasts with standard Bayesian learning models, which often fail to predict the emergence of high-payoff equilibria. In the process, we also demonstrate the existence of a "bifurcation point" within the space of prior beliefs. Beyond the existing literature on cognitive hierarchies in single-stage games, this research advances the understanding of such hierarchies in multi-stage games under insufficient information. Our findings hold significant implications for modeling behavior in economic and biological systems, as well as for understanding the dynamics of strategic interactions. Furthermore, our approach facilitates the analysis of how the depth of cognition influences the selection of high-payoff equilibria. Finally, our findings contribute to the broader field of social learning, particularly in scenarios involving multiple agents with heterogeneous cognitive depths. By employing Bayesian cognitive hierarchy equilibrium, we provide a new perspective on the existence of Bayesian selection toward high-payoff equilibria, complementing the existing body of work on the emergence of such phenomena. This study demonstrates the technical viability of generating sustainable census estimates of total population and population density for remote, hard-to-reach areas in Southern Mozambique, specifically the Maputo Province, by integrating high-resolution satellite imagery with deep learning algorithms. We developed a high-quality, heterogeneous dataset comprising 1,000 satellite images from diverse locations across the province, from coastal to inland regions, to train and evaluate a series of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures. Furthermore, we successfully deployed a pre-trained ResNet50 model within a Raspberry Pi device to estimate population and population density for new, unseen areas in the province, proving the system's portability and energy efficiency. Approximate membership checking is a fundamental task in computer science designed to reduce the memory required for storing sets. It operates as a probabilistic data structure that occasionally produces false positives, meaning it might indicate a element is in the set when it is not, though this happens rarely. This paper revisits the class of filters based on minimal perfect hash functions (MPHH), which are highly efficient structures that store only positive elements without false negatives. We demonstrate that this category inherently functions as a filter by simply keeping an independent collection dedicated exclusively to false positives. Leveraging this insight, we introduce multiple filters utilizing MPHH; these are rapid to execute, require less memory, and are the first of their kind to offer true space efficiency with an optimal linear space lower bound. Furthermore, we propose the use of false positive-free collections as a novel technical approach for constructing probabilistic data structures. Our method involves defining the boolean complement of the MPHH-based structure, which functions as a perfect hash function for false positives. This technique represents a significant advancement in the field. Additionally, we examine how to enhance the quality of filters by integrating our proposed approach with conventional bit vector methods. Finally, we validate the practicality of our structures through memory and execution time comparisons against other probabilistic data structures. To our knowledge, this work introduces the first probabilistic data structure family to be both practically and theoretically optimal. This study introduces a multi-resolution Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) approach designed for complex fluid-structure interaction (FSI) scenarios. The framework is built upon an adaptive kernel approximation using a multi-resolution technique. These methods are implemented to calculate a high-resolution, anisotropic meshless kernel in fluid regions surrounding solid boundaries. We validate and expand this framework by examining a challenging multi-component FSI problem: a flexible plate within a vortex ring. In this study, particles are subjected to multi-phase forces, and a fine SPH mesh is required to accurately resolve both the fluid and the boundary. Our results demonstrate that the proposed adaptive kernel effectively captures the fine fluid mesh and successfully captures the vortex ring interacting with the plate. Furthermore, the method is capable of resolving the complex dynamics of the plate, including its bending, fluttering, and flutter-bending motions. Consequently, this method is particularly well-suited for FSI problems featuring complex fluid dynamics and highly nonlinear structural behaviors. Finally, we discuss potential applications in geophysical flows, such as sediment transport and fluid-structure interactions involving geotechnical structures. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChengweiZhang1991/MultiResolutionSPH. Video files documenting our findings will be uploaded to the same repository. Additionally, we acknowledge that the multi-resolution SPH method is not yet fully mature and is currently being refined. We aim to further improve the technique and explore applications in geophysics and geotechnical engineering. Our goal is to provide a more accessible and user-friendly open-source code for the community. We welcome collaborations with researchers in geophysics and geotechnical engineering. This study explores quantum machine learning applications within the NISQ era, focusing on unsupervised learning for quantum-processed data using a superconducting processor. We introduce a quantum-guided approach leveraging a variational unsupervised algorithm to analyze quantum data via graph partitioning and principal component analysis (Q-PCA). This method is applied to quantum data derived from the classical Heisenberg model on a square lattice, exhibiting strong Ising correlation, as well as data from two- and three-particle quantum collision kernels. Ultimately, the research demonstrates the viability of quantum methods for pattern analysis and graph processing, establishing a foundation for future quantum-enhanced supervised learning. By integrating these findings into the AI-driven scientific discovery loop, we illustrate how quantum computers can serve as a critical link in this cycle. Specifically, we highlight that superconducting processors can function as either classical CPUs or hybrid CPUs, capable of guided learning through AI workloads that provide target labels and evaluation metrics. Furthermore, we demonstrate the integration of quantum-enhanced superconducting processors with quantum-enhanced GPUs for pattern analysis on quantum data, representing a significant step toward the emerging field of quantum-informed scientific discovery. Finally, this work underscores the value of superconducting processors as a vital intermediate step toward fully quantum-informed scientific discovery. Although the Pitch-timed FastSpeech2 (TPS) has demonstrated significant improvements in naturalness, speech intensity, and intelligibility by enabling pitch-controlled TTS, it suffers from limited pitch controllability due to the scarcity of high-pitch training data. To address this, we introduce a novel pitch augmentation technique called Varying F0 (VF), designed to enhance pitch controllability in TPS. VF synthesizes high-pitch samples from low-pitch ones while maintaining timbre characteristics. Specifically, VF generates high-pitch waves by shifting the fundamental frequency (F0) upward, applying a sampling rate adjustment to preserve the waveform's duration, and incorporating noise during the up-sampling process to avoid timbre degradation. Additionally, the TPS architecture is modified to accommodate timbre variations introduced by VF. Training results confirm that VF significantly improves pitch controllability, whereas simply providing extra training data without VF yields negligible gains. This study introduces Hopper, a novel multi-hop transformer designed for the inference of spatiotemporal data. While deep learning methods, particularly transformers, have achieved significant success across various domains, they face substantial challenges within the spatiotemporal inductive bias, primarily due to unaddressed long-term dependencies. We validated our approach on three real-world datasets—Air Quality, Traffic Flow, and Weather Prediction—demonstrating that Hopper surpasses state-of-the-art models in both accuracy and efficiency. This work introduces a method for determining the mass of the $W$ boson by analyzing the cross section of lepton-pair production in association with a $b\bar{b}$ pair at the LHC. In this framework, the primary production mechanism for the lepton-pair and the $b\bar{b}$ pair is the associated production of a top quark pair. The primary motivation for this approach is that the resulting sample is highly contaminated by $t\bar{t}$ events, where the $W$ boson mass is already well-established. Consequently, the derived value for the $W$ mass will serve as a consistency check. The study provides a systematic uncertainty estimate, yielding a total uncertainty of 1.2%. Furthermore, the precision is expected to be improved by approximately a factor of three through the inclusion of data from high-luminosity LHC runs. Additionally, the technique is applicable to associated production scenarios involving $b$-quarks and other particles. Implementing this method at a future high-luminosity, high-energy machine could enable precision measurements of $W$-boson properties, including its mass, thereby offering a consistency test for the $SU(2)_L$ doublet nature of the top quark. All results are calculated within the SM. The analysis was performed using next-to-leading order QCD simulations for $t\bar{b}$ production, alongside leading-order predictions for the $b$-quark density. The uncertainty is dominated by uncertainties in the $t$-quark and $b$-quark parton distribution functions. The $b$-quark density uncertainty is estimated at 10%, a figure that could be reduced by incorporating data from associated $t\bar{b}$ production. The method was tested using a simulated sample of $10$ fb$^{-1}$, and the final result is presented as the ratio of the measured $M_W$ to the predicted $M_W$. This ratio was found to be 1.001, with a total uncertainty of 1.2%. A future measurement of the $W$ boson mass with an uncertainty of 100 MeV is anticipated once the data volume from a 300 fb$^{-1}$ run of the LHC is utilized. Mafia, or Werewolf, serves as the quintessential social deduction game. In this format, participants are randomly divided into opposing factions: Civilian, Mafia, or Werewolf. Each pair of Mafia-type roles functions as a unified team that cooperates to eliminate players. During gameplay, mafia-style votes are cast to target civilian players. This game has been featured on over 300 TV programs across 20 countries, and online surveys indicate it is the most favored board game among teenagers. This paper introduces a mathematical framework for Mafia-type games, where two distinct mafia-style roles may join forces. We present a random process modeling the random allocation of roles and derive a formula calculating the probability of a specific assignment for a group of $N$ players. Furthermore, we examine scenarios involving a single role that allows mafia-style players to coordinate, deriving a recursive relationship for the likelihood of elimination when the initial player counts for Civilian and Mafia-type roles are known. We also analyze the randomness of the mafia-style elimination process under this framework. Our research offers a tool for investigating various Mafia game variations and differentiates between the "Mafia" and "Werewolf" mathematical models. These findings facilitate a deeper understanding of the game's mechanics and may inform the design of new variations or assist in the development of automated opponents. Additionally, our methodology has been applied to specific game configurations, yielding counter-intuitive results. We conclude with several open questions and potential directions for future research. To our knowledge, this represents the first mathematical analysis of Mafia-type games. The framework established in this study has been adopted in undergraduate mathematics curricula, and we have utilized it to train mathematics teachers. We anticipate that this research will be valuable for mathematics education as well. This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 11771018). The accumulation of accreted gas by multiple giant planets significantly influences their ultimate mass and orbital evolution. This study investigates gas accretion dynamics around a single central star and its disk containing two giant planets. We employ a model utilizing hydrodynamic equations for the disk and classical accretion theory for the planets. Our findings indicate that gas accretion by both planets occurs concurrently, with the system exhausting the disk within approximately 1.5 million years. During this phase, the inner planet gains mass at a rate of 1.5 Earth masses per 100,000 years, while the outer planet accretes at a rate ten times slower. The model reveals that the migrating outer planet induces the formation of a gap in the disk, whereas the slowly migrating inner planet creates a pronounced density peak. This inner density peak persists until the gap-forming planet carves through it, after which mass accretion rates drop substantially. We conclude that the observed variation in accretion rates and the structural features of young disks around central stars may serve as a method for detecting the presence of multiple planets within the disks. Additionally, we demonstrate that a high density peak in a disk can halt accretion onto a migrating planet, potentially explaining the low masses of some hot Jupiters. This outcome contrasts sharply with the standard core accretion theory, which predicts rapid, uninterrupted accretion once a gap forms. Consequently, our proposed mechanism offers a potential explanation for planets with masses below 1 Jupiter mass that have migrated to very close orbits around their host stars. Finally, we suggest that the migration and mass accumulation of Jupiter and Saturn can be attributed to this mechanism. By analyzing their orbital spacing and current masses, we can constrain the duration of their gas accretion phase to roughly 1.5 million years. Electronic transport within armchair carbon nanotubes (CNTs) is primarily governed by ball-like tunneling along the tube axis, whereas phonon-assisted one-dimensional scattering is expected to significantly influence conductivity near charge neutrality. However, conclusively identifying this mechanism in macroscopic CNT films has remained elusive. In this study, we demonstrate clear evidence of such a process by analyzing the temperature and gate voltage dependencies of conductivity in high-quality C50-Ar/SCN-based CNT films. Our results reveal distinct phonon-assisted tunneling signatures, including a conductivity variation with temperature that aligns with the density of states near the CNT band edge and a pronounced conductivity peak at the CNT charge neutrality point. We further confirm these findings through numerical simulations. This substantial phonon-assisted scattering indicates weak links between the metallic and semiconducting regions of the CNT, thereby enabling the design of switchable CNT-based devices. The observed phenomena are attributed to grain boundary defects, which have profound implications for the development of functional CNT-based materials. Specifically, optimizing CNT films by mitigating these defects is essential for achieving high-performance, uniform electronic devices. Finally, our methodology for elucidating the physical mechanisms in macroscopic CNT films can be readily extended to other two-dimensional materials. By elucidating the physical mechanisms in macroscopic CNT films, our work paves the way for further investigations into the electronic properties of other CNT architectures and CNT-based materials. This study introduces a novel fuzzy k-means algorithm designed for high-dimensional data, which may contain redundant or irrelevant features. In many real-world scenarios, a single data point comprises multiple attributes that can be replaced by a smaller set of reduced features. Existing methods often fail to effectively manage high-dimensional data due to the absence of variable weights; instead, traditional approaches assign equal weights to all features. To address this, we propose an enhanced fuzzy k-means algorithm utilizing variable feature weights. We develop a high-dimensional data structure incorporating these feature weights and utilize Shannon entropy to assess feature relevance. The core mechanism involves iteratively calculating both feature weights and centroid values. The process begins with an initial data partition, where variable weights are computed based on data distribution, and initial centroids are derived by removing outliers. The algorithm then executes two parallel operations: updating centroid values and reassigning cluster memberships. Iterations continue until the objective function stabilizes. Experimental results indicate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods. Furthermore, the effectiveness of introducing variable feature weights is demonstrated through comparisons with simplified versions of the algorithm. Finally, comparisons with other clustering methods confirm that the proposed algorithm achieves superior performance. Performance is evaluated using high-dimensional datasets with synthetic features, random features, and real features. The algorithm's computational efficiency is demonstrated through comparisons of execution time and iteration counts against other models. These findings highlight the significance of variable feature weights in high-dimensional data clustering. The mixture-of-experts (MoE) model is extensively used across various machine learning domains, such as natural language processing and computer vision, due to its capacity to yield highly accurate results. Despite this, analyzing the convergence of nonconvex-nonnconvex gradient descent methods for learning MoE remains an open challenge, a barrier that has hindered the development of efficient learning procedures for this model class. This paper offers two primary advancements. First, we resolve the consistency issue in learning linear MoE by introducing the first provably consistent gradient descent algorithm capable of learning such models under mild conditions. Second, we tackle the inefficiency problem by presenting the first provably efficient algorithm for learning quadratic MoE, effectively balancing model expressiveness with computational tractability. Our approaches are versatile and extend to other structured models, including factor models, operator models, and autoencoders. We demonstrate the empirical effectiveness of our algorithms using linear and quadratic operator models on extensive datasets, showing that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/taehyungkim1213/moe}. Furthermore, our findings have broader implications for optimization theory by advancing the understanding of gradient-based methods in nonconvex-nonnconvex settings. Specifically, we establish a general convergence guarantee for gradient descent applied to a nonconvex-nonnconvex bi-level optimization problem, a result that is inherently consistent with current theory and potentially useful for analyzing other problems. Additionally, our work suggests new research directions for future investigations. Finally, this manuscript serves as a comprehensive tutorial on the learning theory of structured models, offering an in-depth treatment of recent advances in the field. However, the absence of exactly global symmetries in a quantum theory of gravity remains a contentious issue. Burnat's straightforward yet intricate principle serves as a fundamental tool in topology, offering a criterion to determine whether the topological structure of a space can be reconstructed solely from the cohomology of its skeleton. Although the principle maintains relative simplicity, its underlying methods are so delicate that numerous attempts to broaden its scope have failed. A notable advancement by Cohen-Ghienne-Grady achieves this long-desired extension to relative settings; however, this achievement remains a delicate mathematical result that is unlikely to be generalized further. This article examines the various proofs of the Mumford conjecture, with a specific focus on how they rely on Burnat's principle. The content is intended for a broader audience, particularly graduate students and researchers interested in the foundational concepts of the conjecture. A key component of the discussion is the demonstration of one proof utilizing the techniques of stable homotopy theory. The analysis excludes other approaches, such as those rooted in geometric group theory, which are significantly more complex and require additional time to explore.

A significant challenge in deep learning research involves ensuring that models trained on one domain can generalize to another. Transferability describes how this capability functions across three key dimensions: source-target task alignment, model architecture, and training objectives. Research by Liu et al. (2019) established two key agreements: an ordinal relationship between task similarity and transferability, and a strong correlation between model representational similarity and transferability. This study expands upon the second agreement by eliminating the confounding effect of task similarity. We propose evaluating multiple tasks with a single shared model to isolate the impact of representational similarity. Through our experiments, we observed that while an exponential relationship exists between representational similarity and transferability, it is non-monotonic, indicating that higher representability does not always enhance transferability. This finding underscores the critical role of task similarity in transfer learning. Additionally, we conducted experiments without the confounding effect of architectural differences to further clarify the relationship between representational similarity and transferability. Our results demonstrate that the $\ell_2$-distance between contextualized embeddings effectively captures this dynamic. Finally, we examined how training objectives influence transferability and the resulting relationship. To assess this, we compared the effects of pretraining with and without task adaptation, measuring representational similarity via fine-tuning results on unseen datasets. Our analysis reveals that the impact of contextualized embeddings on transferability diminishes as task similarity increases. Collectively, these experiments support the following refined agreements regarding the relationship between task similarity, representational similarity, and transferability:
(1) When task similarity remains constant, a higher degree of representational similarity generally leads to greater transferability.
(2) Representational similarity exerts a non-linear influence on transferability.
(3) An inverse relationship exists between task similarity and the impact of representational similarity on transferability.
These conclusions offer valuable insights for advancing transferability research, particularly regarding the design of inter-task models. Furthermore, the ordinal relationship between task similarity and transferability remains valid. Containing and orchestrating workloads is a cornerstone of contemporary computing, where containers have become the leading solution for building scalable systems. First introduced in 2013, containers have become the standard for developing and running large-scale data processing systems. This paper presents Ozy, a universal container designed to enable universal orchestration, effectively bridging the traditional divide between container runtime and orchestration layers. Ozy shares the same root namespace with the host, shares only minimal resources, and incurs negligible overhead. By providing full system-level isolation, Ozy allows multiple workloads to run concurrently on a single machine while supporting both offline and online container migrations. System evaluations demonstrate that Ozy can host up to 100 containers per machine with a per-container overhead as low as 1.5%, and online migrations within 10 milliseconds. Furthermore, we illustrate that integrating universal orchestration with Ozy can enhance the performance of prominent big data processing systems by up to 1.7 times. Ozy is built upon our recent enhancements to the Linux kernel and is intended to serve as the foundation for future Linux container distributions. Research at the Los Alamos National Laboratory's Quantum Hall Phase Diagram Group indicates that a reentrant, incompressible semiquantum crystal with 5/2 quasiparticles emerges in the 5/2 quantum Hall phase when the Landau level mismatch parameter is elevated. This reentrant regime extends toward higher power supply current, resulting in high strain and low conductivity. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy reveals that within the reentrant regime, the sample transitions from an incompressible semiquantum crystal to a metallic state characterized by gapped bulk excitations and propagating semiquantum crystal domain walls. Additionally, the study observes two distinct types of 5/2 quantum Hall incompressible semiquantum crystal phases: one driven by Landau level mismatch and another caused by strong interactions between the semiquantum crystal and the sample edges. These findings demonstrate that the 5/2 quantum Hall phase exhibits greater complexity than previously anticipated. By mapping the 5/2 quantum Hall phase diagram, our research offers new insights into the nature of this phase and establishes a foundation for future investigations into its critical phenomena. Astronomical black holes, specifically supermassive and primordially black holes (SPBH/PBH), are hypothesized to evaporate into cosmic radiation via their interaction with the universe. The Thakurta metric models the spacetime of such evading PBHs, incorporating the Grunberg radiation field. The stability of this metric was previously examined by Thakurta, who identified a critical point where the radiation field diminishes and the solution transitions to the Kerr metric; he argued that this critical radius defines the event horizon. This study revisits the evolution equations and the physical significance of that critical point. We demonstrate that the physics at this critical radius closely mirrors the behavior of an atomic system during the electron's fall from the first excited state to the ground state. Furthermore, we show that the frequency of radiation emitted by the Kerr solution beyond the critical point is approximately $10^{14}$ times higher than that inside it. Consequently, we conclude that cosmological black holes are not accurately represented by the Thakurta metric at the critical point, and therefore, the current LIGO-Virgo constraints on PBHs remain valid. Additionally, we explore the potential for using this metric to investigate the spacetime of other cosmic objects. Finally, the paper includes an appendix detailing the numerical results of our analysis. These findings may also be relevant to the study of Hawking radiation from black holes. Accretion of small particles onto large bodies is a critical mechanism in the evolution of planetary systems, yet its relationship with gas density fluctuations remains unclear. To investigate this, we developed a model that accounts for dust and gas density variations. Our results indicate that regions with higher dust density fluctuations significantly accelerate planetesimal formation. Furthermore, these planetesimals generate distinct gravitational imprints on the surrounding dust ring, which can be observed via ALMA. This model offers a means to explain the rapid assembly of planetesimals and provides fresh insights into planet formation, including the origin of gaps around young stars and the early development of planetary systems. It is widely recognized that statistical learning models are frequently maintained at sizes smaller than the number of training samples to ensure unique parameter estimation. In contrast, brain neural networks operate with vast numbers of parameters relative to the data, prompting the question of how such high overparameterization aids generalization. This paper investigates the mechanisms enabling generalization in large-scale models and its relationship to computational constraints. We contend that this relationship is complex: although large models can indeed generalize effectively, they may also lead researchers to draw misleading conclusions. Drawing on recent advances in non-convex optimization, we demonstrate how the minimization of large-scale models results in models that appear to perform significantly better than they actually do. Consequently, we emphasize the necessity of evaluating whether the optimal performance of large-scale models truly exceeds that of smaller ones. To address this, we introduce a practical approach for comparing large and small models, illustrated through examples on both synthetic tasks and established datasets. This proposed methodology is particularly relevant for machine learning research conducted on limited datasets and computational resources. Our findings reveal a trade-off between model expressivity and the ease of achieving good generalization. While large models can represent representations that small models cannot, they also exhibit significantly higher optimization barriers, rendering them more computationally challenging to optimize. This suggests that the advantages of large models are less pronounced than currently perceived, underscoring the value of smaller, more efficient alternatives. Finally, we illustrate the utility of this perspective in re-examining the benefits of extreme model sizes, including those found in transformers and biological systems. Specifically, we demonstrate that small neural networks can represent language models as effectively as much larger ones. These results provide a potential explanation for the parameter efficiency observed in neural language modeling and the language capabilities present in small brains. Overall, this work aims to foster a more nuanced understanding of the trade-offs between model size and performance. By doing so, it encourages the development of smaller models that achieve comparable results, thereby promoting more responsible research practices, reduced resource consumption, and greater accessibility in the field. Let $G$ be an infinite abelian group with rank 1. Suppose $A$ is a symmetric subset of $G$ such that the sumset $A + A$ contains a nontrivial Bohr set $B$. Then, the set $A$ must include a Bohr set $B'$ whose parameters are strictly better than those found in any Bohr set contained within $A$. This result holds true for all groups except $\mathbb{Q}^d$ and $\bigoplus_{i=1}^\infty \mathbb{Z}_2$. In each identified case, we can construct a subset $A$ such that $A + A$ contains a Bohr set, yet $A$ does not. Furthermore, for the specific case of $\bigoplus_{i=1}^\infty \mathbb{Z}_2$, we demonstrate the existence of a subset $A$ where $A + A$ includes a Bohr set $B$, yet $A$ fails to contain any Bohr set with parameters at least half of those in $B$. This resolves a question posed by Balog and Szemerédi. Finally, we provide a generalization of our primary theorem and its corresponding failure cases. Specifically, if the conditions of the theorem are met, then $A$ necessarily contains a Bohr set; however, if $A$ is infinite, it exists such that $A + A$ contains a Bohr set while $A$ itself contains none. These findings are applicable to groups where the rank is at least 1. Additionally, for the case of $\bigoplus_{i=1}^\infty \mathbb{Z}_2$, we establish that for any Bohr set $B$ contained in $A + A$, there exists a Bohr set $B'$ within $A$ possessing at least half the parameters of $B$. This confirms that the failure to contain such a set $B'$ is exclusive to the $\mathbb{Q}^d$ and $\bigoplus_{i=1}^\infty \mathbb{Z}_2$ scenarios. To achieve this, we introduce a variant of the Fourier transform and the associated Bohr rank that accommodates functions valued in $\bigoplus_{i=1}^\infty \mathbb{Z}_{p_i}$, where $\{p_i\}$ represents an arbitrary sequence of distinct primes. This study examines a dial-a-ride problem tailored for elderly individuals in a densely populated urban setting. Rather than focusing on minimizing travel distance, the primary goal is to reduce the total ride time, which encompasses waiting periods, driving durations, and passenger travel time. The model allows for partial service, permitting some elderly people to be left unserved as long as the total time—summing ride times for both seniors and non-seniors—remains within a specified limit. Numerical experiments were conducted to evaluate the proposed formulation. Additionally, a heuristic incorporating machine learning was developed; numerical results demonstrate that this approach outperforms a classical heuristic. Furthermore, collaborations with operators and service users enabled the collection of real-world data, including actual requests and routes, which were used to test the computational efficiency of the experiments. Finally, a pilot deployment of the machine learning-based heuristic with a partner company in Marseille yielded encouraging results. The paper concludes with a discussion on computing time and potential future research directions. The computational performance of the branch-and-cut algorithm was analyzed based on four key factors: the vehicle type, planning horizon length, budget constraint, and the percentage of seniors included in the request. Notably, reducing the number of seniors in the input significantly increases the computational power of the algorithm. Future research could explore dynamic problems and the potential for the heuristic to serve as a pre-processor for the branch-and-cut method. A Python library is available for reproducing the numerical experiments, and the authors welcome collaborations to develop a user interface for the algorithm. As multi-modal pre-trained models have advanced rapidly, researchers have increasingly focused on applying them to meta tasks. However, this approach often neglects the specific characteristics of individual tasks, resulting in sub-optimal performance. To address this, we introduce KUMM, a two-stage framework that integrates domain-specific knowledge into the pre-training process. In the first stage, a multi-modal pre-trained model undergoes fine-tuning alongside the extraction of multi-dimensional task-specific knowledge. In the second stage, this extracted knowledge is utilized to guide the pre-trained model, enabling it to better adapt to and comprehend the nuances of single-modal data within multi-modal contexts. Extensive experiments across eight e-commerce e-commerce sub-modal datasets demonstrate that KUMM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our analysis and visualization reveal the rich knowledge understood by our framework, highlighting its effectiveness and robustness. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/akimichi/KUMM.

Toxoplasma gondii (T. gondii) infection is known to cause neuroinflammation in the brains of both humans and animals. This study investigates whether T. gondii infection accelerates the onset of Alzheimer's disease (AD) by inducing chronic systemic inflammation. The research involved a longitudinal analysis of 1,000 subjects from the Cardiovascular Health Study (CHS), which collected data on T. gondii seropositivity, cognitive function, and brain atrophy. The findings reveal that individuals with T. gondii infection experience a faster rate of cognitive decline. Furthermore, atrophy in the medial temporal lobe shows a stronger correlation with cognitive decline than atrophy in the whole brain, suggesting that T. gondii-induced AD pathology may specifically target the medial temporal lobe. These results provide the first evidence linking T. gondii infection to AD pathogenesis, with T. gondii emerging as a potential risk factor for the disease. Additionally, the study underscores the value of well-designed longitudinal studies in elucidating risk factors for neurodegenerative conditions. This study introduces the detailed semantic intricacies of word and phrase semantics, which are crucial for effective language understanding. We propose a new model, the Interaction-based Recurrent Neural Network (I-RNN), which employs a two-layer recurrent architecture. The initial layer sequentially ingests words from a sentence, while the second layer iteratively processes pairs of a query's words and a context sentence's words. The I-RNN demonstrates superior performance on two widely used benchmarks: the ConceptNet 17 SemEval dataset and the MS MARCO dataset. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis of both the generated semantic representations and the I-RNN model architecture to enhance transparency. We contend that our approach not only achieves state-of-the-art results in comprehending word and phrase semantics but also offers deeper insights into the underlying mechanisms of semantic representation and the generation process. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/zhongyuan1992/I-RNN.

In metals exhibiting strong electron-electron interactions, the spin-orbit coupling (SOC) experienced by individual electrons can be significantly amplified. This occurs because the SOC-driven spin-flip transitions are facilitated by the many-body Hamiltonian, which incorporates an effective spin-dependent exchange field. This phenomenon is illustrated through the correlated topological Kondo insulator Bi$_2$Se$_3$_-Sb$_2$Te$_3$. This study employs a self-consistent many-body perturbation theory to analyze how SOC is enhanced in a correlated metal. Within a three-band model, we demonstrate that many-body effects can increase SOC by two to three orders of magnitude, contingent upon the magnitude of the band gap. Furthermore, we establish that this SOC amplification is intrinsically linked to the emergence of a topological band gap, a finding supported by both many-body self-energy calculations and DFT+DMFT studies. Finally, we illustrate how the strengthened SOC manifests in spin-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. Specifically, we show that the self-energy can be self-consistently derived from spin-resolved photoemission data, enabling the measurement of the self-energy's magnitude and sign. This capability is crucial for investigating the fundamental interactions between strong electron correlations and spin-orbit coupling. Additionally, we observe that the self-energy can exhibit a sign change, a feature that can be attributed to the self-consistent self-energy method. We introduce a novel dark sector featuring metastable conformal dynamics, which serves as a promising candidate for conformal shadow matter. This matter could constitute the majority of cold dark matter, with its decay into the visible sector occurring on astrophysically relevant timescales. Our preferred model accounts for both gravitationally generated warm dark matter and dark matter annihilations observed in dwarf galaxy rotation curves. Additionally, the model predicts a small cold dark matter component, alongside potential signals detectable in direct detection experiments and the cosmic gamma-ray background. We also explore the implications of our findings for collider phenomenology. This framework offers a viable alternative to previously proposed dark matter models based on conformal shadow matter. Furthermore, it resolves the conflict between constraints from dwarf galaxy annihilation data and those derived from structure formation. Finally, our proposal suggests that warm dark matter may exist, a concept that contrasts sharply with the traditional view of dark matter as entirely cold. Consequently, investigating the nature of dark matter through cosmological observables remains crucial for determining whether it is cold, warm, or hot. In this context, our work provides the first concrete evidence for a dark matter candidate with a mass exceeding several GeV that is both conformal and warm. We have made public all code and parameter sets necessary to reproduce our results. Additionally, we have released a user-friendly interface, implemented in Python, that enables rapid generation of gamma-ray spectra and dark matter density profiles for the simplest version of our model. This tool is accessible at https://github.com/ConformalShadowMatter/ConformalShadowMatter. We anticipate that our approach will inspire further research into conformal dynamics within dark sector models. Specifically, we propose that detailed investigations of gamma-ray spectra and dwarf galaxy rotation curves could uncover new physics in the dark sector and help establish the fundamental parameters of these conformal candidates. Enhanced sampling methods in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are crucial for investigating the conformational dynamics of biomolecules. Although these techniques have been extensively applied to investigate the folding of proteins and nucleic acids, their potential on rigid substrates remains largely unexplored. In this study, we demonstrate that simulation enhanced sampling on a rigid substrate unexpectedly yields profound biological insights into the topology and topology transitions of DNA. Specifically, we show that simulating DNA on a rigid substrate within the canonical ensemble allows for the observation of DNA conformations that are statistically impossible under standard MD simulation conditions. Consequently, we conclude that simulations performed on a rigid substrate within the canonical ensemble can uncover data-rich, topology-specific phenomena regarding the topology and topology transitions of DNA. Furthermore, we illustrate that this approach enables the discovery of new data regarding the interaction between DNA and small molecules. Overall, our findings indicate that utilizing a rigid substrate represents a viable and practical strategy for applying enhanced sampling to DNA, offering novel biological and chemical insights that are unattainable through the application of these techniques in bulk. This work provides a framework for simulating DNA topology and topology transitions in the canonical ensemble, thereby advancing the field of topology-specific MD simulation science. Finally, we show that this methodology can be applied to various nucleic acid topologies, including supercoiled DNA, trefoil DNA, and catenanes. To facilitate the application of this approach, we have developed a Python-based code named "TopoEnsemble" (available at https://github.com/TopoEnsemble/TopoEnsemble), which calculates the statistical mechanical partition function and the probability of topology-specific observables for DNA on a rigid substrate using the GROMACS MD simulation package. TopoEnsemble is an open-source tool that can be seamlessly integrated into any MD simulation workflow. This advancement allows for the quantification of topology-specific phenomena in DNA, thereby enabling enhanced sampling on a rigid substrate to provide a wealth of topology-specific observables for DNA. We anticipate that these findings will significantly impact the fields of topology-specific MD simulation science and topology-specific MD simulation enhancement sampling science. Furthermore, our results may advance the fields of topology-specific drug discovery and topology-specific DNA sequencing. The Arithmetic Normal Form represents a significant advancement over the standard arithmetic encoding method proposed by R. Davis in 1949. This encoding scheme achieves two primary objectives: first, it enables the representation of any real number within the closed interval $[0,1]$ as a finite sequence of digits from a specified base $b$; second, when applied to joint distributions, it maintains correlation structures between random variables much more effectively than conventional encoding methods. By employing the Shannon entropy $H(X)$ to determine the distribution of bases $b$ across a set of codewords, the resulting entropy $H_X$ can be calculated. The ANS encoding scheme proved effective in my PhD thesis, demonstrating superiority over other methods regarding both time and space complexity. This paper presents the computational outcomes of utilizing the ANS encoding scheme for the arithmetic computation of $H_X$. The study focuses on $n$-tuples of random variables $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$, where each $X_i$ is defined over a finite set of cardinality $k$. The research examines various configurations of $n$ and $k$, specifically analyzing scenarios where $n$ is small and $k$ is large, as well as cases where both $n$ and $k$ are moderate. Furthermore, the ANS encoding scheme was applied to two real-world datasets: the UCI Wine dataset, which consists of 178 samples with 13 attributes, and the MNIST dataset, comprising handwritten digits. The results indicate that the ANS encoding scheme is effective for both synthetic and real-world datasets. Finally, the paper discusses the effectiveness of ANS encoding in light of the inverse entropy decoding scheme, $\text{InverseEntropyDecoding}(H_X)$, which allows for the recovery of the original $n$-tuple $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ from its ANS-encoded representation. This approach successfully recovers the original sample along with its assigned wine class or handwritten digit class. The dielectric properties of cement-based construction materials have garnered significant interest due to their potential for structural health monitoring. However, a comprehensive understanding of the dielectric behavior of concrete remains elusive, largely because the dielectric properties of the aggregate component are not well understood. While the dielectric characteristics of pure pore solution have been studied, there is still a lack of detailed data regarding those of the aggregate solution. This study investigates the frequency-dependent dielectric response of solutions found in both aggregate and cementitious matrices, as well as the resulting heterogeneous cement-aggregate mixtures, across a temperature range of 20 to 60 °C. These solutions were analyzed using an open-ended coaxial probe technique combined with ion-exchange chromatography. The dielectric frequency response of the pore solutions in cementitious mixtures was well-described by the Debye model, with parameters showing strong correlations to pH value and temperature. The spectral characteristics of the heterogeneous mixtures under investigation were interpreted using the series Debye model, which accounts for the series arrangement of aggregate and cementitious solutions. This model demonstrated accuracy across the entire measurement frequency spectrum, with series resistances for both solutions exhibiting clear dependencies on both pH and temperature. Furthermore, the resistance of the cementitious mixture solution showed greater sensitivity to changes in temperature and pH compared to the aggregate solution. Finally, the resistance of the cementitious matrix exhibited the highest sensitivity to variations in both the cement and aggregate solutions, with the cementitious solution consistently exhibiting the higher resistance value. These findings provide a foundation for future research aimed at developing methods to quantify the internal condition of concrete structures based on their dielectric properties. Furthermore, they enable the interpretation of dielectric measurements obtained from real concrete, which contains both cementitious and aggregate phases. Specifically, the study demonstrates that dielectric measurements are more sensitive to chemical changes in the cementitious solution than in the aggregate solution. This suggests that, in the event of chemical attacks, dielectric measurements could serve as an early warning system to detect deterioration in the cementitious matrix before it affects the aggregate. Additionally, the research indicates that dielectric measurements are more sensitive to chemical changes in the cementitious matrix when the cement is highly alkaline, such as in high-performance concrete, compared to normal concrete. This is because the cementitious matrix in high-performance concrete is generally less permeable, making it more susceptible to chemical changes in the pore solution. This work provides a review of recent theoretical findings concerning massive-heavy hadronic molecules. We begin by outlining the fundamental properties of molecular binding, followed by an analysis of the quantum numbers, sizes, strong decay widths, and experimental signatures of these candidates. Subsequently, we examine the theoretical frameworks used to construct binding potentials within the chromo-magnetic interaction and the one-gluon exchange potential. We then present calculations of the binding energies and wave functions for these states using the variational method. Finally, we summarize our conclusions and propose directions for future research. This study extends the physical scope of hadronic molecules to include massive-heavy systems and employs straightforward theoretical techniques to substantiate the feasibility of such molecules. Furthermore, we demonstrate that chromo-magnetic interactions can bind these states more effectively than one-gluon exchange potentials. We also note that two chromo-magnetic molecules, potentially a tetraquark and an antitetraquark, exhibit degenerate binding energies. The inclusion of chromo-magnetic interactions in theoretical models is essential for achieving a realistic understanding of these exotic hadrons. Our findings indicate that these states are bound by gluons, with strong decay widths resulting from diquark-antidiquark annihilation. We emphasize the necessity of experimental investigations to verify the existence of these predicted states. We have structured this report to serve as a comprehensive resource on the theoretical underpinnings of hadronic molecules, offering detailed derivations alongside our results. This report is intended to assist researchers in advancing the theoretical field of exotic hadronic molecules. Additionally, we have omitted detailed discussions of the meson-baryon molecule, as this topic is addressed in a separate paper. Overall, this work represents the first study to calculate binding energies for massive-heavy hadronic molecules, and we believe it will significantly contribute to the theoretical development of the field. Our goal is to provide readers with all relevant information regarding the theoretical aspects of these exotic hadrons. We have included all necessary theoretical details to facilitate research in this area. This paper is designed to be read as a complete resource on the theoretical side of hadronic molecules, offering thorough explanations of the underlying concepts. We have endeavored to present all relevant information clearly and concisely, ensuring that readers can gain a full understanding of the theoretical framework governing these exotic states. Our intention is to equip readers with a solid foundation for future research in this field. We have included all pertinent theoretical details to support readers in their own investigations. The Lyman-$\alpha$ forest serves as a valuable tool for cosmological studies, yet its direct application remains underutilized. We introduce a technique for extracting cosmological parameters by examining the three-dimensional correlations of Lyman-$\alpha$ forest absorption. This approach enables the deduction of cosmological parameters without relying on large-scale structure simulations. By analyzing the auto-correlation of the forest absorption distribution, we can determine the baryon density ($\Omega_b$) and the mean metallicity of the intergalactic medium ($\langle Z \rangle$). The cross-correlation between the forest and the quasar sample reveals the distance-redshift relation, which helps constrain the Hubble constant ($H_0$) and the baryon-to-dark matter ratio. Furthermore, the cross-correlation between absorbers identifies the redshift at which the intergalactic medium transitions from neutral to ionized, known as the percolation redshift. Finally, the forest auto-correlation provides constraints on the baryon density. This work demonstrates the direct extraction of the baryon density and mean intergalactic metallicity from the three-dimensional correlation of quasar samples utilizing the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, thereby opening a new pathway for cosmological research. This paper introduces a novel, vision-based Human-Swarm Interaction (HSI) method designed for a Human-Robot Team (HRT) vision subsystem. In this decentralized approach, each robot independently and concurrently captures and processes the operator's hand gestures and forearm positioning. These individual perceptions are then integrated to achieve a precise overall estimation of the gesture. The system relies on the interaction between human arms and forearms, which are covered by high-contrast colored sleeves to facilitate reliable detection by the robot's vision module. By leveraging state-of-the-art hand pose estimation and deep learning techniques, the HSI framework translates these gestures into discrete commands that the swarm can execute. To evaluate the proposed solution, we conducted extensive experiments using a dataset of real-world hand gestures involving two operators and three different arm configurations. Our results demonstrate that this approach enables reliable and precise HSI among multiple robots, thereby significantly advancing the reliability and robustness of HRI and HRT. The code and the gesture collection will be made available online. Furthermore, we have successfully tested the proposed solution on a quadrotor swarm, and we will present video demonstrations of the HSI solution in action. Finally, we will discuss the limitations of this approach and suggest potential avenues for future research. The proliferation of smartphone-based digital microscopy has enhanced both the accessibility and efficiency of clinical cell analysis. However, manually examining cells in peripheral blood smears or bone marrow samples remains a labor-intensive and error-prone process. Although current neural network models can automate cell typing, they often struggle with low confidence when encountering atypical cell forms. To address this, we introduce a multi-model fusion system designed to boost the accuracy of cell classification. In this approach, multiple neural network models trained on distinct architectures process the same input, and their outputs are aggregated via an ensemble method to determine the final classification. We evaluated the performance of seven individual cell classification models and four ensemble configurations using 1,300 images containing 13 cell types. The results indicate that model ensembles significantly outperform single models, raising the average classification accuracy from 71.5% to 82.1% and increasing the proportion of correctly classified rare cell types from 42.9% to 66.7%. Furthermore, the most effective ensemble configuration utilizes seven different neural network models, comprising three convolutional neural networks, three recurrent neural networks, and one autoencoder. This study demonstrates the efficacy of multi-model ensembles in improving overall and rare cell type classification accuracy, offering a promising solution for the automated analysis of blood cells. The source code and data are accessible at: https://github.com/DeepHealth/CellNet-Ensemble. Keywords: blood cell classification, deep learning, neural networks, ensemble methods. Counterdiabatic (CD) protocols have emerged as effective tools for designing quantum operations, yet their high control-order demands often hinder practical implementation. This study presents a variable CD protocol tailored for the two-dimensional Hubbard model, utilizing only two local variable fields alongside a standard LD driving field. Variations in the first control field reduce the LD field's dimensionality, while the second control field further constrains the system's dynamics. The CD Lagrangian is constructed based on these two control fields, with its value evaluated under periodic boundary conditions. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed protocol achieves near-perfect ground-state initialization across a broad spectrum of interaction strengths. Furthermore, an analytical formula is derived to determine the optimal configuration of the two control fields. Finally, the study investigates the impact of control field noise on quantum performance, revealing that the protocol remains robust against noise. These findings provide a foundation for developing efficient variable CD protocols applicable to other relevant models. The source code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/zhongqiangwang/CD_Hubbard}. Additionally, this work is supported by the Computational Science Center at Fuzhou University, with details available at \url{http://www.csc.fzu.edu.cn/}. Source code and publication details can also be found at \url{https://github.com/zhongqiangwang/CD_Hubbard}. Additionally, the Computational Science Center, Fuzhou University, \url{http://www.csc.fzu.edu.cn/}.

This study introduces a high-dynamic-range (HDR) tone-mapping approach that presagates local discoloration in a scene using a two-stage method. The initial stage employs a tone-mapping operator grounded in color temperature, which adjusts the overall tint by blending the contributions of a warm color channel and a cool color channel based on a calculated ratio. The subsequent stage applies a non-linear contrast adjustment to each individual channel. Evaluations demonstrate that this technique outperforms current methods in preserving both color fidelity and texture details within highly contrasting regions of HDR images. Furthermore, the approach is computationally efficient, requiring less than 10 milliseconds to process a 1920x1080 image on a standard CPU. To our knowledge, a color-temperature-based tone-mapping strategy has not been previously explored for visual enhancement. The proposed method is implemented in OpenCV and is available as an independent C++ library at https://github.com/SeokhoonLee/ColorTemperatureOperator. The accompanying paper provides a tutorial on developing your own color-temperature operator. Both C++ and Python versions of the code are included in the supplementary materials. Additionally, the source code is hosted on the first author's GitHub account at https://github.com/SeokhoonLee. The tutorial can be accessed here: https://github.com/SeokhoonLee/ToneMappingTutorial. Various color temperature examples are available at https://github.com/SeokhoonLee/ColorTemperatureOperator/tree/master/examples. The tutorial is also accessible at: https://github.com/SeokhoonLee/ToneMappingTutorial. The paper itself is available at: https://github.com/SeokhoonLee/ToneMappingTutorial.
