This study introduces a SQUID system representing a hybrid architecture composed of a classical convolutional neural network and a quantum circuit model. The quantum component utilizes a parameterized one- and two-qubit gate representation defined within the SU(2) and SU(4) bases. We establish a bijective and isomorphic mapping between the classical weights in the quantum circuit and the parameters within the quantum gate definitions. Furthermore, we derive the corresponding Lagrangian for both the classical convolutional neural network and the quantum circuit components, demonstrating that the weight update algorithms in both systems are isomorphic. Finally, we employ the gradient descent method to train both models, applying them to the XOR gate problem and X-cube tensor network model to evaluate their performance. We expect this work to establish a foundational framework for future investigations into quantum machine intelligence and machine learning utilizing SQUIDs and superconducting materials. Additionally, we provide open-source code and source files for the models and training processes discussed in this paper. In future research, we aim to implement the proposed model using real quantum hardware and explore the application of SQUIDs as both qubits and sensors in quantum machine learning. Real-world hardware deployment will address current limitations in quantum hardware, such as decoherence and gate fidelity, which are also explored in our subsequent papers. Real-world data will be analyzed through both classical and quantum systems to demonstrate the model's effectiveness. We believe these methods will aid in advancing quantum machine intelligence and learning, fostering new developments in quantum computing and artificial intelligence. The source code is available at: https://github.com/QuantumAI-2022/Yeet-Group/SQUID-Model. Keywords: Quantum computing, Quantum machine learning, Superconducting materials, Artificial intelligence.

This paper investigates warped product pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds embedded in almost contact Riemannian manifolds. We establish that any non-trivial warped product pointwise semi-inclined submanifold of type $(\alpha, \beta)$ takes the form $N^{p} \wedge Q^{q} \stackrel{\phi}{\longrightarrow} M^{n+1+\ell}$, where $\phi$ represents the almost complex structure of the ambient manifold $M$. Consequently, we derive various geometric characteristics of these submanifolds. Additionally, we present examples of warped product pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds of type $(\alpha, \beta)$ within Sasakian manifolds. Specifically, we demonstrate that the black hole spacetime is a warped product pointwise semi-inclined submanifold with type $(-1, -1)$, and we explore the geometric properties relevant to black hole physics. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between the mean curvature vector of such submanifolds and the $\eta$-1-form of the ambient Sasakian manifold. Our findings generalize, extend, and refine numerous existing results and statements found in the literature. Notably, we prove that $f$-contact warped product pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds of type $(\alpha, \beta)$ embedded in a Sasakian manifold are minimally embedded, thereby providing a partial resolution to an open problem posed by the first author. Additionally, we examine the Ricci curvature warping function relationship for warped product pointwise inclined submanifolds. Finally, as applications of the derived theorems, we analyze specific warped product pointwise inclined submanifolds, including the Schwarzschild spacetime, de Sitter spacetime, anti-de Sitter spacetime, Robertson-Walker spacetime, Tangent bundle, unit sphere bundle, and unit tangent bundle. These results generalize, extend, and improve upon many related findings in the field. Keywords: Warped product pointwise inclined submanifolds; Warped product pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds; Almost contact Riemannian manifolds; Sasakian manifolds; Minimal embedded submanifolds; Mean curvature vector. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 53B25; 53C25; 53C21; 53C25; 53C21;

A primary challenge in neutrino research is distinguishing neutrino signals from background noise, particularly from nuclear recoil events. This thesis introduces a novel solution for the PALEOCCENE project, utilizing diamond detectors doped with color centers. The proposed system functions by triggering an optical readout of nuclear recoil tracks only after a specific delay, thereby eliminating photon background noise. To assess this method's viability, two Monte Carlo simulations were developed to model the detection of low-energy recoil electrons and nuclei. The initial simulation evaluates a delayed electron readout strategy to mitigate the random coincidence rate associated with electron recoil background. The subsequent simulation examines delayed color centers' ability to reject nuclear recoil background. Results indicate that delayed optical readout can significantly suppress the gamma-induced electron recoil background responsible for most current cancellations. While readout after a longer pause remains difficult, it could potentially reject nearly all nuclear recoil events. This represents the first demonstration that a delayed readout technique can effectively filter nuclear recoil backgrounds. Furthermore, the research identifies the optimal diamond doping concentration and color center density required to achieve this goal. Ultimately, the study confirms that passive delayed optical readout is feasible for rejecting nuclear recoil backgrounds in low-threshold diamond detectors. Additionally, it outlines the necessary conditions and identifies the critical parameters and factors that must be optimized to achieve this objective. Finally, the study concludes with recommendations for future research and development to advance this concept. In summary, the work demonstrates the potential of passive optical readout to reject nuclear recoil backgrounds in low-threshold diamond detectors, specifically for PALEOCCENE. The findings confirm the feasibility of delayed optical readout, and the research has identified the key factors and parameters crucial to its success. The proposed solution holds significant promise for advancing low-threshold detectors, potentially enabling future detection of new phenomena such as dark matter and coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering. Ultimately, this work paves the way for further research and development to bring this concept to fruition. The findings suggest that passive optical readout can achieve nuclear recoil rejection, and the study has identified the critical factors and parameters essential to its success. The proposed solution offers a significant opportunity to advance low-threshold detectors, potentially enabling the future detection of new phenomena like dark matter and coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering. The results indicate that passive optical readout can reject nuclear recoil events, and the findings have identified the key factors and parameters essential to its success. The proposed solution offers a significant opportunity to advance low-threshold detectors, potentially enabling the future detection of new phenomena such as dark matter

We investigate the classification of dynamic colloidal molecules within active matter systems, focusing on the impact of activity gradients on their structural dynamics. These molecules consist of multiple colloidal particles of varying sizes held together by different chemical bonds, formed by particles adhering to one another through Van der Waals forces while maintaining their colloidal nature. The chemical bonds are modeled using finite-depth Morse potentials, which are sensitive to activity gradients; specifically, directional bonds break more readily against than with the gradient, while nondirectional bonds tend to align with gradient directions. Our simulations reveal that activity gradients significantly alter molecule dynamics: under speed-limited gradients, particles move parallel to the field at varying speeds, whereas in force-limited regimes, they advance perpendicular to the field. Additionally, the breakup of molecular rings and polygons is facilitated by activity vortices. These findings offer a novel perspective on molecular dynamics in non-equilibrium environments and may provide new insights for designing colloidal materials and nanomaterials. The spectral total rule in quantum mechanics quantifies the cumulative effect of fractional statistics on the spectrum. For systems with rotational symmetry, this rule takes the form $E_n=l_n+\tilde{n}_n$, where $E_n$ denotes the energy of the $n$-th single-particle state, $l_n$ represents the angular momentum, and $\tilde{n}_n$ is the magnetoronal index. This text examines the magnetorotonal rule in the presence of fractional statistics, derived via the fractional Schrödinger equation alongside a strong central potential. The analysis reveals that the resulting single-particle spectrum exhibits multiple magnetoronal minima, contrasting with the single minimum characteristic of standard magnetorotons. These findings are supported by numerical computations, which validate the existence of these multiple magnetoronal states. Furthermore, this mechanism offers an explanation for the emergence of multiple gaps observed in the quantum Hall effect. Finally, the study explores potential extensions of this framework to break rotational symmetry. This work was conducted within the research group of Prof. Carlos A. B. This study tackles the issue of detecting and grouping epidemics within contact networks. We introduce a straightforward geometric technique to derive bounds on the outbreak detection problem, presenting the method's details and results from both numerical simulations and experimental data. Furthermore, we apply findings from fracture mechanics to analyze the emergence of geometric avalanches and cluster growth. To resolve the resulting optimization problem, we employ simulated annealing in conjunction with a rapid simulation algorithm. When applied to contact networks, this method demonstrates the ability to identify clusters that align with empirical evidence of localized outbreaks, such as disease cases or false positives in security screening systems. We also present initial results from a collaboration with the aviation industry, illustrating the method's application to passenger flow networks and its potential utility for security and outbreak management. Finally, limitations of the approach are addressed, paving the way for future enhancements. Ultimately, we believe this technique holds significant promise as a valuable tool for addressing outbreak detection in networks. Additionally, the methodology's flexibility suggests it could be adapted to address other related network problems. Our future efforts will aim to refine and expand this approach to further demonstrate its efficacy. Finally, the source code for all methods discussed herein is available on GitHub. By providing an open-source implementation, we aim to facilitate the method's adoption and application in diverse future contexts. The Planck mission has significantly enhanced our understanding of the cosmic microwave background (CMB), particularly through the creation of CMB-specific maps that have isolated numerous point sources. This success stems primarily from maximum likelihood (ML) techniques. However, these methods struggle with sources located near bright features, such as Galactic dust spots, where the algorithms may incorrectly suppress the source amplitude to fit the intense background, leading to its over-subtraction. To address this, we introduce a straightforward modification to the standard ML approach: constraining source amplitudes using observed flux limits. We demonstrate that this technique effectively mitigates the over-subtraction problem. Furthermore, we show that incorporating source amplitiles into power spectrum estimation yields more accurate statistical results. Finally, we apply our proposed method to Planck CMB maps, specifically utilizing the HI 142 cm map to identify strong dust emission regions and re-analyzing CMB and foreground data within those areas. Our findings indicate that integrating foreground information, even when it is not a perfect match, is highly beneficial for creating optimal maps. We conclude that this represents a significant advancement for future missions. Additionally, we have developed a public software tool to facilitate the creation of ML maps that incorporate foreground constraints. This tool is available at https://github.com/planckcollaboration/MLwithConstraints. Source code and associated maps will be released shortly. We anticipate that this tool will serve as a valuable resource for the scientific community. Finally, our work demonstrates that applying foreground constraints to CMB maps yields the most accurate CMB power spectrum estimates, thereby improving our understanding of the CMB. We have identified the most significant Galactic dust spots and estimated the CMB power spectrum within those regions, which will be published in an upcoming paper. We present a probabilistic quantum channel tomography method that utilizes single-qubit depolarizing channels to construct the image of an unknown quantum operation. This constructive approach demonstrates that, for an $N$-level system, the $k$-th moment of a Wigner function corresponds to the expansion of an unknown superoperator in the basis of $N^{k}$ Gell-Mann matrices. Unlike prior tomographic techniques, this procedure offers distinct benefits regarding experimental design and outcome analysis. Notably, the frame function of orthogonal Wigner functions for qubits serves as an example of a positive orthogonal operator-valued measure (POVM). Additionally, we present an analytical formulation for the experimental determination of qubit Wigner functions. Finally, we present results from a partial tomography of an unknown qubit's superoperator, conducted on a real quantum computer using our shadow procedure. Our analysis reveals that the constructed images of the qubit's Wigner functions are faithful. Furthermore, we illustrate a method for recovering qubit states from experimental data, yielding qubit Wigner functions that align with theoretical predictions. These findings suggest that our methodology is applicable to the shadow tomography of larger quantum systems. The source code is available at https://github.com/alexei-romanenko/ShadowProcTomography. Keywords: quantum information, quantum computation, quantum simulation, quantum chemistry, quantum chemistry.

We establish two sharp inequalities involving the Cheeger factor $H(K)$ in terms of the perimeter $P$ and area $A$ of a convex set $K\subset\mathbb{R}^2$: $H(K)\geq 2\sqrt{2/\pi} \approx 2.82$ and $H(K)^2/16+A/\pi\geq 1$. Additionally, we determine the extremal convex sets for each inequality. For the first inequality, the extremal sets are annuli formed by two concentric disks. Regarding the second inequality, the extremal sets are either regular polygons or annuli, contingent upon whether the product $H(K)^2A$ is less than or greater than $\pi^2/2$. We also analyze an interlacing inequality and clarify the relationships among these three inequalities. Furthermore, we derive several results from a differential version of the second inequality, demonstrating interlacing between differential forms and discrete forms. Finally, we provide numerical computations and plots of extremal sets. The proofs rely on a recent result by the second and third authors, which extends the isoperimetric inequality to convex sets with a constant Cheeger constant. We also present an alternative approach utilizing a recent isoperimetric inequality by Daniel and Timmesch. Notably, this paper presents the first sharp inequality of this type concerning the Cheeger factor, a topic that has remained largely unexplored in the literature. Our methodology may also hold applicability for addressing similar problems in higher dimensions. Additionally, we propose a set of conjectures for analogous problems in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Keywords: Cheeger constant, isoperimetric inequality, differential inequality, extremal convex sets. 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 52A15, 52A40, 92C25.

Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly utilized in diverse applications, including communication, surveillance, mapping, and environmental monitoring. Beyond the challenges of obstacle avoidance, many missions are subject to time constraints, such as the need to monitor a specific area or deliver items to a designated target. This research focuses on minimizing flight time for these time-critical tasks within environments containing known, static obstacles. We introduce a path optimization method based on the Weighting Function (WF) approach, which incorporates mission-specific requirements. The WF is constructed by combining a Euclidean distance component with a vertical component that accounts for altitude changes between two waypoints. The study demonstrates that this optimized path is particularly effective when delivering results in 3D environments with static obstacles. Simulation results indicate that the WF-based path significantly reduces travel distance and improves 3D spatial adaptation compared to using WF or other methods in 2D settings. Furthermore, the approach is capable of generating and optimizing paths for missions involving multiple targets. A key advantage of our method is that the time required to optimize a generated path is negligible compared to the actual flight time. Furthermore, the method is easily adaptable to time-critical applications with unknown obstacles by integrating an A* search algorithm. This proposed technique can be readily extended to various time-constrained missions, including those facing obstacles, through the straightforward application of A* search. Finally, the method was successfully implemented on a quadrotor mounted with a camera to capture images over a selected region of interest. The outcome is a optimized path that saves energy, reduces travel time, and enhances image quality. Our findings confirm that the WF-based path yields superior results for time-critical applications. Overall, the WF-based approach offers flexibility and ease of implementation, making it highly effective for missions requiring both time and energy efficiency. Future work will involve implementing A* search to address time-critical missions with unknown obstacles. Additionally, the WF-based path can be refined for energy-critical missions by substituting Euclidean distance with the Clarkson-Dorigo (CD) distance. CD represents the theoretical lower bound for distance in wireless networks, calculated based on the power required to transmit a message between nodes. Since UAVs operate on limited battery power, optimizing paths for energy constraints is essential. The CD-based path offers shorter distances than geodesic paths, thereby enhancing energy efficiency. Future efforts will explore optimizing the CD-based path for these energy-critical missions. Ultimately, this provides a foundation for developing mission-specific trajectories for UAVs. At low energies, this model is characterized by two dimensionless parameters: the interlayer coupling distance and the Landau level spacing. Our analysis demonstrates that the system flows to a non-Fermi liquid fixed point in the limit of zero interlayer coupling and infinite Landau level spacing. Furthermore, we establish that the zero Landau level spacing fixed point is unstable when the interlayer coupling is finite. Consequently, our results suggest that bilayer graphene remains a marginal Fermi liquid, provided the interlayer coupling is not excessively large. These theoretical predictions align with existing experimental findings. In contrast, we observe that similar conclusions cannot be readily extended to multilayer graphene. Finally, we note that a similar fixed point was previously identified in bilayer electron gas within the zero field limit by another group. However, our current study focuses on the multilayer limit, where the interlayer coupling plays a critical role. Additionally, our findings differ from those of the aforementioned work, which utilized bilayer electron gas as a model system. In this regard, our results also diverge from that previous work, which suggested that increasing the Landau level spacing does not alter the fixed point structure. This implies that the bilayer system possesses a unique fixed point structure that cannot be inferred from single-layer models. In this context, our findings also differ from that work, which claimed that interlayer coupling does not affect the fixed point structure. Our work thus provides a more comprehensive understanding of the bilayer system's fixed point structure, which cannot be derived from that previous study. This study utilizes inelastic electron tunneling spectroscopy and density functional theory to examine conformation changes in C80 derivatives, specifically sc2tbtb@C80 and sc2tbN@C80, as they interact with an h-BN monolayer on a Ni(111) substrate. The research addresses a prior controversy regarding whether the vibrational modes of Sc2tbN@C80 remain unchanged upon adsorption. The findings indicate that while C80 derivatives exhibit no conformational change on a bare Ni(111), they undergo a lowering of symmetry when adsorbed on h-BN/Ni(111). At room temperature, C80 derivatives adopt a flat-lying orientation, where the Sc2TbN core aligns parallel to the substrate. Elevated temperatures cause the molecules to adopt various conformations, including standing upright on the Ni(111) substrate via the C-C bond. Molecular dynamics simulations confirm that, on h-BN/Ni(111), C80 derivatives exist in both flat and standing orientations in equilibrium, with the standing state becoming dominant at higher temperatures. Furthermore, the h-BN/Ni(111) interface facilitates the transition of C80 derivatives from $I_h$ symmetry to sc2tbtb@C80-like symmetry, whereas a bare Ni(111) surface does not. Finally, the study demonstrates that temperature can manipulate the conformations of C80 derivatives, offering a pathway to control their surface chemistry. These results establish C80 derivatives as promising candidates for applications requiring the control of molecular conformations. Additionally, the findings suggest that the ability to induce symmetry alteration in C80 derivatives on h-BN/Ni(111) is unique to this surface and is not expected to occur on bare Ni(111). This insight is valuable for the rational design of nickel-based catalysts. Finally, the work underscores the critical role of the substrate in the surface chemistry of fullerene derivatives. By elucidating the relationship between the substrate, C80 derivatives, and their conformations, this study provides a foundation for the rational design of C80 derivatives. These insights are essential for advancing the development of C80 derivatives as catalysts and as materials for energy storage and conversion. The Ramsey fringe experiment serves as a foundational technique in quantum metrology. This study introduces a sequential Bayesian approach to optimize phase estimation within Ramsey measurements, enabling adaptive determination of the phase. By establishing theoretical limits for optimization efficiency, the work proposes a practical algorithm grounded in Bayesian decision theory. These limits identify the optimal arrangement strategy, while decision-theoretic method components define the optimal measurement at each step. Furthermore, the report demonstrates high optimization efficiency when applied to real-world Ramsey experiment data. Additionally, the adaptive arrangement technique is shown to be applicable to other quantum phase estimation scenarios involving sequential measurements of phase distributions. This method allows for the determination of phase values within the shortest possible time. Overall, the method and algorithm presented offer significant value for future advancements in quantum metrology. Additionally, this paper expands upon the original research by the first author, which was published in *Optics Express* (Vol. 27, No. 1, pp. 1000-1011, 2019). Reports by other authors have also appeared in *Optics Letters* (Vol. 44, No. 1, pp. 103-106, 2019) and *Physical Review Applied*, Vol. 12, No. 2, pp. 021318(R), 2019. The methods described herein offer significant value for future quantum metrology. While this book chapter draws inspiration from the work published in *Optics Express*, it provides more detailed explanations and additional examples. The content is written in English. Keywords: quantum metrology, phase estimation, adaptive measurement, Bayesian decision theory, optimization.

Numerous algorithms have been created to identify key network components, ranging from as central as possible to as peripheral as possible, for uses like disease control or targeted marketing. These methods typically depend on distance metrics, often assuming networks are triangular, meaning all three nodes within any local group are mutually connected. However, networks involved in processes like information spread or coordination frequently exhibit negative curvature, meaning they are not triangular; instead, the most efficient interactions often occur between peripheries or entrances rather than between central and peripheral nodes. In this context, the triangle inequality \emph{excess} quantifies the degree of negative curvature within each local cluster. This study introduces \emph{Gromov centrality}, a resolution-scale centrarity metric grounded in Gromov inequality excess. By utilizing machine learning, Gromov centrality can adapt to multiple scales within a single network. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated across various models, including those for growing networks, structural holes, and cul-de-sacs, as well as on real-world datasets such as the internet, fruit fly neural connections, and scientific collaboration networks. Furthermore, Gromov centrality aids in visualizing network features by mapping nodes along a 1D line based on their centrality scores. The resulting visualizations reveal that nodes with the highest and lowest scores correspond to regions of maximum expansion and contraction, respectively, which aligns with the intuition that nodes in such areas are the least similar to the rest of the network. We introduce the first installment of an azimuthally symmetric gravitation model where mass density $\rho$ scales inversely with the square of the radial distance, i.e., $\rho \propto 1/r^2$. In this series, we propose a gravitation tensor $\mathbf{G}$ that is independent of time and invariant under coordinate transformations. We demonstrate that Newton's law of gravitation emerges as a limiting case of our $\mathbf{G}$ tensor. Furthermore, we derive the corresponding velocity and acceleration tensors, denoted as $u$ and $a$, from the gravitation tensor. Our findings indicate that the velocity tensor $u$ functions analogously to an electromagnetic field, while the acceleration tensor $a$ is anisotropic. In the subsequent paper, we will present the complete set of field equations. Additionally, we will establish various conservation laws, including the conservation of gravitation flux, mass, energy, and momentum. Finally, we will derive the equations of motion for gravitons. This series is titled "Azimuthally Symmetric Model of Gravitation." In the following publication, the title will be "Azimuthally Symmetric Model of Gravitation (II)." This paper, however, is designated as the first installment of the series. The corresponding manuscript is named: Azimuthally Symmetric Model of Gravitation I. A2M-G I. ASM-G I. ASM-G I. ZBM-G I.

This work outlines an approach to constructing low-rank approximations matrix bundles, which represent low-rank approximations of matrix operators. Our method is grounded in the concept of data-dependent low-rank approximation for matrix bundles under strict equivalence. We demonstrate that both the adaptive cross approximation and the randomized sparse approximate low-rank approximation (SALR) algorithms satisfy data-dependent SALR for matrix bundles within the strict equivalence relation. Furthermore, we establish that both algorithms produce matrix bundle approximations with an error term of $O(n^{-\alpha-1/2})$. This error bound is significantly more favorable than the $O(n^{-\alpha})$ error rate of standard SALR approximations in the weak equivalence setting. Finally, we apply these algorithms to the matrix operator associated with the Gaussian K-Bessel kernel. Beginning with a coarse grid of $N_0=100$ points, we successively refine the grid using matrix operator approximations, thereby generating increasingly accurate matrix operator approximations in the process. We compare the computational efficiency of these two algorithms against the Nyström method, which constructs matrix operator approximations under weak equivalence. Our findings indicate that for matrix operators in both $L_1$ and $L_\infty$ norms, the algorithms produce matrix bundle approximations of nearly equal quality. However, for matrix bundles arising from K-Bessel kernel operators, the error-dependent SALR approximation via the Nyström method is substantially more costly than the error-adaptive versions of either adaptive cross approximation or randomized SALR. Additionally, we illustrate that adaptive cross approximation can be viewed as a data-dependent low-rank Nyström method. This implies that quality errors in matrix operator approximations stem not only from data-independent SALR approximation errors but also from a data-dependent SALR approximation error. Crucially, this data-dependent SALR approximation error is of higher order than the data-independent SALR approximation error. These insights regarding adaptive cross approximation may prove valuable for developing new matrix operator approximation techniques. For instance, when constructing a matrix operator approximation from a matrix bundle, one could first compute a matrix bundle approximation, followed by a data-independent SALR approximation of that result. This strategy would likely yield a quality error comparable to standard Nyström approximations while offering superior computational efficiency. Finally, we propose a novel application of adaptive cross approximation to matrix operators: a Krylov subspace method for data-dependent low-rank approximation. Graphs equipped with length constraints can be visualized as maps, where edges follow prescribed paths within a model space. In this work, we demonstrate that certain maps possess low treewidth. Specifically, we construct maps for minor-free graphs, maps featuring edge weights, and maps of planar graphs within hyperbolic spaces. Our methodology relies on a graph-theoretic concept termed "almost embeddability," which we define and explore. Furthermore, we establish the limitation that general metrics cannot exhibit low treewidth representation. To our knowledge, this research marks the initial application of treewidth representations to maps. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides a review of graph minors and treewidth. Section 3 introduces the concept of almost embeddability. Section 4 examines treewidth representations of maps, with Sections 5 through 7 dedicated to proving the main theorems. We examine general discrete-time systems that evolve smoothly on a compact manifold without boundary, incorporating a weak monotonicity condition. For an extensive range of parameters, the dynamics are predominantly characterized by the presence of hyperbolic periodic orbits which are both globally attracting and repelling, alongside trajectories that converge to these orbits in either forward or backward time (or both). In the context of the logistic map, this property manifests as the ubiquity of superstable periodic orbits. This extensively chaotic characteristic extends to a wide spectrum of strongly monotone systems, encompassing self-interacting fields and discrete-time quantum maps, thereby yielding novel dynamical regimes in quantum and statistical field theories. We further link this prevalent phenomenon to the concept of "almost global attraction" within continuous-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity or concavity, a feature known to trigger reparametrization instabilities in time-dependent quantum states. These dynamics are expected to emerge in various "large" systems where "repelling" trajectories are constrained by monotonicity, leading to an effective attraction toward periodic orbits while retaining complex trajectory structures. We illustrate this using the example of the Vlasov equation featuring a strongly monotone force. Established links between strongly monotone systems and deformed oscillator algebras suggest that these ubiquitous dynamics could be engineered in quantum systems via appropriately deformed metrics on Fock spaces. Finally, we outline broader implications for the concept of "warp factor" solutions in cosmology and elucidate connections to recent findings regarding "dynamical" group theory. Notably, the ubiquity of superstable periodic orbits in strongly monotone systems offers a unifying framework for interpreting recent findings on periodic orbits within certain non-cryptographic chaotic maps. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the dynamics of the logistic map align with the periodic-doubling route to chaos, providing a fresh perspective on this well-known phenomenon. Ultimately, we propose that strongly monotone systems serve as a paradigm for revealing hidden patterns within the vast landscape of all possible dynamical behaviors. This includes elucidating "unexplained" features in widely utilized systems across mathematics, physics, and engineering, and may guide the search for new systems exhibiting "unusual" behaviors in both classical and quantum contexts. This proposal holds significant promise for advancing the general understanding of dynamical systems and for harnessing the inherent complexity of strongly monotone systems in quantum information applications. Additionally, it may inspire the development of novel techniques for numerical simulations and the design of new approaches to discrete control theory. This proposal stands in contrast to the conventional view of monotonicity

We introduce a method for reading neural networks by employing a variational autoencoder trained with variational inference, where the mean-field posterior is utilized. We demonstrate that this approach successfully identifies semantic concepts within the neural representations of both artificial networks and those used in conftastic. Furthermore, we find that applying this technique to natural language models yields surprisingly more semantic and less entangled concepts compared to those derived from vision models. The code for our method is accessible on GitHub. Additionally, we have released pre-trained models for CLIP, ViT, DeiT, RoBERTa, and XLM-R, which can assist in understanding these models without requiring manual training. We demonstrate that Clusters of Representations (CoRs) discovered using DeGenerative semantic models (DGls) are semantically meaningful. Specifically, we show that CoRs exhibit greater semantic inter-cluster separation and smaller intra-cluster sizes compared to those produced by other representation learning models. The gravitational-wave backdrop observed by the NANOGrav 15-year dataset and recently by the European Pulsar Timing Array (15yrp) is typically attributed to the gravitational-wave galaxy around the Milky Way. However, an alternative hypothesis suggests that both signals originate from a gravitational-wave backdrop generated in the early universe. We demonstrate that the latter model can resolve the Hubble tension. Specifically, a stiff-matter-dominated early universe amplifies primordial gravitational waves, resulting in a frequency-dependent, isotropic, and stochastic gravitational-wave background. This analysis reveals that NANOGrav 15yr and 15yrp place stringent limits on cosmological parameters, allowing us to establish tight constraints on the amplitude and slope of this backdrop. By employing NANOGrav 15yr and 1YR1 data, we derive tight constraints on these parameters and establish a lower bound for the cosmic jerk parameter. Furthermore, the best-fit model indicates that early universe physics, rather than galaxy physics, is primarily responsible for the NANOGrav 15yr observations. Additionally, the 1YR1 signal is more complex than previously noted, showing a rise at lower frequencies and a plateau at higher frequencies, which aligns with predictions from the gravitational-wave backdrop model. This model necessitates a search for a plateau in the 1YR1 signal, followed by a sharp decline at high frequencies. Future observations from NANOGrav and pulsar timing arrays will be able to distinguish between the galaxy and backdrop origin theories. The upcoming LISA mission will also investigate this gravitational-wave backdrop and its implications for cosmic acceleration. Moreover, future enhancements to Pulsar Timing Arrays, such as CHIME, will provide the means to test this hypothesis with greater precision. Ultimately, investigating and understanding the gravitational-wave backdrop is essential for a comprehensive account of cosmic history. This study serves as a proof of concept, demonstrating that a gravitational-wave backdrop model is viable and that future datasets can effectively constrain this hypothesis. Our findings are consistent with early-universe models featuring a large tensor-to-scalar ratio, such as the KKLLT model. Furthermore, we have developed a Python package named GWBACK to facilitate future research in this area. GWBACK is available on GitHub. Finally, Pulsar Timing Array data can constrain the stochastic gravitational-wave amplitude at nanohertz frequencies, while LIGO-Virgo data can constrain it at kilohertz frequencies. Our analysis reveals a spatially diffuse emission of carbon monosulfide (CS) that lacks a point source, suggesting a dispersed origin. This emission is best explained by a CS production rate of $Q_{CS} = (1.1 \pm 0.1) \times 10^{27}$ s$^{-1}$, derived from a Gaussian fit to the data. This finding supports the hypothesis that the nucleus is chemically active, a trait also observed in other comets. Unsupervised Speech Synthesis (USSS) aims to generate speech for arbitrary words without requiring annotated speech-data pairs during training. To achieve this, the field typically relies on the conventional end-to-end neural TTS (ET) architecture augmented with an unsupervised phoneme alignment (PA) module. However, the PA module often demands complex loss functions and a word corpus with phoneme transcriptions to train the encoder-decoder alignment network, creating a dependency that contradicts the core principle of unsupervised training. To resolve this inconsistency, we propose a speech generation framework that eliminates the need for PA modules and their associated losses. Our approach consists of two components: first, a speech-to-text model converts acoustic features from the ET architecture into discrete speech tokens; second, a word-to-speech model directly synthesizes speech from these tokens based on input words. This setup enables training and inference to proceed directly from words to speech features, bypassing the traditional PA module. Furthermore, we incorporate a Cycle Consistency constraint to enhance synthesis quality and reduce the data requirements. Experimental results demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms the traditional ET approach with sparse training data and achieves performance nearly on par with the ET model + PA module + Cycle Consistency method when provided with sufficient training data. The code is available at: https://github.com/ruixiangwang/Simple_and_Efficient_Unsupervised_Speech_Synthesis. The parameter $\alpha$ is constrained to the range $[-2,2]$, with values near zero implying the $\Lambda$CDM model. Results indicate that $r_c$ decreases over time, while $\omega_{de}$ transitions from a quintessence phase to a phantom regime. The availability of high-quality data is essential for both data-driven and hypothesis-driven research in healthcare and biology. However, sharing data often presents significant hurdles, particularly regarding privacy, security, and intellectual property rights. While data access control and de-identification are critical, they should not be viewed as obstacles but rather as integral components of a secure data-sharing process. We propose leveraging cyberinfrastructure gateways to manage sharing, ensuring that sensitive information is securely transferred to authorized researchers who can access it within the gateway environment. We outline specific requirements for gateway cyberinfrastructure to support effective and secure collaboration, demonstrating how it supports a sharing lifecycle that encompasses sharing policies, data access requests, de-identification, access control, usage monitoring, security, and collaboration infrastructure. This approach supports various use cases, including the dissemination of public data, preclinical data sharing, and the provision of secure, effective environments for clinical data collaboration. Furthermore, we demonstrate how scientific computing environments, such as Scientific Databases, can function as gateways to facilitate effective data sharing. Finally, we describe an ongoing implementation within the Clinical Data Repository, a biomedical data repository, which serves as a gateway for secure, effective collaboration via a cloud-based scientific computing environment. This collaborative infrastructure not only supports scientific computation but also facilitates data sharing, usage monitoring, and secure collaboration through integrated communication and web conferencing tools. Additionally, we highlight how a gateway collaboration environment can serve as a testing ground for sharing policies, helping to resolve issues before they arise in production systems. We discuss how this approach can accelerate scientific discovery and provide a foundation for developing more sophisticated data-sharing policies. Ultimately, we argue that the combination of secure biomedical data sharing, effective collaboration, and enhanced data quality will significantly enhance data quality as a key enabler for this process. Furthermore, we contend that adopting a gateway-based model will become the standard for secure data sharing in the biomedical domain, thereby substantially improving the quality of healthcare and biology. This study examines the design of robust secure multiuser communication networks utilizing a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) and an active intelligent reflecting surface (AIRS) within the presence of hardware impairments. The primary goal is to maximize the sum secrecy rate (SSR) by jointly optimizing the AIIRS active reflection coefficients, RIS passive coefficients, and hardware impairment parameters. Due to the complexity of the SSR, the problem is initially reformulated into an equivalent convex form, which is then decomposed into two independent subproblems. Since the AIIRS active coefficients are complex, they are converted into simple phase shifts. Furthermore, the resulting subproblems are non-convex; therefore, the successive convex approximation (SCA) method is employed, and the ellipsoidal generator (ELGEN) algorithm is used to address a non-convex quadratic constraint. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms other schemes. Additionally, an analytical expression for the SSR is derived. Finally, the impact of hardware impairments is analyzed, and the algorithm's computational complexity is calculated. Notably, the proposed approach is more efficient than existing methods, and its performance is substantially influenced by hardware impairments. To mitigate these impairments, the AIIRS active coefficients should be optimized, and the number of elements in the AIIRS should be increased. Furthermore, the proposed method achieves a higher SSR than other schemes, with a maximum improvement of 10.81%. The computational complexity of the proposed algorithm is O(K^3), where K represents the number of AIIRS active coefficients. Given that K is small, the algorithm exhibits low computational complexity. In conclusion, the proposed algorithm is highly effective for optimizing secure multiuser communication networks with RIS and AIRS despite the presence of hardware impairments. This effectiveness stems from the joint optimization of AIIRS active coefficients, RIS passive coefficients, and hardware impairment parameters, resulting in secure, reliable, and robust communication networks. This paper offers a comprehensive analysis of the proposed algorithm's performance, computational complexity, and robustness, providing valuable insights for researchers and practitioners working on secure multiuser communication networks with RIS and AIRS in the presence of hardware impairments. The paper also discusses the algorithm's limitations and potential future research directions. This work is significant for the field of wireless communications, particularly for the design and optimization of secure multiuser communication networks with RIS and AIRS under the influence of hardware impairments. The proposed algorithm is also applicable to other related areas, such as wireless sensor networks, IoT networks, and military communication networks

Executive function (EF) encompasses a wide range of skills, from managing emotions and controlling impulses to solving problems and making decisions. These capabilities are vital for independent living and have been studied across disciplines such as medicine, psychology, and computer science. Despite these efforts, the intricate nature of EF has prevented the field from reaching a consensus on a single definition or research methodology. Consequently, studies on EF often concentrate on just one or a few specific definitions. This paper aims to elucidate the concepts of EF, perception, and decision-making to offer a unified, holistic definition of EF. Furthermore, we propose a contrastive learning approach to model human-like EF, which simultaneously resamples and relabels perceptions through summarization from the perspective of optimal strategies. Finally, we evaluate our model's performance in controllable decision-making tasks that explicitly incorporate EF concepts, demonstrating that our contrastive learning method effectively captures the definition of executive function. Our findings indicate that the proposed definition and the contrastive learning approach successfully capture the essence of EF, while our resampling and relabeling mechanisms enhance both the efficiency and effectiveness of perceiving and deciding under the EF framework. Additionally, our empirical evidence suggests that this definition and modeling technique may offer new insights for unifying and extending EF research within decision-making domains.

The solar breeze represents a distinct solar wind structure characterized by a core temperature near the ionization point, with protons and alpha particles flowing at speeds significantly exceeding this temperature. This study presents initial findings from the Parker Solar Probe mission using data collected between July 2018 and April 2019, analyzing energy flux energy density (EFE) plots for solar breeze events. These plots were generated using Parker Solar Probe instruments alongside in-situ measurements from Advanced Composition Explorer (ACE) and Wind spacecraft at 1 AU. The analysis identifies two categories of breeze events: Type 1, where all EFEs peak near solar wind flow speed ($V_{sw}$), and Type 2, where the proton EFE peak aligns with $V_{sw}$ while the alpha particle peak appears at a higher speed. These results are compared with previous observations from the Ulysses mission. The paper discusses the energy distribution characteristics of these Parker Solar Probe events, their relationship with coronal hole properties, and the potential for these events to be classified as intermittent turbulent structures. Additionally, the study explores implications for heating and acceleration mechanisms of the solar breeze, solar coronal magnetic field configurations, and the existence of interplanetary shocks. Finally, it examines how these factors influence the evolution of solar breeze turbulence and the formation of intermittent structures. Overall, this analysis quantifies the energy content of the Parker Solar Probe across various plasma species, offering a new perspective on the inner heliosphere's energy budget. This data is critical for calibrating and validating inner heliosphere plasma models and for investigating the fundamental heating mechanisms of the solar wind.

This study presents a Clarity Diagram (CD) for a $q$-deformed optomechanical system (QDOM) featuring both radiation and motion modes quantized via the $q$-deformation parameter. The CD plots the system's dispersion properties against the $q$-deformation parameter and the intracavity field amplitude. We observe that the CD offers a more intuitive and visual representation of the phase diagram compared to the potential diagram. Additionally, the CD reveals hidden features of dispersion properties, such as distinct linear, Lorentzian, and Gaussian regions, and demonstrates how to access these areas. These findings are supported by numerical results. Our research indicates that the QDOM's dispersion properties are highly sensitive to the clariﬁcation parameter $\gamma$. By analyzing the CD, we determine the optimal $\gamma$ value that maximizes the system's dispersion properties. Furthermore, we find that the CD effectively identifies optimal parameters for enhancing dispersion effects, including the optomechanical coupling constant $g_1$, the mechanical frequency $\omega_m$, and the laser drive field amplitude $\Omega_d$. These results are validated by numerical data regarding system gain and bandwidth. Ultimately, the QDOM's CD provides a comprehensive and efficient method for investigating the system's dispersion properties and for parameter optimization to achieve superior dispersion effects. These findings hold significant potential for enhancing quantum memory, enhancing sensing, and improving quantum communication. Finally, the proposed CD approach is general and can be extended to other relevant quantized deformed optomechanical systems. Rotational spectra observed in even-even nuclei from A=100 to A=190 are successfully modeled by the Two-Rotors Model, which incorporates two quantum mechanical rotors linked via a single sigma-type excitation. The rotors' angular momenta align with, or are opposed to, the collective angular momentum. The R-parity of the spectrum is defined by the R-parity of the lowest excited single-excitation state. This study examines the R-parity inversion phenomenon in the Two-Rotors Model by integrating classical instability analysis with quantum mechanical investigations of rotors coupled through a harmonic oscillator. By employing a large-scale basis set, we investigate R-parity inversion caused by the interaction between the rotors and the oscillator, identifying a new instability within the quantum system that lacks a clear classical equivalent. Furthermore, we present R-parity inverted states with significant overlap with the classical unstable orbit, termed adverse scissors modes, and derive their properties and decay channels. The existence of these adverse scissors modes offers potential for resolving the long-standing issue of low-lying negative bandheads in well-established rotational spectra. Additionally, these modes provide a novel feature in nuclear rotational spectra, offering further understanding of the interplay between the quantum and classical regimes. Ultimately, the Two-Rotors Model demonstrates rich behavior in its R-parity inverted spectra, with quantum-averaged observables in these regions expected to differ from those in the well-known quasi-classical range. This study also explores the implications of these findings for the interpretation of nuclear spectra. To facilitate further investigation, the code used in this research will be made publicly available. (A version of this work was presented at the 12th International Conference on Cluster Physics, held in Tallinn, Estonia, from June 25 to July 1, 2023.) Although machine learning has led to significant advancements in physics-informed methods for solving partial differential equations (PDEs), these techniques are currently restricted to specific equation types, primarily relying on finite element or finite difference basis functions. This study introduces a novel physics-informed neural network (PiNN) method grounded in cell-mean values. By applying integration by parts, the model enforces weak formulations of hyperbolic and parabolic PDEs using only the neural network's values, without requiring its derivatives. This approach employs a weak deep residual hyperbolic formulation (WDRH) and a weak deep residual parabolic formulation (WDPH). The cell-mean structure of the deep residual operators ensures that the resulting deep formulations remain consistent with classical strong hyperbolic and parabolic methods based on cell-average and flux variables, while retaining the advantages of flux variables. Numerical experiments confirm that the proposed PiNN approaches are equivalent to strong deep formulations (DDF and DPF based on flux variables) and demonstrate superior performance compared to finite element-based deep methods. Furthermore, these results extend to inhomogeneous cases where source terms depend on neural function variables. Notably, the WDPH formulation is unconditionally stable within the L2 norm. Additionally, the method is highly parallelizable, as the forward and backward propagation of these wDEs can be executed concurrently. Ultimately, this paper presents a new physics-informed deep formulation that is both stable and accurate for hyperbolic and parabolic equations. Additionally, the research offers a unified framework for hyperbolic and parabolic problems, facilitating the extension of these methodologies to more complex scenarios. Finally, the authors demonstrate that the proposed formulations are equivalent to existing deep formulations, thereby providing a foundational reference for future developments in this field. For instance, while previous studies have primarily focused on Lagrangian deep methods for wave equations, this study investigates the equivalence between hyperbolic and parabolic deep formulations, which has not been previously explored. These equivalence results serve as a basis for advancing future research. The code is available at: https://github.com/zhengxianyi/PiNN. Keywords: Physics-informed neural networks, hyperbolic equations, parabolic equations, cell-mean value, flux variable, stability.

The ALICE experiment, operating in heavy-ion and $p+p$ collisions at the LHC's Heavy Ion Collider (LHC), is dedicated to investigating the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) within heavy ion collisions and in the context of heavy-flavor hadron spectroscopy driven by charmonium state removal in $p+$Pb collisions. The ALICE upgrade is designed to significantly expand the experiment's capabilities in terms of luminosity, data volume, and event-by-event multiplicity. The current plan involves upgrading the experiment in phases 0, 3, and I (with anticipated start dates of 2020, 2025, and 2028, respectively) and concluding the experiment's participation in LHC Phase III (starting in 2023) in its post-upgrade configuration. This contribution details the anticipated ALICE upgrade following Phase 0 and during Phase 3, as well as the event selection criteria and anticipated physics results for LHC Phase III while the experiment is still operational. The primary focus will be on the development and deployment of new tracking detectors, specifically the upgraded Time-Projection Chamber (TPC), Pixel Detector (PD), and Pad-Readout Detector (pRD). Additionally, new detectors for particle identification will be implemented, including the Electron Spectrometer (ES) and the Electromagnetic Calorimeter (EMC). The text will also outline the upgrade of the Muon Spectrometer (MSP), the timing detector (TOF), and the Central Barrel Calorimeter (CBC). Furthermore, updates to the ALICE data acquisition system, trigger logic, and data processing framework will be presented. Finally, new ALICE physics results from the most recent heavy-ion runs will be included. The proposed upgrade is expected to deliver significant advancements in heavy-ion collision research, notably regarding quarkonium suppression patterns, strangeness production, and open charm properties. Furthermore, the experiment aims to achieve unprecedented statistics for charmed hadron production in binary nucleon-nucleon collisions, a goal unique to ALICE. Ultimately, the outcome of LHC Phase III will be a fully upgraded ALICE experiment with enhanced capabilities in both heavy-ion and hadronic physics. The completion of this upgrade will result in a substantial increase in the production cross-sections for both light and heavy hadrons, as well as a tenfold improvement in the reconstruction rates for weakly decaying particles. Furthermore, the analysis of decays involving baryons is expected to see significant gains

The Unruh effect predicts that uniform acceleration induces entanglement between future and past light cones, despite their inherent separation. This study demonstrates that the geometric phase associated with a qubit interacting with these cones serves as a detectable signature of that entanglement. We calculate the geometric phase of a Berry-defining Hamiltonian involving an accelerated observer and their local quantum field, accounting for both timelike and spacelike segments of the observer's trajectory. Our primary finding is the identification of Unruh effect signatures within the calculated geometric phase. Specifically, the phase exhibits oscillations as a function of the acceleration parameter, with signal amplitude and oscillation frequency scaling linearly with the mentioned timelike Unruh effect. Furthermore, our analysis of spacelike slices reveals that the entanglement between the future and past light cones diminishes as their spatial separation increases; consequently, signatures of the Unruh effect present in the spacelike slice of the entangled region gradually fade into the white noise characteristic of the Unruh effect observed in fully disentangled spacelike slices far from the future and past light cones. These results suggest that geometric phases offer a viable alternative framework for detecting the Unruh effect and provide additional support for the entanglement between the future and past light cones. The low-mass X-ray binary Cyg X-1 exhibits a complex and evolving relationship between the accretion disk and its companion star during the hard state. In this study, we utilized the 2019 hard state data from the Wide Field Camera on Chandra to investigate how the stellar breeze influences the spectral and timing characteristics of the most luminous hard-state systems. To isolate the specific contribution of the stellar breeze, we employed a physically motivated phenomenological model that incorporates the stellar component and a pressure-supported inner disk structure. By comparing our results with earlier Chandra observations, we determined that the breeze's effect on the inner disk's pressure structure is minimal when the disk is significantly truncated, but it becomes substantial as the disk moves closer to the compact object. Furthermore, we established that the stellar breeze can account for a substantial portion of the count rate in the 2–10 keV range, a factor that must be considered when interpreting timing properties at these energies. Specifically, the power spectral density of count fluctuations in the 2–10 keV band is significantly higher than that above 10 keV, a discrepancy fully explained by the variable stellar component. Consequently, the correlation between the power spectral density and the fractional contribution of the stellar component to the total count rate in the 2–10 keV range is particularly strong. This study demonstrates that the stellar breeze can generate significant low-frequency fluctuations in the hard state, and our findings indicate that the breeze's contribution to spectral and timing properties is substantial as the disk transitions from a fully hard state to a quasi-parallel state. These results suggest that similar effects may be present in other hard-state low-mass X-ray binaries. Finally, our analysis reveals a potential link between the accretion disk and the stellar companion in Cyg X-1, which may be more readily detected in the soft state. Overall, this research highlights the critical role of the stellar breeze in shaping the spectral and timing behavior of the hard state in Cyg X-1. To further explore the interaction between the accretion disk and the stellar companion, future efforts should focus on obtaining higher time resolution and improved spectral coverage. Additionally, we should continue to develop and apply more precise models to better isolate the contributions of the stellar component and the inner accretion flow to the observed spectral and timing properties. We investigate the influence of thermal fluctuations on a scalar field coupled to an adjoint gauge field within a Yang-Mills theory. This coupling, identified as a "non-abelian epheter-like term," functions as an effective operator in the high-energy limit of a four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric gauge theory. In this framework, the scalar field represents an adjoint fermion, while the "ether-like" derivative corresponds to an adjoint gaugino. We demonstrate that the effective description via this non-abelian ether-like term remains valid across both infrared and ultraviolet regimes, spanning both weak and strong coupling. The calculated energy spectrum reveals a transition from an insulating to a metallic state, a phenomenon that may be interpreted as deconfinement. Furthermore, the calculated specific heat indicates that the metal behaves as a non-Fermi liquid. Additionally, we demonstrate that the effective Lagrangian can be solved exactly using an expansion in inverse powers of the scalar field. Finally, we explore how introducing the non-abelian derivative into $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory alters the renormalization group flow of the gauge coupling. These findings are anticipated to be relevant for understanding the dynamics of non-abelian black holes in the context of anti-de Sitter space. To facilitate this, we also detail the construction of such black holes by coupling an $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric matter multiplet to the anti-de Sitter background. In this configuration, the matter multiplet includes a non-abelian derivative, and the Killing spinor condition is satisfied by a fermionic superpartner of the scalar field. Consequently, the resulting black hole possesses a fermionic supercharge, and we explicitly calculate this charge. Furthermore, we show that the scalar field remains uncondensed in this background. Finally, we establish that the non-abelian ether-like term does not affect the renormalization group flow of the gauge coupling. These conclusions are consistent with the specific heat analysis, which identifies the black hole as an example of a non-Fermi liquid. Additionally, the vanishing of the scalar field in the matter multiplet provides a mechanism for deconfinement.

We utilize deep imaging from the Hyper Suprime Cam Survey (HSC-SSP) to analyze 10,000 early-type galaxies (ETGs) within the redshift range $0.01 \leq z \leq 0.15$. By applying an automated edge detection method, we identify and quantify tidal features in these ETGs, specifically measuring the flux fractions of tails and bridges. Our findings indicate that the average flux fraction for early features (defined as those with apparent magnitudes $>19.5$) is approximately 10%, while the rate of galaxies possessing at least one such feature is about 15%. We observe that the flux fractions of these early features are inversely proportional to galaxy mass, a relationship that remains consistent regardless of whether the features are classified as early or late. Furthermore, the fraction of ETGs showing evidence of recent or ongoing mergers is roughly 20%, with the associated flux fraction also being approximately 10%. Finally, the measured early and recent/ongoing merger rates for ETGs are $2.0 \pm 0.1$ and $1.6 \pm 0.1$ Gyr$^{-1}$, respectively. These results align with previous literature, and the high precision of our merger rate estimates is attributed to the extensive sample size and the accuracy of our feature detection and flux fraction measurement techniques. The latter is further supported by our demonstration that the flux fraction correlates with seeing conditions, which we account for using a Gaussian function. Ultimately, we confirm that ETG merger rates are lower than those of disk galaxies but consistent with the rates observed in elliptical galaxies. Additionally, the early merger rates for ETGs are found to be proportional to $L_{\rm Ks}^{-0.2} \proq M_{\rm h}^{-0.1}$. These conclusions are expected to hold for the HSC-SSP survey up to redshifts of $z \sim 0.3$. This study is the first in a series to be based on the complete HSC-SSP sample. This study extends the previous work in this series by deriving the azimuthally symmetric analog of the new gravitational potential and associated field. Unlike the spherically symmetric case, the 3D Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (3D-ASTGT) retains the core principle of bipolar outflows as a repellent effect while preserving the conservation of gravitational energy. The paper first presents the general solution to the Laplace equation under 3D-ASTGT, demonstrating that it comprises a linear combination of Legendre's azimuthally symmetric solutions. The azimuthally symmetric gravitational potential is defined as the gravitational equivalent of a specific component of the electrostatic system. This equivalence enables the use of established concepts from the spherically symmetric 3D-ASTGT regarding point-like and surface-like mass distributions. Furthermore, based on the spherically symmetric framework, the gravitational energy conservation law is derived for 3D-ASTGT, and the azimuthally symmetric gravitational field is formulated. The gravitational energy conservation law is shown to depend on the absence of non-conservative field terms. The polar component of the field is identified as attractive, whereas the latitudinal component acts as a centrifugal-like repulsive force. The influence of this repellent effect on bipolar outflow formation is analyzed. The paper concludes by detailing properties of the azimuthally symmetric field within specific space regions and presenting expressions for the energy flux of outflowing matter. These findings suggest that bipolar outflows originate from a gravitational repellent effect, with their structure determined by the geometry of the source mass distribution. Additionally, the analysis indicates that the latitudinal component of the bipolar outflow corresponds to matter moving along geodesics. The azimuthally symmetric flux of gravitational energy is derived, exhibiting properties analogous to those of electric energy flux in the corresponding electrostatic system. Finally, the flux of gravitational energy is expressed through the azimuthally symmetric component of the gravitational field. Overall, 3D-ASTGT is presented as a viable alternative theory capable of describing and explaining observed bipolar outflows. The study also addresses the issue of the missing mass problem. This study examines optical emission from five well-defined fast radio bursts (FRBs) that were not detected by radio telescopes during their radio bursts. We establish stringent upper limits on the optical flux associated with these FRBs, utilizing both simultaneous and delayed emission scenarios. The observed radio silence is best explained by either a compact core with a size of approximately 100 km or an optically thick jet oriented nearly perpendicular to our line of sight. For the FRB 20210514A event, the radio non-detection can be attributed to an obscuring dusty torus. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the upper limits derived in this work are more restrictive than the optical flux lower limits inferred from the dispersion measure of FRB 20200110A and the features seen in the light curve of FRB 20220610A. Consequently, we conclude that a jet is the most probable engine driving these FRBs. Finally, we propose that the fast radio emission is likely generated by a compact engine, such as a black hole or neutron star, rather than an external shock. These findings have significant implications for the potential use of ground-based optical telescopes in future FRB research. Additionally, we discuss the broader implications of these results for the current models regarding the origin of FRBs. In our conclusion, we advocate for the deployment of a next-generation optical telescope, such as the proposed Vera C. Rubin Observatory, to investigate the physical nature of FRBs. This instrument would be capable of studying the optical emission from the most luminous FRBs, thereby providing a critical new window into these enigmatic phenomena. We also suggest that the Rubin Observatory will facilitate the simultaneous detection of a large number of FRBs, offering valuable insights into their physical nature. Finally, we argue that the data quality achieved in this work sets a new standard for future FRB research. We emphasize that the optical emission from FRBs is likely to be observed in the near future, and we advocate for the adoption of new strategies and facilities to investigate this emission. In the end, we express our hope that this work will inspire further research into the optical emission of FRBs. Our primary goal is to encourage the broader FRB community to pursue the study of FRB optical emission. We believe that the optical emission from FRBs will play a crucial role in advancing our understanding of these mysterious objects. High-energy lasers serve diverse applications, including laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy, directed energy, directed propulsion, and particle acceleration. However, the deployment of these systems often encounters complications stemming from numerous non-linear effects within high-power laser media. To address challenges related to laser-plasma interactions and the degrading influence of non-linearities, this study proposes analyzing the propagation of perturbations along coupled laser beams. By employing a multi-dimensional perturbation model, we examine how perturbations propagate within a chirped grating, thereby enabling the correction of phase errors in high-power laser systems. Additionally, we investigate propagation dynamics across various coupled laser beam configurations using both analytical and numerical methods. These findings offer a significant basis for effectively mitigating the detrimental effects of non-linearities in high-energy laser systems. Furthermore, the research explores the reverse engineering of such lasers by providing insights into their internal design and operational mechanisms. The models and methodologies developed in this work are also applicable to other nonlinear optical systems. Ultimately, this research aids in understanding the complex interactions occurring inside high-energy laser systems and addresses associated problems. The proposed methodology is also extendable to other nonlinear coupled laser systems for potential new applications. The results are documented in Design, Enhancement, and Reverse Engineering of High-Power Laser Systems, a dissertation by Youssef El-Diab, completed at the University of Central Florida under the direction of Dr. Mohamed El-Diab and Dr. Mohamed El-Shaakhawy. The work encompasses five chapters covering coupled laser beam propagation and its application to laser plasma, laser plasma spectroscopy, multi-dimensional perturbations in high-power laser systems, and the reverse engineering of high-power laser systems. The material is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. Keywords include: High-power lasers, coupled laser beams, laser plasma, laser plasma spectroscopy, and reverse engineering.

Text generation using pretrained language models (PLMs) typically proceeds without visual input, yet a clear need exists to integrate visual controls to fine-tune PLMs for generating descriptions of visual data. We introduce a framework that connects visual representations of images or videos to text-based PLMs via a visual control tower. This tower comprises a text encoder to process input descriptions and a visual encoder to handle either specific visual states or dynamic motions. These components interact through a state gate that regulates a decoder to produce output text. Trained in an end-to-end manner on datasets like COCO and DIANa, the model can generate descriptions that explicitly or implicitly align with visual states or motions. Evaluations demonstrate that the generated text accurately matches the intended visual states or movements and achieves a competitive balance between accuracy and diversity compared to models without visual guidance. Furthermore, the model excels at controlling the complexity of descriptions when directed by visual states. Additionally, we present a training-free method that leverages our model's visual constraints to automatically reorder sentences for summarizing motion, achieving superior automatic evaluation scores over textual-only baselines. Finally, extensive ablation studies confirm the model's robustness and highlight the distinct contributions of individual components within the framework. The brightness profile of a particle beam along one or multiple axes can be determined by analyzing the spatial distribution of a secondary beam within a screenless cross-spectroscopy detector. Currently, data-driven approaches are increasingly utilized to tackle various scientific and engineering challenges. However, existing methods often suffer from significant accuracy issues due to inherent limitations in data, models, or their integration. This study introduces the concept of a data repository and examines the data provenance within collaborative data-driven science and engineering. A new framework, named collaborative data-driven modeling (CDDM), is proposed to address data-related challenges. The core philosophy of CDDM involves iteratively enhancing data quality through modeling, thereby enhancing the overall accuracy of data-driven solutions. To demonstrate CDDM, two examples are provided: one where modeling refines data representation, and another where data informs the selection of the most suitable model. These cases highlight the flexibility and broad applicability of the CDDM approach. The first example applies CDDM to the inversion problem involving the identification of material properties within complex structures. The second instance investigates the reverse design of a data-driven constitutive model for a new class of materials. Numerical experiments confirm the effectiveness of the proposed CDDM methodology. This research paves the way for data-driven modeling, design, and inverse design utilizing complex data repositories. The CDDM framework is anticipated to foster innovative methodologies within the fields of data-driven science and engineering. Furthermore, this work offers valuable insights for advancing data science initiatives in scientific and engineering contexts. Additionally, the findings may benefit the broader communities of science and engineering, as well as business and social science domains involving scientific data repositories. These disciplines are increasingly adopting data-driven solutions, necessitating a deeper understanding of the origins of their input data. Consequently, the concept of a data repository and the associated CDDM research are expected to be highly relevant to a wide array of users. The paper includes supplementary materials, such as videos and executable code, to facilitate the implementation of CDDM. Specifically, a Jupyter notebook is provided to enable readers to run the numerical examples presented in the study. The findings are also available at: https://github.com/zhongxiao/CDDM. Soft robotics has gained significant traction due to the unique capabilities offered by these technologies. At the core of every soft robot lies a control system that translates the robot's physical characteristics into performance. Although soft robots exhibit a wide range of behaviors, their controllers are often designed using trial-and-error methods rather than being derived from the robot's properties. While model-based approaches offer a solution, the inherent nonlinearity and deformable nature of soft robots make them difficult to model, leaving an essential research gap in the field. This paper reviews the current state-of-the-art in modeling and control techniques for soft robots. It begins with a brief introduction to the technology, followed by a systematic categorization of existing methods, with each category accompanied by specific examples and explanations. Finally, the paper outlines the current challenges and future opportunities in the domain. By providing a clear classification and research map, this survey aims to facilitate further advancements in soft robot control and encourage more systematic, model-driven designs to enhance their capabilities.
