We establish a metaplectic version of the Frobenius reciprocity theorem for the "genuine" Jacobi group associated with a general compact automorphic form within the "general" Jacobi group. This result serves as an extension of the metaplectic Frobenius reciprocity established by S. Kim and U. Shin in 2007, which applied specifically to genuine compact automorphic forms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the space of Whittaker coefficients corresponding to a square-integrable automorphic form on a metaplectic cover of the standard Jacobi group is isomorphic to the space of automorphic forms on a metaplectic cover of the genuine Jacobi group. Finally, to establish this main theorem, we investigate key properties of metaplectic covers of the Jacobi group and their respective dual groups. Specifically, we prove that the metaplectic kernel for the genuine Jacobi group is either $2$ or $1$, and we examine the structure of metaplectic central forms by reducing the problem to a finite-dimensional Lie algebra. Additionally, in this investigation, we provide a constructive model for the metaplectic cover of the genuine Jacobi group using $L^2$-completion, a practice not previously addressed in the literature. This work also contributes to the broader objective of extending metaplectic reciprocity to the full covering groups of the general linear group. To achieve this, we analyze the geometry of the symmetric space associated with the genuine Jacobi group and its dual. By examining the geometry of the product space of the general linear group with the symmetric space of the genuine Jacobi group, we elucidate the relationship between the spaces of square-integrable automorphic forms on these groups and their metaplectic covers. Leveraging this property, we derive an explicit integral formula for the metaplectic Fourier-Cohen-Veltman transform of a function on the genuine Jacobi group. Table-based fact verification involves verifying claims within a factual query frame using only information from tables provided in question context. Existing approaches tend to treat this task as fully end-to-end, often resulting in inadequate handling of partial claims and limited exploration of model interpretability. To address these issues, we introduce a novel disassembly-based framework that: 1) decomposes fact verification into two distinct sub-tasks—claim identification and claim classification—and 2) leverages intermediate representations from the identification model to analyze the fine-grained verification process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our disassembly-based approach achieves an accuracy of 86.32%, surpassing the best-end-to-end method by 1.72%, while offering greater model interpretability. Furthermore, our analysis of intermediate representations uncovers both the strengths and limitations of the FActEval dataset, revealing both effective verification strategies and potential biases. The dataset and code are accessible at https://github.com/ruoyangliu/ExploringDisassembly_for_Table-based_Fact_Verification. Finally, we hope that our work will inspire future research to prioritize interpretability and the design of more interpretable verification systems in the field of fact verification. Beyond enhancing human understanding of AI decision-making, these efforts will also improve the reliability of AI systems in real-world applications. Specifically, our intermediate representations can serve as a foundation for developing more interpretable and trustworthy verification systems, thereby fostering greater trust between humans and AI. Looking ahead, we aim to investigate the generalizability of our proposed disassembly-based approach to other areas of table information processing. Specifically, by separating claim identification from FactCheck, table extraction, and table reading, we plan to explore whether our disassembly methodology can yield similar performance gains in those contexts. Furthermore, extending our approach to temporal fact verification presents a promising avenue for enhancing both performance and interpretability, particularly by incorporating temporal knowledge graphs and reasoning mechanisms. Finally, we intend to deepen the analysis of intermediate representations to uncover more effective verification strategies and reduce dataset biases, building upon the insights already generated. We anticipate that these future directions will advance the broader objectives of interpretability and trustworthiness within fact verification research. To achieve this, we propose implementing techniques such as saliency maps, counterfactuals, and natural language explanations to make decision-making processes more transparent and understandable. Ultimately, we hope these efforts will contribute to the development of more interpretable and trustworthy AI systems in practical applications. To further support this goal, we plan to conduct research on human-in-the-loop evaluation

We present a novel technique for incorporating conditional information into generative adversarial networks through a transformed latent space. Bayesian model comparison frequently employs Nested Sampling, where the choice of algorithm governing how sampling steps are selected significantly influences outcomes. This study introduces an algorithm using simulated annealing to explore the posterior, modeling the process as an annealing schedule. We evaluate the resulting simulated annealing step selector against two existing methods: uniform and exponential. Through an exact calculation, we demonstrate that the Nested Sampling evidence for the uniform selector exceeds that of the exponential selector. Furthermore, Nuts tests indicate that for moderate problem sizes, the uniform selector performs comparably to or better than the exponential selector. Finally, we examine the step selection mechanism of the uniform selector in the limit as the nested volume approaches zero. This limit yields the tail selector, which draws samples exclusively from the model's posterior tail, highlighting how the original step selection implicitly determines the Nested Sampling significance selector. Finally, we illustrate an application of the nested volume quantile selector to a real-world dataset and provide links to the various algorithm implementations used in this study. This work serves as a practical guide for choosing algorithms and step selection strategies when applying Nested Sampling to real-world problems. The various algorithm implementations are available under the unified nested_sampling namespace on PyPI. The objective of distance labeling in graphs is to assign $n$ labels to the vertices of an $n$-vertex graph such that the pairwise distances between these labels in an appropriate metric space remain bounded and reveal the distance between their corresponding vertices in the original graph. Initially proposed by Diestel and Lehman in 2016 for general graphs, this concept was later adapted to planar graphs by Diestel et al. in 2020 to investigate its resilience against adversarial faults. In this updated framework, an adversary is permitted to alter up to $k$ labels in an $n$-vertex planar graph; subsequently, vertices must still be identifiable based on their distances from a designated source $s$. Diestel et al. demonstrated a lower bound of $\Omega((k+1)^2)$ bits for the label size under these conditions. In this paper, we present a new distance labeling scheme for $s$-identifiable labels on planar graphs with a bit complexity of $O(k + \log n)$. Our approach builds upon the successful scheme by Diestel et al., which utilizes a labeling of size $O(\log n)$. Finally, we conjecture that the upper bound can be further optimized to $O(k)$. Additionally, we propose that the lower bound can be strengthened to $\Omega(k + \log n)$, thereby matching our construction up to lower-order terms. To support this, we construct a family of planar graphs featuring $k$ vertex cuts, where identifying a vertex's position relative to the cut necessitates at least $\Omega(k + \log n)$ bits. We investigate two-particle correlations within a driven, dissipative Bose-Hubbard model featuring nearest-neighbor boson-boson interactions. These correlations are characterized by the joint time and frequency-domain response of two sites to a weak probe. The study addresses both the separationless and large-separation limits of the bosons.

Recent research has increasingly prioritized out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. However, the majority of existing methods evaluate OOD samples individually rather than analyzing them collectively, which hinders a comprehensive understanding of their characteristics and the identification of common traits. This paper introduces a novel Bayesian Gaussian Process model that provides a joint posterior for the latent features of OOD samples. By integrating this joint posterior into the Bayesian evidence formula, we derive an evidence-based metric for OOD detection. Additionally, we derive an analytical expression for the covariance between a data point and its features, which enables efficient and accurate model training. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in small-data scenarios and when dealing with multiple in-distribution classes. Furthermore, the method offers valuable insights into collective characteristics, such as the diversity and dimensionality of latent features within the OOD space. Finally, the code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhonghaonan1993/dgpsods.

Periodic driving of a quantum system typically induces heating, a phenomenon known as Floquet heating, which is particularly prominent in open systems subject to particle exchange with an external reservoir. This study demonstrates that Floquet heating can be avoided within specific subspaces of driven open systems by leveraging quantum coherent effects. Utilizing a two-dimensional optical lattice coupled to a reservoir as a model, we reveal that Bose condensation within a non-equilibrium "scar-like" subspace protects the system against universal Floquet heating. The reservoir acts to suppress condensation by dephasing off-diagonal terms in the density matrix; however, this suppression is partially counteracted by the periodic driving, which alters the eigenbasis of the master equation, thereby preserving certain terms. The resulting steady state, characterized by enhanced diagonal elements in the Floquet mode basis, constitutes a non-equilibrium scarred state. This system exhibits extended lifetime regarding thermalization, a property potentially valuable for quantum memory applications. Furthermore, we establish that this scarred state can be characterized by a negative Laplace transform of the time-dependent dynamics. Such states are frequently observed in both natural and engineered systems, and our findings may extend to diverse driven open systems, offering new insights into non-equilibrium quantum statistical mechanics. The primary contribution of this work is a unified proof establishing the enhanced Alexandrov maximum principle and uniform Hölder continuity for uniformly convex solutions to the Monge–Ampère equation with a bounded right-hand side, addressing the long-standing challenge identified by Chen, Leung, and Wang in \cite{CWL15}. This principle is fundamental to the study of the Monge–Ampère equation, particularly when proving $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity. By integrating key ideas from multiple existing proofs, the proof presented here is notably more concise and straightforward than previous approaches. Additionally, the discussion on uniform continuity incorporates an original contribution. Through the application of the enhanced Alexandrov maximum principle, the $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity of uniformly convex solutions to the Monge–Ampère equation with a continuous right-hand side, as demonstrated in [Li85], can be derived. Furthermore, the $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity for uniformly convex solutions to a specific class of anisotropic Monge–Ampère equations is proven using the principles established herein. The discussion also highlights the necessity of certain assumptions found in [Li85]. Finally, the paper concludes with a review of various proof techniques for the Alexandrov maximum principle, aiming to inspire future research. Given the significant role of the Alexandrov maximum principle in the theory of the Monge–Ampère equation, this comprehensive overview and the original contributions provided are expected to inspire further advancements in the field. The primary motivation behind this work is the desire to unify existing proofs and to offer the original contribution regarding the issue of uniform continuity. We demonstrate that the standard time-domain analysis method is adaptable for investigating the stability of stochastic, non-periodic optical clocks. This approach demands minimal a priori knowledge of the clock noise sources, enabling the detection of transient anomalies in the time series. We validate the efficacy of this technique using synthetic data generated from stochastic models. Subsequently, we apply the method to analyze high-precision optical clocks based on Yb$^+$, Ac$^+$, and Al$^+$ ions, which are under active development. The methodology is accessible via an open-source Python package. Our findings indicate that stochastic optical clocks adhere to the superposition hypothesis, implying that period-based analysis methods remain applicable for characterizing their short-term stability. Furthermore, we observe that the period-based analysis of synthetic data yields comparable outcomes to the standard method. However, for non-synthetic experimental data, the period-based approach yields slightly different stability estimates and offers the distinct advantage of revealing the temporal evolution of noise sources. We suggest that these newly presented methods will serve as valuable tools for the development of optical clocks. These findings are supported by the following video. Optical atomic clocks utilize a quantum two-level system to maintain time by oscillating between two energy states at a highly stable frequency. In optical clocks, transitions occur within the optical spectrum, whereas microwave atomic clocks operate in the microwave band. Although optical clocks have been demonstrated experimentally, they have not yet been integrated into the global timekeeping system. A primary obstacle is the lack of agreement between short-term and long-term frequencies; while optical clocks demonstrate superior long-term stability, their frequencies are not fixed by international agreements. To identify the various noise sources in optical clocks and determine their characteristics, standard time-domain analysis methods are employed. These techniques typically involve filtering the time series into discrete frequency bands and calculating the resulting time interval. The resulting stability characteristics are subsequently used to distinguish between different types of optical clocks. However, these conventional methods are specifically designed for periodic signals, limiting their utility for non-periodic stochastic optical clocks. In this work, we show that standard time-domain analysis can be adapted for such non-periodic signals. This study introduces a fog-assisted Software Defined Network (SDN) architecture designed to enhance Service Function Chain (SFC) resilience and stability. The primary objective is to minimize the costs associated with virtual network functions (VNFs) and traffic engineering when responding to service failures caused by faults or Denial of Service (DoS) attacks. To achieve this, we propose an integrated solution that jointly addresses real-time failure restoration, fault prevention, and energy-efficient resource management. This framework dynamically reconfigures network resources to mitigate real-time failures and predictively prevent energy-related issues. Specifically, an Expectation Maximization (EM) algorithm is employed to optimize failure restoration by simultaneously selecting fault prediction intervals, VNF types, and their deployment locations. Furthermore, a Machine Learning (ML)-based prediction model forecasts energy consumption to aperiodically trigger resource adjustments, thereby preventing future faults. These proposed schemes are expected to significantly improve SFX network resilience and stability. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the joint solutions reduce VNF deployment and traffic engineering costs by 17% and 21%, respectively, outperforming existing approaches. Additionally, the EM algorithm exhibits superior convergence performance. These findings highlight the potential of joint solutions to deliver SFC services more efficiently. Finally, we outline future research directions, including the development of intelligent self-healing mechanisms for SFCNs, the application of AI-driven resource management, and the use of ML to dynamically adjust network resources based on historical fault recovery data. This would enable networks to transition from reactive to proactive fault prevention. Furthermore, we aim to enhance SFCN security by detecting and preventing DoS attacks, alongside other threats, to further strengthen network resilience. Ultimately, the proposed joint solutions offer a promising pathway for future research. Deep learning models frequently rely on specific objective functions, such as mean squared error (MSE) or cross-entropy loss, yet the influence of these functions on model interpretability remains largely unexplored. To address this, we introduce GSLNet, a novel gradient surgery technique capable of reverse-engineering the impact of various loss functions on interpretable attributes. By applying this method, we developed GSLNet-MSE and GSLCross-Entropy, which generate visualizations from images processed by models trained under different loss functions. Empirical results demonstrate that these GSLNet visualizations offer new insights into the distinctions between learned obfuscations for MSE and cross-entropy losses, revealing that human obfuscations associated with each are nearly identical. Furthermore, these findings align obfuscations within the same semantic framework and expose the internal mechanisms of both MSE and cross-entropy losses, ultimately explaining the effects these losses produce. To our knowledge, GSLNet represents the first visualization method capable of revealing the internal mechanisms of loss functions. Our code and experiments are available at https://github.com/ChenchenLi2018/GSLNet. Additionally, GSLNet offers a new tool for exploring the internal workings of obfuscated images. Our results indicate that GSLNet visualizations are more interpretable than prior methods, as evidenced by higher mutual information scores. Finally, human studies confirm that GSLNet visualizations outperform existing approaches in terms of interpretability. To our knowledge, GSLNet marks the first visualization method capable of uncovering the internal mechanisms of loss functions. The success of GSLNet also validates the obfuscations generated, suggesting that these representations may hold significant value for security research. Our results further show that the internal mechanisms identified by GSLNet are highly robust, as these GSLNet visualizations resist the obfuscations generated by other methods. In summary, GSLNet provides a fresh perspective for interpreting obfuscated images. All related materials can be found at https://github.com/ChenchenLi2018/GSLNet. We introduce a new holographic quantum error correction code constructed by iteratively applying a unitary Haarni transformation. This process generates a hyper-invariant topologically stable code that outperforms the 1D XY spin chain in maintaining entanglement under random bond noise. By employing a real-sparse tensor network representation, we develop a variational algorithm that successfully maps the spin chain's density matrix into a hyper-invariant MERA structure. This code emulates the self-similar distribution of entanglement found in critical quantum many-body systems, specifically those with power-law dependence. Furthermore, we identify a family of functions capable of encoding the density matrix for ground states of power-law dependent Hamiltonians, such as those governing critical 1D spin chains and electrons on a 1D lattice. Finally, we demonstrate that this construction can be extended to create a topologically stable, locally invariant tensor network for the ground state of the toric code in any dimension $d$. These findings are supported by results from classical computer simulations. Our work paves the way for investigating novel, efficient, and robust quantum error correction codes that are locally stable and capable of correcting highly correlated errors. Additionally, since these codes are constructed from strongly correlated ground states, they hold significant potential for applications in quantum chemistry. This approach is expected to advance our understanding of many-body Hamiltonians and facilitate the simulation of quantum field theories. (See also Phys. Rev. D 102, 046001 (2020)). This study investigates the axial spacing between filaments within the Galactic Center to assess the homogeneity of the filaments identified in Paper I. Analysis reveals that the mean spacing along the filaments' primary axis is $0.37 \pm 0.02$ pc, with the median ($0.36$ pc) and mode ($0.35$ pc) showing minimal deviation from the mean. The observed spacing distribution is primarily driven by two distinct components: the dominant filament-filament axis parallel pair population, which accounts for $70\%$ of the total population, and an isotropic pair population. Furthermore, the characteristics of filaments included in the Paper I selection are highly representative of the broader population, as the properties of all filaments, regardless of whether they were selected, are nearly identical. These findings collectively support the homogeneity of the population identified in Paper I. Additionally, the axis-axis spacing distribution is compared against theoretical distributions derived from random point clouds and homogeneous, anisotropic filament networks, both of which fail to adequately describe the observed data. Finally, an investigation into the relationship between filament separation and the properties of the interfilamentary medium suggests that the gas density within the space between filaments is linked to their separation. Specifically, higher gas densities are associated with smaller separations, and this relationship is examined using the spatial distribution of ionized gas. Ultimately, this relationship is best modeled by a power law with a slope of $-1.7 \pm 0.2$. This study introduces a delay-stochastic bandit framework featuring arm-dependent delays and introduces the concept of an "advisory algorithm," wherein delays affect only the utilization of a specific arm rather than every action. We investigate the problem using an advisor that provides optimal arm recommendations, analyzing both regret and "delay square regret" for these advisory algorithms. While the delay square regret concept is novel in this context, it aligns with established definitions from delay-stochastic control literature. For each bandit type, we propose an advisory algorithm achieving the optimal delay square regret, while also proposing adaptive algorithms capable of operating without advisor input and attaining the same regret bound. These results represent the first of their kind for any delay-stochastic bandit model. Furthermore, we extend these findings to scenarios involving correlated arms. Notably, our algorithms achieve near-optimal performance even when functioning without advisor input, as evidenced by their regret bounds. Finally, we demonstrate that a correlation-based, zero-input algorithm reaches optimal regret for kernels with a rank of 1. Our analysis encompasses a broad spectrum of bandit models, encompassing piecewise stationary, piecewise homogeneous, piecewise deterministic, deterministic, correlated, correlated sub-Gaussian, and independent sub-Gaussian variants. Additionally, we establish novel theoretical results for correlated sub-Gaussian bandits. Finally, the paper reports empirical results that validate our theoretical findings.

Text-generation algorithms are becoming increasingly common, yet current models often fail to capture the full spectrum of human dialogue capabilities. Specifically, they struggle with (i) maintaining conversational context and (ii) steering discussions toward specific topics. To address these shortcomings, we present a new framework for creating context-aware, discourse-controlled, human-like dialogue. Our system employs latent space conditioning to enhance context awareness and utilizes discourse-driven sampling to guide attention toward particular topics. We validated our approach by measuring its impact on contextual sensitivity, topic control, and overall human-like quality, with results showing marked improvements. Furthermore, we conducted extensive human evaluations, where our generated dialogue was deemed more human-like than that of state-of-the-art models. The code is accessible at https://github.com/roberta10/LEATHER.

This brief presentation will highlight recent findings from the German QCD collaboration (QCD-GSI) at non-vanishing temperature and density, derived via lattice QCD using 2+1 flavor sea quarks with dynamical charm. The results focus on light baryon structure and the chiral evolution of various QCD order parameters under changing temperature and density. Furthermore, a recent study on the heavy flavor transition region through lattice QCD will be presented. This approach employs the heavy quark effective theory (HQET) to reduce systematic uncertainties linked to the finite mass of the bottom quark. Consequently, this work enables a first principles determination of the heavy flavor fragmentation function for $b \to d$. Finally, the study will address the QCD contribution to flavor changing neutral currents (FCNC) and the mixing of $B_s$ mesons, utilizing the same HQET framework. The analysis also examines the impact of heavy quark mass and lattice spacing on the determination of the $B_s$ meson mass difference, $\Delta m_{B_s}$. Ultimately, the calculated value, $(17.757(15)_{\rm stat}(0.9)_{\rm syst})\, {\rm ps}^{-1}$, aligns well with the experimental measurement of $(17.757(0.010(2))\, {\rm ps}^{-1}$. This study examines the structure of a probabilistic surrogate model designed for predicting stress distributions along the tower and drive-train of an offshore wind turbine. The surrogate, which incorporates uncertainty quantification, is constructed by sequentially chaining multiple Gaussian processes. Validation results demonstrate that the surrogate successfully generates accurate and reliable stress realizations for the turbine. Furthermore, the study confirms the model's ability to replicate key statistical metrics, including the mean, variance, and probability of failure. Finally, an assessment of the surrogate's uncertainty budget reveals the contributions of each chained Gaussian process and the impact of inter-model uncertainty on the final stress prediction. These findings indicate that a chained Gaussian process network is a viable approach for building probabilistic surrogate models for wind turbines and potentially other complex systems. Additionally, this research highlights a methodology for developing modular, hierarchical probabilistic models that can be effectively utilized for uncertainty budgeting. These techniques are expected to facilitate the creation of more robust probabilistic surrogates for wind turbines in the future. This study utilizes Twitter data to analyze the Izmir Earthquake that occurred on October 30, 2023. Given Twitter's role in disseminating information, the platform was actively used during the event. The analysis focuses on the English language, which encompasses a broader global reach than Turkish. Employing both quantitative and qualitative methods, the research examines user demographics, activity timelines, the most frequent hashtags, and the primary themes discussed within the English-speaking community. The findings provide insights into the earthquake's information dynamics, the needs of English-speaking users, and the types of content they engaged with. This research not only contributes to the existing body of knowledge on using social media for disaster management but also paves the way for future studies. These studies could adopt similar methodologies to investigate other disasters or explore the events from the perspective of different languages. The data was collected on a sample basis to ensure efficiency and was accessed from the Google n-grams website. This approach to information analysis is anticipated to be of interest to researchers in the fields of data analysis, information analysis, and disaster management. Additionally, the study provides Python code to facilitate replicating the analysis. While the focus is on disaster management, the methodology is also applicable to other information analysis tasks, such as brand analysis. The paper is structured into six sections, beginning with an introduction to the significance of information analysis and its relevance in disaster management. The second section outlines the data sources and the method used to extract the sample. The third section details the steps taken to analyze the extracted data prior to examination. The fourth section presents the results of the analysis, while the fifth section offers a discussion of the outcomes. Finally, the sixth section provides the conclusion. Given the volume of information generated by Twitter, the authors believe this approach is the most effective for analyzing such data. Furthermore, the paper includes Python code designed to be easily adaptable for similar analyses. The study demonstrates that information analysis can yield valuable results in disaster management, offering insights into user activities, engaged content, and the themes discussed. These insights are highly beneficial for disaster management efforts. The authors have also conducted this analysis for other disasters, including the Gaza War, the 2023 Turkey-Syria Earthquakes, the 2015 Syrian Civil War, the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh War, the 2023 Israel-Hamas War, and the 2022 Russia-Ukraine War. This paper introduces a new method for reconstructing time-resolved data using forward-optimization terminated at the measurement time. The approach relies on the hypothesis that an inversion method should maximize the likelihood of observing the in-sensor data given the unknown source. We demonstrate that this hypothesis leads to a variational formulation, where the source is represented by a data-driven trajectory basis. This basis is generated by integrating the forward model over random inputs for all times up to the measurement instant. This basis is adaptable to various time-resolved measurements across different modalities and configurations, provided the forward model is known. Numerical experiments indicate that the proposed forward-optimization strategy is highly efficient, stable, and robust, particularly in noisy conditions. The framework is demonstrated using time-resolved optical coherence tomography and computed tomography. Furthermore, the approach is shown to be applicable for recovering time-resolved images from data acquired at multiple instants, such as in dynamic computed tomography. Notably, in the case of optical coherence tomography, the method enables the reconstruction of time-resolved data from data acquired at several time instants, thereby facilitating time-resolved reconstruction from sparse sampling. This capability is particularly advantageous for scenarios where measurements are difficult and time-consuming. Finally, for both computed tomography and optical coherence tomography, we demonstrate that the proposed forward-optimization framework yields superior results compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Both simulations and experimental data confirm these findings. Overall, the forward-optimization framework is versatile for time-resolved reconstructions, applicable to both sparse and dense data acquisition scenarios. In sparse data cases, it enables the design of in-sensor optimization objectives, resulting in reconstructions that accurately reflect the uncertainty of the observed data. In dense data scenarios, it facilitates reconstructions that surpass current state-of-the-art performance. Notably, in both scenarios, the forward-optimization framework ensures that the source representation remains tractable. This is achieved through the use of a data-driven trajectory basis, which is constructed by integrating the forward model with respect to random inputs. Consequently, the proposed framework is applicable to any time-resolved measurement where the forward model is known. For model-based reconstruction, this allows for the development of efficient algorithms that are robust to both model and data uncertainties. In data-driven reconstruction, it facilitates the creation of efficient algorithms that are robust to data uncertainties and sensitive to model discrepancies. In both scenarios, the resulting reconstructions are more accurate and reliable. These features are especially relevant for future research aimed at designing next-generation imaging

We introduce SceNDD, a situation-based naturalistic driving dataset designed to facilitate research into advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and autonomous vehicles (AVs). Driving scenario databases are essential for algorithmic research, planning, and learning, yet they are difficult to generate, necessitating the collection of real-world driving data. While most existing datasets rely on professional drivers following scripted instructions, our approach utilizes everyday drivers traveling on public roads. We employed the Driving Recorder System (DRS) developed at TU Delft to automatically capture vehicle trajectories and surrounding environmental information. Additionally, on-board sensors recorded driver biometrics, including steering torque, acceleration, and steering angle. The resulting data comprises 20 hours of driving from 15 drivers, annotated with 1,100 driving scenarios, 35 event types, and 15 biometric modalities. This work demonstrates how to construct a driving scenario database from naturalistic driving data and underscores the value of such resources for advancing ADAS and AV technologies. Boundary entropy represents an additional component of entropy that emerges when a bulk conformal field theory (CFT) interacts with a boundary. This boundary entropy arises from the intrinsic entropy of the boundary itself and its interaction with the bulk CFT. Recently, the concept of reflected entropy has been introduced for two boundary entropy segments, $b_1$ and $b_2$, situated on opposite sides of the boundary. This metric quantifies the quantum entanglement between $b_1$ and $b_2$. In this study, we calculate the reflected entropy $E_R$ between $b_1$ and $b_2$ within a boundary CFT using both Cardy and Zamolodchikov boundary conformal field theory models. Furthermore, we examine a specific interface conformal field theory (iCFT) model involving two $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry breaking interfaces and determine the reflected entropy between these interfaces. The results indicate that $E_R$ remains invariant between boundary (or interface) symmetry breaking patterns in both boundary CFT and iCFT scenarios. Additionally, we find that the reflected entropy between two interfaces is non-zero. These findings suggest that boundary and interface entanglements can be characterized by the reflected entropy between two such interfaces. The framework established here for analyzing reflected entropy in boundary and interface configurations may be applicable to other systems, including those involving topological defects. Finally, we explore the potential for connecting boundary entropy to boundary entanglement entropy through the reflected entropy method. This paper investigates the simultaneous optimization of the meta-surface in a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) alongside the optimization of an orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) transmitter, within a scenario characterized by an imperfect channel state information (CSI) database and hardware imperfections. The objective is to maximize the average received signal power at the receiver. To achieve this, the transmission is divided into two distinct phases: during data transmission, a standard ELM-based system operates using imperfect CSI to transmit data; however, for evaluating and optimizing the RIS, a modified ELM-based system is employed. This modification involves shortening the signal's cyclic prefix (CP) and quantizing the ELM's weights. The resulting joint optimization problem is non-convex, but it can be simplified into two separate subproblems: ELM weight optimization and unitary matrix optimization. Utilizing the modified ELM-based system, the optimization is performed in the low-sample regime. Furthermore, the unitary matrix optimization is enhanced using the Riemannian manifold framework, which utilizes the Nakanishi transformation and the Householder transformation. Simulation results indicate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches. Specifically, it surpasses traditional ELM-based systems by leveraging an enhanced architecture and reduced sample complexity. Additionally, it outperforms other state-of-the-art solutions by utilizing a shorter channel measurement period and jointly optimizing both the ELM and the unitary matrix. This strategy compensates for the reduced CP and quantization effects, thereby significantly lowering the required number of channel samples for convergence. Finally, the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art solutions, which rely on high sample complexity and perfect CSI. This is because those solutions are not optimized for low-sample regimes, are limited to perfect CSI conditions, and are constrained by the use of a short CP. To address these limitations, the paper introduces novel enhancements to the ELM-based system, resulting in substantial improvements in both performance and energy efficiency. Consequently, the proposed method is well-suited for low-sample regimes and energy-efficient applications. This approach is particularly beneficial for RIS-assisted ELM-based systems, ELM-based OFDM systems with a short CP, energy-efficient ELM-based systems, RIS-assisted ELM-based OFDM systems with a short CP, and ELM-based OFDM systems that experience hardware imperfections. Keywords: ELM, RIS, OFDM, Joint optimization, Sub-optimal solution, Simultaneous optimization, Low sample regime, Riemann

We establish a more comprehensive version of the Heisenberg measurement error-precision inequality, specifically tailored for quantum state discrimination tasks. This version incorporates both the intrinsic limits of the quantum mechanical process and the strategic elements involving the user's prior knowledge and their selection of a specific measurement strategy. Additionally, we demonstrate that according to this inequality, the optimal strategy to minimize the intrinsic quantum uncertainty is achieved by a non-projective measurement, which distinctly contrasts with the outcomes of quantum optimal state merging and the standard quantum measurement scenario. Finally, we explore the connections this inequality has with the data processing inequality regarding the mutual information between the prior and post-measurement states, as well as its relation to the abstract formulation of the Ollivier-Audenaert quantum Wasserstein distance. Notably, this relationship offers a novel method for constructing quantum distances based on information-theoretic principles. Furthermore, it suggests a potential alternative definition for quantum relative entropy. This work examines the stability of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons within nearly parallel $\mathrm{G}_2$ geometries. By employing deformation theory, we demonstrate that instantons associated with cohomogeneity-one spaces admit a unique deformation class for each deformation parameter. Furthermore, we investigate large deformations and outline the conditions under which the resulting deformed instantons define new geometric structures. Finally, we apply this general theory to analyze the deformation classes of all known $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons in $\mathrm{G}_2$ cohomogeneity-one spaces. Specifically, we identify eight deformation families and determine that none of these instantons remain parallel after deformation. In the context of cohomogeneity-one spaces arising from Lie algebras, we find seven deformation families, comprising abelian and non-abelian cases; however, only the abelian instance possesses a deformation class representing exactly seven distinct parameters. For the $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton derived from an exceptional real-form of $E_6$, we observe that it admits deformation families of both cohomogeneity-one and cohomogeneity-two. Additionally, this instanton exhibits a deformation class containing precisely seven members when the underlying space is nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$. This class is parameterized by nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$-deformations of the Lie algebra and specific non-abelian bi-invariant 3-forms on compact simple Lie groups. We explicitly construct these geometries and corresponding instantons, demonstrating that they induce $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons on various $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds. In the final section, we present numerical computations regarding the deformations of the $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton on the $G_2$-Hopf manifold $S^1 \times \mathbb{CP}^3$. Our findings indicate that this manifold's instanton is rigid. However, the numerical data suggests that the $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton on $S^1 \times \mathbb{CP}^2$ deforms into the bi-invariant case on $SU(3)$ across a continuous family of nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ deformations. This implies the existence of deformation families with at least cohomogeneity-one, though computational constraints prevent us from identifying additional cohomogeneity-two families. The early 21st century witnessed a significant surge in digital technology adoption, with social media and messaging platforms becoming integral to daily human interaction. This digital transformation extended rapidly to the workplace, where email and collaboration tools replaced many face-to-face activities. However, the value of these digital systems was further underscored by the COVID-19 pandemic, which necessitated their use for national contact tracing applications to manage virus spread. This research evaluates the privacy implications of such applications, specifically analyzing data collection methods, limitations, and user consent within Germany's official COVID-19 app. The study employs Dwork's decision tree model and the GDPR framework, focusing on Germany's legal and technical environment. Our findings reveal that the application violates the principle of purpose limitation under German law, as it was designed solely for tracing purposes yet mandated the installation of additional software for testing. This issue is particularly acute in Bavaria, where the app is the only permitted tool for tracing. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that users utilizing this application are not adequately informed regarding the risks associated with the software. This lack of awareness stems partly from the German government's failure to conduct a thorough pre-deployment risk assessment regarding privacy violations. Additionally, the study addresses data protection concerns inherent to the SUS.DAT technology, highlighting that the system faces challenges in de-identifying data, making it susceptible to re-identification attacks. Ultimately, this paper underscores the critical importance of privacy considerations in the design and implementation of any application utilizing SUS.DAT technology. Specifically, it examines how purpose limitation affects data collection, storage, and usage, and how these factors influence informed user consent. Ultimately, the conclusion emphasizes that the development of tracing applications must adhere to established technical and legal privacy standards. This ensures that users remain vigilant about the risks of installing such software and understand the necessity of strict government oversight to prevent purpose limitation violations. Without proper regulation, users may inadvertently expose themselves to privacy threats, thereby compromising their right to privacy. This framework establishes a foundation for future contact tracing applications to balance data protection with the effectiveness of virus containment efforts. Specifically, it outlines the steps required to achieve purpose limitation, such as separating data collection, storage, and usage across different applications, and ensures that users are adequately informed about associated risks. This approach promotes informed user consent, thereby safeguarding individual privacy rights. The significance of this study extends beyond Germany, as the methodology and conclusions can guide other nations in the development and deployment of similar applications. Ultimately, this work contributes to the broader goal of maintaining privacy rights in the digital

Quantum information represents a distinct category of data that, despite being valuable for specific computational tasks, remains limited in scope compared to the broad applications of classical data. This study introduces a novel class of hybrid neural systems dedicated to learning quantum data. Although the systems utilize classical neurons, they employ quantum bits as connectivity weights. These weighties constitute hybrid entities that merge properties of both quantum and classical data, enabling neural systems to harness the advantages of both information types. As a practical application, we investigate climate data, demonstrating the system's effectiveness in identifying air mass types from atmospheric conditions. The results highlight significant benefits regarding generalization, general-purpose utility, and cost-efficiency. Furthermore, this hybrid approach offers a versatile framework for developing future quantum-classical hybrid neural systems. By enabling the creation of quantum neural systems capable of processing quantum data, this framework facilitates deeper investigations into the fundamental trade-offs and benefits associated with neural processing of quantum information. These insights are essential for determining the optimal balance between classical and quantum data processing. Additionally, this framework holds potential for discovering hybrid quantum-inspired neural systems distinct from the quantum neural systems analyzed in this work. Such a development could lead to more efficient quantum algorithms for neural processing and reveal fundamental principles regarding the learning capabilities of such systems. Finally, this research provides fundamental guidance for practical decisions concerning the deployment of quantum computing in the context of neural data processing. Keywords: Quantum information, Quantum computing, Quantum machine learning, Quantum neural learning, Classical machine learning, Climate data.

This paper presents a C code creator derived from a shallow embedding of C within ACL2. Unlike the authors' prior work on an ACL2-to-Verilog synthesizer, which is now PLS-certified, this new tool works in the opposite direction, translating ACL2 to C. Our primary objective is to automatically generate C code from ACL2 models of programming languages. By leveraging the existing ACL2-to-Verilog synthesizer, we can subsequently convert the generated Verilog into FPGA hardware. We demonstrate the use of this code generator in constructing a simple ACL2-based domain-specific language (DSL) and in modeling two DSLs for instruction sets, specifically the x86 and ARM architectures. The paper includes source code for the C code generator and an ACL2 specification for a C DSL, illustrating how to define C programs in ACL2 that faithfully represent this DSL. Furthermore, we show that ACL2 can formally verify properties of C programs within this DSL using the ACL2-to-Verilog-based flow, all automated by the code generator. Ultimately, this generates formally verified code, a capability we aim to extend to hardware synthesis in the future. To achieve this, we require not only ACL2-to-C and C-to-Verilog synthesis but also hardware extraction from Verilog. Although the Verilog-to-FPGA synthesis step currently lacks formal certification, we demonstrate a C-to-FPGA flow for a subset of C using an ACL2 model, providing a proof of concept for the future development of a fully certified toolchain. Following the code generation process, we illustrate a formal verification flow comprising C-to-Verilog and Verilog-to-FPGA synthesis, followed by FPGA implementation. This approach enables us to verify properties of the resulting hardware using ABC and various FPGA vendors' tools. We conclude by discussing the challenges and limitations of this flow, which rely on commercial synthesis and implementation tools, and present our vision for achieving formal verification using this process. Specifically, we advocate for open-source tools capable of formally verifying hardware properties, such as those offered by the SYNTHEZ project. The C-to-Verilog and Verilog-to-FPGA synthesis steps would need to be proven equivalent to SYNTHEZ's formal verification to ensure that all properties verified by SYNTHEZ are sound. This study analyzes the orbital elements of 106 asteroids belonging to the (39991) Iochroma family, utilizing astrometric data from the Small-Aperture Survey for Cometary Asteroids (SASCA). We confirm the family's dynamical cohesion by demonstrating that its mass constitutes 0.04% of the total mass within the heliocentric semi-major axis distribution. Furthermore, we achieve this while maintaining a degree of "arithmetic" by adhering to an elliptic cohomology theory. By incorporating both circle and $q$-symmetries, we derive $K$-theoretic results for projective spaces and their $q$-extensions. A time schedule for the symposium is also provided. Specifically, the corrections to the transverse momentum distribution reach approximately 100% at $q_{\perp}^2 \to 0$. Although 2-Factor Authentication (2FA) is a prevalent and widely accepted security measure, user perceptions and understandings of its specific mechanisms remain underexplored. This study investigates the views, mental models, and practical experiences of Signal users regarding PIN-based 2FA. Through a survey of 184 Signal users and a qualitative analysis of 30 in-depth interviews, we reveal that users largely prioritize convenience over security, leading many to adopt practices that may inadvertently compromise the integrity of the 2FA process. Our research identifies four distinct mental models of PIN security and highlights four primary barriers to the effective implementation of 2FA within this user group. Finally, we offer recommendations for improving the design and deployment of 2FA systems that are attuned to the needs and realities of these users. These findings collectively foster a deeper understanding of how users engage with 2FA and suggest potential pathways for enhancing the security and usability of such mechanisms. Furthermore, this work underscores the necessity of conducting empirical studies on user perceptions and practices regarding established security protocols, even in the context of a platform like Signal, renowned for its strong security culture. This insight may inspire similar research within other technical communities. Our study underscores the significance of empathy-driven security practices and establishes a foundation for future initiatives, such as the Signal Security Ambassadors program. Finally, this research exemplifies the value of an interdisciplinary approach to studying human-computer interaction and security. By integrating the technical expertise of a computer science researcher with the qualitative skills of a sociology researcher, we demonstrate how diverse perspectives can yield richer, more nuanced insights into user behavior. This collaborative model holds promise for advancing security research across various communities. The study is grounded in the work presented at the 57th Hawaii International International Conference on System Sciences, 2024. The rising adoption of solar power has led to increasingly erratic solar energy consumption patterns, driven by the combination of cloud cover and the discrete nature of individual appliances. This paper introduces solar quadrature rules, a suite of numerical methods designed to align with the diurnal cycle of solar irradiance. We begin by reparameterizing solar time using the fractional solar constant, which swings between 0 and 1 over a 24-hour period, rather than the conventional total solar irradiance. Next, we apply the Stieltjes transform to generate a rational parametrization of this cycle, which closely mirrors the shape of solar irradiance. By utilizing the measure derived from this parameterization, we construct solar-Gaussian quadrature rules. These rules adapt their node locations and integration weights to the specific, highly variable profile of solar irradiance, offering a superior approach for light-load computing environments compared to traditional methods. The study includes both analytical and numerical investigations into the characteristics of these quadrature rules, demonstrating their precise efficacy in harnessing solar energy. Furthermore, we illustrate their potential utility in a stochastic scheduling framework for cloud computing and analogous systems. Our proposed solar-weighted geometric progressive scheduling strategy reduces overall energy costs while maintaining service-level agreement (SLA) compliance. Additionally, our approach ensures robustness against the highly stochastic and unpredictable nature of solar irradiance. Finally, numerical simulations confirm the advantages of our solar-weighted geometric progressive scheduling algorithm, showing that it achieves significant energy savings compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. Notably, our method reduces energy consumption by 10.7% relative to a randomized algorithm and by 24.4% compared to the current state-of-the-art approach. Moreover, our solar-weighted quadrature method is capable of adapting to varying solar profiles. In this context, our algorithm achieves energy savings of 10.4% over the existing state-of-the-art solution. Overall, our method proves highly effective in energy-efficient scheduling, even in scenarios where the solar profile remains unknown. Keywords: Solar energy, solar-powered cloud computing, stochastic scheduling, quadrature rules, geometric progressive algorithm.

The curvature of a loss landscape is a fundamental component of the optimization landscape, influencing both the convergence rate and the final solution of the training process. This paper introduces a low-rank approximation of the generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) matrix that utilizes mini-batch-wise second-order statistics to model the Hessian of individual loss components. We demonstrate that this approximation is equivalent to the curvature term within the recently proposed Variational Vision Transformer (ViViT). Our theoretical and experimental findings indicate that our approach yields the same approximate curvature structure as ViViT but is more computationally efficient, as it eliminates the need for an additional projection layer. Furthermore, we apply our method to classification and regression tasks to prove its effectiveness. Finally, we offer a comprehensive discussion of the method's practical applications and potential extensions. Code and experimental results are available at https://github.com/sergiorodriguez22/vivit-curvature. The source code for the demonstrated applications and results can be found at the same location. Grammatical gender influences how nouns are mentally represented in languages where this categorization is expressed through inflectional endings, such as Spanish, French, and German. Research indicates that gender affects both the categorization of nouns and the development of mental representations, often leading to semantic categorization based on gender despite the lack of inherent meaning in these categories. This study investigates how gender systematically alters neural representations of words in such languages by analyzing embeddings derived from annotated corpora across three specific languages: French, Spanish, and German. The study examines various inflectional annotations, including articles, adjective endings, and suppletive forms like "der Mond" (the moon) versus "die Sonne" (the sun). Results demonstrate a consistent pattern: gender-related neural representations align closely with the inflectional data across all three languages, confirming that gender-related effects are robust and consistent within the same language family. Furthermore, these gender representations demonstrate "zero-shot" transfer to tasks involving animacy and personhood. Finally, the analysis explores the relationship between gender representations and diachronic language change, specifically examining how gender has shifted over time in these languages. The paper concludes by discussing the broader implications of these findings for theories regarding the origins of grammatical gender. (Code and data available at: https://github.com/josh-lee-11/gender-reps)

Let $G$ be a connected semisimple Lie group defined over the reals, assume its real rank is at least 2, and suppose it does not fall under conditions where $(G,F) \simeq (\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{R})$ or $(\mathrm{Sp}(4,\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{R})$. For any prime $p$, consider a finite index subgroup $\Gamma$ of $G(\mathbb{R})$ that arises from arithmetic construction. We define $c_p(\Gamma)$ as the smallest index of a normal subgroup $\Lambda$ within $\Gamma$ such that $\Lambda$ contains all elements of $\Gamma$ with word length at most $R_p(\Gamma)$, where $R_p(\Gamma)$ denotes the relative length in the quotient $\Gamma/\Gamma^{ab}$. Our primary finding establishes that $c_p(\Gamma)$ is bounded by a function $F(G,\Gamma)$ that depends solely on the local characteristics of the defining form of $\Gamma$ and the index $[\Gamma:\mathrm{G}(\mathbb{R})]$. This result implies that arithmetic lattices exhibit a form of uniformity in their subgroups, a property we term uniform charm. Leveraging this discovery, we demonstrate that both uniform charm and the uniform hyperbolicity of exponential spaces associated with nilpotent groups of dimension at most 7 for $\Gamma$ are equivalent to the stiffness of $\Gamma$. Furthermore, we extend these equivalence theorems to broader contexts, including uniform lattices and arithmetic supersingular Drinfeld modular groups. Our proof integrates methods from algebraic groups, geometry, combinatorics, and probability. Notably, uniform charm was previously known for uniform lattices due to work by Björner, Chan, Chiu, and Poonen, and for arithmetic supersingular Drinfeld modular groups based on research by Chen, Liu-Vladut, and Yu. Our research was conducted while the fourth author held positions as a Visiting Assistant Professor at the University of Washington, Seattle, and as a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Notre Dame. We extend our gratitude to both institutions for their support. Additionally, we acknowledge the University of Notre Dame's Center for Geometric Group Theory for providing a stimulating environment that significantly benefited the collaboration. This paper introduces an efficient framework for large-scale attribute extraction in massive sparse traffic forecasting environments. First, to lower the computational complexity of model training, we utilize a city block distance metric to measure similarity between traffic networks across different cities. Second, leveraging this similarity, we perform attribute extraction using heuristic rules to establish transfer learning between cities. Finally, we develop a large-scale sparse traffic forecasting model capable of predicting traffic flow at the road segment level across multiple cities. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework reduces computational complexity by at least 90% compared to standard recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and outperforms them in prediction accuracy. Additionally, our model achieves a 10% to 20% improvement in accuracy over state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning approaches. The source code will be made publicly available. VACA extends beyond purely interventional settings by incorporating latent variables and employing a dynamic noise distribution for interventional queries. Experiments across multiple synthetic datasets demonstrate that VACA can accurately recover the underlying target graph, even when the true additive noise model is unknown. Additionally, the method successfully handles both interventional and counterfactual queries. While numerous studies have examined how pre-release attributes influence box office success, identifying which attributes drive revenue remains challenging due to inconsistencies in findings across different research papers. These discrepancies often stem from variations in datasets, as prior studies rely on limited sample sizes that lack comprehensive coverage of exogenous factors. This paper addresses that gap by analyzing over 1,000 films from 2000 to 2019. By focusing on ticket sales growth rates rather than cumulative revenue, the research effectively controls for revenue fluctuations caused by factors such as the number of operating theaters and the duration of a film's run. The findings indicate that marketing expenditure, release type, and film length are the most significant drivers of revenue. Additionally, the study demonstrates that machine learning models utilizing these pre-release attributes can accurately predict a film's revenue growth. Finally, the analysis reveals that increasing marketing spend is the most effective strategy for short films, whereas long films benefit more from a wide release. Furthermore, the research confirms that animated films generate higher revenue than live-action films. These insights into the film industry aim to assist producers and distributors by providing a means to forecast earnings and enable audiences to make more informed decisions. This study examines the interaction between frequency and voltage within an AC network modeled under steady-state frequency regulation, a common setup for analyzing the transition to alternative frequency control systems. While prior research has primarily addressed linear interactions, this paper focuses on nonlinearities by proposing a functional approximation method. By converting the nonlinear problem into a parameter-dependent linear one, we evaluate the stability of voltage fluctuations through linear stability analysis across various networks. Furthermore, numerical simulations illustrate how these analytical findings apply to actual networks, offering guidance on modeling such systems. Specifically, our model reveals that the ratio between voltage and frequency deviation is not constant, a result that aligns with empirical evidence. These insights demonstrate that the stability of voltage fluctuations is governed by the eigenvalues of the frequency and conductance matrices, distinguishing it from linear models. Additionally, we quantify the impact of nonlinearities on model parameters and their influence on system stability. Finally, our results indicate that modeling nonlinearities significantly affects the characterization of alternative frequency control, thereby influencing the design of control systems intended to stabilize fluctuations. In this context, we show that the traditional 1:1 coupling assumption for alternative control is overly simplistic, as it overlooks the existence of nonlinearities. Furthermore, our analysis of nonlinear effects uncovers a new class of stable networks, expanding upon existing classifications derived from linear models. Notably, these additional stable networks exhibit the same stability margins as those identified by linear analysis. Overall, this work underscores the necessity of accounting for nonlinearities when modeling nonlinear problems. Notably, our findings regarding alternative frequency control systems provide a framework for analyzing the stability margins of emerging active distribution networks. Finally, our results highlight the critical role of conductance in determining system stability, underscoring the need for shunt compensation strategies to mitigate unstable voltage dynamics. Excess emission in the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray (SXR) bands is frequently observed in the spectra of active galactic nuclei (AGN). This study introduces a new approach to modeling this excess via hard X-ray photons from the jet that scatter off thermal electrons within the broad-line region (BLR). Specifically, we demonstrate that the UV/SXR excess in these sources arises from external-Compton scattering of thermal X-rays, which are a natural emission product of AGN jets. To validate this hypothesis, we developed a novel Monte-Carlo simulation code named MAPPIES (Monte-Carlo Applications for Partially Polarized inverse external-Compton Scattering). Utilizing MAPPIES, we modeled the BLR as a collection of hot clouds and simulated the scattering of pre-polarized inverse Compton X-rays. Our results indicate that the polarization degree of the UV/SXR excess can reach up to 10%, aligning with current observational data. Furthermore, our model successfully explains the origin of the UV/SXR excess in AGN spectra. The proposed model and the MAPPIES code will be applicable to analyzing the physical properties of the BLR. Additionally, we suggest that the UV/SXR excess in AGN spectra serves as a new diagnostic tool for investigating BLR physics. We also discuss the implications of our findings for the underlying physical processes occurring within the BLR. Finally, we demonstrate the capabilities of the MAPPIES code using the broad-line region of the blazar 3C 279 as a case study. This work presents a quantum detector designed to identify an unknown, but symmetric, pure state with high fidelity within an online framework using the minimum number of measurements possible. We demonstrate that the detector's fidelity can be expressed through the population of the highest total angular momentum subspace in the measurement basis states. Based on this analytical formulation, we developed a simulation of the detector in Python. Additionally, we explore a potential physical implementation using cavity QED systems. This approach requires no tuning of experimental parameters, involves only a single interaction between the analyzer and the signal, involves no signal loss, involves no inefficient readout, and can process a signal at a rate of 1 MHz. Our calculations indicate a detector fidelity of 99.9999%. We conclude by outlining future extensions of this work. These include generalizing the detector to observe a combination of multiple symmetric pure states with known relative coefficients; this generalization maintains the same computational complexity and could be realized experimentally by preparing the signal in a superposition state via quantum interference and preparing the detector in a signal basis state corresponding to the relative coefficients among the observed states. Other extensions involve adapting the detector for observation of mixed symmetric states with known densities within a online framework at a minimum rate, which would involve evolving both the signal and the detector over time. This proposal also demonstrates that the detector's fidelity scales exponentially with the detector size, offering a way to achieve ultra-high fidelity. Finally, we discuss the experimental feasibility of these proposals and their potential impact on future research. Specifically, we show that these schemes offer new opportunities for high-precision spectroscopy, quantum state tomography, and the observation of highly entangled states. These applications achieve record-breaking precision and require significantly fewer measurement settings than comparable techniques in the literature. Furthermore, the ultra-high fidelity of our detector suggests that these methods could help resolve the current "precision puzzle" in spectroscopy, where further improvements in measurement precision are becoming increasingly difficult to achieve. In summary, our work demonstrates that large-scale quantum detectors can significantly impact high-precision measurement and quantum information processing. This insight may inspire further research into quantum detectors with scalable fidelity. In the near future, leveraging the ultra-high fidelity of these detectors, quantum detectors larger than the signal could become a viable alternative to traditional large-scale quantum computing architectures for high-precision spectroscopy and quantum state tomography. In the long term, the ultra-high fidelity of our proposed detector may enable new discoveries in fundamental physics. Solar oscillations are highly sensitive to the Sun's surface magnetic fields, making helioseismic travel-time measurements a powerful tool for detecting currents and flows near sunspot groups and active regions (ARs). This study characterizes the 3D velocity and current structures within and around ARs that generate these travel-time anomalies. By applying the helioseismic local time (HLT) method to HMI Dopplergrams, we identified 100 events with travel-time shifts exceeding the noise level. Using Gaussian process regression on the resulting LT maps, we reconstructed 3D velocity fields to extract travel-time shifts. We selected 60 events from this dataset that showed no significant correlation with travel-time anomalies arising from internal AR flows. For the remaining events, we derived travel-time shifts from the reconstructed 3D velocity fields. Finally, we compared the travel-time shifts of the 30 events exhibiting the largest shifts with the time derivatives of magnetic currents crossing the solar surface. A strong correlation was found between time derivatives of magnetic currents and travel-time shifts, suggesting that currents surrounding ARs contribute significantly to the observed LT variations. Our findings indicate that if a break in the GW strain spectrum exists between 10–30 nHz, magnetic field evolution cannot explain it; however, the signal below 10 nHz could potentially be attributed to primordial GWs generated during inflation. This hypothesis is supported by recent research demonstrating that primordial GWs can produce a strain spectrum matching recent LIGO data, with the break frequency aligning well with the magnetic field strength of $B_0=10^{-9}$ G. Consequently, we utilized this constraint to establish an upper limit on the magnetic field strength at the end of inflation, showing that this bound scales with the reionization epoch, $N_{\rm end}$. Furthermore, under specific assumptions, we derived additional constraints that suggest the break frequency may be located at or below 10 nHz. We conclude that future PTAs will enhance sensitivity to GW signals in this frequency band, potentially enabling the detection of primordial GW signals and offering a method to constrain magnetic field strengths during inflation. Additionally, we note that the PTAs currently under analysis include the European Pulsar Timing Array, International Pulsar Timing Array, Chinese Pulsar Timing Array, and Indian Pulsar Timing Array. Light field technology has garnered significant interest due to its capacity to capture extra spatial and temporal data via spatial and temporal multiplexing, a feature highly valuable for applications like light field displays and automotive systems. However, the high dimensionality of light field data presents storage and transmission challenges. A promising solution to these issues is image compression leveraging neural networks. This paper introduces a novel learning-based framework designed for the compression of light field images, specifically targeting synthetic aperture radar (SAR) automotive applications. This approach separates the compression and decomposition stages into distinct processes. To enhance efficiency and quality, we propose a new parallax-aware model for compressing light field images. This model utilizes a lightweight convolutional neural network to decompose the compressed representation into directional image planes. During the compression phase, the system encodes the first plane and predicts the remaining ones using a recurrent neural network (RNN). Additionally, a customized RNN architecture is developed to better model long-range dependencies. Experimental outcomes confirm that our parallax-aware model surpasses existing methods in both compression performance and quality, as measured by PSNR and SSIM metrics. Furthermore, qualitative comparisons demonstrate that our model effectively handles complex light field images. Ultimately, we demonstrate that our parallax-aware model achieves superior results compared to current state-of-the-art approaches. The concept of utilizing quantum operators as returns for stochastic kinetic processes originates in [3], where it was demonstrated that this approach yields non-classical steady-state distributions while preserving classical momentum distributions. The origin of protoplanetary disks remains a fundamental unanswered question in disk and planet formation research. This study investigates the relationship between the collapse of prestellar cores and the subsequent formation of protoplanetary disks. Through 3D simulations of prestellar core collapse, we demonstrate the direct formation of protoplanetary disks from the fragmentation of a prestellar core. Our findings indicate that the mass of the resulting disk is primarily governed by the density profile of the prestellar cloud, with our results suggesting a linear mass budget between the core and the disk. Additionally, the rotation of the prestellar core largely determines the final disk mass and structure, as rotational flattening converts the central dense core into a disk. We also observed that magnetic fields can significantly influence disk formation; specifically, they can suppress cloud collapse, leading to the creation of multiple disks and, in some cases, only a single disk. These results provide valuable insights into the processes of disk formation and evolution. Ultimately, the prestellar core plays a pivotal role in shaping the characteristics of the final protoplanetary disk. Our model offers a comprehensive framework for understanding the link between prestellar cores and protoplanetary disks, which is a key factor in explaining the origin of planetary systems. This study addresses multi-period time series modeling by introducing a Bayesian Variational Inference (BVIE) framework that integrates a group Lasso penalty with an Gamma prior. The proposed model is computationally efficient, requiring only $O(T\times D)$ memory and demonstrating linear scalability with respect to the number of variables $D$. Its performance was evaluated using two real-world datasets: the S\&P500 Index (1992–2012) and the Chinese SSE Index (2007–2017), which were split into training (80%) and testing (20%) sets. The results indicate that the number of selected variables in the BVIE model correlates positively with the actual number of significant variables underlying the data. Furthermore, BVIE outperforms traditional models, including ARIMA, VAR, and LASSO, as well as machine learning approaches such as SVM, Random Forest, and XGBoost. Additionally, an analysis of the underlying mechanism reveals that BVIE is equivalent to a kernel-based model, specifically a kernel Lasso, which can be viewed as a special case of kernel SVM with L1 loss. Consequently, BVIE is highly effective at identifying the most critical time points in a multi-period time series model. Finally, we demonstrate that BVIE exhibits robustness against noise in both inputs and parameters. These findings suggest that BVIE holds significant promise for financial forecasting and risk management. Our code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/zhongtao2017/BVIE}.

We propose a new constant expansion of the logic $G_{1,\omega}$ tailored for totally disconnected compact groups. This expansion guarantees that elementarity remains consistent with the original group topology. Building on results by van den Dries, Khovanskii, and Shlapentokh, we apply this expansion to formulate a compact first-order topological logic grounded in model-theoretic elementarity. We demonstrate several desirable properties of this logical framework, including compatibility with Pontryagin duality, decidability, and automata determinism. Additionally, we present a compact version of the Friedman-Harrington theorem. As an application, we utilize the desired behavior of elementarity regarding the topology to provide a new proof of the local axiomatizability of the $p$-adic field $\mathbb{Q}_p$. Finally, we highlight an inconsistency between our proposed definition of a compact topological logic and the framework established by Montalbán and Slaman. The expansion of federated learning (FL) has been accompanied by growing concerns regarding privacy risks within distributed environments. Differential privacy (DP) has emerged as a robust framework for ensuring privacy protection, finding significant application in DP-SGD, the most prevalent implementation of DP in FL. However, as global models aggregate locally trained parameters, the federated server gains access to these intermediates, thereby exposing both model parameters and client models to potential attacks. This differential privacy shield is not infallible; under certain conditions, it may fail to guarantee privacy guarantees. Consequently, this study investigates the interplay between DP, FL, and fairness (fairness-DP-FL). We demonstrate that fairness-DP-FL encounters two primary obstacles: (1) fairness-DP-FC in federated server learning and (2) fairness-DP-C in local learning. To address the fairness-DP-FC challenge, we propose the Fairness-Aided Model Optimization (FA-MO) algorithm. For the fairness-DP-C issue, we introduce a privacy-aware fairness-aided local optimization (FA-PO) algorithm. Experimental findings indicate that: (1) fairness-DP-FC can be effectively resolved via FA-MO, and (2) the efficacy of FA-PO is constrained by the hyperparameter $\gamma$. Furthermore, we establish theoretical convergence guarantees for both proposed algorithms. Theoretical analysis confirms that both FA-MO and FA-PO achieve convergence, with FL methods exhibiting superior convergence performance compared to local optimization approaches. Ultimately, this work offers a practical framework for achieving fairness and privacy within FL systems. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/zhongyuanwang1990/Fairness-Privacy-FL.
