We investigate the connections between different dark matter models and leptogenesis scenarios. Specifically, we examine a scalar field responsible for dark matter that interacts with the visible sector, alongside right-handed neutrinos. Through one-loop corrections involving this interacting scalar, the otherwise stable right-handed neutrinos acquire a finite lifetime, enabling their decay into visible particles and generating neutrino asymmetry through CP-violating terms. Finally, we compute the dark matter relic density and correlation with the neutrino mixing angle $\theta_{13}$. This framework allows us to explore a broad parameter space encompassing both cold and warm dark matter scenarios. In particular, the warm dark matter case can account for the structure of small-scale structures in the universe. We also discuss the potential to constrain the parameter space through LHC collisions and future neutrino experiments. Finally, we present our findings. \newline

We introduce a learning-based control framework designed for systems with unknown dynamics operating in diverse environments. The approach utilizes multiple linear regression to estimate system dynamics from minimal data, alongside a greedy control policy for locomotion and manipulation. Furthermore, we propose two novel techniques to mitigate parameter estimation errors arising from model structure mismatches. The first method, called the Mixture Model, treats the true system as a convex combination of multiple candidate models. The second method, named Divergence Minimization Control, explicitly incorporates an unknown divergence term into the cost function of a model-based control policy. We demonstrate that this term can be efficiently approximated using the Bregman divergence between the learned and true models. Our analysis establishes the convergence of both methods toward model-based control policies when model mismatches are small. We validate our approach across various simulated and real-world scenarios, including robotic locomotion, manipulation, and even a mouse model, effectively handling model mismatches and parameter uncertainties. These results highlight the method's ability to learn effective policies with high sample efficiency. The numerical experiments illustrate the framework's versatility in handling both real-world and biological systems. Finally, we emphasize that the proposed methods offer significant advantages in computational efficiency, scalability, and robustness. The entire codebase is made available to facilitate reproducibility. This work demonstrates that data-driven control can outperform traditional model-based control when dealing with model mismatches and uncertainties with limited data. This requires minimal modifications to existing model-based control policies and can be seamlessly integrated into learning frameworks. Twin-field quantum key exchange (TF-QKE) serves as a method for generating encryption keys between distant nodes using quantum techniques, leveraging the twin-field protocol to overcome the rate-distance limitation found in standard QKE methods. This bottleneck occurs when feasible secret key rates at large distances drop to levels comparable to noise, enabling eavesdroppers using photon-number-splitting attacks to transmit only slightly fewer bits than the honest users, thus compromising security. To address this, TF-QKE requires comparing the relative phases of coherent states at the transmitter and receiver; however, traditional implementations demand that both users maintain this phase at identical frequencies with negligible drift over time. We demonstrate that by employing a modified TF-QKE protocol, the phase-locking requirement can be substantially relaxed. This modified approach involves characterizing local phase fluctuations and utilizing them during post-processing rather than enforcing strict real-time stability. Our findings indicate that the secret key rate of this modified protocol is only marginally lower than that of twin-field protocols with real-time phase locking, even at distances extending to thousands of kilometers. Furthermore, we show that the absolute secret key rate can be further enhanced by deploying entangled coherent states and implementing the optimal cross-correlated measurement strategy during local key reconciliation. Together, these modifications position TF-QKE as a highly promising solution for secure communication across ultra-long distances. Additionally, we anticipate that the technique of compensating for local phase fluctuations, as used in our modified TF-QKE, could be applicable to other quantum communication protocols that rely on coherent states and do necessitate real-time phase locking. Identifying novel vocabularies during inference is a difficult and largely unresolved challenge. We introduce a method that eschews the need for example data by utilizing pseudo bounding-box annotations. Our findings indicate that this approach facilitates the identification of novel classes, surpassing methods reliant on examples, particularly when both limited time and computational resources are available. Furthermore, we observe that even without explicit bounding-box examples, visual perception models can be effectively fine-tuned to extract features useful for learning object identification. To facilitate the clear and unambiguous detection of novel vocabularies, we propose a new metric: the False Positive Rate. Our results demonstrate that this method can identify novel vocabularies comprising objects with distinct visual appearances, sizes, and orientations. Additionally, we show that the method is robust against background clutter and partial occlusions. The approach is occlusion and background-aware, allowing it to adapt to specific environments and identify vocabularies unique to those settings. Finally, we illustrate that the method is computationally efficient, enabling the deployment of large visual representation models that are otherwise too costly to run on edge devices. The young massive star S1 in the Rho Oph A cloud is a candidate for being the first known high-mass multiple sequence (HMS) object. This study investigates the gas distribution surrounding S1 by analyzing the spatial relationship between ionized gas, atomic gas, and photodissociation regions (PDRs). We employed radio recombination lines (RRL) to map ionized gas, the RRL line ratio method to trace atomic gas, and the 21 cm line to identify PDRs. Our results indicate that the ionized gas forms a bipolar outflow structure oriented along the North-South axis, with a size of approximately 0.2 pc. The atomic gas exhibits a clumpy morphology, with dense clumps situated at the edges of the ionized gas lobes. Additionally, the PDR gas displays a thin shell-like structure aligned with the North-South axis, exhibiting a width of roughly 0.01 pc. We conclude that the ionized gas originates from S1's bipolar outflow, while both the atomic and PDR gas are driven by photoevaporation from S1. The spatial configuration of the ionized, atomic, and PDR gas is primarily shaped by the collimation of the outflow and the magnetic field orientation. This configuration may facilitate the formation of a massive O-type star within the PDR gas. These findings offer a novel perspective on the gas distribution around high-mass multiple stars and the interplay between outflows and magnetic fields in star-forming regions. Furthermore, this research underscores the necessity of using multi-wavelength observations to study the gas environment around HMS objects. Finally, the study provides constraints on the nature of S1, suggesting it is likely a high-mass multiple star rather than a protostar. These results also provide valuable insights into the nature of HMS objects and their role in the formation of O-type stars. The data from this study will be valuable for understanding the gas distribution around high-mass multiple stars and the feedback mechanisms they exert on star formation. The study of textual veracity has gained significant momentum over the last few years. This field involves classifying statements as true, false, or mixed, a process that depends on additional context. While traditional methods relied on statistical language models like LSTM and CNN, recent advancements have introduced Transformer-based architectures. This survey paper comprehensively reviews these recent approaches, covering both pre-trained and post-trained Transformer variants. Furthermore, we analyze the associated datasets and evaluate the current state of the art. Our goal is to provide a consolidated resource that will aid future research in the area of textual veracity. Additionally, we identify key challenges and outline potential directions for advancing Transformer-based solutions in verifying factual claimness. Finally, we conclude by proposing strategies to foster future research in textual veracity. Our insights are intended to assist researchers in selecting the most appropriate tasks and effectively leveraging large-scale language models for factual claim verification. A summary table is also provided in the Appendix for the convenience of readers. This study employs a factor model with unobserved common forces for mortality prediction, utilizing a dynamic factor model with time-varying loadings (DFM) and a structural factor model with time-invariant loadings (SFM). The primary distinction lies in how each approach treats common mortality forces: the DFM allows these forces to evolve over time, whereas the SFM assumes they remain constant. Both methods are evaluated using real mortality data from 13 countries. The results indicate that the DFM with time-varying loadings yields superior predictive performance compared to the SFM with time-invariant loadings. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the loadings in the DFM represent the time-invariant loadings of the SFM, effectively linking the two models. Finally, it is shown that the covariance matrix of the DFM's time-varying common forces can be estimated; this estimated covariance enables prediction via an equivalent structural factor model. This paper details the formulation of that model and its resulting predictive performance. The DFM with time-varying loadings is recommended for forecasting periods where mortality rates fluctuate significantly, while the SFM with time-invariant loadings is more suitable for longer-term predictions. Additionally, an extension of the factor model with time-invariant loadings is proposed to accommodate non-linear trends in mortality rates. This approach treats the change rates of level-shifting and slope-shifting common forces as time-invariant, thereby allowing for non-linear trends while maintaining the simplicity of an additive factor model with time-invariant loadings. This extended model is found to be the most effective for medium- and long-term mortality prediction. Finally, the paper provides recommendations for future research. Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) serve as the cornerstone of Deep Learning, which has achieved remarkable success across various fields, including image classification. To further enhance existing models and explore new architectures, Research Scientists and Engineers rely on Deep Learning experts or rely on their intuition to guide decisions. However, this reliance on human expertise is both time-intensive and laborious. To alleviate this burden, we introduce a neural architecture search method that automatically designs neural architectures for specific tasks. This approach employs reinforcement learning to identify optimal architectures, where the reward signal is derived from accuracy and F1 scores on validation datasets. During the learning process, the agent may encounter conflicting tasks, leading to interference between different architectures. This paper examines the causes of such interference and proposes a dual memory system to mitigate it. The algorithm successfully generated high-performance architectures across four distinct datasets. Specifically, for the ImageNet dataset, it achieved a 76.7% validation accuracy with 1.1 billion parameters and a forward pass time of 0.1 seconds per image. For the Pascal VOC dataset, it reached 76.8% accuracy using 20 million parameters with a faster pace of 0.004 seconds per image. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm significantly reduces interference, yielding higher performance and more consistent architecture quality compared to the baseline, while also requiring fewer parameters. The source code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/DeepLearningTechnologies/NAS}. Furthermore, additional results and source code can be found at \url{https://github.com/DeepLearningTechnologies/DualMemoryNAS}. Finally, this work was presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems 2019. Dual Memory Neural Architecture Search automatically discovers neural architectures that outperform manually designed ones by up to 10% in accuracy across multiple datasets. To further refine these discovered architectures and eliminate their interference, we propose a dual memory mechanism. The controller memory stores high-performing architectures, while the population memory retains those that have not yet been evaluated. By separating architectures with conflicting search dynamics into these two distinct memory pools, the algorithm effectively mitigates interference. This dual memory approach enables the discovery of high-performance architectures for diverse tasks. Time series data is extensively utilized across various scientific and industrial sectors, often demanding rigorous examination to derive valuable insights. While numerous techniques exist for this purpose, we present a comprehensive analysis of a feature-based approach implemented in R via the theft package. These methods support both multivariate and univariate datasets, covering stationary and non-stationary data as well as time series with irregular intervals. We demonstrate how theft facilitates the analysis and visualization of diverse features, including periodicity, entropy, linearity, and stationarity. Furthermore, all methods in the package are vectorized, enabling parallel execution for real-time data streams. The theft package contains more than 50 features and offers a simple yet extensible interface that allows users to easily add new features. We evaluate the theft interface against popular competitors, demonstrating that it is significantly more than 10 times faster than R's tsfeatures package and achieving similar speed performance with tsfresh when applied to industrial data. Finally, we illustrate several simple yet effective applications of theft-based features using data from a real-world industrial use case. In human translation workflows, reliability assessments are essential for ensuring that translators consistently deliver high-quality results. This paper introduces a novel Bayesian framework for evaluating a translatator's reliability, modeled as a sequence of binary outcomes. While the translatator's reliability constitutes the primary unknown parameter, the study also considers unknown counts of reliable and unreliable opportunities. The reliability metric is represented by a Bernoulli process, with its prior distribution defined as a Beta law. Since the true values of these counts are typically unobservable, they are estimated using a Bayesian approach. The resulting methodology is straightforward to implement and yields reliable estimates even with limited data. A case study involving the assessment of a specific translatator's reliability demonstrates the approach's effectiveness. Furthermore, additional simulations and two real-world examples illustrate that the proposed methodology successfully recovers reliable estimates even when the observed series is relatively short. Overall, the method is recommended for its ability to enhance the quality of reliability assessments in translation projects. Finally, the authors acknowledge that, as an initial contribution to Bayesian reliability assessment in machine translation, further research is required to explore extensions of the model and develop techniques for comparing the performance of multiple translatators. **Keywords:** Machine Translation, Translation Services, Translatator Reliability,可靠性, 翻译专家可靠性. **Acknowledgments:** The authors extend their gratitude to the translatators who generously agreed to have their reliability assessed. Pruning techniques aim to remove redundant neural network components while preserving performance. A primary challenge remains identifying the specific characteristics that distinguish redundant parts from essential ones. By analyzing the properties of these winning subnetworks, we can refine pruning strategies to achieve better performance with fewer parameters. Our findings indicate that minimal convolutional networks identified by weight-magnitude pruning exhibit four key traits: they are highly sparse, concentrate most parameters within few channels, are significantly deeper, and broader than non-winning networks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these minimal networks are not isolated outliers but rather represent the dominant trend across the solution space. The characteristics of these small subnetworks offer valuable insights for future pruning algorithms. Additionally, we trained subnetworks using our proposed algorithm based on these insights and empirically confirmed that it outperforms the standard Weighted Magnitude Pruning algorithm. Finally, we highlight that these results are particularly pronounced in convolutional networks, leading us to pose a question about whether fully connected networks can also serve as the winning lottery ticket for convolutional networks. Empirical evidence confirms that they can. This study introduces a new framework for analyzing lottery games by incorporating the concept of future players. Within this approach, the "anticipated value" of a ticket is defined as the expected net profit for an individual buyer, accounting for the competition against all other contestants. This model demonstrates that a lottery ticket possesses positive value if and only if the price is reduced to a level below the cost of value information; under these conditions, paying a premium is suboptimal. We apply this theory to determine the optimal strategies for buying and selling "how-to" guides. Furthermore, preliminary empirical results from a controlled experiment validate these predictions. Consequently, this research offers a novel economic perspective on the "hot hand" phenomenon in lotteries, which suggests that when the price is low enough to make value information profitable, the probability of a ticket yielding a positive return increases as the number of future players rises. Ultimately, this indicates that lotto players should be more wary of the house when they possess early knowledge of the draw outcomes. Finally, we examine the implications of this finding for time-dependent price setting in dynamic pricing scenarios. Specifically, the model suggests that when the cost of value information is low, revenue can be maximized by initially underpricing the ticket to encourage widespread adoption of "how-to" information, followed by raising prices once this information becomes available to future players. Furthermore, to capitalize on the increased likelihood of positive returns among informed agents, revenue can be maximized by raising prices immediately after the draw once the value of this information begins to decay. Finally, we demonstrate that standard revenue-maximization models fail to account for the impact of value information, and our framework offers new insights into understanding and mitigating the potential harms of gambling addiction. By providing new empirical evidence, we show that price increases can lead to both higher revenue and the destruction of positive-value tickets, thereby exacerbating the problem of gambling addiction. Finally, we outline how our framework can offer guidance on establishing appropriate price points to prevent lotteries from becoming addictive. **Keywords:** Gambling, Gambling Addiction, Dynamic Pricing, Price Discrimination, Time-Dependent Pricing, Rationality, Information Asymmetry. **JEL Classification:** D03, D81, L81, L82. **Acknowledgments:** We are grateful to the participants of our experiment, as well as to Michael Adler, David Babcock, David Beshears, Matthew Johnson, David Laibson, Matthew List, Matthew Niederle, David Reilly, Matthew Shapiro, Matthew Weinzierl, and

Valley physics has gained significant attention for its potential to revolutionize information processing and security. This study investigates how new electron-phonon coupling pathways influence valley transport within two-dimensional materials. We introduce a non-equilibrium valley model that incorporates both intravalley and intervalley deformation potential couplings, as well as phonon-assisted scattering, to account for phenomena such as non-zero phonon current, the valley Hall effect, and phonon-driven charge current. These effects arise from the interaction between intervalley and intravalley coupling channels, alongside phonon-assisted scattering events connecting the same valleys. To validate the model, we analyzed graphene, graphene nanoribbons, and transition metal dichalcogenides. Our findings indicate that the predicted effects are most pronounced in graphene nanoribbons due to the presence of a local minimum near the valleys. This region facilitates the opening of additional intravalley coupling channels and enables phonon-assected scattering, leading to the observed physical phenomena. Consequently, the valley Hall effect in graphene nanoribbons is anticipated to be more distinct than in other two-dimensional materials, making them ideal candidates for the development of phonon-assisted valley devices. Additionally, we demonstrate that the non-equilibrium valley structure can be manipulated by adjusting external parameters, such as the nanoribbon width. This controllability offers a promising avenue for designing systems capable of achieving the desired valley states. These results are expected to advance the understanding of electron-phonon interactions in two-dimensional materials and facilitate the creation of novel devices utilizing these interactions. Ultimately, this research holds great promise for driving future advancements in the field of valley physics. This study presents diagrammatic Monte Carlo results for the 2D Fermi polaron in the presence of a single attractive impurity. We calculate the polaron binding energy and effective mass, comparing our polaronic series of diagrams with established variational energies and mass estimates for 2D Fermi systems with a single impurity and/or an additional bosonic particle. Our diagrammatic Monte Carlo energies align well with variational ones, while our computed binding ratios for mass show good agreement with prior diagrammatic findings and variational methods. We demonstrate that the series of diagrams we sample exhibits moderate signs of alternating character, allowing for the resummation of the series to significantly reduce the systematic error of truncated calculations. This approach extends the valid range of polaron binding energies and effectively addresses the mass, for which no equivalent diagrammatic series exists. We also determine the polaron decay width via diagrams for the self-energy that surpass the order of the polaronic expansion, showing excellent agreement with variational estimates. Finally, we demonstrate that the polaron series converges for a binding energy ratio of approximately $-0.45$, which corresponds to the Mott transition in the impurity-doped superfluid phase. This marks the first time the impurity-driven superfluid-to-insulator transition has been reached through direct diagrammatic Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we examine the diagrams and find that the leading contributions to the mass arise from the same class of diagrams as those for the energy, resulting in a slower convergence for the mass series. Consequently, the mass exhibits greater divergence, with the polaron series becoming non-convergent at a binding energy ratio of roughly $-0.3$. We discuss these findings in the context of other methods and previous diagrammatic Monte Carlo calculations. Our findings offer a comprehensive and direct validation of the impurity-driven Mott transition within the impurity-doped superfluid phase. Furthermore, we have identified a new diagrammatic series for the two-particle Green's function that converges in the range of binding energy ratios between $-0.15$ and $-0.45$, covering the ground state to the strongly bound state. This enables a direct observation of the two-particle gap closing at the two-particle Mott transition. We also present the first calculation of the excitation spectrum of the impurity, revealing a flat band at the bottom of the continuum and a direct gap to the two-particle continuum. While the primary focus is on $4\times 4$ cases, we also examine specific instances of $5\times 5$ and $6\times 6$ arrowhead matrices. By leveraging these properties, we can generalize the theorems to cover a broader class of matrices. The analysis indicates that the choice of $h$ significantly impacts stability, as it directly alters the determinant's sign. Consequently, we establish a necessary condition for $h$ to ensure stability. The CMS Collaboration reports measurements of electrons generated from the semi-leptonic decays of charm hadrons at midrapidity, derived from Pb-Pb collisions at a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The differential elliptic flow, defined as $v_2/\langle v_2\rangle^\pi$, is analyzed across various electron $p_{\rm T}$ bins for events with 0–60% centrality. Comparisons with theoretical models incorporating both initial- and final-state mechanisms indicate that the observed elliptic flow results from a combination of path-length-dependent partonic energy loss during propagation through the quark-gluon plasma and the final-state hadronization of deconfined partons. The study concludes that an elliptic flow ellipticity of approximately 10% is required to reconcile the CMS experimental data with these theoretical models. These findings support the existence of a hot, strongly interacting medium capable of generating significant collective motion for semi-leptonic charm decay electrons. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that final-state models successfully describe the measured $v_2/\langle v_2\rangle^\pi$ ratios, with a path-length-dependent partonic energy loss during propagation through the quark-gluon plasma being essential. This confirms that final-state models can effectively account for elliptic flow in semi-leptonic charm decays, offering valuable insights into the production of high-$p_{\rm T}$ charm quarks. Additionally, the paper addresses several aspects of the CMS experimental results, including the selection of leptons from semi-leptonic charm hadron decays, the measurement of $v_2$, and the comparison with both initial- and final-state models. Finally, the study underscores the necessity of incorporating final-state effects into the interpretation of semi-leptonic charm decay electron data. This research investigates Christian M. M. Maes's chromatic $\alpha$-structure within persistent homology. We begin by defining chromatic $\alpha$-structures as sequences of nested chromatic complexes generated by a specific coloring of a space $X$. Subsequently, we move beyond the original geometric motivation to introduce "motivic" $\alpha$-structures, which consist of chromatic (co)homology groups featuring chromatic maps and connecting (co)boundary maps. Leveraging this general framework, we examine $\alpha$-structures arising from a finite vertex-weighted graph $G$, demonstrating that they are chromatically equivalent to a specific $G$-motif. Furthermore, we explore $\alpha$-structures linked to a two-coloring of a simplicial complex $\Delta$, which yield an explicit expression for the persistent homology of these structures. Finally, we analyze the persistent homology of chromatic (co)homology within the context of a two-coloring of $\Delta$, yielding explicit formulas for the rank invariants of this persistent (co)homology. Notably, when $G$ is an $n$-cycle, our findings regarding two-colored chromatic (co)homology align with previous results by Maes et al. and by Farber et al. on persistent homology for $G$-motifs in the case of $n=4$. These results establish a new connection between the persistent homology of $4$-gons and the persistent homology of 2-colorings of simplicial complexes. In this sense, this work extends Maes's initial findings on $4$-gons to motivic and 2-colored $\alpha$-structures. Through the persistent homology of $n$-gons, we aim to uncover a persistent pattern for $n$-ary $\alpha$-structures. This potential pattern elucidates the intricate relationships among chromatic (co)homology, $\alpha$-structures, patterns, and persistent homology across various contexts. Ultimately, this persistent pattern serves as a foundation for the persistent homology of $n$-ary $\alpha$-structures. Notably, our approach to 2-colored $\alpha$-structures offers a distinct alternative to the persistent homology of $n$-gons, which relies on the persistent homology of $n$-ary $\alpha$-structures. This study examines the $K$-user Gaussian interference channel (GIC), evaluating the maximum generalized degrees of freedom (GDoF) benefit of optimal non-linear power control over binary power control. Assuming each user must achieve at least $\kappa$ GDoFs, constraints are established for $K$ interference-aligned subspaces, aiming to maximize the total network sum-rate GDoF. The resulting optimization problem demonstrates that the extreme GDoF-rate gain of optimal power control relative to binary control (where users are either active at maximum GDoF or silent) scales as $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ for a fixed $\kappa$. Furthermore, utilizing the convexity of the optimization problem, we prove that the $K$ optimal transmit power levels used for interference alignment within the downlink GIC ($\mathrm{GIC}_{\mathrm{D}}$) form an arithmetic progression. This finding confirms the conjecture proposed in [1] regarding the power spectrum of the $\mathrm{GIC}_{\mathrm{D}}$. Finally, we present numerical results supporting these conclusions.

Data categorization serves as a fundamental mechanism for managing information in large-scale systems, where categorizing information assets is essential for effective security and privacy controls. However, data attributes can become inconsistent or evolve over time, causing categories to become outdated and necessitating updates. The primary challenge lies in determining the optimal categorization strategy, which involves selecting not only the correct categories but also the proper depth, as excessive granularity can hinder practical security and privacy management. This paper introduces a method for adapting information categorizations that simultaneously optimizes both the depth and the specific chosen categories. The proposed algorithm utilizes formal concept analysis and Dempster-Shafer theory to dynamically refine the categorization of information assets based on real-time attribute changes. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the method's utility in developing a tool that generates multiple candidate categorizations, allowing domain experts to select the most suitable option from various alternatives. This approach supports multi-perspective categorization, facilitating the integration of diverse viewpoints, such as those of security and privacy specialists. Finally, the paper concludes by discussing the method's applicability to other domains. Additionally, the authors identify current limitations and propose future research directions aimed at enhancing the algorithm's efficiency and scalability. The Strauss process is a inhomogeneous point process defined by an intensity function, with the additional constraint that no two points can be placed within a specific mutual range. This paper investigates the "creating from" formulation of this process, which focuses solely on the distribution of point configurations within a bounded region, independent of the rest of the space. We demonstrate that if point patterns outside a given bounded domain are \emph{stitched} together in an appropriate manner, the resulting configuration can be modeled as a point process on a new domain. Specifically, we establish that the creating-from Strauss process can be reconstructed using standard point process techniques, provided the stitching method satisfies a simple verifiable condition. Furthermore, we introduce a stitching technique based on the \emph{interval factorization measure} developed by \cite{Bilham2019}. This factorization decomposes the partition function into a product of one-dimensional marginal functions, a property we extend to higher dimensions. We provide a negative result indicating that this modeling approach is limited to Strauss processes with very simple intensity functions. However, by combining this method with another recently developed technique, we show that our strategy can successfully stitch together more complex piecewise functions. Finally, we extend our findings to a generalized Strauss process where the exclusion constraint allows for the existence of small clusters. In this context, we utilize \emph{conditioned partition functions} instead of the partition function to track changes in point configurations and employ \emph{conditioned interval factorization} rather than the standard version. This yields a sufficient condition for stitching that is nearly as permissive as our initial condition. We conclude by outlining how these findings can be applied to create a creation-from model for the Ising model. \textbf{Keywords:} point process, partition function factorization, Ising model, exclusion process. \textbf{MSC 2010:} 60D05, 60G60, 82B21, 82B26. \textbf{AMS 2010:} 60D05, 60G60, 82B21, 82B26. \textbf{Primary 2010:} 60D05, 60G60, 82B21, 82B26. \textbf{Classification:} 60D05, 60G60

The generalized uncertainty principle (GUP), which extends the Heisenberg uncertainty principle (GUP) and is motivated by string theory and quantum gravity, is examined in detail. This exploration reveals that the GUP inherently introduces an ultraviolet (UV) cutoff, implying a minimum resolvable length. A fundamental inquiry arises: can this minimum length be absolute, or is it subject to Lorentz contraction at high energies? Two distinct scenarios are analyzed. The first posits an absolute minimum length, leading to a modified Galilean transformation (GUT) that remains consistent with the invariance of the generalized commutation relation (GGR). The second scenario assumes Lorentz invariance, where the minimum length is not contracted; this necessitates a deformation of the Lorentz transformation (LTRANS) to preserve the GGR. In both cases, the algebra involving position and momentum operators is derived, and the superposition principle is confirmed. Furthermore, both the modified Galilean and Lorentz transformations maintain the form invariance of the GGR. Finally, the composition of velocities under these modified Lorentz transformations is calculated. These findings demonstrate that the GUP, combined with the generalized Lorentz transformation (GLT), offers a consistent framework for describing quantum systems at very short distances. Notably, the GLT deviates from standard Lorentz transformations, indicating that Lorentz transformations require modification in the presence of quantum gravity effects. Consequently, these results provide a rigorous foundation for the claim that quantum gravity fundamentally alters the Lorentz transformation. The study concludes by outlining potential experimental tests for these predictions. Additionally, an appendix is included to derive the explicit time-dependent form of the modified energy-momentum relation. Finally, various references are provided, which could serve as the basis for an alternative approach to quantum gravity. Overall, this work represents a significant advancement in the ongoing quest for a quantum theory of gravity. This study addresses a multitasking service systems problem rooted in cloud computing, where multiple customers share services across various tasks. In this framework, time is divided into units, and each unit for a given customer constitutes a "call," which can be processed either individually or jointly with other calls from different customers. When processed jointly, multiple calls consume one unit of time through shared processing. The primary design challenge involves determining the probability with which each call should be selected for shared processing. We examine scenarios involving both known and unknown call arrival patterns. For both scenarios, we demonstrate that a specific design maximizes total revenue (equivalent to minimizing cost) by achieving the highest possible average progress for each customer, contingent upon respecting service level agreements (SLAs). These results hold even when joint processing is subject to capacity limits. Furthermore, we extend our findings to settings where capacity is uncertain and capacity-constrained call processing is governed by a Markov decision process. Additionally, we consider a setting where call arrival patterns are unknown but can be inferred from historical data. Finally, we provide a comprehensive numerical analysis comparing our proposed designs against naive alternatives. Specifically, we utilize real-world data from Amazon EC2 to illustrate the significant revenue gains achievable with our methods. Additionally, we establish a lower bound on the number of calls required to accurately estimate an arrival pattern and show that our designs remain effective even when this bound is nearly met. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first work to systematically and rigorously analyze the allocation of shared processing for call-like services. Furthermore, we believe that many techniques employed in this study are applicable to a broad range of practical shared processing problems. **Keywords:** Multitasking, Cloud Computing, Call Processing, Call Center, Resource Allocation. **MSC2010:** 90B35, 90C39, 90C25, 90C27, 90C31, 60J10. **AMS:** 90B35, 90C39, 90C25, 90C27, 90C31, 60J10. **DOI:** 10.1287/epoc.2021.0160. **History:** October 2021. **Affiliation:** Cornell University. **Date:** October 14, 2021. **Time:** 11:11. **Location

To enhance terrain adaptability for legged robots, this paper introduces a flexible footpad design based on a monopod and viscoelastic structure. Utilizing the contact dynamics framework, the model equations are established, and the Poincaré map, which maps the state at the beginning of the flight phase to that at its end, is derived for numerical simulation. The viscoelastic structure, modeled using the Kelvin-Voigt framework, exhibits nonlinear damping force behavior relative to oscillation frequency. Consequently, the robot demonstrates increased sensitivity to footpad deformation even under minor impacts. Theoretically, the energy loss within the footpad serves as the primary mechanism for achieving stable hopping. Numerically, the energy dissipation is significantly greater during the foot-terrain interaction phase compared to the viscoelastic structure itself. Furthermore, the model predicts that the footpad's behavior shifts from single to multi-valued as the compression amplitude increases. This multi-valued characteristic results in multiple stable hopping orbits, thereby boosting sensitivity to initial conditions and reducing the robot's adaptability to sudden impacts. To mitigate this, the damping coefficient of the footpad's viscoelastic structure must be increased. This finding was validated experimentally, where an optimized model with an enhanced damping coefficient demonstrated superior adaptability to terrain undulations. The proposed model and design offer a method to balance stable hopping and terrain adaptability in biologically inspired robots. The methodologies utilized in this study can be extended to other monopod viscoelastic structures. Additionally, the developed modeling and analysis techniques are applicable to various systems, including the bipedal robot introduced in our prior work. Internet of Things (IoT) firmware updates (FUTs) are essential for enhancing cybersecurity and functionality, yet FUT-enabled infrastructure often suffers from reliability issues, particularly during deployments, leading to prolonged outages. This study evaluates FUT reliability and human intervention requirements across various wireless technologies and network scales. We conducted extensive live network experiments across four distinct environments—campus, city, industrial, and home—using LoRaWAN and Zigbee protocols, involving 2,000 devices and 100 users. Our findings indicate that successful FUT execution depends on three critical factors: the size of the de-centralized mesh network, the volume of users, and the density of the De-centralized Mesh Network (DMN). Consequently, our results demonstrate that FUTs are most effective when applied to LoRaWAN in large-scale, high-density DMN settings. Furthermore, we observed that while configuring and managing FUTs requires more time than the update process itself, human involvement is necessary to mitigate reliability challenges, especially in bigger networks. Finally, we introduce an open-source framework that facilitates easy-to-use, reliable, and scalable FUT deployments, with the LoRaWAN implementation available on GitHub. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale, real-world investigation of FUTs across diverse environments, protocols, and densities. The associated data can be accessed at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7108104. Our ultimate goal is to assist practitioners in selecting the optimal wireless technology and planning FUT deployments to ensure reliability and security. We believe this work will significantly advance the reliability of FUTs in practical settings. The entire paper is available at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7108095. We demonstrate that the scaling of the Fock space propagator across the many-body localization (MBL) phase transition, as a function of the deviation from the critical point $f$, exhibits a distinct variation as the number of bodies $N$ increases. This scaling relation holds valid for systems with up to $N=15$ bodies. Our findings indicate that the shift in the scaling law for $f$ experienced by the MBL phase remains constant as $N$ grows, a stark contrast to the linear scaling of the shift in the phase transition point $h_c$ with respect to $N$. We attribute this differing scaling behavior to the sensitivity of $h_c$ to the spectral density near zero energy, which is influenced by multifractal characteristics. This sensitivity proves robust even at the phase transition, where these properties are independent of system size. Additionally, we calculate the scaling of the spectral density with respect to $N$ and establish a lower bound for the multifractality index, which scales linearly with $N$ at the phase transition. This linear scaling of the multifractality index applies specifically to the smallest Krylov space, which is capable of resolving the spectral density. Our results provide a clear quantitative framework for the scaling behavior of the Fock space propagator near the phase transition. We conclude by discussing the implications of these findings for the existence of MBL in the thermodynamic limit. Finally, we note that the observed scaling behavior is not unique to the MBL phase; it also appears in other well-studied systems, such as the one-dimensional transverse field Ising model and the Kitaev model. In the latter case, the shift in the phase transition point shows excellent scaling behavior with $N$, which is essential for accurately locating the transition. We also examine the presence or absence of a thermodynamic phase transition in the free-fermion model. We begin with a review of the MBL phase, followed by the numerical exact diagonalization (ED) scheme used in this study. Interactive search offers a flexible framework for modeling real-world retrieval scenarios where a user collaborates with a system to identify target objects. In this process, the user provides input in each iteration, and the system responds with a directed question to the next retrieval system, ultimately presenting a recommended set of objects. This loop continues until the budget is exhausted. Previous research on interactive search typically assumed a single target; however, many practical applications involve multiple targets. For instance, a user might simultaneously seek both the highest-grossing animated film and the highest-grossing live-action film. This study examines interactive search under a shared budget constraint for multiple targets, a setting that presents unique challenges. We propose a novel objective function designed to balance the number of targets identified with the search efficiency. To address this challenge, we develop several algorithms, including a new method called the consensus-based algorithm (CBA), which constructs the next query based on the consensus of a set of recommended objects. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing baseline methods in interactive search for multiple targets. To our knowledge, this represents the first research on interactive search targeting multiple objects. The code and data are accessible at https://github.com/1148102266/BILIS4MLSD19. Furthermore, we showcase a web application for interactive image search built upon our method, which is available at https://interactive.search/. Finally, we discuss the application of interactive search to graph retrieval and list several potential directions for future research. Quantum classifiers hold potential for realizing speedups in machine learning classification, though their reliance on probability distributions makes them susceptible to adversarial attacks. This study investigates the adversarial robustness of quantum classifiers, demonstrating the existence of adversarial examples that induce classification errors. Furthermore, we reveal that the Reduction Principle allows the transfer of adversarial instances from classical classifiers to the universal threat model applicable to quantum classifiers. Additionally, we explore the concept of quantum classifier hardening, where applying specific transformations to the input can enhance adversarial robustness. Experimental results indicate that the classical Hadamard-Walsh transform is an effective hardening technique, and we provide recommendations for input transformations that facilitate adversarial robustness in quantum classifiers. Finally, we examine the quantum adversarial training problem, showing that applying gradient descent to quantum adversarial training input data produces similar outcomes to training quantum neural networks using the Variational Quantum Gradient Descent algorithm. These findings offer a foundation for universally securing quantum classifiers against adversarial attacks. As a practical application, we utilize quantum adversarial training to detect anomalies in industrial equipment. In this study, the input is represented as an angle-encoded quantum state, and we train a quantum neural network trained input-wise. Our results demonstrate that this approach enables the detection of anomalies in industrial machinery. We conclude that these findings establish a basis for developing security protocols to protect quantum classifiers from adversarial threats. This serves as a significant step toward the broader goal of safeguarding quantum computing systems against adversarial attacks. To facilitate practical implementation, we have made our source code available on GitHub. This work represents a step forward in securing quantum classifiers and paves the way for future research in quantum machine learning security. Source code is available at: https://github.com/quantum-machine-learning-security. Conformance checking is a key element of process mining, focusing on identifying deviations between actual process executions and normative models. However, real-world scenarios often result in noisy event logs containing noise三类 (missing, false, and reordered events). To address this, recent research has introduced trace fragment alignments and algorithms for detection. This paper presents an infix alignment-based algorithm to verify the conformance of trace fragments against WS-BPEL and BPEL4WS process models. It also outlines how to derive the negative post-hoc process mine using trace negatives. Finally, an algorithm based on postfix alignment is proposed for detecting conformance violations in positive trace fragments. In both approaches, logarithmic time complexity is achieved for calculating, generating, and mining trace fragments, while conformance checking itself is proven to be NP-hard. Additionally, the paper proposes an algorithm for extracting trace fragments and their corresponding sub-process models from conformance violation reports. The proposed methods were implemented in the FCONCO checkers suite and validated using various benchmark event logs. Results demonstrate that the approach is highly effective for managing noisy event logs. Notably, in several cases, noise-induced conformance violations were successfully resolved, and significant insights were gained regarding the trace fragments and their sources. Furthermore, in other instances, the method identified the specific sub-processes responsible for noise, offering a valuable alternative to prior noise removal techniques. Finally, an empirical evaluation of an application case study was conducted to illustrate the method's practical utility. This case study involved verifying the compliance of trace fragments with specific business scenarios. In this analysis, the approach effectively highlighted potential risks and provided actionable recommendations for decision-makers. Overall, the proposed methodology supports business process monitoring and management by enabling conformance checking and violation detection on trace fragments. Moreover, it facilitates the investigation of noisy event log sections through negative post-hoc mining of trace fragments. Ultimately, this work offers a valuable alternative for post-hoc analysis of noisy event logs. The widespread adoption of 5G technology has led to larger cells and increased user density within coverage areas. This shift causes radio signals from different base stations to overlap, resulting in interference that degrades network quality. To evaluate and track these signal interactions, accurate models are essential. However, traditional radio propagation models often fail to capture the complex interactions between signal transmission and environmental factors like terrain and building materials. This study proposes a deep convolutional neural network as an alternative modeling approach, trained on real-world field measurements. The resulting model is tested in an office environment, and its performance is compared against standard models such as the 3GPP TR 38.901. Additionally, we demonstrate how this method can be extended to both predict and reconstruct interference patterns. The experimental results indicate that the proposed deep learning model outperforms standard approaches in predicting received signal strength, while showing comparable accuracy in interference prediction. Furthermore, the results confirm that the model is capable of accurately recovering real-time transmission data. Consequently, we conclude that deep learning-based modeling offers superior accuracy and provides a more comprehensive representation of radio transmission environments. These findings suggest that such models could enhance wireless coverage planning and support next-generation applications, including mobile augmented reality and digital twins. We introduce an extended temporal planning language that incorporates support for both non-deterministic functions and probabilistic constraints. For each program written in this language, we develop a corresponding probabilistic temporal Prolog representation and provide a proof of soundness regarding the verification process, utilizing Prolog's closed-world assumption. Furthermore, we demonstrate a general methodology for generating such probabilistic temporal Prolog representations for any temporal planning language that meets specific, easily verifiable criteria. This representation faithfully represents the original program's semantics under Prolog's closed-world assumption and employs a straightforward probabilistic logic program to model the program's non-deterministic and probabilistic aspects. Additionally, we establish a sound and complete connection between the temporal planning language and the temporal Prolog representation it generates, thereby enabling the application of existing formal verified verifiers to temporal planning programs. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first instance of a verified verifier operating on any probabilistic language beyond Prolog. Our experiments indicate that the generated probabilistic temporal Prolog programs can be executed efficiently by current probabilistic logic programming systems. Finally, we outline pathways to extend this representation generation process to other temporal planning languages and probabilistic logic programming systems. The results of our work constitute the most extensive and broadest coverage of verified verifiers for temporal planning to date. All definitions, proofs, and experimental code are derived from our previously published work, ensuring that this achievement represents the current state of the art in verified verifiers for temporal planning. Specifically, our work provides the most extensive collection of formal semantic definitions and their associated sound and complete verified verifiers for temporal planning known in the field. Power system expansion planning (PSEP) models are typically solved to identify optimal future network configurations, yet their results can be highly sensitive to input parameters. This study examines the model's responsiveness to variations in power costs, demand forecasts, and the probability distributions of renewable energy inputs. We introduce the Local Responsiveness (LR) metric, which quantifies the relative change in costs resulting from a small, localized increase in the unit investment expense of a specific technology. Utilizing the analytic model structure, we derive a formula for the LR density of this planning problem. The analysis confirms that the LR density remains positive, indicating that the total cost of an optimal solution always increases when a technology's investment expense rises. Furthermore, the density is highly sensitive to the mix of technologies, particularly when renewable sources are present. This insight is utilized to develop a new term for a generalized PSEP objective function; minimizing this objective yields a complete set of PSEP problem solutions that are significantly more robust to model parameter uncertainties. Consequently, this approach generates a solution set that is less responsive to parameter changes compared to other methods, such as linearly varying model parameters. Finally, we apply these findings to a simple power system, revealing that the generalized objective function provides a more diverse technology mix than the standard model. This diversity includes greater flexibility in renewable energy usage, thereby enhancing the model's ability to adapt to uncertainties regarding fuel prices and demand. Ultimately, the proposed objective function offers a practical tool for decision-makers to address uncertainties in power system planning. Additionally, it can be applied to other parametric optimization problems to manage parametric uncertainty. This potential application is demonstrated by applying the model to a quadratic optimization problem and subsequently comparing the resulting solution sets. This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for Vlasov-type equations coupled with boundary conditions linking electric fields in bounded regions, thereby addressing a longstanding challenge. Specifically, we prove that the Vlasov-Poisson system can globalize when incorporating Dirichlet, Neumann, or mixed boundary conditions. Furthermore, regarding a class of hard-core potential models, the paper demonstrates global well-posedness and analyzes the stability of stationary solutions. Additionally, we derive global regularity results for a low-dimensional Fokker-Planck-Fourier system under Neumann conditions on a bounded domain. Finally, to address a conjecture by Adams and Lions concerning mixed boundary conditions, we show that the local regularity established in this work is optimal. However, it becomes evident that global well-posedness for the classical Vlasov-Poisson model in bounded domains with mixed boundary conditions remains an unresolved and difficult problem. To address this, we explore an extension of the model by incorporating Poisson's boundary conditions, which significantly simplifies the boundary conditions for both the distribution function and the electric field. This approach yields global well-posedness results where none previously existed. Additionally, for Dirichlet conditions, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the long-term behavior of solutions. We demonstrate that solutions globalize even with only $L^\infty$ initial data for the distribution function, and we establish the regularity of stationary solutions, revealing qualitative differences compared to the unbounded case. Furthermore, we investigate stability issues in both bounded and unbounded settings. Our findings indicate that, in contrast to the standard model in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the extended model exhibits remarkable stability properties, including those involving negative charges. Finally, we examine a hybrid condition applicable to specific problems, thereby confirming the previously mentioned conjecture. This concludes our investigation into the long-standing issue of global well-posedness for Vlasov's equation in bounded domains with mixed boundary conditions. To achieve this, we have developed a novel and general framework for the electrostatic problem within bounded regions, a task that has historically proven extremely complex. Our methodology is designed to be versatile and applicable to various problems in both pure mathematics and physics. We have also addressed certain limitations of this generalization, with the hope of inspiring further research into the fundamental problem of global well-posedness for the Vlasov-Poisson system in bounded domains. Despite significant advancements in software development, software maintenance remains the most time-consuming and costly phase, largely because of efficient concept location. This process involves determining whether a specific concept exists within software and, if so, identifying all of its locations. We introduce STRICT, the first stack trace inference tool capable of handling both binary and source-level implementations. STRICT first parses software units to generate precise abstract syntax tree (AST) metadata. It then processes software call logs to derive multi-query key sets that represent concepts. Finally, STRICT computes similarity scores using retrieval metrics to pinpoint concepts within the unit. In extensive empirical studies, STRICT demonstrates promising performance, outperforming existing tools in various scenarios. This article examines the significance of the Collatz Conjecture in both mathematics and computer science. Although its proof remains elusive, the article explores why the conjecture is believed to be true by analyzing computer-generated graphs. Beyond its theoretical importance, special attention is also given to its popular cultural impact. Through examples and illustrations, we aim to make the article engaging for readers by demonstrating the simplicity of the problem, which invites intuitive approaches. Ultimately, we highlight that enjoying the mystery behind unsolved problems is a natural and valuable part of the mathematical experience.

This paper explores a method for leveraging mathematical entity linking to enhance STEM document understanding. We introduce a novel document re-ranking strategy that employs mathematical entity links as features for calculation, applied documents on a large corpus of raw papers and another on the ArXiv Synthetic Dataset. Furthermore, our method yields substantial improvements in the precision of mathematical entity extraction. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed approach substantially reduces error rates, thereby offering a step toward the automatic comprehension of mathematical expressions in STEM documents. While the stable marriage problem traditionally assumes knowledgable agents to derive optimal outcomes, many real-world contexts involve agents with limited information regarding others' preferences. This paper presents a study on best-proposing deferred acceptance when agents only possess a subset of known preferences. We evaluate multiple agent types—including independent, benchmark-aware, and optimal-agent benchmarks—and propose novel structures for agents to transmit to the matching mechanism, such as exhaustive-proposing chains and optimal-matching chains. These chains are selected based on the most probable known preferences of the agents involved. Finally, we assess the solution quality of these proposals by comparing them against both the benchmark-aware and benchmark-optimal scenarios. Experimental results indicate that for exhaustive-proposing chains, the first two alternatives are consistently chosen, whereas for optimal-matching chains, the second alternative is generally preferred. Furthermore, results show that known preferences significantly enhance solution quality, with approximately an 80% increase observed in the benchmark-optimal case. Notably, even a single agent's known preferences are sufficient to substantially improve outcomes. Finally, we recommend that matching mechanisms accept proposals from chains, as this approach yields substantially better results than random selection among all possible matching solutions. Overall, this study demonstrates that available known preferences can significantly improve the solution quality of stable matching problems. The proposed method is particularly beneficial for mechanisms serving large numbers of agents, where acquiring extensive known information may be costly or impractical. This research is the first to explore how known preferences can enhance solution quality, offering a novel approach to this challenge. Additionally, it is applicable to various mechanisms, including those with unstable outcomes like the top-trading cycles mechanism. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 outlines problem definitions and definitions; Section 4 details the method for generating known information; Section 5 defines solution quality; Section 6 outlines solution algorithms; Section 7 presents experimental results; and Section 8 concludes the paper. This work introduces a novel algorithm for reconstructing a multivariate signal with sparse structural sparsity using quadratic measurements. The proposed method is an iterative quadratic domain domain-driven dictionary learning approach named QDDLE. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that under specific conditions, the convergence of QDDLE within the local convergence framework guarantees unique convergence to a global minimizer. Furthermore, it illustrates that QDDLE can yield a near-minimizer for a more practical reconstruction problem. Additionally, we prove that both QDDLE and a related sparsity-constrained variant, QSDE, are stable even with high-compression ratios, enabling efficient reconstruction of high-dimensional signals from very limited data. Numerical simulations on multivariate random signals and data arising from electrical impedance tomography effectively validate the stability of the proposed algorithms. Furthermore, the theoretical results for the stability of QSDE are extended to handle noisy data. Finally, the paper provides examples of noisy data reconstruction across various application fields, highlighting the advantages of the new methods. Overall, this study advances the understanding and application of stable signal recovery from quadratic measurements. Fusion approaches combining camera and LiDAR data have become increasingly popular in autonomous driving research. Nevertheless, most existing methods first project LiDAR points into 2D image space for pixel-level fusion, which introduces various errors stemming from point cloud quantization and irregular sampling. In this paper, we introduce BEVFusion, a novel framework that performs multi-sensor fusion within the bird's-eye view (BEV) representation. Our approach projects each LiDAR point cloud sample into BEV space and directly fuses it with the BEV features extracted by a camera backbone. This fusion is achieved through a simple yet effective mechanism: a multi-layer convolutional network that processes camera features conditioned by the corresponding LiDAR point features. Additionally, we explore a variant that initializes the camera backbone's feature input using LiDAR point features, termed "fusion from low-level features." Experimental results demonstrate that BEVFusion is not only computationally efficient but also achieves state-of-the-art performance in detection and segmentation tasks. Our source code is available at https://github.com/PPV-AD/BEVFusion. We hope this work will be beneficial to the community.

This study examines dissipation-range turbulence statistics in the context of energy transfer and thermal fluctuations. We analyze the energy flux $\varepsilon_{\mathbf{k}}$ across three distinct scales: the injection range, where turbulence is driven by a single mode, and the dissipation range, governed by viscous effects. Our findings indicate that both inertial and dissipation ranges exhibit statistical symmetry, a characteristic typically associated with dissipation-range effects. Consequently, these effects must be considered alongside those in the injection range when scaling turbulent quantities. Furthermore, we observe that thermal fluctuations are damped by viscosity at high wavenumbers, a result consistent with prior research. Finally, we conclude that the seemingly contradictory behaviors of energy flux and thermal disturbance, as reported in existing literature, can be reconciled through the observed scaling properties of $\varepsilon_{\mathbf{k}}$. This represents the first such resolution to the apparent paradox. These conclusions are derived from a nonlinear framework incorporating linear physical mechanisms, which is supported by both numerical simulations and experimental data. While our model accurately predicts the behavior of turbulent and thermal systems, it also addresses unresolved issues in the field. Specifically, it offers a comprehensive explanation for the properties of statistically asymmetric turbulence and the data similarities between the energy cascade and thermal disturbance. Additionally, our data reveals a power-law scaling for $\varepsilon_{\mathbf{k}}$ at both injection and dissipation scales, a feature absent in both direct numerical simulations and linear theories. This suggests that linear mechanisms, including the backscatter effect, are more significant in fluid turbulence than previously believed. Overall, this work provides a holistic perspective on dissipation-range fluid turbulence. Notably, the scenario of statistically asymmetric turbulence, which has remained unexplained for nearly four decades, is now fully elucidated, thereby resolving a long-standing mystery in the field. This achievement is made possible by our nonlinear model, which extends the Kraichnan oblique shockwave theory by incorporating physical mechanisms. Our results demonstrate that such theories can effectively address the mystery of statistically asymmetric turbulence. Furthermore, the dissipation-range properties of $\varepsilon_{\mathbf{k}}$ predicted by the Kraichnan backscatter model have been experimentally confirmed, providing the first direct evidence of backscatter. These discoveries have significantly advanced our understanding of dissipation-range fluid turbulence. Finally, we have successfully predicted the physical data governing the interaction between thermal fluctuations and viscosity, thereby concluding the discussion on dissipation-range fluid turbulence. This study presents a multi-faceted analysis of heat transfer within a confined liquid using transparent liquid crystals. By employing both experimental methods and numerical simulations, we investigate the thermally refractive profile generated in the medium by a single pulsed laser beam. Our approach utilizes a pulsed top-hat laser and a lens to create a thermal lens, with the resulting focal power and its evolution over time measured via digital in-line holography. We track the temporal and spatial characteristics of the thermal profile across various experimental conditions. To address the strong coupling between the liquid's thermal and hydrodynamic properties, we developed a comprehensive numerical model incorporating the thermo-optic effect, heat transfer, and fluid motion. This model successfully replicates the experimental data and provides deep insights into the complex interactions between heat and fluid dynamics, thereby clarifying the mechanisms behind the observed phenomena. Furthermore, the complete description of the liquid's thermal profile enables the prediction of intricate diffraction patterns produced by straight laser lines in the liquid crystal. This capability facilitates the design of complex vector beams and multi-structured light patterns through straightforward laser scanning of the liquid crystal. Ultimately, this research underscores the significant interplay between fluid dynamics and the thermal-optic effect in liquids, a factor that must be accounted for in numerous applications. Key applications include thermal optics, liquid lenses, liquid-on-a-chip systems, and photonic devices. Additionally, the presented numerical model serves as a valuable tool for simulations in these specific fields. Design discussions in software development are frequently considered complex and prone to chaos, a view supported by existing literature. This paper challenges that perspective, proposing instead that such discussions are structured and adhere to a specific format that ensures stability. We define conclusion stability as the property where a conversation's end reaches a definitive conclusion regarding a particular topic, maintaining this state even after further discussion. Our approach involves identifying a formal grammar for natural language design discussions, which enables the detection of conclusion stability. Additionally, this grammar facilitates the creation of tools for extracting and managing discussions from software systems, a process demonstrated through two case studies. Ultimately, the paper argues that the concept of conclusion stability is valuable for developers engaged in systems requiring extensive design discussions. By providing clear answers to critical questions, these discussions can guide developers through complex design issues and prevent errors during implementation. Specifically, we examine whether conclusion stability can be utilized to address scenarios where developers struggle to initiate or sustain discussion threads. Finally, the paper explores how software systems with stable design conclusions can be effectively developed. To demonstrate this, we have released a tool that automatically generates comments from natural language discussions, which can subsequently be used to drive implementation. The authors argue that this capability enhances the value of the discussion by directly supporting the implementation process. Furthermore, a tool has been developed to extract comments from the Java source code of JUnit 4, a library known for having active and detailed design discussions, serving as a proof of concept. This tool successfully generates comments for 90% of the discussion points, thereby improving the quality of the Java code in JUnit 4. Ultimately, the paper posits that software systems equipped with the ability to extract value from natural language design discussions will exhibit higher code quality and require less effort during implementation. This is because developers can leverage these discussions to avoid errors and achieve successful outcomes. This work presents a series of illustrative simulations of cross-section data for single production of top and bottom partners across various scenarios, both featuring and excluding resonances. The resulting constraints are comparable to, and in certain regions exceed, those derived from analyses focused on resonant production. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has become a standard tool for knowledge base union operations, facilitating tasks like cross-lingual Natural Language to Knowledge Base (NL2B) and Knowledge Base to Natural Language (KB2NL) translations, as well as cross-lingual entity alignment. Specifically, within the SPARQL NMT framework, neural transducers have emerged as state-of-the-art solutions for end-to-end query generation from natural language. This paper addresses a practical challenge in knowledge base union operations: handling duplicate triplets, which are frequent in large-scale datasets. We introduce the Copy Transformer, a novel architecture that treats repeated triplets as special tokens within the query generation process. Evaluated against traditional Transformer models, the Copy Transformer demonstrates superior performance in producing consistent queries for duplicate triples while significantly reducing Query-Vector Space (QVS) size by minimizing the storage of redundant repetitive tokens. We introduce a new method for evaluating scientific papers that substitutes traditional citation-based (or impact) metrics. Unlike conventional approaches, our framework relies on analyzing the scholarly communities associated with each publication venue. By extracting structured data from citations, we construct a graph where nodes represent venues and weighted directed edges reflect citation relationships. Using community detection algorithms, we identify groups of venues with similar impact levels. Our core hypothesis is that a paper's importance can be adequately gauged by the communities to which its various venues belong. To validate this, we tested several methods on a dataset of 135,000 venues and 3.2 million citations from the Computer Science domain. We compared their performance against key, well-established citation-based metrics, demonstrating that community membership reliably predicts classical metrics such as CiteScore, total citations, normalized citations, field normalized citations, and relative influence. Additionally, we show that venues publishing the same paper tend to belong to similar communities, further supporting the use of publication venue analysis for assessing a paper's significance. Finally, we demonstrate that our approach effectively filters out venues known for low-quality publications. Given that our methodology requires no user input, is computationally efficient, and scales to very large datasets, we argue that it serves as a robust alternative to the increasingly problematic and manipulative citation-based metrics. Furthermore, we provide open-source implementations of all our methods. To illustrate the practical utility of these techniques, we developed tools for analyzing and comparing venues, detecting potentially low-quality venues, and evaluating a specific venue's standing relative to others in the same or different disciplines. Grouping is a fundamental capability for computer vision systems, facilitating complex tasks like map generation, place recognition, and 3D reconstruction. While most state-of-the-art grouping techniques are limited to identifying disjoint associations, real-world scenarios often demand the modeling of overlapping relationships. This paper presents a place recognition pipeline that leverages functorial hierarchical grouping to simultaneously extract landmarks, features, and overlaps from images. By employing category theory to define the overall structure of data processing, this approach offers a novel perspective on the field. We demonstrate that category theory serves as an effective framework for analyzing image processing workflows and propose a specific functorial grouping method. Experimental results show that this method performs competitively with recent disjoint grouping algorithms and establishes a new state-of-the-art in place recognition when utilizing overlaps. Furthermore, we find that carefully selecting which overlaps to model can significantly enhance performance. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianSchaeffler/functorial-grouping. Additionally, we have released a dataset comprising 2 million images of urban scenes from 1,000 cities, featuring annotations for landmarks, features, and overlaps to support research in this area. The dataset can be downloaded from https://github.com/SebastianSchaeffler/LandmarkDataset. Its usage is further detailed in a companion paper, also available at the same repository. Ultimately, this work aims to advance the community's understanding of functorial hierarchical grouping with overlaps, highlighting its potential to generate valuable insights for place recognition research. The proposed methodology is expected to yield significant improvements in place recognition outcomes. The paper concludes by outlining several promising avenues for future research in this domain. We anticipate that these contributions will inspire new directions and innovations within functorial hierarchical grouping and place recognition.
