Recent advancements in wireless communication technologies have enabled the emergence of the Internet of Vehicles (IoV), a system comprising interconnected vehicles within the broader Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem. IoV facilitates efficient data exchange between vehicles and road-side units to support critical applications such as traffic management, road safety, and autonomous driving. However, the rapid proliferation of connected vehicles introduces significant challenges, particularly concerning data privacy and security, as vehicles frequently transmit sensitive information to road-side units. To address these risks, Federated Learning (FL) has been proposed as a framework for training machine learning models using local data without direct exchange. Nevertheless, FL is not a complete solution, as it still requires the transmission of sensitive data. Consequently, the integration of Blockchain (BC) with FL has been suggested to resolve these remaining privacy and security issues. This paper presents a systematic literature review of recent research on blockchain-enabled federated learning frameworks for IoV, analyzing 27 studies to identify key contributions and advancements in this field. Based on this analysis, we propose an open research problem concerning resource-constrained edge nodes in IoV and outline potential avenues for future research. Additionally, we offer insights and suggestions to guide subsequent scholars in this domain. We believe this review will assist researchers in gaining a deeper understanding of the subject and exploring new directions for blockchain-powered federated learning in IoV. Furthermore, it serves as a foundation for advancing this field and will provide guidance to newcomers. **Keywords:** Internet of Vehicles (IoV), Federated Learning (FL), Blockchain (BC), Systematic Literature Review (SLR). 2018. 10.1109/ACCESS.2021.3055581. 2019. 10.1109/ACCESS.2019.2908102. 2018. 10.1109/ACCESS.2018.2722816. 2017. 10.1109/ACCESS.2017.2689119. 2016. 10.1109/ACCESS.2016.2567369. 2015. 10.1109/ACCESS.2015.2480528. 2014. 10.1109

This paper introduces a large-scale automatic tagging system for geospatial data within the VALUE project. Given the expansive scope of the data, our method relies on automatic processing rather than semi-automatic or manual labeling. We utilize open-source software to generate labels derived from diverse data sources, such as satellite imagery, point-of-interest information, and existing maps. The proposed pipeline processes and aggregates these individual contributions to produce and maintain up-to-date, robust tags for every image. VALUE represents the most comprehensive automatic tagging system currently available for large-scale urban imagery, handling a dataset of 1,000,000 images across 100 cities. We assess the system's performance regarding city-level tag accuracy and the temporal stability of tags, demonstrating that VALUE consistently provides reliable labeling for massive urban image datasets. The source code is accessible at https://value-project.github.io/value/. Our methodology is distinct from other large-scale systems, including Wikitude, which depends on semi-automatic tagging by volunteers and struggles to sustain image annotation over time. In contrast, VALUE is specifically engineered to deliver automatic tagging for large datasets with a focus on long-term maintenance. We evaluate the performance of VALUE-captured tags and compare them against tags from other sources, such as DeepMap. We demonstrate that the distribution of VALUE tags closely matches that of manually annotated manually labeled data, and after just six months, the accuracy of VALUE tags improves by 10% compared to manually labeled data. Ultimately, VALUE offers a practical solution for large-scale automatic urban tagging, capable of operating in real-time for satellite imagery and efficiently processing datasets of any size. This capability is essential for supporting decision-making in autonomous driving and robot navigation. VALUE can be deployed on any machine with a CPU, including cloud environments, and is not restricted to Stavanger. To facilitate this, we have developed a Docker image that encapsulates the VALUE processing environment, allowing for the automatic application of tags to any dataset. By deploying VALUE in Stavanger, we have successfully demonstrated a large-scale automatic tagging workflow for urban imagery. VALUE is now ready to assist other cities in implementing similar large-scale automatic tagging workflows for their urban imagery. Additionally, VALUE can be easily deployed in any city by simply providing a list of object occurrences within the city. VALUE is designed to be extensible, allowing for the addition of new labels through: (i) providing a city-specific occurrence list of objects, and (VALUE) (ii) training a new object classifier to extract labels from the city's imagery. This study addresses the nonuniform sparsity prior within the Bayesian framework. By integrating the proximal average method with Bayesian techniques, we derive a closed-form solution for posterior inference regarding both the hyperparameter and the image. Furthermore, we introduce NuSPAN, a proximal average network designed to learn the nonuniform sparsity prior. Our approach is validated through 2D synthetic seismic data, demonstrating enhanced sparsity and noise attenuation compared to the L1 norm. The NuSPAN network is subsequently applied to 3D seismic reflectivity inversion data. The methodology is versatile and can be utilized in other inverse problems, such as blind deconvolution and denoising. Additionally, the code is publicly accessible via GitHub. We demonstrate that the "wavefunction intersection" method effectively calculates universal finite-size corrections within scaling dimensions. First, we present data supporting the conjecture that the secondary peaks appearing in wavefunction intersection distributions correspond to every primary peak shifted by the complex shifts associated with the fused conformal family $\mathbb{1}\otimes \bar{\mathbb{1}}$. Subsequently, we apply this finding to the Haagerup model, deriving fusion rules for the fused family. Our results show strong agreement with predictions derived from the model's chiral algebra, enabling the complete determination of fusion rules through the measurement of the fused scaling dimension. Furthermore, by combining our findings with algebraic constructions, we establish lower and upper bounds on the number of primary scaling dimensions for the Haagerup model, which are $256$ and $288$, respectively. Additionally, we observe that the secondary peak distribution aligns with a Poisson distribution, and we prove that this phenomenon applies to all fusion processes. This observation facilitates the estimation of the total count of secondary peaks in the chiral primary peak distribution, yielding a lower bound of $256$ and an upper bound of $288$ for the number of primary scaling dimensions in the Haagerup model. Finally, we note that the techniques employed in this study are broadly applicable to other lattice models. Specifically, we utilize the technique to determine the scaling dimension of a specific operator in the critical transverse field Ising model, achieving a value consistent with the known exact result. This outcome demonstrates that our approach can accurately resolve scaling dimensions for operators in models where the operator fusion process is non-trivial. Overall, our findings indicate that operator scaling dimensions can be accurately determined through lattice methods without relying on the chiral algebra of the model. This conclusion is further reinforced by the recent measurement of the central charge in the critical transverse field Ising model, which was achieved without knowledge of the model's chiral algebra. Consequently, our results suggest that a lattice-based method for determining operator scaling dimensions is both feasible and effective. This development is expected to significantly advance the investigation of non-abelian lattice models, which are currently less understood compared to their non-abelian conformal field theory counterparts. Historical texts present significant challenges for computational linguistic applications, including natural language processing and text mining, due to deep syntactic, lexical, and contextual variations even over brief time spans. Part-of-speech (POS) tagging serves as a critical pre-processing stage for many text mining applications on historical data; however, the inherent uncertainty in determining a historical word's specific meaning renders standard single-value prediction inadequate. Consequently, we propose treating POS tagging of historical texts as a dependable set-valued prediction task, utilizing an enhanced probability-based confidence score to ensure robustness against annotation uncertainties, temporal drift, and lexical ambiguities. Evaluations using gold-standard datasets for 17 different 150-year-old languages across various time periods demonstrate that this novel approach consistently outperforms traditional single-value methods, achieving up to a 100% increase in confidence scores. Furthermore, we show that the reliability of set-valued predictions can be further improved by integrating etymological relatives and employing a part-of-speech-specific ensemble of transformer-based POS tagging models. To facilitate high-quality set-valued prediction for historical corpora, we introduce TIESPOS, a multilingual transformer-based POS tagging model enhanced with etymological relatives and adapted through domain-specific pre-training. TIESPOS enables the generation of multiset-valued predictions for 17 languages, spanning from the 9th to the 21st centuries. Our experimental results indicate that this multilingual approach yields up to a 16% improvement in POS tagging accuracy for historical corpora compared to state-of-the-art monolingual methods. The code and models for TIESPOS will be made publicly available. (Accepted to EMNLP 2021) https://nlp.cs.uni-siegen.de/nlt/pos_tagging/

This paper presents non-continuous integrability theory based on Deby's work, which developed a non-continuous form of Riemann's summation. Deby's contributions have historically been overlooked, despite the fact that his derived formula is equivalent to the modern Cauchy principal value. We outline the key properties and advantages of non-continuous integrability, demonstrating how it effectively handles functions exhibiting non-integrable singularities. Additionally, we explore various application methods, including finding primitives of non-continuous functions and developing a non-continuous form of Green's theorem. The study concludes by presenting findings from a specific case analysis of the square function. Finally, we propose a series of open problems aimed at further developing non-continuous integrability, with a specific focus on defining a non-continuous version of Stieltjès integrability. This extension is essential for maintaining a strong analogy with classical continuous integrability. Furthermore, we intend to generalize both continuous and non-continuous integrability by incorporating other well-known mathematical concepts. Specifically, we aim to develop hyper-complex integrability, which relies on the hyper-complex number system, and Fractional integrability, which is based on the concept of fractal dimension. The latter is particularly relevant given the significant role of fractals in modern mathematical research. In the final section, we present the historical context of Deby's work and analyze the impact of the non-continuous approach on the evolution of mathematics and its various applications. We also address the social implications of these outcomes. It is our hope that non-continuous integrability will gain the recognition it deserves within the broader mathematical community. Ultimately, we aim to foster further research into this area, thereby advancing mathematical understanding and knowledge. Through such efforts, we contribute to a more profound comprehension of the world and its underlying laws. Most significantly, we believe that non-continuous integrability holds the potential to enhance human lives. By promoting this field of research, we strive to create opportunities for individuals to achieve their dreams, thereby improving human existence. This perspective reflects our personal commitment to the non-continuous approach, which has been our primary focus throughout our lives. The effective execution of software projects relying on software-defined appliances for city services hinges heavily on accurately translating stakeholder needs into precise software speculations. This research introduces a formal framework designed to enhance project efficiency by automatically converting requirements into formal speculations. By employing an IoT appliance, specifically a Raspberry Pi, as a case study, we developed an automatic requirement collection system that integrates both hardware and software components. Furthermore, we implemented an automated conversion mechanism using a requirement engineering tool, QFlex, which extracts data from natural language statements via the Azure speech service. Finally, we outline strategies to further refine this system to facilitate the development of smart city initiatives. The proposed formal specification language, ISC, introduces novel constructs to more accurately model requirements, while the system successfully generates the corresponding software code necessary for the Raspberry Pi appliance. The complete code is accessible at: https://github.com/raufkhan123/Smart-City-Assistant. Our findings indicate that developing software projects within the smart city domain necessitates both embedded system requirements and software requirements. This approach significantly reduces costs and accelerates software development, thereby enhancing overall efficiency. Additionally, the method improves requirement quality, leading to superior software outcomes. This system offers a foundational solution for deriving software requirements in smart city projects, with the ability to be extended for extracting additional requirements. Future work will involve testing the system's effectiveness through both manual and automated means. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that smart city projects utilizing software-defined appliances can be developed with high precision, accuracy, and effectiveness. We anticipate that this system will serve as a valuable foundation for future research. The code is available at: https://github.com/raufkhan123/Smart-City-Assistant. Surface codes are widely regarded as the most promising quantum error correction framework, yet the development of low-overhead error correction circuits remains a significant challenge for near-term superconducting quantum devices. This paper introduces the hidden inverse (HI) protocol to construct surface code-based quantum error correction circuits. The HI approach effectively addresses faulty syndrome measurements and performs effective fault detection to mitigate cumulative errors. When applied to quantum error correction, the HI protocol successfully corrects single-qubit errors within the cluster. Simulation results demonstrate that a complete surface code decoding cycle utilizing the HI protocol can successfully detect and correct multiple faults. Furthermore, the HI protocol enables the implementation of quantum error correction circuits with substantially fewer physical qubits compared to conventional methods. Consequently, this work offers a viable solution for advancing quantum error correction technology in near-term superconducting quantum systems. Additionally, the proposed HI-based surface code error correction scheme is expected to benefit other applications relying on surface codes, such as quantum computing algorithms and quantum communication. The HI-based surface code implementation is available at: https://github.com/Quantum-Computing-Group/HiddenInverse. Keywords: quantum error correction, hidden inverse protocol, surface code, superconducting quantum devices.

In a regular category $\mathcal C$, we examine preorders and define their cocartesian representation, which involves mapping an object $A$ to a morphism $f_A:\mathcal C(a,A)\to \mathcal C(1,A)$ for every object $A$. We demonstrate that preorders possessing a cocartesian representation are equivalent to images of right exact functors that are both $a$-multiple and presheafable, as well as to images of representable functors that are right exact and both $a$-multiple and presheafable. Furthermore, we prove that any preorder with a cocartesian representation is isomorphic to the image of a direct limit of a diagram composed of subobjects of $a$-multiples. We also introduce and analyze the concepts of an equivalence relation with a cocartesian representation and the cocartesian representation of the "quasi-e" relation between objects in $\mathcal C$. Additionally, we establish that in a regular category $\mathcal C$, a preorder has a cocartesian representation if and only if it does in the category obtained by inverting epimorphisms. Within this framework of inverted epimorphisms, we investigate how to determine when morphisms represent an equivalence relation with a cocartesian representation. We provide sufficient conditions for an equivalence relation to possess a cocartesian representation within both the original category $\mathcal C$ and the category formed by inverting epimorphisms. Finally, we note that while the category of rings does not admit a complete representation of preorders with cocartesian representations via objects, such a complete representation exists for many other categories, including those of groups, commutative rings, graphs, sets, graphs, topological spaces, and those arising as completions of small categories along full subcategories closed under limits. We also explore the possibility of constructing a functor that assigns to each preorder with a cocartesian representation an object representing it. Specifically, within the category of sets, we prove that every preorder with a cocartesian representation is isomorphic to one represented by an object, and we characterize preorders with third-order representations that are isomorphic to ones having second-order representations. Additionally, we characterize preorders with second-order representation that are isomorphic to ones with first-order representations. Finally, we characterize preorders with first-order representations over the category of sets that admit second-order or first-order representations. The study investigates spatial extremal dependence within marine environments, motivated by the observation that multiple variables in marine extreme events often exhibit conditional dependence. To address this, a multivariate spatial conditional extremes (MultisCo) model is developed, which extends multivariate spatial conditional extremes (MulticCo) distributions by incorporating a multivariate copula with unique parameters for each pair of components. The MultisCo model enables the analysis of spatial conditional dependence across a multivariate point process by defining multivariate CopulaS conditional extremes (MulticCoS) margins. Parameters are estimated using the pseudo-maximum likelihood method in a multivariate block-maxima framework. A simulation study demonstrates that these estimation methods accurately recover the multivariate spatial conditional dependence structure. Furthermore, a case study analyzes multivariate extreme marine environments, with results indicating that sea surface temperature and chlorophyll- $a$ concentration display strong positive conditional dependence, whereas wind speed and sea surface temperature show strong negative conditional dependence. The findings suggest that these two variables may serve as effective predictors for identifying extreme marine conditions. Finally, the limitations of MultisCo-based inference are examined, and a potential improvement is proposed to enhance spatial MulticCoS margin estimation. Overall, MultisCo serves as a flexible tool for inferring spatial conditional dependence among extreme events in marine settings. Enhancing pre-trained vision-language models (VLPs) is a pivotal area of research with numerous applications, notably in vision tasks such as image captioning and detection. Most current approaches focus on constructing large-scale, high-quality datasets through data augmentation or generation to refine VLPs. However, since existing augmented datasets often retain the same biases and inconsistencies as the original data, they fail to significantly boost model performance. This paper introduces a novel method leveraging generated visual-directed images to improve pre-trained VLPs. Unlike text-directed images, visual-directed images offer higher fidelity and greater diversity. To achieve this, we propose a new model, VT-CLIP, which integrates text representations from CLIP with visual guidance from encoded images to generate diverse visual-directed images. Specifically, VT-CLIP employs a visual encoder to create image embeddings and utilizes a generator to produce varied visual-directed images based on these embeddings. We evaluate VT-CLIP across various tasks including image classification, object detection, and scene recognition, demonstrating substantial improvements on standard benchmarks. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the generated images and their impact on model performance. Our results and code are available at https://github.com/ruigzhang/VT-CLIP. The model can be accessed at https://huggingface.co/ruigzhang/VT-CLIP. This study develops a unified framework for linear operator transitions designed to address the control of noisy matrix systems within quantum technologies. By integrating the concepts of noise virtuality and complete noise virtuality, we establish the conditions required for an operator transition to function as a controller within a closed-loop noisy system. Specifically, the existence of a (complete) controller is equivalent to the existence of an operator transition that renders the resulting closed-loop system (completely) nilpotent. Furthermore, we formulate (complete) state feedback controllers based on this design principle, successfully solving the state control problem for various quantum technologies affected by Pauli noise. To demonstrate practical utility, we apply this method to construct controllers for the 1D cluster state preparation circuit, the cluster generation process within the noiseless quasi-adaptive stochastic quantum iteration model, and a quantum random access memory exposed to Pauli noise in the quantum read phase. These examples illustrate that our approach achieves state controllability in scenarios where traditional state control methods fail. Additionally, we analyze the existence and construction of controllers for quantum systems subjected to arbitrary Lie algebra noise, with potential applications in quantum error correction codes such as surface codes and color codes. Ultimately, this work proposes a novel method for constructing quantum controllers that expands the scope of solvable noise control problems in quantum systems. Image annotation is essential for tasks involving diagnostic assistance, such as identifying cancer metastasis in histopathology slides or pneumonia indicators in chest X-rays. These annotations typically consist of bounding boxes, segmentation masks, or scores for pre-defined classes like metastasis or granuloma. While deep learning techniques have advanced the field of computational pathology and radiology, manually performing and evaluating task-specific annotations remains a time-intensive process. DICOM, the standard for encoding image-related metadata, is extensively used in radiology and increasingly relevant in pathology, where digital scanners generate well-annotated slides. However, the current DICOM standard suffers from complexity and lacks specific tags for certain annotation types, such as scores. To address these challenges, we introduce highdicom, a Python library that extends DICOM to facilitate the storage, exchange, and evaluation of inferred labels and annotations. By providing standard encoding for common annotations and assisting users in creating new tags for custom requirements, highdicom offers a more robust solution than current workarounds. Additionally, it includes validation tools to ensure annotation quality and offers developer-friendly utilities for generating new tags. We investigate the boundary term within the Einstein-Hilbert action, demonstrating that it yields a Noether charge whose boundary contribution to the field equations defines a gauge transformation. This charge is non-zero in curved spacetime, whereas it becomes non-zero only at the boundary when applied to the pure Einstein-Hilbert action. We further show that the Noether charge associated with the boundary term generates the Virasoro algebra. Additionally, we establish that the entropy term utilizing the Noether charge of the boundary term of the Einstein-Hilbert action is equivalent to the Euclidean action term of a black hole, thereby achieving consistency with the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy formula. Furthermore, the null energy condition is satisfied, ensuring the second law of thermodynamics remains valid. Finally, we propose an interpretation of the boundary term in the Einstein-Hilbert action, suggesting it represents the entropy of gravitational degrees of freedom. These findings may have significant implications for quantum gravity research.

Current deep learning approaches that rely on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are primarily employed to extract features directly from DNA sequences. This paper introduces a feature representation derived through an unsupervised, high-dimensional Gaussian process latent variable model. By directly learning from DNA sequences, this representation implicitly captures fundamental biological insights without the need for sequence alignment. The resulting generic features prove highly transferable, enabling the training of multiple downstream classifiers to identify both coding and regulatory sequences. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method surpasses other feature learning techniques and establishes a robust baseline for downstream sequence classification tasks. Our method's source code is publicly available at https://github.com/SebastianSchwartz/DNA-GP. In this work, we concentrate on modeling exonic sequences. For the broader application of our method across various genomic regions, please refer to our subsequent publication: Seitz et al. (2021). Unsupervised feature learning in DNA sequences. Bioinformatics. 37(10):3001-3008. doi: 10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa1090. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa1090. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8024877/. Our findings indicate that coding sequence features extracted via our method (referred to as GP) are superior to those obtained using k-mers, k-mers+RNN, or DeepSig (an existing sequence alignment-based approach). While an alignment-free RNN-based approach yields the strongest performance for regulatory sequence classification, our GPs achieve comparable results. When applied to all sequences, our GPs successfully capture fundamental regulatory motifs, such as transcription factor binding sites. Our GPs exhibit transferability across different organisms, allowing for the identification of both human and mouse transcription factor binding sites when trained on human data and tested on mouse data. Our approach is complementary to our previous research (Seitz et al., 2021), which addresses a different aspect of unsupervised learning in DNA sequences. In that prior work, we demonstrated that GPs trained on sliding windows across the entire genome can identify evolutionary constraints, gene bodies, and regulatory regions. The current study focuses on training GPs on coding sequences to extract gene-level features. The role of surface modifications in inducing metal-insulator transitions (MIT) within V$_2$O$_3$ ultrathin films has been investigated using density functional theory (DFT) and density functional perturbation theory (DFPT). Our findings indicate that oxygen vacancies and oxygen adsorption on the (0001) surface significantly alter the MIT. Specifically, oxygen vacancy concentrations ranging from 12.5% to 50% shift the MIT from insulating to metallic states, whereas oxygen adsorption at 0.25 monolayer coverage on tetrahedral surface vanadium sites reverses this transition. Furthermore, the presence of oxygen in tetrahedral sites enhances the electron-phonon coupling constant, $\lambda$, in the insulating phase but reduces it in the metallic phase. These results demonstrate that the MIT in ultrathin V$_2$O$_3$ films is highly sensitive to surface modifications, a factor that must be accounted for when studying the MIT in vanadates. Additionally, these results may offer a pathway for developing oxygen vacancy switches based on vanadates. Finally, the MIT in V$_2$O$_3$ ultrathin films can be studied experimentally via photoemission spectroscopy at the (0001) surface orientation. We apply a specialized version of the Clebsch rule to transform arbitrary Lie-Poisson structures into a canonical form. In this process, we identify the links between functions residing in both the co-adjoint orbit and the Fock space associated with the Lie algebra's cohomology. This methodology simplifies the quadratic Lie-Poisson equations into a fully decoupled system. As an application, we utilize this canonical form to construct general solutions for the Euler equations of an incompressible heavy fluid with a specific domain. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to derive general solutions for the Euler equations of incompressible fluids from these canonical solutions. Additionally, we extend this solution scheme to barotropic fluids. Notably, our approach relies solely on solving decoupled first-order ordinary differential equations. Furthermore, we show that this canonical form yields a significant simplification of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation defined on Lie algebras. Finally, we highlight that this canonical representation recovers the established canonical models for ideal fluids. Solutions to these canonical equations represent general solutions for ideal fluids whose vorticity remains invariant under the co-adjoint action. This result holds true regardless of the dimension of the fluid's spatial domain. Consequently, this provides a novel solution to the Euler equations, a problem that has been a focal point of research for over a century. Finally, we present some open questions and potential future research directions inspired by these findings. This work extends the research presented in [1].

[1] V. V. Kozlov, Yu. V. Kozlov, and A. A. Kozlov, "Canonical solutions of the Euler equations for an incompressible fluid in terms of periodic functions," *Dokl. Math.*, vol. 100, pp. 1001–1004, 2019. https://doi.org/10.1070/DM8176.

Building on the research by F. Zhang and B. Hanack regarding conservation law controls, this study extends the work to systems exhibiting nearly conserved quantities. The study addresses both 1-D conservation laws and n-D compressible Navier-Stokes equations, demonstrating the input-entropy stability of the numerical approximations proposed. Furthermore, it confirms the network effect within non-linear conservation law systems using numerical examples, and numerical results for the compressible Navier-Stokes equations illustrate stability alongside near-conservation and entropy properties. Notably, unlike the conservation laws scenario, the network effect is not observable in the numerical solutions for the compressible Navier-Stokes equations. Additionally, the numerical examples regarding conservation laws were developed in collaboration with B. Székely. For readers interested in the relationship between conservation law controls and network science, a related paper is also recommended. Keywords: Conservation laws, Conservation principles, Conservation controls, Input-entropy stability, Numerical approximation, Network science. MSC2020: 35L65, 35Q35, 76N15, 65M99. Predicting the likelihood of a bank client becoming non-performing (NP) is a critical task for financial institutions, as identifying NP loans early allows for the recovery of lost profits and the mitigation of reputational damage. Recently, machine learning (ML) models have become prevalent in banking applications due to their superior performance compared to traditional methods, though this often comes with reduced interpretability. Consequently, there is a pressing need to evaluate the trade-off between model performance and interpretability to assist banks in selecting the most suitable ML models. This study evaluates the performance and interpretability of the top 10 most frequently used in-scope NP prediction ML models using a dataset containing 1,000 clients with 20 features. The findings indicate that the last 10 ML models achieve accuracy rates between 80% and 90%, closely matching that of linear regression, which serves as the first benchmark. Additionally, Shapley additive explanation (SHAP) was employed to perform feature importance analysis across these 11 models, revealing that the last 10 in-scope NP prediction ML models rely on similar client features to distinguish NP clients from healthy clients, while linear regression depends on more features. Overall, the last 10 in-scope NP prediction ML models demonstrate both high performance and interpretability, making them well-suited for practical application. Future research should expand the NP client dataset and develop methods to automatically tune the number of client features for linear regression and other in-scope ML models. Furthermore, additional analysis is required to identify the most distinctive features for NP clients versus healthy clients and to investigate the invariance of these predictive features across different periods. Finally, comparative analysis using data from other banks is necessary to determine if similar conclusions hold in different banking contexts. We define chromatic symmetric functions for Dyck trails and establish their connection to q-rook theory. This relationship enables a characterization of the functions using difference tables. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck trails are positively linear combinations of chromatic symmetric functions associated with disconnected graphs. Finally, we provide explicit expansions of these functions in terms of both elementary and complete homogeneous polynomials. Notably, the q-analogs of Dyck trail numbers appear as the coefficients of the q-polynomial, thereby validating the Conjecture by Carlitz regarding chromatic symmetric functions for Dyck trails. Additionally, we offer an explicit formula for the coefficients in the expansion involving elementary polynomials, which confirms the validity of the statement for minor dimensions.

Direction Convolutional Networks (DCN) augment standard DCNNs by appending a supplementary convolutional layer to the architecture's end, enabling the model to capture directional contextual cues for feature enhancement. This added layer utilizes directional convolutional kernels, where each kernel is represented as a collection of point features arranged in a specific spatial configuration. By employing directional convolutions, the networks acquire the capacity to capture contextual information from diverse directions. Comprehensive evaluations on diverse datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1000, across both training and testing phases, demonstrate the efficacy of DCN. The results indicate that DCN surpasses traditional DCNNs and establishes DCNN-GB as the superior model. Furthermore, our final DCNN-152 achieves the highest performance on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-2012 among all systems, securing the first-place ranking on CIFAR-100 and a second-place finish on ImageNet-2012. We present several applications of this relative trace formula, including a generalized version of Waldspurger's theorem, comparisons of periods between curved and standard groups, and the identification of linear forms invariant under both curved linear groups and their Lie algebra analogs. Additionally, we utilize this formula to establish the positivity of eigenvalues for the twisted Laplacian on curved Drinfeld modular curves; this result follows from an identity derived via the trace formula, which also connects to a relationship between local zeta functions of Drinfeld modular curves and their Drinfeld–Manin counterparts. This study revisits the top quark pole mass extraction from the differential distribution $d\sigma/m_Tdm_T$, derived from the main 2015/2016 LHC $t\bar{t}$ dataset. The investigation focuses on the impact of light quark masses on the measured top mass and other pertinent quantities. The analysis demonstrates that, given the current level of statistical and systematic uncertainties, this method yields a top quark pole mass of $m_Q=172.9\pm 0.8$ GeV, reflecting a slight but detectable flavor dependence. Furthermore, we compare the reconstructed transverse mass $m_T$ and the differential cross section at high $Q^2$ against findings from the 2015/2016 LHC $t\bar{t}$ measurements. Our results indicate that $m_Q$ exhibits a more pronounced flavor dependence than both $m_T$ and $d\sigma/dQ^2$, suggesting that measurements utilizing high-$Q^2$ data could offer greater sensitivity to the underlying flavor dependence of the top quark mass. Additionally, we examine the dependence on the renormalization and factorization scales, as well as the number of massless partons included in the analysis. Finally, we explore the relationship between the laboratory-frame reconstructed invariant mass $M_{t\bar{t}}$ and the pole mass, noting that $M_{t\bar{t}}$ shows an even stronger dependence on flavor. These observations are consistent with earlier studies. Overall, the paper confirms that the pole mass displays a light level of dependence on quark masses, which must be accounted for in high-precision mass measurements. The scale dependencies identified in this work may inform the design of $t\bar{t}$ analyses aimed at maximizing sensitivity to the top quark mass's flavor dependence. This paper proves that for any $k \geq 2$ colors and an integer $r$, there exists a constant $N$ such that every almost $k$-regular graph $G$ with $|V(G)| \geq N$ contains a subgraph $H$ induced by a vertex set of size $r$, where the edges of $H$ use at most $k-1$ colors. The degree of each vertex in $H$ differs from $k$ by no more than 1, and colors are assigned via a proper edge-tinting. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the bound $N$ grows exponentially with respect to $r$. The definition and initial exploration of almost regular graphs were introduced by Dvo\v{r}\'{a}k, Kr\'{a}li\v{c}, and Sudakov, who famously posed the question: Does there exist a constant $N$ such that every almost $3$-regular graph with at least $N$ vertices contains an octahedron? Our findings affirmatively answer this: For $k=3$ and $r=6$, there is a constant $N$ ensuring that all subsets of $V(G)$ of size $r$ induce subgraphs with at least one mismatching color. We believe this result is optimal. Additionally, we derive several corollaries that either resolve or significantly refine problems and bounds previously established in the literature. Finally, we examine the relationship between this problem and the graph coloring problem. For each $k$, we demonstrate that the bound $N$ grows factorially as $r$ approaches infinity. The global COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread fear and significant loss of life, yet diagnosing the disease remains challenging due to its nonspecific symptoms and limitations in current testing methods. Consequently, there is a critical need for a highly effective diagnostic tool that can rapidly identify infected individuals. This study introduces a two-stage time-distributed capsule network (TD-CN) leveraging neural differential equations to achieve human-level accuracy in detecting COVID-19 from low-dose chest CT scans. In this framework, a convolutional neural network (CNN) first estimates motion parameters for the TD-CN, which subsequently classifies the condition. We demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both classification accuracy and inference time. Specifically, compared to the best existing model, our method achieves a 0.7% improvement in accuracy while reducing prediction time by 50%. Furthermore, experimental results indicate that the model maintains human-level performance when trained on synthetic capsule tensors generated from synthetic CT images created from X-rays through diffusion processes. These findings suggest that our model could potentially enable human-level COVID-19 detection from low-dose chest CT scans using only chest X-rays as input. This paper introduces a mathematical framework for modeling the growth of low-Earth orbit (LEO) mega-constellations and examines the trajectory of increasing space density. We propose a metric known as space utilization, which represents the ratio of occupied spherical volume in radial direction within the orbital shell to the total volume of the shell. We analyze this metric across various satellite orbits and levels of space utilization, highlighting its utility in assessing the potential for new launches. Additionally, we explore methods for optimizing spherical volume allocation in LEO mega-constellations and address the challenges encountered when high inclination and eccentricity orbits are mixed. The study includes simulations of space utilization under different orbital configurations and constellation growth patterns. We also model the evolution of space utilization considering both temporal and spatial factors, while briefly discussing its reduction mechanisms due to de-orbiting satellites and natural decay. Finally, the paper concludes with suggestions for future research. Our findings indicate that once space utilization exceeds 50%, mega-constellations exhibit a strong tendency to aggregate, which significantly impacts the availability of adjacent orbits. Furthermore, we observed that the rate of space density increase accelerates as utilization approaches 100%. These results offer valuable insights for guiding the development of LEO mega-constellations. We introduce a new framework for generating coarse quadrilateral meshes on CAD models by mapping them onto an underlying quadrilateral grid. This process results in a coarse mesh free of T-junctions, ensuring that every quadrilateral connects exclusively at its vertices. The method supports CAD models with curved surfaces, mapping them to polyhedral domains defined by quadrilateral faces, with the specific mesh introduced as an optimization variable solved via an integer linear program. The system prioritizes producing meshes with an appropriate quadrilateral count and distribution, while enabling users to define regions with a high density of elements. These optimizations can either be executed automatically or according to specific user requirements. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in generating coarse quadrilateral meshes and highlight its flexibility in accommodating various user-specified requirements. Furthermore, the design facilitates the extension of existing quadrilateral refinement techniques, allowing them to produce high-quality refined meshes directly from the generated coarse precursors. The proposed system is implemented within the open-source ParaSolid suite, which is accessible at https://parasolid.org. Additionally, examples of CAD models from various industries, along with their associated coarse and refined meshes, are available at https://parasolid.org/quadmesh-examples. Finally, our open-source software is also accessible via the ParaDeps package available on Ubuntu's software repositories. This capability allows users to easily apply our technology to any CAD model utilizing standard file formats supported by ParaSolid. Specifically, users can execute our algorithm through the ParaModeler command-line tool, which provides user-friendly options for specifying regions requiring increased element density. To utilize this, users must simply provide a CAD model and the file name of the region to be refined. Through ParaModeler, users can also access various ParaSolid utilities for visualizing and analyzing CAD models and their associated meshes. These capabilities include identifying and eliminating T-junctions, as well as performing user-directed refinements. All outputs can be directly imported into ParaSolid for further examination and manipulation. Specifically, users can employ the QuadCheck utility within ParaSolid to assess the quality of the resulting meshes. In summary, our technology offers users precise control over specific regions of a CAD model, ensuring that quadrilaterals are densely packed where necessary. This represents a significant advancement over prior methods, which generally produced meshes with suboptimal distributions. Our approach delivers superior results by automatically generating high-quality coarse precursors, thereby enhancing the overall mesh quality. The system achieves this without imposing additional computational overhead, as our algorithm is highly efficient and produces results in a fraction of a second.

The correlation coefficient serves as a robust metric for linear relationships between two continuous variables, yet its expected value over random permutations of discrete data is challenging to determine analytically. Consequently, researchers typically rely on Monte-Carlo simulations to estimate these values, a process that introduces significant computational costs and potential estimation errors. This article derives analytic formulas for the moments of the correlation coefficient under random data permutations, specifically addressing the two-sample case. These formulas are computationally efficient, enabling the rapid calculation of moments without the associated costs and inaccuracies of simulations. The efficacy of these analytic formulas is demonstrated in the moments' application to identifying outlier-free subsets within bivariate data. All computational methods and the case study presented in this article are available in the accompanying Python package, which can be accessed at: https://github.com/alextorres12345/outlier-free-subset. Additionally, the Python package includes formulas for higher-order moments that extend the primary results of this work. Keywords: Correlation coefficient, Outlier-free subset, Analytic formula. This study establishes the uniform stabilization of 2-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations, defined on a bounded domain $\Omega$ with smooth, possibly irregular, boundaries, by implementing finite-dimensional localized feedback controls. The stabilization is achieved by measuring the solution within a feedback loop to determine a control $u$ applied in an arbitrary open subset $\omega \subset \Omega$, which may differ from the actuation region. This control regulates the flow velocity to drive the system to zero as $t$ approaches infinity. This setup constitutes a boundary-value stabilization problem, which extends the classic Backsteem stabilization method originally used for 1-dimensional wave equations on a half-line. The primary challenge lies in the fact that the Navier-Stokes equations are not parabolic, and existing stabilization results are limited to parabolic equations, whereas non-parabolic systems typically rely on spatial translations for stabilization. To address this, the authors develop a novel feedback stabilization technique that translates the required translations into localized measurements. The resulting stabilization rates are optimal within the framework of critical $L^q$-based Sobolev and Besov spaces. This framework is significant because it ensures uniform stabilization across all initial conditions, regardless of their regularity. Consequently, the problem of uniform stabilization using localized feedback is resolved in critical $L^q$-based Sobolev and Besov spaces. It remains an open question whether uniform stabilization can be achieved in more regular spaces where initial data are required to be in higher-order Sobolev spaces. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate uniform stabilization using localized feedback controls that are parabolic in nature. This parabolic stabilization serves as a foundation for achieving stabilization using localized *algebraic* feedback controls, where the uniform stabilization rates are again optimal. Finally, the problem of uniform stabilization via localized *static* (time-independent) feedback controls is addressed, yielding optimal stabilization rates. Notably, the uniform stabilization using static feedback controls is derived through an indirect method involving uniform *asymptotic* stabilization first, followed by a second step utilizing standard techniques from control theory. This final step relies on standard control-theoretic arguments rather than the novel techniques developed in this work. Thus, this research represents a first step toward achieving uniform stabilization using static feedback controls. A key outcome of this work is the successful extension of uniform stabilization results from critical $L^q$-based Sobolev spaces to the broader context of critical $L^q$-based Besov spaces. Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are extensively employed in Recommendation Models; however, their "black box" characteristics hinder full user trust, necessitating research into explainable artificial intelligence. Local Interpreted Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) stands out as a leading approach for ANN interpretability, recently extended to recommenders (LIME-RS) to identify influential items for specific user-item interactions. Despite its model-agnostic flexibility, the specific limitations of LIME-RS remain unclear. This study investigates these properties by evaluating LIME-RS on seven recommendation models using various similarity metrics and hyperparameters. The results, which correlate with human ratings of explanation quality, highlight significant limitations of LIME-RS and offer practical guidelines for selecting result parameters to enhance interpretability. Additionally, we propose several modifications to LIME-RS and present preliminary evidence that they improve the model's properties. Finally, we outline potential future research directions. The code and data are accessible at https://github.com/fernandocosta/LIME-RIME. These findings are partially presented in our recent work (Costa et al., 2021).

The sensitivity of two-dimensional (2D) electron gases (2DEGs) to surface adsorbates stems from charge transfer between the surface and the bulk, which can shift the Fermi level and alter transport characteristics. In this study, we demonstrate that this adsorption-induced pinning of the Fermi level in near-surface InAs (NSIQWs) can be mitigated by engineering an appropriate band structure. By applying an external gate voltage to modify the Fermi level, we show that this adjustment lowers the formation energy of surface defects. Consequently, this mechanism enables the removal of surface adsorbates and significantly reduces the sensitivity of NSIQWs to surface contamination. These findings have broad implications for enhancing the stability of semiconductor-based quantum devices. Furthermore, this strategy is applicable to other topological materials, such as InAs/InSb quantum wells, thereby advancing their realization as topological superconducting qubits. Our results underscore the critical role of the Fermi level position in the stability of quantum devices. This is validated by comparing experimental data on NSIQW conductivity before and after annealing, which reveals that the annealing process restores the Fermi level to its optimal position. This observation highlights the necessity of optimizing the Fermi level to ensure the stability of quantum devices. Our findings provide a pathway to mitigate the detrimental effects of surface adsorbates on device stability. Specifically, this is achieved by designing quantum wells with suitable band structures that prevent surface defect formation and adsorbate accumulation. These outcomes are realized through careful heterostructure design and the strategic use of quantum confinement effects. Ultimately, the stability of quantum devices can be improved by optimizing the Fermi level to avoid surface defect formation and adsorbate accumulation. This study investigates how incorporating local inquiries can enhance the sample efficiency of robust learning. We first demonstrate that for a broad category of problems, any algorithm relying solely on noisy local inquiries cannot be both accurate and sample-efficient. Subsequently, we introduce a general framework that integrates two distinct types of local inquiries, proving that with these inquiries, computation can significantly reduce the sample complexity required for accurate learning. Our work offers two frameworks grounded in various local inquiries, advancing both theoretical understanding and practical progress in this field. First, we establish that any algorithm utilizing exclusively noisy local inquiries will fail to achieve both accuracy and sample efficiency across a wide range of scenarios. Next, we propose a framework incorporating two different local inquiry types, illustrating that computation utilizing these inquiries can substantially lower the sample complexity needed for accurate learning. Finally, we introduce a practical robust robustness verification system based on a vision-inspired local inquiry framework, which empirically confirms that our approach leverages local inquiries to substantially improve sample complexity. Overall, this paper establishes both theoretical and practical foundations for integrating local inquiries into robust learning. The resulting methods hold both practical utility and significant potential for further theoretical investigation. Additionally, our code is publicly available to foster continued research and exploration in this area. This paper introduces Fast Sinkhorn II, an algorithm designed to calculate the exact Sinkhorn norm for optimal transport problems characterized by a collinear transport map. By leveraging the structure of a specific class of invertible matrices known as upper (or lower) triangular matrices, we reduce the computational complexity of Sinkhorn iterations to linear time, resulting in precise results without incurring the approximation errors common to current linear-time approximate methods. This structural advantage also enables the natural extension of our linear-time algorithm to scenarios involving more than two parallel optimal transport problems. Additionally, we demonstrate that our approach supports various kernel functions, thereby enhancing transportation quality and accommodating noise in data distributions. Finally, we highlight that the collinear transport map is particularly relevant for specific applications, such as image processing. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance where the exact Sinkhorn norm has been computed in linear time. The AU Microscopii (AU Mic) system serves as a critical benchmark for understanding the high-energy radiation environments experienced by exoplanets. This study investigates the frequency and intensity of flares in AU Mic's extreme ultraviolet (XUV) and far-ultraviolet (FUV) ranges by analyzing 17 years of data from the GALEX archive. By examining 1,105 epochs of quiescent activity and 18 flare events, we calculated flare rates and their correlation with soft X-rays (S-X-rays). Our results indicate that FUV flare rates are approximately 1.5 times higher than those predicted by S-X-ray correlations, whereas this ratio drops to 0.6 for FUV events occurring during S-X-ray flares. These findings suggest that low-energy S-X-ray flares are the primary drivers of FUV variability. Additionally, we observed that FUV variability diminishes at longer integration times, a trend that becomes more pronounced during flares. These results support the hypothesis that both AU Mic's quiescent high-energy output and explosive flares originate from the same magnetically active regions. Finally, we discuss the potential impacts of these diverse high-energy phenomena on the system's exoplanets. The data presented here will facilitate future research into the effects of high-energy radiation on exoplanetary atmospheres and surfaces. Radiation reaction forces are a well-established concept in electrodynamics, appearing in Einstein's maximal acceleration term within the geodesic equation and influencing radiation pressure in climate models. This note examines the drag force exerted by a resistive material medium on charged particles, analyzing its connection to radiation reaction. The most compelling connection arises from modeling the medium as consisting of free electrons. The derived formula aligns with the Birkeland-Langmuir formula under low-field conditions and produces the correct order of magnitude in high-field regimes. Furthermore, this approach offers a novel explanation for the atmospheric polarization gradient. We conclude by proposing that this phenomenon represents an extreme instance of ionization track creation by high-energy charged particles. Additionally, we explore how resistive drag influences cosmic ray deflection, suggesting it may account for the recently observed east-west asymmetry. Finally, we address the relationship between this effect and Cherenkov radiation. These findings are highly relevant to recent experimental and observational advances in understanding charged particle interactions with matter, including ionospheric drag, laboratory particle accelerators, and cosmic ray observations. Specifically, our results may aid in correcting measured particle trajectories in the Earth's atmosphere to accurately determine the cosmic ray charge-to-mass ratio. The paper is intended as an introductory overview for those interested in this subject. No new research is presented. No originality statement is required. No conflict of interest exists. No novel contributions are made. No funding was received. In classification tasks involving significantly imbalanced classes, where one group contains many more instances than others, the decision boundaries between classes are often unclear, particularly between pairs of small, large-small, and largest classes. This study proposes a statistical analysis of k-closest neighbor (k-CNN) voting to better understand how this method affects the resulting classification. Although k-CNN has been employed in closest neighbor classification, its statistical underpinnings regarding the outcomes in imbalanced settings remain unexplored. By integrating the k-CNN voting mechanism with statistical theory, this paper offers insights into how this approach influences decisions when class sizes are disparate and highlights the necessity of using multiple k-CNN votes rather than a single one. These findings offer valuable insights for implementing k-CNN in scenarios with imbalanced classes. Finally, the statistical concepts discussed are expected to assist researchers in selecting the most appropriate algorithm for specific classification problems. A comprehensive online supplementary material accompanies this work to ensure reproducibility. Specifically, it includes all datasets and R functions utilized, along with additional supplementary figures and tables that provide further insights beyond the scope of this article. Additionally, the supplementary file contains detailed information regarding the steps and outputs of the proposed methodology. Finally, the R package `imbalanced-classification` is made available to support the reproducibility of this methodology. This package includes functions for imbalanced class identification, k-CNN voting generation, and the imbalanced-classification-closest-neighbor (ICC-NN) methodology, which is the core contribution of this paper. Users can access the package via the link: https://github.com/ImbalancedData/imbalanced-classification. The functions within this package offer an alternative methodology to that presented in this work for implementing ICC-NN. However, while that methodology offers advantages, it does not provide the same level of statistical understanding regarding the imbalanced-classification-closest-neighbor voting process. Consequently, users are encouraged to utilize the functions in the imbalanced-classification package to gain a more in-depth understanding of the voting process. Keywords: data mining, machine learning, imbalanced data, classification, k-CNN.

We present the sensing of electric signals generated by coherent charge tunneling between a quantum dot and a superconducting island exhibiting superexchange coupling. We show that for dot states with significant overlap with the island, such as the hole at the |1/2, 1/2⟩ configuration, the electrostatic signal generated by an exchanged tunneling charge can be substantial. This effect is verified via dot energy level shifts measured through gate-sensing techniques. Our findings offer fresh perspectives on the exchange mechanism driving spin qubits composed of a quantum dot and superconducting island. Furthermore, this represents the first experimental detection of electrostatic exchange coupling between a quantum dot and a quantum island. We also demonstrate that gate-sensing can facilitate the development of hybrid qubits by enabling access to coherent exchange regimes between a quantum dot and island. Finally, we prove that applying a superconducting gap suppresses exchange coupling, consistent with hole pairing into Cooper pairs. This critical gap marking the transition of exchange coupling from positive to negative serves as a means to investigate the interaction between hole charge and Cooper pairs. Ultimately, our results highlight gate-sensing as a vital tool for exploring hybrid quantum devices capable of accessing diverse charge and spin degrees of freedom. This technique allows for precise tuning of individual dots without disrupting other device components. Additionally, it enables the investigation of hybrid quantum devices under realistic operating conditions. By facilitating access to charge dynamics in hybrid quantum devices, gate-serving paves the way for novel hybrid qubits based on dot-Cooper pair coupling. Such inductance-modulating qubits could utilize microwave photons to encode and read out spin qubit states, thereby integrating spin qubits with established superconducting quantum technologies. Moreover, these gate-sensing measurements provide a pathway to investigate the fundamental physics of coherent exchange coupling between a quantum dot and a superconducting island. Specifically, our measurements of the dependence of the exchange Hamiltonian on the superconducting gap reveal a hole-phonon interaction that competes with hole-Cooper pair interaction, resulting in the sign flip of the exchange Hamiltonian. This finding suggests that gate sensing can be a valuable tool for investigating the fundamental physics governing hybrid qubits. In this work, we focus on gate sensing to advance the development of hybrid qubits. Future research will explore microwave sensing to further investigate the physics of charge dynamics in hybrid qubits. By combining gate and microwave sensing, we can achieve a more comprehensive understanding of the physics underlying hybrid qubits, ultimately leading to the creation of fully functional devices. The Murozuma-Jiannelli (MJ) contraction is defined on the same q-TV space utilized by the Engelquist (E) contraction, yet it exhibits distinct characteristics. Specifically, the MJ contraction remains a contraction across the entire q-TV space, whereas the E contraction only functions as such within open cones defined by entropic pairs. While both methods yield the same solution for contact discontinuities, they diverge in their treatment of shock contractions. Furthermore, the MJ method generally produces a more regular solution, quantified by a higher value of k in bounded k-annular functions. This paper presents initial numerical experiments comparing the two contraction definitions, followed by an outline of future research directions. The results indicate that MJ contractions successfully converge to a solution that aligns with the expected physical behavior of the system. Additionally, numerical comparisons between the m=1 case under both contraction types and an operator-splitting scheme demonstrate that all three approaches yield consistent solutions, thereby validating their application to multi-dimensional problems. Finally, we outline potential extensions of the MJ contraction to higher dimensions. These findings provide a foundational framework for the subsequent book chapter, where we will present further numerical evidence supporting both the validity and effectiveness of MJ contractions. Notably, the evidence regarding convergence to the correct solution is particularly compelling, as it relies on extensive numerical experiments rather than theoretical proofs. Additionally, the analysis of multivariate problems offers further insight into why MJ contractions produce accurate solutions. Crucially, this validation does not depend on operator splitting, which, despite its practical utility, poses significant theoretical challenges. Consequently, these results substantiate the assertion that MJ contractions fulfill the necessary conditions for well-posedness. Ultimately, this body of evidence establishes a solid basis for the arguments presented in this book, supporting the claim that MJ contractions ensure a well-posed problem. Specifically, they guarantee both the existence and uniqueness of solutions, as well as their stability. Uniqueness is further reinforced by the demonstration that any two solutions must be monotone relative to each other, a property that also serves as an effective stopping criterion for numerical algorithms. In summary, MJ contractions ensure well-posedness, offer effective criteria for terminating numerical computations, and provide a practical tool for analyzing convergence. Notably, these conclusions extend beyond the m=1 case, as evidenced by the successful application of MJ contractions to multivariate problems. Single-view 3D Perpetual Art (SV3PA) represents a novel and emerging challenge focused on generating multiple views from a single image. While 3D Diffusion models have recently advanced SV3PA by producing high-quality, photorealistic, and sharp images, 3D Gaussian Radiance Field models have yielded superior geometry and color consistency. This paper introduces DiffDreamer, a 2D Diffusion model specifically designed for SV3PA. Unlike previous approaches, DiffDreamer represents a unique and reliable direction in the generation process, ensuring high-quality, high-contrast, and high-contrast-free outputs. The model enforces strict control over camera parameters, including rotation, pitch, yaw, and translation, while maintaining smooth object transitions and high-resolution images. To achieve this, we developed a novel 2D Diffusion architecture that is both computationally efficient and easy to train. Our method surpasses the current state-of-the-art 3D Diffusion model, demonstrating that 2D Diffusion models are highly promising and reliable for SV3PA. Networks serve as the primary structure for representing complex systems, with networks of infectious agents being the most prevalent example in literature. While extensive research exists on the prediction and control of such networks, networked processes—defined as networks of agents linked to external inputs—have received significantly less attention. This study introduces a data-driven framework for prediction, optimization, and control of networked processes that relies exclusively on input-output experimental data, eliminating the need for knowledge of physical equations or network topology. The approach utilizes a novel data-driven representation that retains all essential characteristics of the process, including network structure and agent-to-agent connections. Furthermore, the framework enables the optimization of network performance based on selected agent attributes and provides effective control strategies by modeling agent dynamics using time-varying coefficients. The method's effectiveness in prediction, network optimization, and control is demonstrated through its application to various synthetic networks with networked SIS epidemic dynamics. Networked processes extending beyond these cases are anticipated to be effectively modeled using this approach. The underlying code is accessible at: https://github.com/ehsan-hosseini-networks/Networked_Processes. The findings presented here were derived from my thesis [1]. Additionally, I am currently developing a follow-up work [2] that expands upon these results by applying them to real-world networks and introducing additional features. This study theoretically examines the Rayleigh-Plateau instability affecting a liquid film on a rigid, elastic core within a fibre, where surface tension drives the formation of drops. By solving the governing equations for a thin film, we derive an expression for the dispersion relation that accounts for slip at the film's lower interface and elastic lateral stresses. Our findings indicate that slip at the liquid's lower surface can significantly amplify the growth rate of disturbances. Furthermore, we analyze how elastic stresses influence droplet formation on the fibre, ultimately expanding the previously established thin-film instability criterion to include the effects of both slip and elastic stresses. These outcomes are anticipated to be relevant for droplet formation on any thin liquid films bordered by a slip-prone surface and supported by a deformable solid structure. This study investigates the initial-boundary value problem for the Hunter-Saxton model. We establish Lipschitz stability for models featuring $L^2$ initial data and essential boundary measures, as well as for semi-group solutions with $L^2$ initial data, utilizing a direct energy estimate approach alongside generalized Riesz transforms. These findings rely critically on Russell's inequality, recently enhanced by Liu, Shen, and Wang. Additionally, we demonstrate the global existence of solutions satisfying a sufficient condition derived from prior condition numbers. The subsequent sections outline our methodology and present a summary of relevant literature. Section 3 introduces the Hunter-Saxton model, while Section 4 provides a preliminary analysis by reformulating the model into a Cauchy problem. We then address stability in three distinct scenarios: the Cauchy problem (Section 5), boundary value problems (Section 6), and the Hunter-Saxton model itself (Section 7). Finally, Section 8 explores the Hunter-Saxton model under a sufficient condition ensuring the positive definiteness of the Hessian of the energy estimate. This section concludes by proving Lipschitz stability for the model via the sliding interval technique, sliding time method, and induction method. This final section serves as an appendix designed to explore outcomes that extend beyond the scope of the original paper. Notably, the results presented here are original and have not been previously published. Furthermore, Section 10 offers an alternative approach to proving Lipschitz stability for a model satisfying a sufficient condition where condition numbers are positive, employing sliding time and induction methods without requiring a prior proof of global solution existence. This work is also original and represents an extension beyond the scope of the initial paper. Finally, I extend my deepest gratitude to Dr. Yu Chen for his invaluable guidance and support. Thank you. The clinical management of scoliosis relies heavily on ultrasound (US) imaging to evaluate spinal curvature progression. Although it is established that scoliosis curves progress rapidly during growth and that radiological signs of advancement typically match morphological ones, it remains unclear whether computer-aided scoliosis progression detection using US is as reliable as traditional manual radiological assessment. This study aimed to evaluate the reliability of computer-aided scoliosis progression detection using ultrasound compared to manual methods. We developed a pipeline to automatically detect scoliosis progression from US data and compared it against manual detection. The study involved 20 scoliosis patients, with each operator detecting progression twice, resulting in 80 total detections. Results showed that computer-aided detection achieved 100% sensitivity and 95% specificity, yielding a mean absolute error of 1.0 cm and a mean difference of 1.2 cm compared to manual detection. Inter-observer variability for computer-aided detection was 1.4 cm, while manual scanning showed 2.0 cm of inter-observer variability. These findings indicate that computer-aided scoliosis progression detection using ultrasound is as reliable as manual US detection, suggesting its potential to reduce workload and enhance the efficiency of scoliosis monitoring. Furthermore, this technology could facilitate the development of automated scoliosis monitoring systems, potentially making regular monitoring more accessible to underserved populations. Future research will explore the feasibility of creating such automated systems. (Video files are available at: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.14210888). This study evaluates the efficacy of a duration prediction technique for CTDH-MDP DPG-ACM, a DTM&V synthesis framework integrated with the Hidden Domain-Adaptive Control Model. Durance annotations were created through a duration annotation tool (DAT), which applies a specific annotation strategy by selecting the median duration of word instances from a training corpus rather than providing absolute annotated durations. The paper analyzes how DAT annotations influence duration modeling across various corporons, ultimately demonstrating the method's effectiveness for speech synthesis by comparing synthetic outputs generated via median-based duration annotations against those using ground-truth durations. Furthermore, this approach is particularly advantageous when applied to small corporons (SC) derived from large corporons (LC). The primary metric for assessment is perceptual mean opinion score (MOS), supplemented by speech quality (SQ) and naturalness (SN) evaluations. Listening tests confirmed that synthetic speech produced using ground-truth durations exhibits no significant difference in MOS, SQ, or SN compared to speech generated using median-based annotations. Additionally, MOS scores indicate that this method is effective for synthesis using small corporons (SC). Identifying hate speech on social media has become an increasingly significant challenge, driven by the growing demand for fairness and interpretability in machine learning models. While numerous prior studies have employed Natural Language Processing features to detect such content, this paper introduces a novel approach that integrates Content-based automatically generated keywords and NetHate lexicon features with Text automatically generated keywords derived from Social Emotional Learning principles. Additionally, the study examines the impact of combining these feature sets on hate speech detection performance. Evaluated against a widely used dataset in the field, the results demonstrate that models incorporating the proposed combination of features achieve higher accuracy, F1-score, and recall rates compared to baseline models that exclude them. Furthermore, the research analyzes the specific contribution of each feature to the classification process to enhance overall understanding of the mechanisms underlying hate speech detection. By leveraging Content-based and NetHate features, this method uncovers new insights into distinguishing hate speech from other texts while reducing dependency on NLP features. Ultimately, the findings provide critical information for developing more effective strategies to combat hate speech on social media. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/abdullahbaba/HateSpeechDetection. Future research will explore extending this model to multilingual contexts. Abdullah B. Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) architectures aim to enhance inference speed on edge devices by replicating network layers across multiple sub-networks. However, the effectiveness of parameter sharing in existing designs significantly impacts this goal. This paper addresses that limitation through three key contributions. First, we demonstrate that the effective parameters of a typical share-mode in MONAI (Multiple Network Output for Nuclei inference) are often inconsistent within shared layers. Second, inspired by the ECA module, we propose the Asymmetric Share-mode (AS-mode), which applies distinct share-modes to different channels to ensure consistent parameters and improve efficiency. Third, to eliminate redundant computation caused by asymmetric-modes, we introduce the Effective Share-mode (ES-mode), which calculates parameters once and reuses them across multiple shared layers. Experimental results show that ES-mode achieves up to 3.2x inference acceleration with only a 0.3% drop in accuracy on the Kitti dataset, while achieving up to 1.7x speedup and 1.0% accuracy loss on the MONAI dataset. The combination of AS-mode and ES-mode yields up to 1.6x accuracy gains and up to 24% fewer parameters with negligible accuracy loss. The entire model training pipeline, including ablation studies, is available at https://github.com/zhongzhixu/EffShare. Our findings offer valuable insights for future feature-sharing strategies in MIMO architectures. Source code and pre-trained models can be found at https://github.com/zhongzhixu/EffShare.
