Historical documents offer a glimpse into the past by preserving information from three-dimensional objects like books, letters, and letters. Although most existing research on historical document image analysis focuses on digitally captured scans, images from the physical handling of these documents also demand significant attention. The primary obstacle in utilizing such handlings is the scarcity of public datasets for model training. To address this data gap, this paper presents a comprehensive review of publicly available datasets designed to support research on historical manuscript imagery. Our analysis examines 57 datasets across key dimensions relevant to this field: document categories, capture methods, specific research tasks, and statistical metrics. The paper concludes with a discussion on how these datasets can aid historical image analysis research and identifies opportunities for future datasets. We believe this survey will be a valuable resource for researchers entering the field of historical image analysis. Additionally, the document is publicly accessible, and we intend for it to serve as a foundational step toward establishing historical image analysis as a distinct and recognized research domain. Document IDs and links are provided in the paper to facilitate access to these datasets. The complete survey can be found at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.07707. This study addresses the open challenge of achieving high-precision motion control without relying on expensive and complex methods like vision systems or 6-axis robots equipped with encoders. The proposed approach utilizes inexpensive, easy-to-deploy secondary encoders attached to the driven joints of a direct-drive industrial robot (a direct-drive Cartesian robot featuring drive wheels instead of traditional joints). The method combines a data-driven feedforward controller with a feedback controller. The vision of employing secondary encoders for precise control of Driven-by-Motor robots is highly promising for both academic research and industrial applications. **Background:** Accurately modeling health trajectories is essential for understanding how exposures influence multiple health outcomes over time. **Objective:** To demonstrate the Multiple State Examination (MUSE) model for analyzing time-to-event data within a life-course framework. MUSE serves as a multivariate extension of Cox proportional hazards models. **Methods:** MUSE tracks individuals moving among multiple states, including a "dead" state, by generating hazard ratios for various time-varying covariates and transition probabilities between states. This study applies MUSE to multiple time-to-event data from a cohort of myocardial infarction patients, examining transitions between alive states involving cardiovascular and cancer outcomes. **Results:** The analysis successfully estimated hazard ratios for time-varying covariates and transition probabilities across multiple transitions. **Conclusions:** MUSE effectively models time-to-event data within a life-course perspective, accommodating time-varying covariates, unbalanced designs, and right-censored data. Additionally, the model handles multiple transitions among both homogeneous and heterogeneous states. The molecular continuum has been increasingly highlighted for its ability to bridge the gap between molecular and cellular scales, offering a molecular representation of cells that facilitates the integration of molecular mechanisms into cell-wide properties, including tissue behavior. Nevertheless, accurately modeling the molecular continuum remains a significant challenge. In particular, simulating the intra-cellular (cytoplasm) environment demands high spatial resolution, yet such detail necessitates extensive spatial domains and boundary conditions. Given that intra-cellular contents are highly disordered, spatial and temporal heterogeneity must be incorporated into the continuum framework. To address these issues, we introduce a molecular continuum integration scheme that incorporates the spatial distribution of organelles, membranes, and macromolecules. This approach enables the explicit representation of the cytoplasmic environment, thereby facilitating the modeling of molecular diffusion and reactions within a cellular context. We demonstrate that our method achieves spatial heterogeneity and the correct diffusion coefficient for the cytoplasmic continuum. Furthermore, we show that this model can serve as a valuable basis for molecular-scale simulations within a cellular setting. The method is available in an open-source implementation, which can be accessed at https://github.com/akira-koide/MolecularContinuumOrganelle. This implementation integrates the molecular dynamics code MDPK into the cellular continuum framework MOCAP-Cell. We outline how to apply the proposed framework to molecular simulations within a cellular continuum. Additionally, we present results demonstrating the successful modeling of the cytoplasmic environment, diffusion, and macromolecular reactions within a nucleus. These findings provide a foundation for simulating cellular processes at the molecular level. Future efforts will focus on modeling organelle contents, such as the nucleoplasm and mitochondria, to further enable the study of cellular functions at molecular resolution. We demonstrate that this problem is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by the size of a feedback vertex set. Additionally, we establish fixed-parameter tractability for several related problems, including determining if the metric dimension is at most k, whether it changes by at most k upon adding an edge, and whether it decreases by at most k upon removing an edge. Finally, we show that DETERMINING METRIC DIMENSION is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by a combination of vertex counts in cycles and components, as well as by a mixed parameter combining vertex cover and fragment counts. However, we note that no single-parameterized algorithm exists using only cycle size, vertex cover size, or fragment size as the parameter, even when combined with an additional parameter. Furthermore, we prove that the problem is W[1]-hard when parameterized solely by the number of fragments, highlighting the difficulty of identifying a unified structural parameter capable of yielding fixed-parameter tractability. As planetary atmospheres warm into hothouse states, a common expectation is an increase in the frequency of intense downpours. However, both numerical simulations and theoretical frameworks indicate that such extremes can only surge when water vapor concentrations reach very high levels. This study demonstrates that in Earth-like hothouse conditions, the supply of such abundant water is limited to brief episodes. These short-duration phases provide enough moisture to trigger a non-linear explosion in downpours, even though overall precipitation rates remain low. Consequently, despite the prolonged warm climate, these episodes are infrequent, resulting in hothouse Earth exhibiting precipitation patterns that are markedly different from our current climate. These findings are illustrated using an energy balance model with simulated cloud and rain dynamics, supported by complementary results from a global climate model. The mechanisms identified here are also relevant to other planets, particularly those transitioning between cold and warm states. While hothouse phases are characterized by precipitating clouds that are optically thin in the infrared, they remain optically thick in the blue, creating a unique color palette distinct from that of a runaway greenhouse. This distinctive visual is a potential target for future space-based observatories. Furthermore, the presence of such optically thin clouds in the infrared suggests that the upper atmosphere is not trapped in saturation, thereby challenging prevailing theories regarding the runaway greenhouse limit. The ultimate fate of a super-Earth's atmosphere may depend on whether it can radiate sufficient heat through these thin clouds. Finally, the rain generated during these episodic downpours could have significant consequences for surface life. The resulting erosion and nutrient transport could drive rapid geological changes and abrupt shifts in surface environments, potentially causing frequent extinctions. This contrasts sharply with a Runaway Greenhouse scenario, where water is entirely trapped in the atmosphere and never reaches the surface. These outcomes are especially pertinent to exoplanets currently transitioning through a runaway greenhouse event. In such scenarios, even though water is abundant in the atmosphere, it remains dry on the surface, leading to the erosion of the solid surface. This process could strip the planet of its continents, leaving behind a barren, water-covered world. The interplay between these atmospheric and surface dynamics may be crucial for understanding the formation of Super-Earths. During the final stages of their formation, these planets may be heated to a hothouse state by the accretion of material and radiation from their host star. We present the higher-spin generalization of the twistor-space extension of self-dual Yang-Mills theory, framing it as a holomorphic Chern-Simons theory defined on the twistor space of complex Minkowski space. This framework adheres to the linearized higher-spin extensions of the Yang-Mills self-dual equation. Building on the material deformation theory introduced in arXiv:1809.00344, we demonstrate how to construct self-dual Yang-Mills theory at higher-twistor level and subsequently perform "twistor creations" across various higher-spin extensions, exploring the resulting physical implications. Furthermore, we examine the classical and quantum properties of the linearized higher-spin extension, analyzing its gauge symmetries, equations of motion, and a novel class of interactions. These findings suggest that a full non-linear higher-spin extension may exist, potentially possessing a holographic dual in a lower-dimensional anti-de Sitter black hole. Finally, within the context of a ten-dimensional complex manifold, we explore the possibility of higher-spin extensions arising from a holomorphic vector-bundle deformation of F-theory. This process generates a tower of higher-spin fields with increasing spin, characterized by a deformation parameter whose dimension dictates their mass. This mechanism offers a novel approach to exploring the phenomenology of anti-de Sitter black holes. Additionally, by connecting to recent F-theory research, our work offers a unique perspective on the phenomenology of large extra dimensions. These findings may offer fresh insights into the phenomenon of large, nearly-conformal dimensions. Finally, we demonstrate that a related construction in a ten-dimensional complex Kähler manifold can yield a higher-dimensional, lower-dimensional anti-de Sitter black hole with a large deformation parameter. This black hole could serve as the dual theory for a higher-spin theory built upon a holomorphic vector-bundle deformation within a complex Minkowski space. Furthermore, this model may provide the first example of a twistor-space theory that reduces to a well-known space-time theory upon appropriate deformation. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success across numerous computer vision domains, including classification, segmentation, and object detection. Nevertheless, their performance typically degrades significantly when training data contains noisy labels. This study investigates the source of such noise within medical imaging by demonstrating that many images are mislabeled due to annotation errors. To address this, we introduce a deep learning framework that leverages Bayesian statistics to enhance the accuracy of noisy labels in medical images. Our approach employs a Bayesian neural network to approximate the posterior distribution of a neural network, enabling the estimation of predictive uncertainty. By utilizing predictive uncertainty, we refine noisy labels to mitigate the impact of data noise on model training. The efficacy of this method is validated through breast mammography diagnosis and colon cancer histopathology image classification tasks. Consider the transition probability matrix $P$ for the symmetric random walk on $G$. We provide an explicit formula expressing the characteristic polynomial of $P$ in terms of the generating function of the matching polynomials of $G$. This function yields the probability that a walk of length $l$ originating at vertex $u$ and ending at vertex $v$ occurs simultaneously for all pairs of vertices $(u,v)$. Timed definitions represent a specialized category of recursive functions governed by colexicographic ordering. This spatial ordering is appropriate for record-like data structures, such as those found in protocol implementations, where every field must be updated before the record becomes valid. We present an alternative formulation of this concept using a monad that encapsulates all possible computation histories for a protocol state, demonstrating that this monad commutes with certain function applications. Leveraging the equations of a monadic transformer, we develop a more flexible solution that extends timed definitions beyond protocols to any function relying on algebraic types. The timeliness of these functions is essential for protocol verification, as protocols must progress through their state histories, rendering backstates inaccessible. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of timed definitions in a protocol authentication proof using the ProVerif verification tool. The approach involves generating a theorem proving the function's co-termination with a provided state, which ProVerif subsequently utilizes during proof construction. Our methodology also addresses theories involving uninterpreted functions that modify algebraic types, effectively mitigating challenges related to uninterpreted function recursion. All proposed solutions have been implemented in the HOL theorem prover. The implementation occurs at the theorem level, meaning the development of co-termination theorems for specific functions is performed manually by the user. Additionally, we demonstrate how to apply timed definitions within the Isabelle/HOL proof assistant using the HOL42K library. Our implementation successfully handles functions defined via coalescing hole filling, a technique employed in both HOL4 and Isabelle2021. However, our solution does not yet support protocols analyzed by the ProVerif tool, as this requires modifications to the ProtVerif specification language. Furthermore, generating the co-termination theorem for a function defined as timed demands significantly more effort compared to standard function definitions. Our work demonstrates that timed definitions constitute a definitional extension rather than an axiomatic one, allowing for straightforward integration into the HOL kernel alongside other definitional extensions like inductive types. This capability offers a distinct advantage over prior research, which often treated timed definitions as axiomatic. Our approach also diverges from earlier efforts that manually constructed co-termination theorems for specific functions; instead, we provide a generic method for reasoning about the termination of a broad class of functions. These data-driven predictions enable the development of data-enhanced large eddy simulations, yielding data-consistent instantaneous flow fields that refine the understanding of wall turbulence mechanics. Furthermore, we show that these models can predict physical quantities that enhance the accuracy of traditional Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes simulations. Numerical experiments confirm that these data-driven approaches offer significant data-driven theoretical and practical advantages for advancing wall turbulence research and technology. Specifically, we demonstrate that these methods provide (i) significant data-driven insights into the instantaneous dynamics of wall turbulence and (ii) a data-enhanced large eddy simulation framework that improves the accuracy of wall turbulence technology. In the first part of this work, we develop coherent structure-based models grounded in a physics-based theoretical formulation and train them on high-fidelity numerical simulation data. These models utilize a coherent-incoherent structure representation of wall turbulence, where coherent structures like streaks and vortices are identified via data-driven topology optimization algorithms, and vorticity and pressure serve as the primary variables. The resulting models are integrated with large eddy simulations, leveraging a closed-loop data-driven architecture to achieve data-consistent instantaneous field representations. This framework generates physically consistent predictions regarding turbulence statistics, spectra, and transport processes. In the second part, we focus on technology applications, demonstrating that large eddy simulations incorporating data-enhanced models can predict instantaneous wall shear stress with high accuracy. This represents a substantial advancement in wall turbulence technology, as Reynolds-averaged and large eddy simulations currently lack the ability to predict instantaneous wall shear stress with such precision. The data-enhanced large eddy simulation method enables highly accurate predictions of wall shear stress fluctuations, thereby providing a precise and reliable tool for assessing the instantaneous frictional skin drag forces acting on solid walls in complex turbulent flows. This precision is critical for the design and control of various engineering systems, including wind turbines, hydroelectric turbines, and aircraft. Additionally, the data-enhanced large eddy simulation approach facilitates a more precise and reliable quantification of the instantaneous interaction between wall-bounding shear layers and physical obstacles, such as surface-mounted roughness elements. Extending the polynomial Born-Infeld model established by Manton and Sutcliffe, we introduce the \textit{Born-Infeld/infant Skyrme model}. This hybrid approach integrates two complementary mechanisms for soliton stability: a magnetic field constrained by a small parameter $\epsilon$ akin to $\lambda$ in the nonlinear sigma model, and a potential term that flips sign when $\epsilon$ is treated as negative. Leveraging $O(3)$-symmetry, we employ a shooting method grounded in linear interpolation to identify self-dual static solitons. The resulting family of solutions exhibits a magnetic flux approximately ten times larger than that of the nonlinear sigma model, though their energy remains only marginally lower. Furthermore, their decay rate is significantly slower compared to the standard polynomial model. A comprehensive analysis of both decay rates and magnetic flux demonstrates that the \textit{Born-Infeld/infant Skyrme model} offers a viable framework for studying various physical phenomena. Specifically, we investigate the (anti-)self-dual region to explore potential connections with quantum gravity. This study demonstrates that Hofstadertwisting of the electronic spectrum in Hofstadertwisted graphene (HTG) can yield a time-reversal-broken Weyl metal within the Hofstadertwisting regime. Specifically, when subjected to a sufficiently strong magnetic field, HTG exhibits a series of Weyl metals, where the number of Weyl points increases linearly with the magnetic flux. Furthermore, we identify that the Weyl points exist either exclusively on the $K$ point or exclusively on the $K^{\prime}$ point, with no coexistence of these two types. Additionally, we uncover an emergent particle-hole symmetry in Hofstadertwisted graphene, which governs the topological characteristics of the resulting time-reversal-broken Weyl metals. Notably, all chiral modes associated with these time-reversal-broken Weyl points propagate in a single direction, representing a distinct feature compared to that of Hofstadertwisted graphene. Finally, we propose a feasible experimental approach to realize Hofstadertwisted graphene, which involves applying a spatially modulated electric field to graphene alongside a perpendicular magnetic field. This proposal offers a unique experimental avenue to investigate an exotic topological state, the time-reversal-broken Weyl metal, in HTG. Furthermore, this proposal holds the potential to advance the search for Hofstadertwisted graphene, a system recognized for hosting a novel quantum Hall state characterized by fractional Chern numbers. Ultimately, the proposed Hofstadertwisted graphene system is expected to play a crucial role in the ongoing pursuit of Hofstadertwisted graphene. Additionally, our findings regarding HTG may prove instrumental in investigating novel, topologically protected states, such as time-reversal-broken Weyl metals, in other two-dimensional materials, including, but not limited to, transition metal dichalcogenides and transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructures. The interplay between disorder and nonlinearity in stiff granular systems has recently been demonstrated to generate novel phenomena. A key example involves a nonlinear force law with finite stiffness, which reveals an "anomalous screening" effect at distances exceeding the system's Kuhn length. This contrasts with highly nonlinear contact models that feature power-law stiffness extending down to zero, where screening follows standard models. Although this anomalous screening has been predicted for continuous media, its occurrence in discrete systems remains uncertain due to inherent scale cutoffs. We confirm this phenomenon experimentally using a discrete array of stiff plastic spheres, accompanied by numerical simulations and theoretical analysis grounded in a generalized nonlinear Poisson-Boltzmann framework. Furthermore, we explore how anomalous screening influences force propagation in extended sources and the statistical behavior of contact forces within large, uncorrelated granular assemblies. Ultimately, anomalous screening represents a universal effect arising from the complex interaction between finite nonlinear stiffness and disorder. It is anticipated to significantly impact various physical systems involving arrays of charges interacting through nonlinear dielectrics. Beyond granular matter, this includes biological charge transport in cells, geological charge migration within rocks, and charge transport in organic and other materials. In these contexts, finite nonlinear stiffness is expected to be relevant, potentially leading to novel transport phenomena driven by the emergence of anomalous screening. **Keywords:** Granular matter; screening; elasticity; plasticity; dielectrics; universality; percolation; organic and other materials; biology; geology; geophysics; charge transport; charge migration; charge transport in materials; organic materials; organic materials; organic materials. **Acknowledgments:** We thank the anonymous reviewers for their insightful comments. Silicene, a two-dimensional sp²-bonded silicon lattice, has garnered significant interest due to its promising electronic attributes, including a Dirac cone dispersion with a linear band gap and surface states. While various substrates have been investigated to manipulate its electronic properties, recent studies indicate that hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) offers superior stability and structural integrity for silicene compared to other substrates. This work examines the interaction between Mn atoms and silicene as it adsorbs onto hBN. We find that the Mn-silicene-hBN system exhibits favorable stability across all three configurations: Mn on top of silicene, Mn on top of hBN, and Mn embedded within the silicene layer. Sgr A East represents the supernova remnant situated near our Galaxy's center. Although it shares a radio scale height with the Galactic disk, its center appears elevated by approximately 100 pc above the disk, a feature likely attributed to the Galactic bulge's boxy/peanut shape. The supernova that spawned Sgr A East is believed to have occurred roughly 10–12 kyr ago, shortly after the formation of the central star cluster known as NGC 3603. By analyzing the spatial distribution of NGC 3603, we identified a void approximately 10 pc in diameter directly below the center of Sgr A East. This empty space could have served as a cavity where the supernova explosion occurred, shielding the birthplace from the shock wave. Using NGC 3603's spatial distribution as a three-dimensional reference, we identified a localized void approximately 10–12 kyr ago at the Sgr A East location. This finding suggests that supernovae originating within dense star-forming regions like NGC 3603 can inflate bubbles within their immediate surroundings. Furthermore, this study underscores the necessity of high-resolution observations of supernova remnants in the Galactic center to clarify their origins. Finally, we highlight the critical importance of accurately determining the age and location of supernova explosions to comprehend the evolution of massive stars. These factors are particularly vital for investigating the link between supernova explosions and gamma-ray bursts. The methodology proposed here is applicable to any supernova remnant situated near a young HII region. Specifically, the technique involves: (1) measuring the Sgr A East center's position and height, (2) establishing the supernova's age, (3) identifying young HII regions nearby, (4) assessing their age, and (5) examining their spatial distributions. The Sgr A East center is projected to rise further above the Galactic disk in the future due to its location on the long axis of the Galactic bulge. Additionally, the Sgr A East region is expected to host a new generation of stars, the most massive of which could potentially trigger a future gamma-ray burst. This scenario would necessitate a new supernova explosion within Sgr A East, potentially causing a temporary brightening of the region. Such an event would be particularly significant for astronomers studying the Galactic center, given its proximity to the Galactic nucleus. The COVID-19 pandemic has driven significant shifts in how news is consumed, particularly within the United States, where only 18% of adults now obtain local information through online sources, compared to 60% who do so for health data. Despite these changes, experts and news organizations emphasize the continued critical value of local online journalism. This study employs U.S. county-level data to examine the relationship between the extent of local news online coverage and the pandemic's progression, measuring outcomes against COVID cases, deaths, and audience size. Utilizing a difference-in-differences methodology, the analysis compares counties with robust local online coverage against those without, while accounting for pre-pandemic trends and other county-specific variables. The findings indicate that counties within media markets featuring strong local news online coverage exhibited lower COVID case rates and deaths, particularly in the early stages of the outbreak. Additionally, these markets demonstrated greater audience engagement, as reflected by larger social media followings. These results highlight the essential role of local online news in disseminating accurate information and highlight potential avenues for further research. Finally, the study underscores the need for policymakers to sustain local online news coverage, ensuring communities continue to receive vital local information. The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) is a widely utilized technique for accelerating the calculation of pairwise interactions within large systems, achieving exponential speedup for systems containing millions of particles. However, black-box methods like FMM often fail to preserve fundamental physical quantities such as energy, angular momentum, and work. This study presents a modified FMM designed for the rapid calculation of total angular momentum, enabling an error tolerance of approximately $10^{-4}$ in systems of 10 million particles. We also investigate how FMM error tolerance influences individual contributions to total angular momentum, analyzing their relative magnitudes to establish a guideline for selecting appropriate algorithms for specific physical systems. Finally, we explore strategies to enhance computational speed and extend the method's applicability to broader physical systems. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that this proposed approach offers significant computational advantages over traditional methods. Specifically, the new algorithm reduces computation time by a factor of 10 compared to P3M and by a factor of 100 compared to Verlet integration. Furthermore, the results validate that the proposed FMM successfully preserves the total angular momentum of large-scale many-particle systems. Consequently, this work introduces a novel, highly efficient, and physically accurate technique for simulating large systems. Its robust performance makes it particularly well-suited for modeling astrophysical and cosmological systems. This study details a search for Higgs boson pair production in association with a vector boson during 2015 and 2016 proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=$ 13 TeV, utilizing the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The analysis focuses on a final state comprising a vector boson decaying leptonically and the second Higgs boson also decaying leptonically, hadronically, or invisibly. Results are reported for leptonically decaying W and Z bosons, as well as hadronically decaying Higgs bosons in both same- and opposite-charge configurations. The investigation covers the Standard Model single Higgs boson production modes: gluon fusion, associated production with a vector boson, and associated production with the Higgs boson. No significant excess over the expected background was observed. Consequently, 95% confidence level upper limits on the cross section times branching ratio relative to the Standard Model are established for signal models with a Higgs boson mass between 110 and 230 GeV. The derived limits for vector boson-associated production of the Higgs boson pair in lepton-lepton final states reach their minimum values of 1.3 fb and 1.0 fb for WW and ZZ associated production, respectively. For vector boson-associated Higgs boson pair production, the limits are 1.6 fb and 1.2 fb for HH and HH and 1.4 fb and 1.1 fb for same-charge and opposite-charge leptonically decaying Higgs bosons, respectively. The most stringent limit for the WW + HH process is 1.0 fb. Standard Model cross section limits for vector boson-associated production of the Higgs boson pair in leptonically decaying W and Z boson final states are 1.0 fb and 1.1 fb, utilizing all three decay channels. This analysis represents the first observation of Higgs boson pair production in association with a vector boson. The combined result demonstrates sensitivity to vector boson-associated production of the Higgs boson pair for a signal model with a mass of 125 GeV at the 95% confidence level for the first time. Furthermore, the study reports the first search for Higgs boson pair production in association with a leptonically decaying W or Z boson. This study investigates the tasks of identifying hate speech and abusive language in social media contexts within Hindi and Bengali, focusing on classifying offensive tweets into specific target groups (e.g., targeting women, Muslims, the Hindu community, etc.). We developed the first large-scale, fine-grained datasets for these two Indian languages, comprising 70,000 and 45,000 tweets respectively, with an average of 11 labels per tweet. We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of various transformer-based models, including BERT, ALBERT, and Multilingual-roberta, alongside fine-grained topic-aware attention mechanisms. Additionally, we explored transfer learning strategies, demonstrating that pre-training on coarse-grained labels enhances fine-grained classification performance. Our source code and the Hindi and Bengali datasets will be made publicly available. This work represents the first large-scale, fine-grained hate speech detection effort for these languages, offering a valuable resource for future research. Furthermore, our experiments reveal several interesting observations regarding transfer learning and the strategies employed for offensive language classification. Finally, we provide insights and perspectives on the challenges associated with detecting hate speech in Indian languages. Our findings underscore the necessity for: (i) more granular target labels to capture the nuances of offensive content, (ii) a greater emphasis on the diverse forms of offensiveness prevalent in Indian social media, and (iii) a nuanced understanding of the broader socio-cultural landscape of India, which significantly influences the nature of online hate speech. We anticipate that our work will contribute to mitigating hate speech on social media platforms. This approach is demonstrated using a 30 mL tenuous gas TPC, where we show that it enables particle identification in TNT and demonstrates directional recoil observation in CF4. For tenuous gas TPCs, our proposed technique significantly enhances the sensitivity of gravity wave detectors and offsets the primary disadvantages of using such gases. Furthermore, in gas gravity wave detection, this capability allows for distinguishing signal from noise and correcting for partial quenching variations. This study examines the introduction of machine scoring and moderation protocols for evaluating commercial drivers based on their driving behaviors, as observed in automated roadside cameras capturing footage from vehicle-mounted, time-synchronized traffic monitoring systems. The research investigates how moderation systems function as predictive processing mechanisms that integrate bottom-up sensory input with top-down expectations to make top-down judgments. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate the social implications of these systems and how the decision-making processes within machine moderation can be modeled using modern affective computing frameworks. Leveraging concepts from machine intelligence, the paper illustrates how roadside machine analysis and expert moderation interact in a smart contextual intelligent system to ensure fair assessments of commercial driving performance. By combining affective computing with contextual machine intelligence, the study reveals that machine moderation serves as a form of machine emotional labor. Consequently, the research argues that the development of machine rules and procedures must be guided by an ethical framework grounded in social theory. Finally, the study concludes that both machine analysis and expert moderation require transparent reporting of their underlying mechanisms to facilitate continuous refinement. This approach to establishing an ethical framework for machine moderation is essential for the successful adoption of machine intelligence in commercial driving evaluation. The findings are supported by data from a pilot study conducted in Hong Kong, which tested machine rules and procedures for assessing commercial drivers. The results indicate that while machine rules show promise, further refinement is necessary to enhance the accuracy of automated judgments. Additionally, evidence suggests that while machine moderation can improve consistency, it may also introduce biases that require mitigation through the application of machine intelligence principles. Overall, the study confirms that ethical machine intelligence is essential for the successful deployment of machine analysis in commercial driving assessments. This conclusion is derived from an in-depth analysis of the decision-making processes involved in machine moderation, which were examined through the lens of machine intelligence, emotion, and ethics. This paper presents the results of the Out-of-Categories challenge, which sought to identify if specific deep learning network architectures are superior for classification tasks involving categories significantly distant from those in the training data. The competition utilized three distinct challenges based on pre-print models from Li et al. (2019), Xu et al. (2019), and Liu et al. (2019), with all comparisons made against the ResNet50 baseline. The findings indicate that while the average accuracy of the three models proposed in this work slightly outperforms ResNet50, such performance gains are not consistently achieved across individual challenges or even within the same category. Consequently, the study concludes that there is no definitive evidence to suggest that certain architectures are inherently better than ResNet50 on this specific validation set. However, the authors note that their models did surpass the ResNet50 baseline in approximately 40% of the combinations analyzed, highlighting that these models are capable of outperforming the baseline in certain scenarios. The authors aim for this research to encourage the development of more effective knowledge transfer models that can handle the distribution shifts characteristic of out-of-category tasks. In recent years, Gaussian random fields have gained significant traction as a tool for analyzing data within the human connectome framework. As an extension of this approach, we propose a method for calculating geodesic distances between images on a Gaussian random field manifold and for identifying the corresponding geodesic paths. Our pipeline integrates standard image registration routines with efficient numerical algorithms to address the inherent complexities of distance computation and geodesic optimization in unbounded domains. We validate our algorithm by presenting quantitative and qualitative comparisons of connectome data against synthetic datasets. Additionally, in a collaborative effort with the Human Connectome Project, we have utilized our implementation to derive a geodesic distance matrix for a subset of their participants. This matrix is now made available for the 2019 Data Challenge in the conference series Image Processing with Neural Networks and Applied Machine Learning. To facilitate scientific discovery, we have also released a suite of tools designed for geodesic path analysis on Gaussian random field manifolds. This software is accessible as an independent library alongside our pathway estimation tool, which addresses the challenge of reconstructing geodesic paths on this specific manifold. While our implementation is initially restricted to low-dimensional random fields, it serves as a robust foundation for extending the methodology to broader stochastic spaces. Specifically, our techniques can be adapted for geodesic distance estimation on weighted graphs by constructing the random field to ensure compatibility with the graph's metric structure. Furthermore, although our current implementation does not incorporate probabilistic distance calculations, extending the algorithm to support such estimates is feasible. This enhancement would significantly improve the robustness of the pathway estimation process, which relies on stochastic gradient descent and is currently highly sensitive to initialization. Finally, we demonstrate the practicality of our approach through a proof-of-concept application in a recent data challenge involving the human connectome. This challenge, sponsored by the Human Connectome Project, sought to identify common connectome pathways among participants, with our contribution providing a solution for geodesic pathway estimation. The pathway estimation tool developed to address this challenge is now available for scientific exploration. Overall, our findings indicate that Gaussian random fields, when applied to connectome analysis, can effectively identify pathways connecting brain regions. However, our results also highlight the necessity for probabilistic extensions to our algorithm to ensure that pathway reconstructions are not unduly influenced by initial conditions. We examine a real-world application of word problems involving vocabulary, specifically doublet problems from historical corpora. These puzzles consist of queries like "How many [adjectives] nouns do you count?"; given a corpus of words and their co-occurrence counts, the task is to determine the total occurrences of words that are both adjectives and co-occur with specific named adjectives. We introduce a solution utilizing solution-length automata (SLA), which we demonstrate to be weakly equivalent to the original regular expression defining named languages, while offering superior computational properties. Additionally, we develop an algorithm employing the $O(n^3)$ method to construct SLAs. Finally, we explore the application of SLAs in generating word problems with known solutions, thereby enabling inverse problem solving where one starts with an answer and works backward to construct a valid question. This approach is supported by a weak duality between deletion and substitution. Specifically, regarding duality, we show that while substitution transforms SLAs into equivalent SLAs, deletion results in a loss of length information; consequently, we adapt the SLA definition to address this deficit. Through examples and experiments, we illustrate that this work supports both the practical and theoretical objectives of recent research into problem-pairing. It is established that if a strongly connected digraph $D$ possesses a small maximum size of an independent set, it must be pancyclic. This paper investigates the relationship between independence counts and other characteristics. We demonstrate that for any integer $k \geq 2$, a strongly $k$-hamiltonian digraph $D$ with independence count $id(D) \leq k-1$ is pancyclic. Furthermore, we examine the link between the property of being strongly $k$-hamiltonian and the existence of a spanning strong branchings. This yields the theorem stating: Given two integers $k, \ell$ where $k \geq 2\ell$, any strongly $k$-hamiltonian digraph $D$ containing a spanning strong $(1, \ell)$-factor is pancyclic. We also explore the inverse problem: determining the minimum $\ell$ such that a strongly $k$-hamiltonian digraph $D$ with a $\sqrt{\ell}$-spanning strong $(1, \sqrt{\ell})$-factor is pancyclic. We prove that $\ell = 5$ satisfies this condition. Additionally, we extend this result to multigraphs, showing that a strongly $k$-hamiltonian multigraph $G$ with a $\sqrt{\ell}$-spanning $(1, \sqrt{\ell})$-bifactor is also pancyclic. The converse of this statement is true when $\ell = 1$. Finally, we revisit the problem posed by Brualdi and Goldman (1979): identifying the minimum value of $\ell$ that guarantees that a strongly $k$-hamiltonian multigraph $G$ with a $\ell$-spanning bifactor is pancyclic. We provide a partial resolution to this problem and conclude with several open questions. Notably, one of these inquiries suggests that a strongly $k$-hamiltonian multigraph $G$ with a spanning $B_k$-bifactor (where $B_k$ denotes a union of $k$ vertex-disjoint paths) is pancyclic. Furthermore, the existence of such a $B_k$-bifactor is noted to be a consequence of Conjecture 1 proposed by Thomassen (1999). This study introduces a new algorithm designed to derive a linear Koopman operator representation for dynamical systems. The linear KSK model integrates sparse grid sampling, spectral basis functions, and random matrix techniques. Spectral bases enable the model to capture dynamical features, including nonlinearity, periodicity, and transient behaviors, while sparse grid sampling reduces the computational burden associated with high-dimensional state spaces. Additionally, a randomized Kaczmarz method is employed to efficiently estimate the linear Koopman operator. This approach allows for the simultaneous estimation of the spectral basis and the spectral gap, facilitating the prediction of unobserved system states and the identification of Data-Driven Invariant Manifolds (DDIM). Numerical simulations demonstrate that the linear Koopman representation effectively predicts unobserved system states and isolates DDIMs. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm exhibits high computational efficiency within large-scale, high-dimensional systems. The methodology is validated through a DC-DC buck converter case study. The entire algorithm is implemented in Python and made available via the KSKEst package on GitHub. The method can be extended to address other Koopman-related challenges, such as mode detection, control, and optimization. The method descriptions are detailed in a companion paper. This work represents an expanded and updated version of a study previously published in *IEEE Access* under the title: The sparse-grid-driven adaptive spectral Koopman method for data-driven analysis of dynamical systems. The current publication includes an enhanced discussion on sparsification and DDIM extraction, alongside a significantly broadened range of numerical simulations. Urban environments are renowned for the diversity of interactions they foster, yet it remains unclear how external shocks, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, influence the variety of social contacts. To address this, we examined face-to-face social interactions in London both before and after lockdowns, combining a one-month pre-pandemic survey with three post-pandemic campaigns conducted one month into, between, and after lockdown periods. Our findings indicate that while average encounter sizes remained stable, the income diversity within urban interactions decreased significantly during the pandemic. We attribute this reduction in diversity to behaviorally driven changes in activity patterns, specifically a diminished variety of destinations visited and an overall reduction in movement. These results underscore the vital necessity of face-to-face contact for maintaining social and economic networks. Furthermore, they highlight the critical role of physical spaces in facilitating diverse urban encounters and suggest that movement restrictions can be lifted without risking widespread contact, provided that safety guidelines are adhered to. Finally, the mechanisms underlying these shifts in activity patterns and income diversity can inform the design of targeted behavioral interventions to promote sustainability and resilience in urban systems. **Highlights:** * The pandemic altered human behavior, leading to less diverse urban interactions.

Numerical simulations employing multiphase field-split facilitators are essential for investigating complex multiphase flows, particularly in heterogeneous porous media. This study evaluates the efficacy of popular nonlinear field-split facilitators within a black-box flow simulation framework. To address challenges associated with faceted surface interactions during facettal splitting, we implement the semi-implicit Curvilinear Interface Reconstruction (CIR) method. For the multiphase field equations, we apply the Van-der-Paals (VP) and Multiphase-Capillary-Darcy (MCD) facilitators, comparing them against the standard Van-der-Paals-Friction (VPF) approach. These models are tested using both the incompressible two-phase Darcy equation and a two-equation formulation for multiphase multicomponent flow. The analysis focuses on two- and three-dimensional cases involving a single or multiple active regions of high multiphase saturation. While VPF and VP methods demonstrate comparable performance in simple scenarios, the MCD facilitator yields superior results in complex cases characterized by extensive active regions. Furthermore, VPF produces the most accurate outcomes in three-dimensional settings involving multiple active regions. Across all models, the use of parallel-integrated CIR provides a significant enhancement in multiphase flow simulation results. Finally, the VP and MCD facilitators offer the additional capability to model multicomponent mass transfer between phases. Overall, nonlinear field-split facilitiators based on VP and MCD formulations serve as viable alternatives to VPF, with VPF remaining the most accurate for resolving two-dimensional problems with multiple active regions. Finally, a preliminary discussion on extending two-phase flow facilitators to fully three-dimensional multiphase multicomponent systems is included. This work serves as a foundation for the three-phase flow extension of the CIR method, which is currently under development. Optical resonators are widely used to confine and manipulate light, with certain types exhibiting exceptional capabilities for controlling an light's polarization. This work introduces a novel class of resonators termed single-handedness resonators, which scatter and trap light while maintaining its single-handedness—defined as having only one type of pseudo-polarization state. We provide a definition, physical interpretation, and practical realization of this concept. Additionally, we examine a single-mode single-handedness resonator, highlighting its potential to serve as a platform for investigating fundamental light-particle interactions. This framework also offers a method for constructing photonic chiral devices, a critical component for future quantum technologies. Furthermore, we address single-mode chiral resonators that support only one handedness, proposing them as single-photon sources capable of generating a single output photon with a predetermined polarization. Finally, we outline strategies for generating and detecting single-handedness particles, including photons, electrons, and Weyl fermions. These findings are expected to advance the study of chiral physics and find diverse applications across various fields. This setup yields an action equivalent to an exponential of the Cardy action evaluated at negative central charge, $c=-3/2$. By performing a field redefinition that results in a Liouville-like action with a zero cosmological constant, and by identifying the path integral over the zero mode of the Liouville field with the Penner model, we establish a connection to the $U(N)$ two-matrix model. Additionally, a path integral for a variant of the two-matrix model with a cosine potential is found to correspond to a "double-scaled" version of the JT path integral. Finally, we demonstrate that the large-$N$ free energy of the two-matrix model aligns with the on-shell action of the "dressed" Jackiw-Teitelboim black hole solution. This finding supports the earlier hypothesis regarding the connection between the U(1) reduction of the $U(N)$ four-dimensional Yang-Mills theory and the coherent state of the JT gravity solution featuring a boundary in a Euclidean dilaton black hole background. The TRD (Truncated Regge-Wheeler) equation represents an exact solution to the Einstein equations, functioning as a ideal fluid warp drive solution with negative energy density and the non-zero cosmological constant. By applying a non-zero cosmological constant, the total energy density, pressure, and magnitude of the gravito-electric field are all modified. Specifically, the cosmological constant mitigates the magnitude of the negative energy density, static pressure, and gravito-electric field. The threshold value for the cosmological constant required to revert the spacetime to Minkowski space is established. Furthermore, the implications of the TRD solution for both a universe dominated by dark energy and one where dark energy and matter coexist are examined. The results indicate that the warp field diminishes in magnitude as the cosmological constant approaches the critical value that restores Minkowski space. Additionally, the magnitude of the negative energy density is directly proportional to that of the warp field. Finally, the gravito-electric field exerts the strongest repulsive force on the warp bubble in a universe containing dark energy and matter compared to the scenario involving only the cosmological constant. This suggests that a more complex dark energy model, such as the interaction between dark energy and dark matter, may be more viable than a model containing only the cosmological constant. Specifically, the interaction between dark energy and matter generates a more complex dark energy equation of state, which in turn produces a more complex warp field. Furthermore, the warp field's magnitude is negatively correlated with the distance from the warp ring. Consequently, the warp ring must be positioned far enough from the destination to generate a sufficiently strong warp field. Additionally, the warp ring should be placed as close as possible to the target to maximize the warp field's magnitude. Additionally, the warp bubble's velocity is influenced by the cosmological constant. Specifically, when the cosmological constant is positive, the warp bubble's velocity increases as it moves away from the warp ring. Conversely, when the cosmological constant is negative, the warp bubble's velocity decreases with distance from the warp ring. However, there exists a critical negative value for the cosmological constant; if its magnitude exceeds this threshold, the warp bubble's velocity will decrease with distance when far from the warp ring but increase when it is very close. If the magnitude of the negative cosmological constant is less than this critical value, the warp bubble's velocity will increase as it moves away from the warp ring. Cities are increasingly becoming complex, heterogeneous environments, prompting the creation of numerous new applications that depend on high-quality geospatial data. However, these applications face significant hurdles due to the fragmented nature of this data across various governmental and private organizations, each operating with distinct priorities and standards. Consequently, there is a pressing need for new methods to manage and share these information resources. This chapter outlines two innovative approaches: the GUIDES initiative and the GEOS platform. Both provide a flexible framework for integrating geospatial data through a shared reference framework and for delivering geographic information on-demand. This high-level overview highlights the core principles and key features of GUIDES and GEOS, which are currently being implemented within the CITYLIGHTS project. It also presents two use cases: providing geospatial infrastructure data to support bicycle route planning and enabling the creation of a geographic information system to assist project managers in urban construction projects. Finally, this discussion explores how the proposed solutions can address the complex challenges associated with geospatial data management and sharing in urban settings. Specifically, it examines the benefits of a service-oriented approach for accessing geographic information and the associated difficulties in designing and implementing such a solution. The CITYLIGHTS project aims to validate these solutions in two major European cities: Madrid and Turin. The chapter concludes by identifying future research directions and potential applications in this field. The dynamics of motional excitation and deexcitation are central to the design of practical quantum algorithms and the analysis of experimental data in trapped-ion quantum computing. However, in large ion crystals, the coupling of modes, as well as temperature and motional state distributions, are difficult to characterize. Additionally, because heating is an inherent aspect of ion trap operations, there is a need to quantify the rates at which modes and the crystal as a whole gain energy. This study addresses these challenges by utilizing collective spin dephasing as a method to measure mode temperatures, motional state distributions, and heating velocities in a 2D calcium ion crystal. The approach leverages the large spin coherence times achievable with the highly scalable F1+ ion. We demonstrate that, at low temperatures, the ground state of the collective vibrational modes is occupied with a Gaussian distribution, and the heating rates of these modes are nearly independent of their excitation numbers. Furthermore, the heating rates of the global center-of-mass mode and the m=2 mode vary with temperature, a phenomenon attributed to the mechanical response of the crystal. These findings offer a quantitative framework for understanding the factors influencing heating rates in large ion crystals. Additionally, the research confirms that motional state distributions can be tailored at will by adjusting the relative amplitudes of individual laser beams used to drive spin-dependent motional sidebands. Finally, we propose a method to extract the heating rate of a specific mode from the time evolution of its dephasing rate. Collectively, these results provide a comprehensive toolset for investigating the dynamics of mode coupling, temperature, motional state distributions, and heating rates in large trapped-ion crystals. Such data is essential for developing error correction schemes in quantum computing and for designing and analyzing the outputs of quantum simulation experiments. Specifically, we present the first measurement of heating rates for a sideband mode, revealing it to be approximately an order of magnitude slower than the response of other modes. This measurement was achieved by analyzing the time evolution of the dephasing rate, a technique that may serve as a general approach for characterizing mode heating in other quantum systems. We introduce a quantum mechanical framework designed to investigate the chemical and electromagnetic contributions of electromagnetic field enhancement in Surface-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (TERS). In this approach, the local electromagnetic field around the silver surface is modeled using the optical dielectric function, while the substrate's electronic structure is described via the Kohn-Sham equation. The study examines and compares the electronic structures of silver and an adenine molecule during the TERS process. Our findings indicate that the electromagnetic contribution in TERS is not uniform across the entire silver surface; instead, it is confined to the region directly beneath the laser hotspot. Additionally, we demonstrate that the excitation of Surface Plasmon Resonance (SPR) is a necessary condition for this contribution to exist. These results are expected to facilitate future quantitative studies on the electromagnetic effects in TERS. This study presents the initial findings of a systematic survey of the central regions of nearby galaxies, utilizing the Sardinia Radio Telescope's (SRT) K-band to detect anomalous microwave emission (AEME). The observations cover a total area of 155 square degrees, featuring 10 galaxies with observed fluxes at K-band (20 GHz) reported for the first time. We identified AEME in Centaurus A, NGC 4435, NGC 4490, NGC 4552, NGC 4631, NGC 4725, NGC 5291, NGC 5474, NGC 6052, and IC 5252. Specifically, AEME was detected in the centers of Centaurus A, NGC 4435, NGC 4490, NGC 4631, NGC 5291, NGC 5474, and NGC 6052, as well as in the eastern lobe of Centaurus A, the southwestern lobe of NGC 5291, the southeastern lobe of NGC 4725, and the northeastern lobe of NGC 5474. Additionally, we observed AEME in the NGC 4435-NGC 4490 pair, the NGC 4427-NGC 4428 pair, and the NGC 4472-NGC 4725 pair. The flux density of the brightest source, Centaurus A, was measured at approximately 1.5 Jy, aligning with previous studies. The second most luminous galaxy, NGC 4435, exhibits an emission of roughly 0.15 Jy, which is about 10% of Centaurus A's emission. The third brightest galaxy, NGC 5291, shows a flux of about 0.05 Jy, roughly one-third that of NGC 4435. We also report the detection of AEME in the NGC 4435-NGC 4490 pair, the NGC 4427-NGC 4428 pair, and the NGC 4472-NGC 4725 pair.

Ammonium sulfate ($\text{(NH}_4$)$^2(\text{HSO}_4)$) is recognized as a strong electrocaloric material, a property attributed to the extensive entropy change resulting from the reorientation of $\text{NH}_4^+$ ions. To investigate the origins of this phenomenon, we conducted first-principles calculations on a $2 \times 2 \times 2$ supercell. By applying symmetry-breaking constraints, we modeled the potential energy landscape and the ion reconfiguration responsible for the observed effects. Our findings indicate that the substantial entropy change arises from the collective realignment of ions within a cluster, a process that creates additional low-energy states. Furthermore, the ferroelectric polarization is linked to a reaction between $\text{HSO}_4^-$ ions, while the $\text{NH}_4^+$ ions exhibit only a minor contribution to polarization. These results offer valuable insights into understanding and designing molecular materials for use as caloric materials. Additionally, we demonstrate that a machine-learning-based normal-mode analysis can identify the entropy contribution from ion rearrangement. This approach isolates the specific vibrational modes driving the ion response, revealing that the atomic displacements in these modes closely mirror the equilibrium configuration of the $\text{HSO}_4^-$ ions. Consequently, the caloric effect in $\text{(NH}_4$)$^2(\text{HSO}_4)$ can be interpreted as an entropic shift from a ferroelectric ground state to a ferroelectrically disordered state. This insight may guide the computational search for new molecular materials with superior caloric performance. Finally, the methodology employed in this study is applicable to modeling other materials, such as ammonium hydrogen phosphate. **Background:** Reinforcement learning (RL) is a widely adopted mathematical framework for modeling how organisms and artificial systems learn from rewards. Within the brain, the midbrain is thought to encode a prediction error signal that drives this process. However, the behavioral correlates of such prediction errors have remained unexplored. Additionally, while various RL theories exist, empirical validation of tactics guiding choices between exploration and exploitation remains absent. Finally, RL theory posits that distinct tactics emerge based on whether learning relies on model-free or model-based mechanisms. **Aims:** This study sought to: (1) identify a midbrain prediction error signal in humans; (2) test whether suboptimal tactics—specifically those driven by "switching" tactics favoring either pure exploration or pure exploitation—"greedy" tactics favoring immediate payoff, and "two-step" tactics anticipating future rewards based on one-step actions; (3) investigate whether individual differences in tactics correlate with inter-individual variations in the prediction error signal; and (4) examine how tactics differ when participants employ model-free versus model-based learning strategies. **Results:** We identified a midbrain prediction error signal exhibiting suboptimal switching tactics correlated with inter-individual variability. Furthermore, we observed a dissociation between model-free and model-based learning tactics, with the latter relying more heavily on model-based processes. **Conclusions:** These findings suggest that (1) subopticular tactics are trait-like and rooted in biological processes, and (2) the midbrain's prediction error signal is influenced by the interaction between individual differences in learning tactics and the specific learning model employed. Finally, we demonstrate that model-based learning is more sensitive to the predictive structure of tasks compared to model-free learning. **New & Noteworthy:** Our results provide the first empirical evidence of a midbrain prediction error signal constrained by task-specific tactics and individual learning styles. These insights offer novel insights into the neural mechanisms underlying human learning. **Keywords:** Reinforcement learning, prediction error, exploration vs. exploitation, model-free, model-based. **Abbreviations:** RL = reinforcement learning; Q = value; TD = temporal difference; HPC = hippocampus; PFC = prefrontal cortex; PFC = posterior parietal cortex; PFC = posterior parietal cortex. **Acknowledgments:** This work was supported by the European Research Council (ERC) under the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme (Grant Agreement No. 679761), the National Research Foundation of Korea

We tackle the approximate close-neighbor search problem for time series under the Fréchet distance within the RAM model, which operates under the Random Access and Discrete Point assumptions. For queries $q$ and a database $\mathcal{D}$ of $d$-dimensional $n$-point time series, we aim to locate the nearest neighbor of a query $q$ under the Fréchet distance, adhering to the following constraints: (i) the algorithm must compute a $\tau$-approximate minimum distance between $q$ and $\mathcal{D}$ for a given $\tau \geq 1$, and (ii) the algorithm must run within a specific time limit $T$. We establish lower bounds on the exponent $e$ for the time complexity $O(n^e T)$ across various scenarios. In the first scenario, we demonstrate that for any valid $T = n^c$, the value of $e$ cannot exceed $2 - c$. This result implies that existing algorithms with a time complexity of $O(n^2 / \log n)$ are nearly optimal. In the second scenario, we show that for any $c \geq 1$, if the minimum distance is exact (meaning $\tau = 1$), then $e$ must be at least $1 + c$. Consequently, for $T = n$, the minimum distance cannot be exact, confirming the lower bound of $\tau = O(\log n)$ proposed by Carmi et al. [ESA'19]. Finally, we present an algorithm that, given $T = n^c$ where $1 < c < 2$, achieves an accuracy parameter of $\tau = \frac{c-1}{2-c+c\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{(c-1)^2}}}$, thereby proving that the lower bound is tight for this range of $c$. Furthermore, when $c=1.01$, the algorithm yields an $\epsilon$-approximate minimum distance with $\epsilon = 0.019$. Our proofs rely on reductions from the 3SUM problem. Our findings are based on the hypothesis that 3SUM cannot be solved in $O(n^1-\delta)$ time for any $\delta > 0$. Additionally, we provide an implementation of our approach under the squared Euclidean distance metric. Measurement error correction is a crucial technique for analyzing data, yet it has largely been overlooked in the machine learning community. Existing methods typically rely on inverting the forward measurement model, but these approaches often suffer from poor scalability and inadequate generalization. This study introduces a novel algorithm named Iterative Bayesian Unfolding. The method is grounded in the Bayesian likelihood principle and demonstrates superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art solutions. Through simulations on synthetic data, the algorithm's effectiveness is validated across various dimensions regarding accuracy, scalability, and memory efficiency. Shared autonomy represents a scenario where multiple robots interact and coordinate through shared decision-making. In this context, robots must exchange data, exchange knowledge, and negotiate to reach consensus. This coordination relies on communication protocols that establish standards governing how robots exchange information. This paper investigates the relationship between communication protocols and shared autonomy tasks. Specifically, it explores how different protocol standards influence shared autonomy operations through simulation. Using a supply chain logistics framework, the study examines two distinct robotic standards: (1) the Control Message Standard (CMS), which defines robot-to robot control directives, and (2 the Communication Interface Standard (CIS), which specifies communication methods. Results indicate that both CMS and CIS significantly impact shared autonomy. Notably, these two standards do not necessarily yield the same outcomes when used independently. Consequently, when developing standards for autonomous systems, researchers should evaluate the specific impacts of those standards on shared autonomy tasks. This paper contributes to the standards development process by offering a quantitative basis for understanding how standards affect shared autonomy operations. Furthermore, it provides a framework that can be adapted to evaluate the effects of other potential standards. Ultimately, this research supports the broader goal of ensuring that robotic technologies deliver value to human users. By enabling users to measure the impact of standards on shared autonomy, we facilitate the development of standards that effectively support collaborative robotic tasks. This approach supports the creation of technologies that generate shared value for both humans and robots within shared work environments. The findings are derived from a simulation of a shared autonomy problem involving two robots tasked with coordinating to remove obstacles from a supply chain. This setup models two CMS and CIS configurations, with performance measured by the time required for robots to clear the line. The study demonstrates that both CMS and CIS affect the efficiency of shared autonomy, with the Control Message Standard exerting a more significant influence than the Communication Interface Standard. Additionally, specific combinations of CMS and CIS can lead to either improved or degraded performance. For instance, certain configurations allow robots to clear obstacles more quickly, while others result in slower clearance. These findings highlight the complex interplay between communication standards and coordinated robot behavior. They also underscore the need for careful consideration of how standards are designed and implemented to ensure optimal performance in shared tasks. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for future research and practice. It suggests that the standards community should consider the impact of standards on shared autonomy and collaborate with the research community to develop standards that support coordinated tasks. We introduce HiTMap, a new topological navigation framework designed for exploration in unknown environments. Distinct from most existing topological map systems, HiTMap maintains an explicit hierarchical structure rooted at the user's current location to facilitate rapid retrieval and efficient traversal. To support both online and offline applications, we developed a novel data structure called the HiT-Graph. This structure enables efficient data loading and allows both forward and backward navigation from the current pose, serving as the foundation for key operations like map retrieval, exploration, and path planning. Furthermore, we address map merging to handle redundant data and propose a new mechanism that enhances navigation by expanding the known area and improving retrieval speed and efficiency. To enhance system throughput in modern communication networks, this paper introduces two new types of complementary code sets (CCS): the inter-group complementary code set (IG-CCS) based on multivariable functions and the two-dimensional Z-supplementary array code set (2D-Z-ASCS) constructed using multivariable functions and supplementary array code sets. The IG-CCS is developed by utilizing functions within a finite field that differ in specific variables, while the 2D-Z-ASCS is formed by arranging CCSs into a two-dimensional array with strategic missing elements. Under the condition that the cardinality of a finite field is a prime power, the proposed CCSs achieve maximum minimum correlation (MCR) performance by fully exploiting functions over finite fields. Specifically, the IG-CCS achieves MCR equal to the lower bound, while the 2D-Z-ASCS reaches MCR of $k^2$, where $k$ represents the order of the CCS. Simulation results validate the feasibility and effectiveness of the CCS construction methods. These novel CCS structures offer superior performance and hold significant potential for practical applications, including spread spectrum communication, code-division multiple access, and two-dimensional radar. Additionally, these methods can be extended to other scenarios by employing functions from algebraic geometry or employing non-perfect CCSs. The corresponding code books are accessible at http://www.2d-z-ASCS.com. Computed Tomography (CT) images are typically reconstructed using convex models like compressed sensing (CS) or total variation (TV), which rely on the assumption of single-energy X-ray projections. However, most practical scanners utilize multiple X-ray energies. While polyenergetic CT reconstruction has been previously addressed, material decomposition has often been neglected. This work introduces a joint reconstruction and decomposition framework for polyenergetic CT that simultaneously achieves image reconstruction, decomposition, and sensor denoising. The proposed method is based on a convex optimization formulation. Furthermore, to enhance computational efficiency, we develop two novel algorithms to solve the variational problem, with the second algorithm offering superior efficiency and accuracy. Numerical experiments on both synthetic data and real measurements demonstrate the proposed framework's advantages over existing state-of-the-art single-energy and polyenergetic CT approaches. The results highlight the method's capabilities in robust sensor denoising, accurate CT reconstruction, and precise material decomposition. Additionally, the framework is shown to be highly computationally efficient. The code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/PolyCT}. Quantum effects, characterized by spatial nonlocality and the absence of wavefunction overlap across the inter-metallic region, become significant when investigating gap-plasmons in the limit of nearly closed nanogaps. This study utilizes the jellium model for metals and employs jellium-plasmon poles within the T-matrix formalism to calculate gap-plasmons and their associated response fields. Our findings indicate that for nanogaps approaching zero separation, gap-plasmons remain extended across the gap despite negligible electron spill-out. The most probable explanation for this phenomenon is the field-like characterization of gap-plasmons; consequently, the inter-metallic space is permeated by electric fields of sufficient intensity to induce electron density displacement in both metals, resulting in extended modes. These insights are corroborated by time-domain simulations of field-pulse excitation within a three-metal system. Furthermore, our theoretical predictions align with experimental measurements conducted on a gold-nanoparticle-cobalt-core configuration. These results suggest that gap-plasmons in nanometallic systems are inherently hybridized combinations of surface and interband plasmons. Finally, we demonstrate that the nonlocal response of electron plasmons can be modeled as a frequency-dependent effective electron mass within the jellium model. Incorporating this nonlocality into our calculations reveals that low-energy gap-plasmons exhibit further extension into the gap, alongside a substantial increase in the inter-metallic region's electron density. These conclusions are supported by comparisons with density functional theory calculations for simpler systems. Ultimately, these results provide a comprehensive understanding of the electronic and field distributions of gap-plasmons as the nanogap尺寸 approaches zero. This understanding is essential for addressing the paradox of electron density depletion observed in the vanishingly small gaps of metallic nano-gaps. Additionally, our conclusions offer valuable insights for the design and operation of field-emission devices and nanometallic nano-electromagnetica. To achieve this, researchers must account for the hybridization of surface and interband plasmons, the nonlocal response of inner-electron shells, and the interaction between electrons and the electric field of gap-plasmons. These factors are particularly critical in the regime of ultra-small nanogaps. Our conclusions are supported by the collaboration of the 3rd author (A.R.) and the experimentalist team (A.P., M.T., and A.N.). The term matching technique is a widely adopted and highly effective approach for contextual named entity retrieval. However, simply retrieving entities containing pre-defined terms often yields results with low relevance to specific contexts, as human relevance encompasses various factors beyond the mere presence of key terms. Consequently, it is essential to assess context for relevance based on individual terms. This paper introduces a novel method called Term Relevance Response (TRR) to enhance contextual named entity retrieval. To implement TRR, we train a neural network to predict the relevance of a context to a given term using bi-directional context representations. We assess the performance of TRR on natural language processing tasks involving fine-grained contextual relevance, such as named entity link-disambiguation and contextually-saturated entity retrieval. Experimental findings demonstrate that TRR consistently and consistently improves the performance of standard context-based entity retrieval methods on real-world datasets. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/11zhangwei/TRR. Furthermore, we plan to explore applying TRR to enhance semantic matching in other fine-grained entity recognition tasks, including named entity semantic similarity and entity resolution.
