We propose a novel observable for the handbag matrix element $\langle 0|j^\mu|P\rangle$ linked to generalized parton distributions, characterized by proton recoil polarization. Developed within the framework of exclusive deep virtual Compton scattering (DVCS) at high momentum transfer, this observable is accessible in experiments featuring an unpolarized lepton beam, an unpolarized target, and a polarized proton remnant. This recoil proton polarization probe offers distinct advantages over traditional DVCS measurements, which typically depend on the beam charge sign to differentiate between bethe-helicity and Bethe interference terms. Notably, this probe yields a complex combination of these terms without requiring beam charge discrimination, thereby providing model-independent direct access to the quark GPD $C_{2q}$. Furthermore, this method remains applicable in DVCS experiments conducted with fixed-target configurations. To demonstrate its utility, we illustrate how this observable can be measured at the Electron Ion Collider using remnant protons obtained via proton dissociation. Our findings indicate a strong potential for extracting the quark GPD $C_{2q}$ from the corresponding cross section, which is dominated by the product of bethe-helicity and Bethe interference terms. Consequently, this method establishes a new pathway for directly determining $C_{2q}$ and may also be extended to other hard exclusive reactions sensitive to $C_{2q}$. Additionally, our approach is readily adaptable to reactions involving other charged hadrons, such as kaons, for which this observable has not yet been investigated. Finally, we note that this methodology is readily extensible to both transversely and longitudinally polarized DVCS reactions. Our findings are directly applicable to upcoming DVCS experiments that will measure proton remnant polarization, such as those planned at the Electron-Ion Collider. This includes a proposed measurement of transverse DVCS on a proton remnant with $L_z$ polarization at $Q^2 = 4 \text{ GeV}^2$, which could enable the first direct determination of $C_{2q}$ with an accuracy of approximately 10%. Such a result would serve as a critical benchmark for testing the reliability of this new methodology, particularly given its independence from beam charge sign. This measurement would also provide a valuable cross-check for the proposed determination of $C_{2q}$ using unpolarized target data with beam-charge- asymmetry. The escalating complexity of socio-technical environments necessitates a more holistic approach to work, one that integrates human cognition with machine intelligence. This paper proposes a novel framework for further integrating human and machine minds, termed "Augmented Synthetic Intelligence" (ASI). Drawing inspiration from the frameworks for Artificial General Intelligence developed by LeCun et al., we define its core components as intention, emotion, and social intelligence. We examine the theoretical foundations of these components, analyze their relevance to human-machine augmentation, and explore applications within augmented intelligence systems. The study concludes by identifying key research challenges and future directions concerning human-machine intelligence collaboration. Finally, we demonstrate the versatility of this framework by illustrating a human-machine team engaged in mental calibration. Overall, this framework serves as a foundation for advancing theories and methodologies for effectively augmenting machine intelligence and facilitating meaningful human-machine collaboration. Furthermore, it supports the design of augmented intelligence systems, including advanced collaborative cognitive systems, and provides a lens for evaluating existing systems through the lens of human-machine cognitive collaboration. The resulting theoretical framework for ASI offers robust guidance for future research and development in this evolving field. We present a theoretical investigation into the ground state and thermal transitions of correlated bosons connected via spin-orbit coupling within an optical lattice, specifically in the band-filling regime. This setup results in a superfluid exhibiting intrinsic spatial modulation. By solving the full many-body problem in the grand canonical ensemble, we determine that the superfluid's modulated state arises from an instability in the Cooper pair fluid. Furthermore, we derive the transition temperature for superfluidity and the deconfinement temperature below which pairs, acting as composite bosons, condense into the spatially modulated Cooper pair fluid. We also calculate the ratio of the transition temperature regarding superfluidity to that of the deconfinement transition regarding spatially modulated pairing, noting that this ratio is governed by the ratio of the bare band gap to the interaction strength. Finally, we discuss the physical implications of these findings. Our theoretical framework aligns with recent experimental evidence indicating modulated pairing in a lattice-orbit coupled system [Phys. Rev. Lett. 127, 033601 (2021)]. These results offer a foundation for designing experiments to investigate the superfluid transition temperature in such systems. Additionally, the proposed model is applicable to various topological contexts, including the topological superconductivity required for Majorana zero modes. The model's parameters can be adjusted to explore a topological superfluid or to achieve the conditions necessary for Majorana zero modes in topological superconductors [Phys. Rev. B 104, 024508 (2021); Phys. Rev. Research 3, 043106 (2021)] within the framework of cold-atom setups. Root graphs, whose vertices represent cosets of a subgroup within a group, are known to universaly encode the group actions of that group. We demonstrate that every finite abelian group admits a root graph that is both regular and girth four, utilizing only a minimal number of colors in its vertex labeling. This minimal color count corresponds to the number of direct cyclic summands needed to decompose the group. Furthermore, we establish that any finite abelian group can be realized by a family of regular root graphs with girth four, requiring at most four colors, with the group size determining the size of these graphs. Our findings are supported by computer searches conducted on nearly 25,000 non-isomorphic graphs of order up to 256. To our knowledge, this work marks the first investigation into the possible degeneration patterns of finite abelian groups into regular girth four graphs. Additionally, we examine the realization of finite non-abelian groups under relaxed constraints, specifically dropping the regularity requirement and limiting the color count to seven. We confirm that all non-abelian groups of orders up to 100 can be realized by root graphs satisfying these conditions, and we categorize all such graphs with five or fewer colors up to order 86. Our work concludes with several open problems and a set of unproven conjectures. Notably, while most groups with orders up to 100 are realized by root graphs with girth four and at most seven colors, the only non-solvable group lacking this realization is $A_5$. We conjecture that every finite non-abelian group can be realized by a root graph with girth four using no more than seven colors. We also propose that every finite group, including the specific case of $A_5$, can be realized by a root graph with girth four using at most five colors. Finally, we assert that any finite group $G$ can be realized by a root graph with girth four using at most $d(G)$ colors, where $d(G)$ denotes the minimum degree of a faithful permutation representation of $G$. We investigate AdS/CFT correspondence in low dimensions derived from massive Type IIA string theory. Specifically, we construct new dual pairs of AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ and AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$, where the bulk theory is massive Type IIA supergravity. The boundary conformal field theories arise from the compactification of 10-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=4$ Chern-Simons theories at specific levels. Our analysis examines various dual pairs characterized by different values of internal fluxes. Furthermore, we compute the central charges for the 2D and 1D conformal field theories and verify that they align with the Wally formula. Additionally, we determine the coefficients of the $c$ and $a$ anomalies for the 2D theories. Finally, we calculate the Casimir energy for the fields within the 1D central charge, showing it matches the conformal dimension of the corresponding field in the compactified AdS$_3$ bulk. These results demonstrate that massive Type IIA provides a framework for constructing a family of non-Abelian dualities in two and one dimensions. Ultimately, our findings support the existence of a symmetry between 1D and 2D conformal field theories. This conclusion is reinforced by the observation that both the central charge $c$ and the $a$ anomaly remain identical across the 1D and 2D theories. These outcomes are consistent with recent developments regarding the conformal bootstrap and the entanglement entropy of 1D and 2D quantum field theories. Consequently, our results bolster the conjecture that the 2D central charge represents a universal quantity across different dimensions. Additionally, we note that massive Type IIA fluxes can be enhanced through various mechanisms. Therefore, our findings suggest the existence of flux vacua within the landscape of 1- and 2-dimensional central charges, offering further insight into the landscape of conformal field theories. This aligns with recent studies on the landscape of 2D central charges. Ultimately, our work contributes to the broader effort of understanding how to explore and comprehend the vast landscape of 1- and 2-dimensional conformal field theories. Finally, our results may prove useful in the ongoing quest to understand the relationship between 1- and 2-dimensional quantum field theories. Specifically, our calculations of central charges and anomalies could serve as additional tools for the ongoing effort to understand the relationship between 1D and 2D conformal field theories. A central challenge in applying Gaussian process (GP) models is selecting appropriate covariance kernels. While numerous well-established kernels exist, they often fail to address specific requirements, and creating new kernels demands deep expertise in GP technology. This paper introduces a framework that facilitates the development of application-specific kernels from basic mathematical expressions. By utilizing this approach, researchers can develop new kernels more easily and effectively combine them to achieve superior fit and generalization. The proposed solution represents every kernel component as a univariate function with a specified domain and employs algebraic operations to assemble these elements into application-tailored covariance functions. The effectiveness of this framework is validated through three case studies: (1) modeling periodic signals with unknown periods, (2. analyzing data streams with abrupt regime shifts, and (3. fitting functions across disparate input regions. Evaluation metrics, including fit, generalization, and interpretability, demonstrate the framework's utility. The maximum a posteriori estimator is selected as the default, and comparisons are made against existing kernels in current literature. All GP models, including model structures and covariance kernels, are provided via the GPyPriorInference tool. The authors anticipate this method will significantly aid future work on creating specialized GP models. The tool is accessible at https://github.com/laurensdavid/gp_elementary. Furthermore, the paper offers guidance on using the framework to achieve optimal fit and generalization while maintaining interpretability. The authors believe this approach will be highly beneficial for designing application-specific GP models. The response is structured to serve as a tutorial on the framework, covering model selection, covariance kernel choices, and hyperparameter analysis. Additionally, the work illustrates how to express GP models using element-wise operations, focusing on input and output transformations. The guide concludes with an analysis of cross-validation results for both framework-based and existing model structures. Finally, recommendations for achieving high fit and generalization with interpretability are provided, emphasizing the fundamental trade-off between these goals. The framework's ability to enable application-specific GP modeling is demonstrated, and its use as a tutorial for creating specialized kernels is explored. Hyperparameter selection methods are reviewed, and the paper outlines how to achieve high fit and generalization while preserving interpretability. GP models developed with the framework express covariance functions as algebraic combinations of univariate functions, allowing modelers to assess fit and generalization independently for each element. This structure supports the use of cross-validation for kernel selection, which is applied to validate the framework. Hyperparameter selection methods are also presented, and the issue of model interpretability is addressed.

Beam-induced background remains a critical challenge for detectors at muon colliders, and mitigating this effect is essential for achieving the science goals of both proposed designs. By deflecting the beam using a closed orbit, we demonstrate that the generation of beam-induced noise can be significantly suppressed. Our analysis indicates that detectors can be positioned as far as 1 to 2 meters from the beamline, resulting in a 100-fold reduction in noise compared to a straight-bell-beam configuration. This reduction is sufficient to enable the precise timing of muon decays, thereby facilitating the extraction of muon polarization and other spin-dependent properties. Additionally, we examine the impact of synchrotron radiation on this noise mitigation strategy and propose the use of a closed orbit in the detector region as a viable approach for minimizing beam-induced background. Furthermore, we explore using an anode with a coarse cell size to further suppress beam-induced noise. Implementing closed orbits or employing coarse anode technologies could enable the construction of muon collider detectors capable of measuring decay times and extracting polarization and other spin-related characteristics. Finally, we address the requirements for a muon collider detector anode. Given that muon decays are highly polarized, the detector must be sensitive to the spin state to observe asymmetries in secondary particles. The coarse anode with cell sizes of 10 to 20 $\mu$m allows for the reconstruction of muon decays with precision matching the muon lifetime, thereby enabling the measurement of polarization. The coarse-anode concept is well-established in the LHC and has been successfully tested at LHC experiments; consequently, developing this technology for a muon collider detector is feasible. The muon collider community is currently investigating the potential of closed orbits as a noise-reduction technique, with initial studies conducted at LHC experiments. We introduce Spartan, a new regularized optimization technique designed to learn sparse solutions within convex optimisation frameworks. By minimising the average transportation cost between a sparse variable and a fixed reference, Spartan offers a straightforward method for deriving structured sparsity in both continuous and discrete domains. This approach unifies various existing sparsity-inducing regularisers, such as the $\ell_0$ norm, $\ell_p$ quasi-norms, and group sparsity, under a single transportation cost framework. Unlike black-box sparsity methods, Spartan integrates seamlessly into a broad spectrum of convex problems because it provides an efficient, closed-form update for the sparse variable. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Spartan yields exact sparsity even at a minimal sparsity level $\eta$ within an $(\epsilon, \eta)$-sparsity framework, which connects to the concept of structured strong sparsity. Empirical results on vision and machine learning tasks, including image denoising, deconvolution, and multi-class classification, show that Spartan can exactlly recover low-sparsity solutions and surpass both grey-box and black-box methods in learning interpretable features. Finally, we analyze Spartan's relationship with the $\ell_0$-norm regularised optimal transport problem, highlighting significant algorithmic and theoretical distinctions between these two approaches. The implementation of Spartan is accessible at https://github.com/DeepVisuals/Spartan. Spartan is also available as a PyTorch module at https://github.com/DeepVisuals/Spartan_pytorch. To facilitate replication, we provide extensive experimental details and data as a supplementary PyTorch module at https://github.com/DeepVisuals/Spartan_experiments. All code and data are accessible at https://github.com/DeepVisuals/Spartan_experiments. Additionally, we have developed a suite of python packages to support our replication efforts, which can be installed via `pip install Spartan_experiments`. The package includes functions for generating synthetic data, solving Spartan using our implementation, solving problems with the Spartan module, and reproducing all experiments. Specifically, the `Spartan_experiments` package contains functions to replicate the complete experimental setup, allowing users to reproduce results by running a single command. Users can verify this within a Jupyter notebook or any other Python environment. We have also provided a `Spartan_notebook` that includes all necessary functions and code to reproduce the experiments in a single environment. This notebook can be accessed at https://github.com/DeepVisuals/Spartan_experiments/tree/master/Spartan

The fermionic sign problem is overcome within the worldline formulation when the flight time between worldline bends is held constant. We demonstrate that an analogous constraint applies to the density of worldline bends, which induces an emergent Pauli obstruction in weakly interacting Bose gases. Through the lattice Monte Carlo method, we examine the validity of maintaining a fixed bend density, identifying specific artifacts in weakly interacting regimes. Furthermore, by calculating the structure factor, we show that this fixed-bend constraint results in an effective increase in the minimum momentum for bends, thereby generating hole excitations. This finding aligns with a theoretical prediction regarding a Pauli-like exclusion effect, confirming that worldline Monte Carlo methods inherently enforce an Pauli-like barrier. Consequently, we anticipate that achieving scale invariance in weakly interacting Bose gases requires moving beyond simple bend constraints toward more complex representations of Pauli blocking. Finally, we discuss potential extensions of this approach to extract ground state properties, such as the equation of state. These insights are expected to advance future worldline Monte Carlo techniques for bosons. Finally, we conclude by addressing implications for fermions and systems exhibiting strong interactions. Test code often exhibits "test smell," indicating poor design similar to "code smell." However, there is currently a lack of consensus among software developers regarding which test smells are truly severe. This study investigates the correlation between developers' perceptions of severity and the actual presence of these test smells. Through a case study of an open-source library, we performed manual code inspection to identify instances of 42 test smells across 1,155 classes and 35,585 lines of code. Subsequently, we conducted a quantitative survey of 20 developers to gauge their perceptions of the severity of 200 test smell instances. Our findings reveal that the perceived severity varies significantly: some smells are widely regarded as severe, while others are largely ignored. Specifically, coupling and cohesion issues are seen as the most severe, whereas poor naming conventions are typically dismissed. Furthermore, we observed that the severity of a test smell is positively influenced by the smell's prevalence and negatively influenced by its complexity. These results offer valuable insights for guiding the selection of test refactoring techniques. Finally, to ensure the reproducibility of this research, we have made our source code, annotations, and survey data available online.

We examine a stochastic brushing process designed for data analysis, derived from the generalizedBrushing method by Smit and Van Zwol [17]. This approach functions as an integro-differential equation where the drift component resembles mean field theory in physics, featuring branching dynamics influenced by both birth and death processes. Furthermore, this equation can be understood as the Hamiltonian formulation of a generalized Langevin equation operating on a tree structure that encodes the brush graph. Its solution yields a time evolution of the brush, with the final state providing data analysis results based on an initial partition of the data graph. The corresponding probability measure defined on this brush graph belongs to the Potts class, making the process linked to Potts dynamics, a connection valuable for understanding data analysis outcomes. We introduce KKMCee, a Monte Carlo event generator designed for electron-positron annihilation processes yielding lepton or quark pairs. The tool comprehensively incorporates QED and QCD radiative corrections, both virtual and real, up to the order indicated by their diagrammatic representations, alongside photon radiation within the final state under the constraints of collinear and soft approximations. Furthermore, it incorporates leading-order corrections of the hard-collinear type for configurations involving two real photons in the final state. KKMCee builds upon the multi-photon exponentiation formalism established in our earlier work regarding hadron production at lepton colliders, extending it into the electroweak sector as necessary. This version of the program is specifically tailored for applications in precision physics research. It enables the simulation of various processes occurring at electron-positron colliders, such as $Z$ boson production and the generation of charged and neutral Higgs bosons, as well as their associated production with fermion pairs. In these scenarios, electroweak box and bubble diagrams are either analytically calculated or approximated as massless and flavor-diagonal propagator corrections. The code supports the investigation of beam polarization effects and the polarization observables of incoming electrons and positrons. KKMCee is released as free software under the GNU General Public License and is publicly accessible via https://theory.physics.ed.ac.uk/~krissl/ee/. Additionally, a detailed manual is available at http://www.edin-kissl.de/ee/. This paper serves as an introduction to the program, offering a systematic overview of its implemented physics and an analysis of its accuracy through a comparison with analytical results for specific observables in model calculations. For each topic discussed, example output files are provided to illustrate the program's capabilities. Finally, this work outlines the primary enhancements made to KKMCee and the key challenges encountered during its development. Measuring inter-beat intervals is essential for diagnosing cardiovascular health and detecting cardiac anomalies. This study introduces the Tiramisu model, a novel approach for estimating these intervals that yields superior results compared to existing methods. The approach is evaluated using synthetic data, the MIMIC-III, and the CSMA databases. Results demonstrate error rates of 0.01, 0.13, and 0.07 for the Tiramisu model on these respective databases, outperforming current state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, the model achieves an inter-rater reliability of 0.999, confirming its robustness and consistency. Ultimately, this method is highly effective for tracking heart rate and supporting clinical decision-making. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/ashishkumar123456789/Tiramisu. Future research will focus on developing an open-source, user-friendly, and mobile-friendly interface for the model. Additionally, the approach is being extended to estimate other physiological metrics, such as respiratory cycles, to assist in diagnosing conditions like asthma. Finally, the framework is being adapted for use in wearable devices to enable real-time inter-beat interval monitoring and analysis. Additional code and resources can be found at: https://github.com/ashishkumar123456789/Tiramisu. We introduce a randomized algorithm for computing the tensor singular value decomposition (TSVD). This approach partitions a high-order tensor into sub-tensors through sampling via the outer product trick, employing a divide-and-conquer strategy. The process begins by identifying a core sub-tensor with minimal dimensions, followed by an initial TSVD estimation. Subsequently, the method extends the solution to larger sub-tensors using an iterative procedure, with the capability to converge to a near-optimal TSVD after a single pass. Finally, the algorithm is applied to reconstruct the original tensor from its sub-tensors. Numerical experiments demonstrate that a few passes over the data significantly enhance TSVD estimation, resulting in substantial improvements in reconstruction accuracy. The method is implemented in Matlab (available on GitHub) and Python (available on PyPI). This implementation facilitates the extension of various matrix and matrix pencil techniques, such as the Q-method, to tensors. The resulting tensor eigenvalue solver, known as the Tensor QR-method, is also provided for testing purposes. Furthermore, the Python version allows the use of NumPy's BLAS routines, making it more memory-efficient compared to the Matlab version. The Python code can be executed directly from PyPI without needing to download additional files. However, the Matlab version offers the advantage of including comprehensive documentation. Both versions support Python versions 2.7 and 3.x. Additionally, we provide a method for calculating the numerical rank of a tensor, which is integral to the Q-method. The Python version of this method is available without requiring extra downloads. Finally, we detail the Q-method for computing singular vectors of tensors, which generalizes the matrix Q-method and is included in both versions to facilitate testing. The Python version utilizes the NumPy package, while the Matlab version requires the Matlab package. Both versions are available without requiring additional downloads. Embedding static, unweighted networks with few layers has become a significant area of research, driven by its capacity to reduce distances between nodes. However, most current studies focus exclusively on static graphs. This paper provides a survey of techniques designed to capture the dynamic nature of evolving graphs through node-level position representations. We examine methods that address graph dynamics at four primary temporal granularities: intra-day, inter-day, weekly, monthly, and inter-temporal. Our objective is to illustrate how graph embeddings can represent the time evolution of networks. Furthermore, we identify key challenges within each temporal category, including assumptions regarding the absence of missing data, an over-emphasis on learned edge weights at the expense of node representations, and a deficiency in benchmark datasets. Finally, we propose several promising research directions for evolving graph embeddings. Based on an analysis of 53 relevant papers, this study aims to guide future researchers in exploring this emerging field. Additionally, it seeks to direct the community toward establishing new benchmarks, given the current lack of standardized datasets for evaluating evolving graph embeddings. Investigating the structure of very neutron-rich nuclei is essential for comprehending the evolution of nuclear forces and addressing questions regarding astrophysical nucleosynthesis. While the neutron-rich isotopes of helium, lithium, and beta decay products have been subjects of recent experimental and theoretical focus, this study specifically examines the validity of the cluster model for the hypothetical $^7$H nucleus. We investigate a $^3$H+4n configuration within the no-core shell model framework, allowing the four valence neutrons to occupy all available states. Our analysis reveals that the $^7$H ground state is an excited state, not the one previously assigned in literature. Instead, the ground state is a three-body $^3$H+2+2n cluster configuration, characterized as 3 3 3 1 in three-body notation and identified as the 5/2$^-$ state. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between this proposed ground state and the $^7$H half-life. These findings underscore the necessity of the three-body H+2+2n model to accurately describe the properties of $^7$H. Neural networks excel at extracting salient features from data, yet their optimal representations often remain opaque and challenging to interpret. Recently, post-training interpreters have been employed to derive meaningful insights from trained models, but these methods typically impose strict constraints on the input space of the final layer, limiting the optimizer's exploration and yielding suboptimal results. To address this, we introduce a novel architecture designed to learn deep optimal representations via gradient descent by integrating Sinkhorn Divergences with Convex Layerwise Training (CLT). Our approach applies Sinkhorn Divergences to penalize excessive confidence in the network's outputs, thereby promoting softer predictions. Furthermore, by calculating gradients independently for each layer, this architecture ensures efficient learning. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that our proposed architecture successfully predicts outcomes while simultaneously learning interpretable features within the neural network's convex layers. Additionally, computational complexity analysis and comparisons regarding training time confirm the efficiency of our architecture. Finally, we validate the architecture's efficacy through case studies involving medical image classification and sentiment analysis on the IMDB dataset. To our knowledge, this serves as the inaugural proposal to learn deep optimal representations utilizing Sinkhorn Divergences within a convex layerwise training framework. The associated code and datasets are accessible at: https://github.com/AmrMohamed12345/Sinkhorn_Divergences_in_DLT. The source code is also available at: https://github.com/AmrMohamed12345/SD-DLT. Voluntary partnerships have significantly influenced how contact tracing apps function within the broader UK strategy to curb community transmission of COVID-19. These partnerships, which involve public health agencies, technology firms, and civil society, are responsible for promoting, hosting, and operating specific apps. The apps developed by technology firms, however, do not share user data with public health authorities. This study evaluates how the presence of these partnerships—specifically the relative contributions of public health agencies versus civil society organizations—affects transmission reduction efforts. Our findings indicate that civil society agencies may offer advantages in reaching certain demographics, yet user adherence remains lower when these apps are used. We conclude that user participation is more strongly driven by public trust in civil society agencies than by user perceptions regarding data privacy. Additionally, we highlight that public health agencies retain control over user adherence, which means that modifications to app features or rebranding initiatives could potentially boost participation rates. Finally, the work underscores the necessity of user surveys to gain deeper insights into the motivations driving app adoption. By integrating insights from public health agencies and user feedback, future apps could be improved to enhance transmission reduction, particularly by targeting demographics that current models suggest are underrepresented in participation. These findings aim to inform decisions that maximize the impact of local tracing partnerships. This study presents the first detailed analysis of Open Cluster Melotte 72 using data from the second Gaia Data Release. We determined the cluster's physical parameters, finding an age of $1.05 \pm 0.05$ Gyr, a distance of $295.7 \pm 1.5$ pc, and a line-of-sight velocity of $-10.0 \pm 0.1$ km/s. The cluster's galactic coordinates are $(l, b) = (11.85, 47.25)$, and its three-dimensional velocity indicates it is moving away from the galactic plane. A sample of 10 multiple-star systems was identified, comprising 7 binaries and 3 triples. Additionally, 12 members were detected as having significant excess flux in the $u$-band relative to the cluster's main sequence. A total of 108 new members, 10 non-members, and 12 previously known members were also classified. Finally, we provide the first detailed discussion of the cluster's structure based on these new findings. These results will be accessible via the cluster's entry in the Catalogue of Nearby Open Clusters. The paper concludes with several appendices: Appendix A details the selection criteria for cluster members, Appendix B lists the 10 multiple-star systems, Appendix C details the 10 newly identified open cluster members, and Appendix D presents the 10 non-member stars. Eyeball Calib is a learning-based algorithm designed to determine camera parameters, specifically extrinsic calibration, using a single image captured by an eye-in-hand setup. This approach leverages visual features within the image to estimate the camera's parameters. The process begins by detecting the object plane and camera center; subsequently, parameters are computed using a modified version of the single-view method proposed by Al-Hady and Mohiuddin. Our method achieves high accuracy, reducing calibration error to under 1 mm, while offering the advantage of requiring no prior knowledge of the environment. Additionally, we demonstrate that even with imperfect parameters, the algorithm produces 3D point clouds of sufficient quality for robotic grasping applications. Experimental results indicate that when applied to data from the Challenge Dataset, the average extrinsic parameter accuracy reaches 99.99%, resulting in an average 3D point deviation of approximately 1 mm. The primary challenge lies in the robust detection of the object plane using the eyeball calibration chain. Furthermore, we show that these learned parameters enable successful grasping on challenging objects, such as a wrench, a screw, and a bolt. Future research will aim to improve robustness by incorporating more diverse training data, including various lighting conditions and occlusions. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/eyeballcalib. The model used in this study was trained on the CACD Challenge Dataset. Additionally, we introduce a new open-source dataset featuring diverse object poses, lighting conditions, and occlusions to facilitate robust plane detection and support future research in this field. We invite researchers to explore this resource and contribute to advancing the field of eyeball calibration and robotic grasping. We welcome your feedback and collaboration. Thank you! Recent years have seen a surge in research on bounded reinforcement learning, focusing primarily on action-constrained settings where only a limited subset of actions is permissible. However, these approaches often perform poorly in exploration when constraints are tight. To address this, we introduce reverse constrained RL, a framework that utilizes state-constraints instead of action constraints to direct the learning agent's exploration. The agent learns a policy that maximizes the count of distinct state-constraints visited during execution. We evaluate our approach in both model-free and model-based contexts, demonstrating that it effectively steers exploration toward under-explored regions of the MDP's state space. Furthermore, we establish arithmetical geometric mean inequalities that bound the exploration bonus of the model-based variant, thereby providing theoretical backing for the method. Empirical results on exploration bonuses, exploration efficiency, and average rewards in dense reward settings confirm that our approach outperforms prior exploration techniques that rely solely on intrinsic motivation. Finally, we highlight reverse constrained RL's utility as a supplementary method for safety-critical tasks, where desired trajectories can be generated by solving a single optimization problem incorporating spatial, temporal, and velocity-based state constraints. This enables the efficient generation of useful trajectories even in highly constrained environments. The code is available at: https://github.com/ashokkathir/ReverseConstrainedRL. Sources: Kathir, A., & Zhang, Y. (2022). Reverse Constrained Reinforcement Learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2202.03008. arXiv:2202.03008 [cs.LG].

A vertex divider for a graph $G$ with treewidth $k$ is defined as a mapping from the vertices of $G$ to its treewidth-defining bag set that maintains $\alpha$-bounded relative distances within a specific metric $\alpha$. These mappings are vital for numerous graph algorithms, spanning from complexity reductions to deterministic black-box solutions for problems like Hamiltonicity and Steiner Tree. For a fixed metric $\alpha$ and graph class, these dividers can be leveraged to develop space-efficient, parallel, and recursive implementations. For instance, when $\alpha$ is the shortest path metric, optimal random shortest path dividers enable Hamiltonicity testing in $2^{O(k^{2.5})} \cdot \text{poly}(\log n)$ time and $O(n)$ space on graphs with treewidth $k$. However, recent black-box algorithms often utilize dividers for metrics $\alpha$ that vary based on specific query instances, creating challenges in terms of runtime, space, and parallelization. This paper introduces a novel, general category of vertex dividers that decouples the metric $\alpha$ from the specific instance dividers. We demonstrate that for any graph class with treewidth $k$ and shortest path metric $\alpha$, efficient $\alpha$-preserving dividers that partition the graph into treewidth $O(k)$ components can be constructed in time proportional to the graph size. Consequently, for any graph class with treewidth $k$ and metric $\alpha$, the query-time and space-efficient dividers previously established by these works can now be executed as a random shortest path divider with a runtime and space complexity of $2^{O(k^{2.5})} \cdot \text{poly}(\log n)$. Recent advancements have enabled the reconstruction of gene regulatory networks using both experimentally derived data and inferences from public datasets, allowing researchers to investigate how network structure influences function. However, current models predominantly focus on binary networks, failing to capture the continuous nature of biological interactions or their directions. Moreover, many studies overlook how the origin of edges—a mix of inferred and measured networks—introduces bias, especially when inferences rely on features other than those being analyzed. We propose a framework for assigning edge weights based on their origin (measured vs. inferred) to enable a more nuanced analysis and assessment of the resulting biases. Through simulations, we demonstrate how binary networks, regardless of whether they are measured or inferred, can be distorted by the features used for inference, thereby altering both network weights and component identification. Furthermore, we present an analysis of a real-world dataset that reveals how both network weight thresholds and edge directionality (when applicable) significantly impact the characteristics of network components. This research provides guidelines for constructing networks from hybrid data and underscores how specific analytical choices can skew both quantitative and qualitative outcomes. Ultimately, these findings highlight how bias manifests in current literature and establish a foundation for future improvements. Specifically, we advocate for the adoption of network weight metrics that reflect biological relevance and the explicit evaluation of component properties in both simulated and real networks when transitioning from binary to weighted models. Additionally, we develop weighting schemes for both directionless and directed networks to address these issues, aiming to enhance the reliability of derived conclusions. Finally, we emphasize how these conclusions are sensitive to various parameters, including weight thresholds, directionality, network size, and the proportion of inferred edges. By understanding these parametric dependencies, researchers can better interpret and generalize their findings. All data and analysis code are made publicly available to ensure reproducibility. These conclusions are particularly relevant to studies utilizing methods like GENIE3, which rely on externally inferred edges. Given how heavily these inferences affect the properties of network components, we provide a comprehensive examination of those effects, which is essential for understanding the validity of many recent publications utilizing GENIE3. Finally, we outline several open questions regarding the selection of appropriate weights and network properties for specific biological contexts. This paper presents a novel a posteriori technique designed to quantify the classification error rate of a physics-informed neural network. By leveraging the formal error analysis of the weak residual, the method establishes an upper bound for the difference between predictions generated by the continuous model and its discrete approximation. The study demonstrates that this weak residual error bound directly translates into a valid estimate of the model's misclassification rate. Furthermore, the approach is extended to models incorporating hyper-singular differential operators and is tested on several representative examples, where it yields tight error bounds in most cases. These results underscore the practical utility of the method in providing a reliable measure of the total classification error for continuous models, a capability that stands in contrast to standard certifications, which currently focus on local perturbation-based error bounds. Ultimately, this technique serves as a crucial step toward achieving physics-informed neural network models that are certifiably reliable. Finally, the paper explores potential future extensions, such as applying similar a posteriori error bounds to other emerging machine learning architectures. Through simple illustrations, it highlights how these error bounds could be leveraged to address challenging practical issues, including the selection of appropriate regularization parameters and the identification of optimal training data subsets. This represents a significant potential advancement over the present state of the art. Overall, the findings indicate that the proposed a posteriori error analysis opens a new avenue for the practical deployment of continuous model solutions in machine learning. Specifically, it enables the direct estimation of the error rate associated with a model's classification errors, a capability that is otherwise unattainable through certification methods relying on local perturbations. This represents a substantial practical benefit, particularly for large-scale models where the local certification paradigm faces inherent limitations. Additionally, the work illustrates a recent innovation in mathematical machine learning: the development of a local weak residual error bound. Unlike traditional pointwise error bounds, this local weak residual bound is capable of quantifying errors in the discontinuous discrete model solutions that are typically unmeasurable in standard machine learning optimization frameworks. This capability marks a significant recent advancement in the mathematical theory of data-driven discovery. Finally, the proposed local weak error bound is shown to be more robust than the classical H1 norm error bound, which is often impractical for large-scale data-driven discovery problems due to the high computational cost of discrete model training. This robustness is essential for the practical implementation of the technique. Finally, the paper illustrates the potential extension of the proposed a posteriori error analysis to establish a local weak error bound, a recent innovation in mathematical data-driven discovery. Air pollution serves as a major risk factor for numerous diseases, including cancer, cardiovascular, and respiratory conditions. The direct attribution of air pollutants to health outcomes is often complicated by factors such as the specific pollutant type, exposure duration, and latency periods. Consequently, epidemiological studies investigating health risks from long-term air pollution are often constrained by challenges in gathering accurate exposure data. To address these limitations, researchers are increasingly employing advanced statistical and machine learning methods. This study aims to evaluate and compare statistical models for predicting air pollutants within an epidemiological context. Itachio et al. [1] suggest integrating geostatistics with machine learning techniques, such as Gaussian Process Regression, to estimate unknown air pollution levels. Therefore, the current work focuses on developing and testing a hybrid machine learning approach for air pollutants that incorporates spatial autocorrelation. By utilizing a dataset of air quality monitoring stations in the province of Treviso, Italy, the study assesses several machine learning models by analyzing their performance regarding spatial and temporal dimensions. Finally, several conclusions are drawn concerning the utilization of machine learning and geostatistics in long-term air pollution studies. Keywords: Air pollution, spatial autocorrelation, machine learning, geostatistics, Gaussian Process Regression.

Our findings indicate that the Majorana signal stands out distinctly against most other signals, except for the Kondo signal. Consequently, we suggest that the most promising experimental candidates for observing the OTSOCMRPE$TRR$ signal are systems where it is anticipated to be the dominant signal. Furthermore, we propose a straightforward experimental criterion to differentiate between a signal originating from the Majorana mode versus one arising from Andreev levels. Finally, we discuss how to eliminate the Kondo signal, which can be mistaken for the Majorana mode signal. These results are expected to aid experimentalists in identifying suitable systems where the OTSOCMRPE$TRR$ signal is expected to dominate. Additionally, we outline key experimental challenges that must be addressed to observe this phenomenon. We conclude that future experimental efforts should focus on developing techniques to observe the OTSOCMRPE$TRR$ signal, given its distinctiveness and the relative ease with which it can be distinguished from other signals. This approach could significantly advance the field of Majorana research. We believe that Majorana modes can be experimentally observed through tunneling spectroscopy with resistive electrodes. We have published our findings in Phys. Rev. B 104, 024507 (2021). However, a notable limitation in current literature is the restriction of action spaces to simple geometric shapes, specifically balls, cubes, or polytopes. This work examines inference within linear bandits characterized by exponentially large action spaces. We establish asymptotic asymptotic normality for linear functionals of treatment effects using linear models fitted via randomized algorithms, provided appropriate conditions are met. Furthermore, we demonstrate that standard methods for assessing uncertainty in linear treatment effects, commonly applied in traditional experimental settings, yield sub-optimal results when applied to linear bandits with high-dimensional action spaces. To address this, we introduce novel approaches that enhance both uncertainty estimation and methodological interpretation. Collectively, these advances facilitate a more comprehensive analysis of the efficacy of rich action spaces in real-world applications. Empirical results are drawn from a randomized social media experiment involving creative assets. Although the orbital Hall effect in time-reversal symmetric systems was predicted over a decade ago, it has been challenging to observe experimentally. In this study, we propose an alternative method to detect it using a mesoscopic graphene ribbon with spatially modulated chemical potential. This system is analogous to a spin Hall setup, where valley pseudospin is replaced by orbital angular momentum. Similar to how electron spin accumulates at the edges of a spin Hall system, the valley and orbital components also accumulate at the rims of the graphene ribbon. We demonstrate that these accumulations can be extracted electrically at the valley filters positioned at the edges. This orbital accumulation is more robust than the valley current and can be harnessed for valleytronics and valley logic devices. Furthermore, we show that the orbital Hall effect can be observed in transport measurements through chiral anomaly. Our findings pave the way for future experimental efforts to observe the orbital Hall effect in a mesoscopic graphene ribbon with a chemically modulated potential. Additionally, our work establishes a new platform for orbital angular momentum-based electronics within condensed matter systems. Finally, we anticipate that our proposed platform will advance orbital Hall effect research by enabling its observation in a system free of intrinsic spin-orbit coupling. This achievement will facilitate investigations into orbital magnetism and provide a pathway to uncovering new orbital magnetic phases in graphene. Moreover, our proposed system will aid in exploring orbital magnetism in other two-dimensional materials, such as transition metal dichalcogenides. Beyond fundamental research, our proposal holds significant potential for applications in spintronics, orbitaltronics, and valleytronics. Furthermore, our proposed device offers a solution to the challenge of achieving high-resolution orbital magnetometry. The sample's orbital magnetization can be precisely tuned by adjusting the chemical potential, and its magnitude can be enhanced by increasing the modulation amplitude. This approach could yield a very high orbital magnetic moment in a solid-state system, potentially enabling high-resolution orbital magnetometry in various applications. Finally, our proposal may advance fundamental research in orbital magnetism. The sample's orbital magnetism is highly sensitive to perturbations, such as strain, which can be exploited to study orbital magnetic phases and their transitions. In summary, our proposal advances fundamental research on orbital magnetism in condensed matter systems. By providing a practical system to study orbital magnetism, we pave the way for new discoveries in this field. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are increasingly utilized to model relationships within graph-based data, making them attractive targets for adversaries seeking to infiltrate systems and disrupt operations. While current research on data contamination in GNNs primarily concentrates on classifying entire labels, our study explores learning contamination strategies by predicting individual node labels. We achieve this by adapting reinforcement learning to the graph learning environment, proposing a Graph-based Data Contamination (GDC) framework. GDC involves an adversary employing reinforcement learning to contaminate node labels within training data, aiming to deceive the model into predicting specific labels for test nodes. Experimental results demonstrate that GDC successfully contaminates node labels even when graph structures remain unaltered, and we observe that the proposed framework can be applied across various GNN models and graph learning tasks. Furthermore, we highlight the necessity of developing new methods to detect and prevent such contamination strategies. The code for our GDC framework is publicly available at https://github.com/ashishkumar1123/GDC.

Catalogue matching serves as a critical method for assigning physical properties to celestial objects, thereby enabling investigations into their formation and evolution. This study examines the catalogues $JWIS$ and $WISE$ to develop an improved catalogue matching technique. We find that the primary limitation of current approaches is the insufficient quality of source coordinates, which hinders accurate matching. Consequently, we evaluate three matching strategies: two cross-match algorithms and one multi-catalogue merge, comparing their performance across three distinct catalogues. Our analysis identifies the optimal approach for each scenario and introduces a novel matching method that leverages multi-catalogue merge capabilities. This new approach utilizes multi-wavelength photometry and astrometry to resolve ambiguities in source coordinates, significantly enhancing matching accuracy. Additionally, we demonstrate that incorporating photometric data from one catalogue as training input can refine coordinates for objects in another catalogue, thereby boosting matching performance. Ultimately, our findings indicate that a multi-wavelength photometric dataset is essential for a successful match, and that our proposed multi-catalogue merge technique offers the best results. These outcomes are particularly relevant for the emerging field of infrared astronomy, which is expected to generate an increasing volume of data from diverse catalogues in the future. Ultimately, our methods facilitate the most efficient identification of source coordinates across multiple wavelengths. By integrating our approach with the recently released $JWIS$ catalogue, we aim to provide a comprehensive dataset covering a wide wavelength range and a vast sky area. This could facilitate the creation of a novel, all-sky multi-wavelength photometric catalogue, thereby advancing the understanding of the universe. We introduce several set-theoretic conditions linked to the infinite pigeonhole principle and establish set-theoretic independent results and questions concerning sets $A$ that hit a sufficient number of large edges. Our analysis relies on extensive combinatorial and set-theoretic machinery, significantly extending the scope of the Erdős, Hahn, and Mayer theorem. Furthermore, we provide a set-theoretic definition of the ideal generated by a family of subsets of a countable set and examine its properties, notably the minimal size of generating families. We also connect this concept to the ideal generated by singletons under the same set-theoretic criteria. Additionally, we explore set-theoretically independent properties regarding vertex sets $A$ that completely intersect all edges, offering set-theoretic definitions for such families and the ideal generated by their elements. We further examine the ideal generated by vertex sets that hit a specified number of edges and its relationship to the ideal generated by sets that completely intersect all edges. Finally, we examine consistency issues concerning the existence of a countable family of sets that generates an ideal containing all sets with positive measure under every probability measure defined on the universe. To address this, we employ consistency results concerning the existence of a countable family of sets whose intersection with any set from the family is empty. Ontologies serve as formal models of concepts and relations, typically visualized through Directed Graph Ontology (DGO) plots. While effective for browsing small ontologies (under 100 concepts), these visualizations fail for large ontologies because their size causes the graph to become overcrowded, obscuring the very patterns the visualization aims to reveal. To address this, we introduce OntoPlot, a new visualization that decomposes the ontology into groups of concepts based on their relational associations. Concept and association queries are mapped onto this grouped structure rather than a flat graph, significantly reducing visual clutter. By leveraging association correlations and advanced layout techniques, OntoPlot organizes large ontologies into a hierarchical arrangement of concept groups, allowing the ontology's structure to emerge from patterns within large datasets. The visualization was stress-tested using the largest available ontologies, which revealed new structural insights about entities and associations in specific domains. Additionally, our results demonstrate that OntoPlot enhances user experience and improves pattern detection for large ontologies. We introduce a method that leverages CycleGAN to establish a mapping between preprocessed speech signals from two distinct domains, enabling the continuation of an end-to-end automatic speech recognition model trained on domain A. This approach allows our system to generate transcriptions for test data originating from domain B. Furthermore, by incorporating inter-domain losses and adversarial loss into our training process, we enhance the model's ability to process speech from domain B. Experimental results demonstrate an 8.4% reduction in Character Error Rate (CER) and a 7.3% reduction in Word Error Rate (WER) on voice-change-noise (VCN) test data. Additionally, the inclusion of inter-domain loss and adversarial loss further improves performance, yielding a 10.2% CER decrease and a 7.9% WER decrease, respectively. Finally, our system was integrated with a related speech enhancement technique to further boost transcription accuracy on domain B data. By combining our method with speech enhancement, we achieved a 12.1% CER reduction and a 9.9% WER reduction on the test data. These findings underscore the potential of our approach for semi-supervised neural speech enhancement and automatic speech recognition applications. While deep neural networks excel in perception tasks within robotics, they lack inherent uncertainty estimates, making them risky for decision-making and control. Although Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) are widely regarded as the most promising approach for learning uncertainty, they face significant challenges in nongaussian decision-making environments, primarily due to high computational costs and poor scalability. This paper introduces a method to mitigate these issues by employing frequency-domain techniques to accelerate gradient descent computations. Additionally, we present the Deep Active Prediction (DAP) framework, designed to enhance nongaussian decision-making by utilizing uncertainty information from Bayes' method. Specifically, DAP utilizes uncertainty metrics for exploration-driven active learning, thereby reducing the number of decision episodes required to learn an effective policy. The efficacy of our Bayes' gradient descent is demonstrated across various perception and control tasks, including image classification, object detection, and reinforcement learning. Furthermore, we show that the DAP framework outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms by achieving superior decision-making results with fewer training episodes. Finally, we validate the robustness and practicality of our proposed algorithms and framework through a real-world robot navigation experiment. The source code will be made publicly available. We conducted systematic molecular dynamics simulations to investigate how the internal degrees of freedom (VW-VDI) in two distinct types of flexible molecules influence the mixture Soret effect, specifically examining systems composed of rigid molecules paired with flexible ones. Our analysis of the time-correlation function (TCF) for VW-VDI revealed that its contribution significantly differs between the two systems, a discrepancy that aligns with the variations in the TCFs related to velocity fluctuations and the orientation of the internal dipole moment. These findings offer systematic insights into the roles of the VW-VDI and its associated components within the V-model framework, a role that appears more critical for a molecule with a strong internal dipole moment, similar to acetone. Additionally, we explored this contribution through the lens of the Langevin equation, which models the stochastic dynamics of flexible molecules. We demonstrated that the correlation time derived from the autocorrelation function of the VW-VDI force plays a pivotal role in determining the TCF of VW-VDI. Finally, we successfully predicted the mixture Soret coefficient using the V-model, thereby providing a rigorous and precise understanding of the internal degrees of freedom of flexible molecules and their connection to the Soret effect. This outcome underscores the potential of the V-model as an efficient and practical method for predicting the Soret effect in flexible molecules. As a preliminary step toward developing a more generalized Langevin equation that incorporates VW-VDI, we also examined the autocorrelation function of the potential energy of the internal degree of freedom. Through these systematic investigations, we have identified two previously unexplored internal degrees of freedom that warrant further study. Ultimately, this work represents a significant step toward a comprehensive and unified understanding of the internal degrees of freedom of flexible molecules and their relationship to the Soret effect. Automated essay scoring represents a longstanding challenge in natural language processing. The primary difficulty involves assessing numerous dimensions of human-written text, including grammatical and structural correctness, as well as content and argumentative quality. This study introduces the application of transformer-based language models for essay evaluation, utilizing various fine-tuning strategies to develop an automated scoring system for text generated in numerous languages. The efficiency of modern transformer architectures enables the processing of multi-turn conversations and long documents, which is particularly relevant for complex tasks like automated essay grading. Furthermore, these pre-trained models offer a more interpretable approach to scoring, moving beyond simple scores toward interpreted feedback that elucidates the reasons behind the scores. This interpretability aids educators in designing curricula and provides students with constructive guidance for future improvements. Consequently, the proposed system demonstrates high accuracy in predicting scores while delivering interpretable feedback regarding grammatical and structural issues. Additionally, it excels at identifying arguments and reasoning issues, which remains an unresolved problem in the field. The system requires minimal labeled data, reducing the need for expensive training resources, and can be deployed within educational settings with limited computational overhead. Overall, the system achieves state-of-the-art accuracy in predicting scores and outperforms other methods in generating interpretable feedback, marking a significant advancement in automated essay assessment. Keywords: Automated Essay Assessment, Interpretable Feedback, Language Models, Transformers, Grammar Scoring, Reasoning Scoring.

Recent domain adaptive (DA) pedestrian detection methods have achieved state-of-the-art results by applying a box re-ranking process to align source domain predictions with target domain ground truth. However, this re-ranking step often generates numerous false positives due to imperfect cross-domain mapping. While an interactive approach could theoretically filter these spurious predictions, it lacks practicality for real-world deployment. To address this limitation, we introduce Box Re-Ranking (BRR), an unsupervised technique for semi-supervised multi-source domain adaptive pedestrian detection that identifies and eliminates spurious predictions. Our key contributions are threefold: (1) BRR is the first method to apply domain adaptation to reduce domain shift in dense box sets; (2) BRR employs an unsupervised domain adaptation strategy to eliminate False Positives (FPs) without requiring target domain ground truth; and (3) We propose a novel FP detection method grounded in the observation that an FP's confidence score is highly correlated with its overlap against True Positives (TPs), allowing FP localization through confidence scores and IoU thresholds alone. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that BRR achieves state-of-the-art performance across various domain adaptation scenarios. The source code will be made available at https://github.com/rogerslab/BoxRe-Ranking. Furthermore, BRR is the first approach to perform DA on the large-scale MS-COCO dataset and delivers state-of-the-art results for pedestrian detection. Recent advancements in voice synthesis and song generation have produced a diverse array of models capable of creating music from text inputs. However, the quality of music produced by current state-of-the-art generators remains significantly inferior to human compositions. This paper investigates enhancing the fidelity of computer-generated music through a two-stage process: first, translating the spectrogram of generated music into the spectrogram of a human composer using a conditional adversarial autoencoder; second, applying music enhancement techniques to this translated spectrogram. The results demonstrate that this approach effectively improves the spectrogram, yielding a music quality score of 0.916, which is 0.19 points higher than the baseline system using original generated music. Additionally, experiments reveal that the image translation method is versatile and highly effective across various source spectrograms. Mastering accurate object release is essential for successful throwing, yet current datasets fail to capture the release phase, forcing researchers to infer it indirectly. This study investigates how mismatches between an object's velocity and size at the point of release affect human performance. To do this, we introduced FauxThrow, a new augmented reality system that manipulates physics by altering throwing dynamics. Our findings indicate that these mismatches significantly hinder users' ability to hit targets. We demonstrated that erroneous release points can generate unrealistic trajectories, leading to an underestimation of horizontal distances and a misjudgment of required force. Ultimately, this work highlights the critical role of the release phase in throwing and establishes a robust framework for exploring its mechanics. The FauxThrow system and this insight into release mechanics will facilitate future research into releasing objects while providing novel augmented reality gaming experiences. This work appears in the Proceedings of SIGGRAPH 2021.

Although Neural Machine Translation (NMT) and Dependency Parsing (DP) are linked by syntactic structure, decoding in both directions currently lacks an explicit syntactic framework. Specifically, NMT does not leverage sentence-level syntax to guide decoding, and DP does not utilize word-level syntactic connections during the process. This study presents a unified tree-structured decoding algorithm for both tasks that models sentence structure and sequences of words simultaneously. The model begins by predicting the depth of each word without referencing other tokens, subsequently refining these predictions by incorporating information from deeper neighbors in the parse tree. We have integrated this algorithm into a standard NMT architecture and dependency models utilizing a tree-structured Transformer encoder. Experiments on English-only data demonstrate that this framework effectively synergetic trains NMT and parsing models while yielding performance improvements for both. Furthermore, we achieve state-of-the-art results in joint NMT and parsing on English monolingual training data. Qualitative analysis reveals that the predicted parse trees align well with human annotations, and the generated translations are accurate and natural. Notably, the joint training approach produces translations that surpass those from vanilla NMT models. On par with other strong baselines, our method offers the distinct advantage of generating the sentence dependency tree alongside the translation. Additionally, on Czech-Czech data, our model yields improved translations and parses while maintaining the ability to output the parse tree with the translation. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/taehyung-lee/TD-Decode. The accompanying paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01037. The binding energies (BEs) of molecules on icy grains are a critical parameter governing the formation and destruction of interstellar molecules. However, the vast range of reported BE values and the lack of context regarding computational methods have made it impossible to assess the reliability of data for the broad atmospheric conditions found in the early Universe. To address this gap, we introduce the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (https://beta.chem.uni-hamburg.de/beap/), an open-access database containing over 100,000 BE values derived from more than 100,000 density functional theory calculations performed across various grain models and chemical environments. These calculations utilize a wide array of widely used methods, including diverse density functional theory functionals, basis sets, and higher-level wavefunction methods. The platform enables users to filter BE values according to their formation conditions and graph theory properties, while also providing details on the computational protocols used. This tool is designed to assist researchers in selecting appropriate BE data for their specific research contexts. The Binding Energy Assessment Platform is freely accessible online and via a desktop application, and it includes a dedicated section with tutorials to guide users through the process. We anticipate that this resource will facilitate the development of robust astrochemical models by allowing researchers to accurately select BE values relevant to their specific environmental conditions. The platform was created through a collaboration between the Chemical Physics and Theoretical Physics departments at the University of Hamburg. The study examines the arithmetic-geometric process $X_n$ defined by $X_0=x_0$, $X_n=\lambda X_{n-1}\eta_n$ for $n\geq 1$, where $\eta_n$ are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables, but features a lower bound that varies with $n$ and is determined by the sample path of $\eta_n$. Specifically, the $\eta_n$ are assumed to be lognormally distributed, although the analysis remains valid for any $\mathbb{R}^+$-valued i.i.d. variables possessing a finite moment generating function in a neighborhood of zero. This work investigates fundamental characteristics of the process, including its finite moments, convergence in probability, and almost sure behavior. Furthermore, applying this framework to the Bitcoin price model, which relies on the Bitcoin Halving event, demonstrates that historical Bitcoin prices align with the proposed stochastic framework. Additionally, empirical evidence indicates that fitting Bitcoin prices using this model yields lower variance compared to utilizing total historical prices. These findings offer potential avenues for enhancing the stability of blockchain technologies. Finally, through simulations of Bitcoin price trajectories, the paper explores the process's potential applications in risk management. We introduce a random Clifford algorithm designed to evaluate "shallow" expectations of the form $\langle\psi\otimes\phi|U^\dagger(U\otimes I)(\psi\otimes I)U^\dagger(U\otimes I)\psi|U^\dagger\phi\rangle$, where $U$ is an arbitrary unitary, $\psi$ represents a specific input state, and $\phi$ denotes either a coherent or incoherent state. This method yields outcomes that differ only by a small additive noise term from the ideal target value $\langle\psi\otimes\phi|\psi\otimes I\phi\rangle$. Our approach employs random Clifford circuits with low depth and limited qubit count, a feature that facilitates parallel execution. Additionally, the parameters are largely independent of the qubit dimension, and the required qubits can be further reduced through techniques such as qubit recycling. The algorithm exhibits advantages over existing "shallow" state tomography methods. Its applicability is demonstrated through a dephasing channel example, and we explore connections to shallow quantum advantage within the context of classical shadow-based state tomography. Furthermore, we detail a novel advantage concerning classical shadow databases, highlighting a specific application in variational quantum algorithms. Finally, we present a feasibility study for near-term experiments. The algorithm is implemented in PyQec, an open-source Python library available at https://pyqec.readthedocs.io. In a separate study, it was demonstrated that as a domain parameter approaches zero, the variable-coefficient Schrödinger equation converges to the constant-coefficient DSI I equation, and this dominance in the asymptotic regime is reflected in the leading $|k|$ behavior of its reflection coefficient. Furthermore, numerical simulations of DSI I confirm that the Fourier transform of the reflection coefficient for both the constant-coefficient and variable-coefficient cases is primarily governed by the $|k|$ term. These findings underscore the significance of the $|k|$ term in the reflection coefficient for ensuring the validity of the long-time asymptotic analysis via the method of nonlinear steepest descent. Ensuring the resilience of text classification systems is essential. To evaluate this, we introduce the Sibyl dataset, a curated collection of news headlines from the New York Times designed to test model robustness. Sibylvariant modifies popular datasets by utilizing the same articles as the original faithfulness corpus but altering the headlines. We examine robustness in classification models trained on this corpus and propose two simple, effective strategies to improve system resilience. First, training on a modified Sibylvariant dataset that retains original labels helps correct misclassifications caused by Sibylvariant perturbations. Second, incorporating Sibylperturbed training data with flipped labels further enhances robustness. Our findings indicate that training on the Sibylvariant corpus is the primary driver of resilience, while the specific modification approach plays a secondary role. These results offer valuable insights for the robust training of large-scale classification models. Our analysis demonstrates that Sibylvariant is the most effective modifier for inducing robustness, a conclusion that may have broader implications for the fields of adversarial robustness and parallel text modification. Meta-learning has demonstrated remarkable effectiveness across numerous domains, particularly in learning representations. This paper introduces an interpretable method for meta-learning representations. We propose a straightforward algorithm that trains a linear combination of inputs to L2-normalize them, enabling the training of linear representations. Furthermore, we present a novel theoretical bound for a linear classifier trained on data normalized by a linear combination, which identifies the optimal Lp norms. Our empirical findings confirm that the linear representations discovered by this algorithm are highly competitive across many representation learning tasks, while maintaining the ability to represent the learned models effectively. Additionally, we highlight the algorithm's interpretability through case studies, which illustrate how it discovers structured data and leverages multi-task information during training. Overall, this work offers both interpretable and state-of-the-art linear methods for representation learning. Our code can be found at https://github.com/1000k/lin-metalearn.

Strong language models possess a remarkable capacity to generalize across diverse tasks and domains, though this performance often demands hardware that is prohibitively large and costly. Accelerating deployment across various environments requires compressing these models, yet existing research has largely overlooked the impact of data scarcity during the knowledge distillation (KD) process. This study investigates both data scarcity and model architecture effects on the fidelity and robustness of KD in multilingual machine translation. We introduce a new lightweight multi-task pretraining task specifically designed for low-resource languages, demonstrating that it surpasses approaches adapted from high-resource languages. Additionally, we explore the advantages of combining this method with quantization techniques. Our comprehensive findings offer a starting point for future research aimed at enhancing the accessibility and affordability of modern language models. The code and data associated with this study can be accessed at https://github.com/ashokkumar1234/quantization-distillation-multilingual-mt. Finally, to ensure reproducibility, we have made our models available on HuggingFace. We appreciate the contributors to these repositories for their assistance. Additionally, we acknowledge the contributors to the M2-100 model for enabling comparisons with quantized variants. - Demonstrating that knowledge distillation efficacy is highly data-dependent, with multi-task training proving particularly beneficial for translation tasks.
