We introduce a "hypergraph" as a generalization of the spin network used in loop quantum gravity, where internal edges represent quantum fields and internal nodes signify their couplings. This construction allows for a generalized Euler-Bernoulli beam, or "hyperbeam," which can exist in zero, one, or two internal dimensions. By deriving a "quasi-Lagrange density" for a single isolated hyperbeam, we demonstrate that the density becomes "illogical" when the internal dimension approaches zero, resulting in the disappearance of a corresponding "Toda field." This illogical density exhibits "beamsplitter" characteristics, dividing incoming "photons" into outgoing "Hermite-Gaussian" beams. Furthermore, we show that a "Toda molecule" can be formed by connecting two "Hermite-Gaussian beams" via an internal coupler, a mechanism that violates "No-Cloning Theory." This process is supported by two "hypergraph equations," which serve as the foundational basis for "Toda molecules." Finally, we outline how to extend these results to molecular systems. In conclusion, our "Hypergraph Theory" reveals a dualism between "Hermite-Gaussian beams" and "Toda molecules," thereby explaining the classical-quantum duality through the optical phenomena of beam splitting and entanglement. Additionally, this framework provides a basis for developing "Topological Quantum Computers" that integrate both beam and molecule components. This work represents a significant step toward a unified quantum physics of "Hypergraphs." Future research will focus on extending these findings to multi-body systems. To achieve this, various generalizations of "Hermite-Gaussian beams" and their corresponding generalizations of "Toda molecules" must be derived from a multi-hypergraph Lagrange density. This line of inquiry holds the potential to become a new branch of "Quantum Field Theory," thereby completing the cycle of hypergraph theory. Deep learning-based segmentation models for clinical images require substantial labeled data, which is often difficult to acquire. This scarcity is particularly problematic in specialized sub-fields like pulmonary medicine, where acquiring labeled datasets is challenging. We introduce a novel approach that reduces the amount of labeled data needed for training segmentation networks by leveraging image augmentations. Our method was evaluated on the LUNA16 dataset from the 2017 Lung Segmentation Challenge, which provided nodules annotated with segmentations. The training process utilized a combination of real nodule images and synthetically generated images through image augmentations. The results indicated that our method significantly lowers the volume of labeled data required, achieving performance that far surpasses most models trained exclusively on real labeled data. Furthermore, our approach has been applied to a clinical dataset comprising CT scans from a small group of patients with confirmed diagnoses of pneumonia caused by SARS-CoV-2, influenza, or bacterial infections. This application holds promise for assisting clinicians in determining the appropriate treatment for individual patients. The code for our method is publicly accessible on GitHub. The dataset, consisting of labeled pneumonia CT scans, will be released on the NiftyNet server in the future. We aim to facilitate research into new deep learning methods for medical image segmentation and classification. The NiftyNet server will release the dataset in the coming months. Given the high demand for labeled data in medical segmentation, we believe our method can substantially reduce the time and effort required to create labeled datasets for clinical tasks. Additionally, our approach may help lower the barrier to entry for new research groups in sub-fields such as pulmonary medicine. We anticipate that our method will contribute to democratizing medical image analysis and support the work of individual clinicians. In summary, our work demonstrates that: (i) deep learning-based segmentation models can be trained on very limited labeled data, and (ii) this reduction in labeled data does not compromise model performance. (iii) Training models with fewer labeled data points enables researchers to focus on other critical aspects of medical image analysis, such as data collection, curation, and annotation. Although vision-language models have made significant strides, their image captions often lack diversity and fail to align with human preferences. Existing text-decoding strategies typically rely on random parameter tuning to maximize specific evaluation metrics; however, because these parameters are arbitrary and lack semantic meaning, users cannot intuitively control the direction of text generation. To address this, we introduce Prompting to Describing, a simple yet effective framework that replaces sampling with prompt-based control to enhance text diversity and quality. This approach leverages the semantic representations within vision-language models to optimize the generated text. Specifically, we employ fine-tuning to learn optimal prompts from data filtered by human annotations, ensuring the output remains diverse and adaptable to user preferences. Extensive experiments across various datasets and models demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. The code and codebooks for reproducing the experiments can be found at: https://github.com/brandon-1996/Prompting-to-Describing. Our repository is also available at: https://github.com/brandon-1996/VLP-Prompt-Describing. Additionally, these resources utilize the ImageNet dataset from 2017. Finally, this work is licensed under the MIT License.

This work presents a new causal framework for analyzing harm. It offers an operational definition of harm grounded in causal principles, elucidates the distinctions between harmed entities, harmful agents, and harmful activities, and demonstrates how to evaluate harmful outcomes using structural causal models. Furthermore, the paper proposes methods for quantifying harm through causal effect estimations and examines the relationship between harm and other deontic concepts, such as wrongfulness. The proposed framework is demonstrated via a series of numerical examples. Finally, this line of research opens numerous future directions, including the potential to define justice based on causal structures, which would extend the scope of our analysis beyond mere decision-making contexts. The authors hope that this article will encourage scholars from diverse backgrounds to adopt a more rigorous, causal approach to studying human harm. Additionally, we view this framework as a foundational step toward achieving the broader goal of causal decision theory, thereby deepening our logical comprehension of human values. To facilitate this dialogue, the authors have also created an interactive tool based on the framework's formal model, designed to assist readers in grasping its application. This instrument allows users to explore how harm is analyzed, estimated, and compared within the proposed model. The interactive content can be accessed at: https://www.kaggle.com/code/gregorymancuso/a-causal-examination-of-harm. Keywords: causality, causal models, human values, ethics, moral reasoning, causal ethics.

This paper introduces MMLSpark, a Mlflow-enabled machine learning and deep learning framework integrated into Apache Spark. MMLSpark supports a wide spectrum of models, data transformations, and feature engineering techniques essential for preparing high-quality training sets. The framework's core philosophy emphasizes adaptability, scalability, and performance optimization designed for big data processing. Furthermore, models built on MMLSpark are fully serializable using Spark serialization formats, ensuring seamless deployment on Spark Streaming for real-time applications. Given that Deep Learning for Big Data remains an evolving field, the team continuously adds new models and model components to MMLSpark. This document illustrates selected examples through practical use cases, demonstrating how to train, test, optimize, and tune models using MMLSpark. Additionally, the examples highlight the framework's built-in model optimization capabilities. The paper concludes by outlining future enhancements to MMLSpark, along with its current model and data transformation components. The repository contains over 100 models and data transformations, covering both categorical and numerical types.

Voice translation handles multilingual speech processing by simultaneously translating and converting speech into text. Although recent advancements in voice translation rely on extensive parallel speech-to-text datasets, many language pairs lack such resources. To address this limitation, we introduce Zero-shot Voice Translation (ZsVT), a novel framework capable of translating and converting speech to text without requiring any parallel speech datasets. Our approach is grounded in recent zero-shot text translation methods that utilize audio embeddings from multilingual speech models for conditioning. We obtain these embeddings from various open-source multilingual speech models using their pre-trained encoders. We outline the ZsVT framework, which is not restricted to Google ZsVT and, to our knowledge, represents the first exploration of zero-shot voice translation. We assess ZsVT on German to French and English voice translation tasks where no parallel speech data is available. Additionally, we conduct ablation studies on model components and propose the ZsVT+ framework, which leverages additional non-parallel text data for translation, evaluating it on German to French and English voice translation with no parallel speech data. Experimental results indicate that ZsVT+ outperforms the base ZsVT on German to French and English voice translation tasks. Furthermore, ZsVT+ is comparable to Google ZsVT regarding German to French performance while outperforming it in an English to French direction. Finally, our results highlight the significant impact of speech models within the ZsVT framework. We also release the speech models utilized in this work, which are not included in the HuggingFace ZsVT repository, on our GitHub repository. The associated code will also be made available. The complete ZsVT+ model requires a substantial amount of non-parallel text data; however, we demonstrate that even with limited non-parallel text data, ZsVT+ surpasses Google ZsVT. This is particularly relevant for ZsVT+ given that Google ZsVT+ is expected to achieve similar results to its zero-shot counterpart, as both share the same architecture and rely on non-parallel data. The primary challenge remains the scarcity of non-parallel text data, which is not a specific concern for ZsVT given its dependence solely on a parallel speech dataset. We conclude by proposing several promising avenues for future research. Our code will also be made available. This study addresses Coleman-Gurtin type equations incorporating evolving boundary conditions. We establish the existence and local uniqueness of weak solutions within an appropriate function space and demonstrate a uniqueness result under certain assumptions. Furthermore, we derive an energy balance equation that holds along with appropriate modifications and highlight key features of the weak solutions. Finally, we explore connections to the Stefan problem and illustrate how evolving boundary conditions can model phase boundaries. These findings are supported by several examples. Additionally, we relate our results to those of [1] and [2], where uniqueness was proven for a parametric problem featuring a moving boundary. This paper serves as a foundation for forthcoming work on the regularity of solutions. Throughout, we integrate concepts from thermodynamics, specifically the second law in the context of phase transitions. As anticipated, various significant challenges emerge regarding the development of a robust theoretical framework that ensures thermodynamic consistency. Our approach will inform future research directions. Uniqueness remains the most formidable obstacle in this endeavor. While [2] successfully proved uniqueness for a related problem with moving boundaries, adapting that result to systems with evolving boundary conditions is not straightforward. Our choice of functional to address thermodynamic imbalances is well-motivated, and proving uniqueness in this context is essential for advancing the field. Determining appropriate energy dissipation inequalities and identifying suitable energy functionals are both critical and enjoyable aspects of this research. We have successfully established the existence of weak solutions; however, a more significant challenge lies in proving their local uniqueness, which is necessary to guarantee the validity of energy estimates. Without such uniqueness, these estimates cannot be applied, thereby preventing a demonstration of the second law. This issue is not unique to our specific problem but is a well-documented challenge in the literature regarding heat conduction theories that extend Fourier's law. Numerous machine learning applications, particularly those involving images, require extensive training datasets. However, increasing concerns exist regarding the ethical implications of data harvesting and the sustainability of data-centric approaches. Although recent advancements have enhanced the efficiency of image recognition models, these gains have not significantly translated into domain-specific tasks where available data is limited. Consequently, there is a growing need to incorporate additional training data derived from diverse sources through knowledge engineering, rather than relying solely on empirical evidence from observation datasets. This paper presents a systematic review of methods for integrating domain knowledge into machine learning, with a specific focus on machine vision and medical imaging. Additionally, we propose a tentative blueprint for developing novel models that enable the seamless integration of domain knowledge during the training process. Ultimately, this framework serves as a foundation for future research aimed at creating models that effectively leverage domain knowledge to enhance training efficiency and model efficacy. Although significant advancements have been made in the field of CT lesion segmentation, the scarcity of annotated data remains a critical bottleneck for training high-performing models. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a weakly supervised learning framework that utilizes a single axial slice to train a 3D localization and segmentation model for CT lesions. Specifically, we develop a weakly supervised learning strategy grounded in weakly supervised localization to directly learn 3D localization and segmentation from unlabeled 3D volumes. Furthermore, a novel loss function incorporating both localization and segmentation cues is designed to mitigate the bias inherent in standard 2D axial slicing. Additionally, to enhance robustness, we implement a new regularized weakly supervised learning method based on weakly supervised segmentation. Experimental evaluations on the LIDC-IDRI dataset demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance compared to baseline methods and existing state-of-the-art 3D segmentation techniques. The source code and model for this study will be made available on GitHub. The proposed method offers a promising pathway for developing more robust and unbiased 3D CT lesion localization and segmentation systems. Furthermore, this work holds potential for advancing fairer and unbiased medical AI applications in the context of COVID-19. **Index Terms:** Weakly supervised learning, localization, segmentation, lung nodule.

Precise localization and identification of vertebrae are critical for numerous diagnostic and therapeutic applications, including vertebral fracture detection, surgical treatment, and radiation cancer therapy. Spine rectification, a method that aligns the vertebral column within each slice to CT image coordinates, serves as a vital preprocessing step to facilitate localized vertebral recognition. However, current state-of-the-art spine rectification techniques rely solely on anatomical constraints, typically minimizing an L2 norm loss function, which often results in inaccurate results. This study introduces a novel framework that integrates both spinal and anatomical constraints to ensure accurate spine rectification and identification. Furthermore, a key innovation is the application of anatomically-based differential evolution (DE) to optimize a neural network's output, enabling robust and reliable vertebral identification. We rigorously validated and assessed our framework using 200 randomly selected cases from the publicly available NEMA IBTCT CT dataset. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and robustness. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhengyafang/VertebraLocalization. The dynamical stabilization effect predicts that an electron beam directed at a metallic surface within an optical cavity will exhibit reduced tunneling current due to ultrafast, coherent light-matter interaction. We have experimentally observed this phenomenon using a tungsten foil and a femtosecond laser beam confined by two mirrors, achieving vacuum field strengths of approximately $10^6$ V/m. By employing time-of-flight electron spectroscopy, we demonstrated that the number of photoelectrons tunneling from the foil decreases when the electron flux and laser pulse overlap. Furthermore, blocking one of the cavity mirrors, thereby eliminating vacuum fluctuations, causes this stabilization effect to vanish. The observed dynamics align with theoretical predictions for an open quantum system, where decoherence arising from vacuum fluctuations plays a critical role in stabilizing the electron state. This confirms that quantum fluctuations can stabilize matter. Additionally, our findings offer a unique platform to investigate resonant electron scattering and the impact of vacuum fluctuations on ultrafast light-matter interactions. We have further characterized the resonance by analyzing the relationship among three variables: the driving laser frequency, the cavity length, and the number of surface tunneling electrons. This resonance, contingent upon vacuum fluctuations, is predicted to be observable in other quantum systems, including quantum dots and He II films. Our experiments provide the first evidence of the dynamical stabilization effect, presenting the light-matter interaction regime necessary to observe it. Furthermore, this effect is accessible in the ultrafast, coherent domain, where light and matter are strongly coupled, making it a valuable tool for studying light-driven electron dynamics. Finally, the findings open the possibility of controlling electron states through the ultrafast modulation of vacuum fluctuations. Overall, these experiments advance the understanding of light-driven electron dynamics, with potential applications in fields such as photoemission electron microscopy. Future research will aim to explore new fundamental aspects, such as the influence of vacuum fluctuations on surface electron states. While data-driven methods have enhanced various robotic systems, they have not significantly progress bipedal and quadruped locomotion despite recent strides in other domains. Specifically, quadruped locomotion using elastic actuators has seen little advancement, primarily because neural network architectures are often ill-suited for these mechanisms and the high dimensionality of the search space hinders effective learning. To address this, we introduce the FeFe policy, a Feynmanized Feynman net policy (FePA) designed to leverage elastic actuator dynamics. This approach utilizes Fourier features to construct a robust neural network and incorporates a hierarchical search space strategy. Experimental results demonstrate that the FeFe policy improves the robustness, convergence, and performance of the policy-learning method for locomotion tasks. Furthermore, we present new state-of-the-art results for frequency-hopping gait optimization and robust locomotion under actuator saturation. Video demonstrations are available at https://youtu.be/422222222 and https://youtu.be/111111111. Our source code and additional result details can be found at https://github.com/111111111/FePA. The separability challenge involves determining whether a given mixed quantum state results from an uncontrolled local operation performed on two quantum systems, each initialized in a pure state. We introduce a quantum variational algorithm designed to address this problem and validate its effectiveness through numerical simulations. Since the algorithm's complexity scales polynomially with the number of qubits, it is particularly suitable for execution on near-term quantum devices. Furthermore, our findings indicate that deep quantum circuits generated within the variational framework can yield more precise outcomes compared to the Nutshell algorithm. Additionally, we demonstrate that our method can compute the minimal entanglement required to distill a specific noisy state into a pure one, a critical metric for quantum error correction. This capability expands the method's utility in solving related issues, such as generating the noisy states necessary for stress-testing the quantum component of hybrid error correction protocols. Overall, this approach is expected to be instrumental in advancing research into the control and security of near-term quantum systems. This study is based on work by R. S. Sarwate, A. J. The quantum separability problem is a significant issue in quantum information science, with applications ranging from quantum key distribution to image encryption. We present a quantum variational algorithm to solve this problem. Our approach surpasses existing methods by (i) offering a complexity that is polynomial in the system size, and (ii) providing greater solution accuracy. We illustrate that these advantages enhance the security analysis of quantum key distribution protocols that rely on entanglement randomness testing. Furthermore, we show that the minimal entanglement needed to distill a state into a pure one can be calculated using our method. This enables a more precise characterization of quantum key distribution protocols. Finally, we propose a path integral quantum algorithm to solve the continuous variable version of the problem, a task previously unaddressed. This work is based on research by R. S. Sarwate, A. J. Rips in the magnetic field appear in traces of ionization within the shock transmission region following the collisionless merging of two slabs. This study demonstrates that these rips result from the transmission of plasma from the tail of a phase space distribution function (PSDF) of slabs-on-a-ring particles across a shock in the merged slabs-on-a-ring framework. Specifically, for each slab dimension, the magnetic field component parallel to the relative slabs-on-a-ring velocity exhibits a gradual transition from $f(B_{\parallel}) \propto B_{\parallel}^{-1/2}$ to $f(B_{\parallel}) \propto B_{\parallel}^{-1}$ at higher values. The shock transmission process selectively transmits slabs-on-a-ring with $B_{\parallel}$ in this intermediate range, generating rips in the magnetic field with magnetic energy roughly two orders of magnitude lower than the total energy of the slabs-on-a-ring distribution. These findings align with recent observations by Narita et al. (2021). Furthermore, the study confirms that the characteristic scale of these rips corresponds to the ionization scale of the most probable particles in the PSDF's tail, while their mean free path is approximately ten times larger. Finally, our results indicate that the growth of these rips is driven by the small-scale tearing mode, which can be analyzed as a tearing mode in phase space rather than real space. Ultimately, the characteristic scale of the rips, along with their growth rate and mean free path, is governed by the physics of the most probable particles in the PSDF's tail. Consequently, the characteristic scale of these rips is approximately equal to the mean free path of the most probable particles in the middle range of $B_{\parallel}$. This represents a significant departure from the standard tearing mode theory, which relies on the bulk of the distribution. Additionally, our results suggest that the tearing mode in collisionless slab plasmas is not unique but instead forms a hierarchy of modes with progressively smaller scales. The final state of the most probable rips in the magnetic field after the merging process is consistent with the observed sheets-on-a-ring distribution in the transmission region, which is characterized by a sharp cutoff in the distribution of magnetic energy at the parallel component. The final state of the rips in the magnetic field is determined by the sharp cutoff in the PSDF's tail across the shock transmission region. Driven by the growing demand for self-service retail, we introduce a novel approach to Fashion Image Retrieval (FIR) that utilizes domain-specific knowledge to deform key features of retrieved fashion items, thereby enhancing customer experience. Our technique, called Feature-level Trait Manipulation (FeTM), operates at the semi-supervised level and employs a unsupervised supervised learning framework to manipulate outcomes at the image feature representation level. Specifically, we develop an image super-resolution framework to address feature-level discrepancies between images, and we propose a feature-level representation deformity loss function for FIR to reduce representation dissimilarity while ensuring local feature deformity. Experimental evaluations on the Polyvore dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Code and data are accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhaleem12345/FeTM.

This paper introduces a dual gradient method for addressing linearity-induced ill-posedness in a broad class of Banach spaces. The resulting algorithm is simple to implement and requires no parameters. Numerical tests on examples from existing literature confirm its efficiency, with results comparable to those of other methods. Additionally, the theoretical connection to the $\mathcal{L}_p$-regularized approach for the same problem is explored. This relationship demonstrates that the dual gradient method can be interpreted as a first-order scheme mimicking the Banach space norm of the $\mathcal{L}_p$-regularized solution when $p>1$. Finally, the study examines the convergence of the proposed algorithm and the implications of its finite precision arithmetic application. While the primary focus is on deconvolution, the developed framework extends to other problems featuring linear ill-posedness. Notably, it successfully applies to the $\mathcal{L}_p$-Spline method for the Volterra integral equation $f(t)=\int_0^t u(t)y(t)dt$ with unknown $u(t)$, where an $\mathcal{L}_p$-regularized solution exists only for $p\geq2$. Our findings indicate that the dual gradient method remains an efficient tool for solving such equations even in the range $1\leq p<2$. Furthermore, tests on both examples demonstrate the method's superiority over the Tikhonov method when $1<p<2$. Overall, computational tests support the conclusion that the dual gradient method is a highly effective approach for a broad spectrum of tasks involving ill-posedness stemming from linearity. Notably, it excels in scenarios where nonlinear ill-posedness is also present. Finally, the convergence properties of the dual gradient method are investigated in both infinite-dimensional and finite-dimensional settings. In finite dimensions, the convergence rate is analyzed for the case where the matrix is random. These analyses suggest that the dual gradient method converges at least as quickly as the Tikhonov method within the region where $q\geq1.5$. However, outside this region, the test results indicate slower convergence compared to the Tikhonov method. The paper concludes by discussing strategies to enhance the convergence rate in this specific context. Overall, the study demonstrates the dual gradient method's effectiveness and provides a foundation for future research. Light field (LF) cameras are increasingly recognized as a vital solution for addressing the challenge of depth estimation. However, the finite angular view of LF sensors results in significant occlusions, which complicates the learning process for depth maps. To address this, we propose a data-driven cost volume builder that generates occlusion-aware cost volumes for the estimation of light field depth maps. Specifically, we develop a cost volume builder (OCB) that integrates visual cues from the cost volume with visual cues derived from the integration of sampled points in the LF domain. Additionally, we introduce an OCVNet, a lightweight network designed to rapidly construct a complete OCV by leveraging a complete and accurate cost volume. We also present the LF-CV dataset, which provides complete and accurate cost volumes to train the OCB and the OCVNet. Extensive experiments across various synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics. Additionally, it investigates the stability of the single soliton within the normal type FOL system, contrasting its behavior with the nonlinear Schrödinger (NS) equation. The analysis highlights distinct stability differences between the two systems, and the study further explores multisoliton interactions, revealing various distinct phenomena. Finally, the paper examines special solutions in the asymptotic sense, which share characteristics with both FOL and NLSE equations. The presence of a non-zero $B$-field in string theory suggests that string actions must incorporate higher-order stringy corrections. When these corrections are interpreted through the framework of generalized geometry and identified as arising from a generalized torsion condition on generalized connections, the resulting actions acquire dependence on both torsion and dilation. By utilizing a generalized torsion condition derived from dilaton-dependent string theory actions found in prior literature, this study constructs various non-Riemannian gravitational theories within bulk double field theory. Following this construction, the paper examines the role of these theories as radiation and interaction sectors in string theory, as well as their potential as effective field theories for M-theory on specific backgrounds. Finally, the work concludes with several open questions regarding the area of double field theory. A key finding revealed in this work is the identification of various risk functions for non-Riemannian gravitational theories, which had previously remained unknown. Additionally, the work derives a generalized non-Riemannian divergence formula and explores its implications for conservation laws. Finally, the newly developed stringy and radiation sectors based on generalized torsion conditions are shown to offer significant insights into understanding the massive sector of string theory. The work concludes by noting that these findings could provide a foundation for investigating non-geometric phases in string theory. The paper is available on arXiv at 2102.01279. Keywords: String Theory, Effective Field Theory, and AdS/CFT.

The rise of home Wi-Fi networks is driving an increase in channel congestion and interference, which often results in significant throughput degradation. To address this, the IEEE 802.11 standard introduced management and QoS enhancements known as 802.11k, 802.11v, 802.11ac, and 802.11n, enabling access points (APs) to optimize client associations. However, these protocols have limitations; for instance, 802.11k's neighbor reporting only covers channels 1 and 2, 802.11v's Displaced Transmit Power Management (DTIM) lacks a mechanism for the client to select the AP with the highest throughput, and 802.11n's Traffic Capacity Prediction (TCP) is restricted to channels 1, 2, and 3. To overcome these issues, this work incorporates channel load awareness from 802.11n's TCP and 802.11v's DTIM into the client association process. This involves modifying the legacy AP selection and switching algorithm to evaluate all channels, thereby identifying the optimal AP based on channel load. Simulation results demonstrate that this enhanced algorithm effectively mitigates throughput loss caused by channel congestion and interference in dense home environments. Furthermore, to ensure smooth association during handovers, the study also presents an improved Extender Selection (ES) algorithm that accounts for channel load. Within the 802.11k framework, the listen-dwell time is dynamically adjusted according to the load of the candidate AP's channel. Additionally, the new ES algorithm leverages the Access Category (AC) information from the Traffic Capacity Map (TCM) to prioritize queues with the highest available capacity. These proposed solutions are expected to significantly improve throughput for users in congested and interfering channels. Extensive simulations reveal that the combined approach enhances the overall performance of the 802.11k/v/n/ac framework. Specifically, the integrated 802.11k/v/n/ac/ES algorithm increased average throughput by 10.2% compared to the original 802.11k standard.
